Mid-Atlantic Agriculture Leaders Praise EPA Action Bringing Closure to 20-Year-Old Agreement and Ending Decades of Uncertainty for American Farms
PHILADELPHIA — Following U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) announcement that it would not develop emissions estimates as part of the 2005 Animal Feeding Operations Consent Agreement and Final Order (2005 Air Compliance Agreement), agriculture leaders from across the nation, including the Mid-Atlantic, are voicing their appreciation. On Friday, October 30, 2026, EPA also announced that the agency’s enforcement office would work to end obligations tied to the agreement. The agency’s announcement brings closure to a two-decade period of uncertainty for thousands of American farmers.
“Agriculture is the backbone of so many communities across the Mid-Atlantic. Farming is a way of life that drives local economies and feeds our nation,” said EPA Mid-Atlantic Regional Administrator Amy Van Blarcom-Lackey. “As a proud Pennsylvania farmer, I know that we need certainty, not years of unanswered questions. I have spoken with hundreds of farmers across our region and have witnessed their commitment to responsible environmental stewardship while providing a safe, affordable, and abundant food supply. This long-overdue announcement delivers the clarity farmers deserve, recognizes the realities of modern agriculture, and affirms the Trump EPA’s commitment to commonsense, science-based moves that strengthen both rural communities and American agriculture.”
Agriculture leaders emphasized that EPA’s action recognizes that farmers should not face uncertainty based on outdated information.
What They’re Saying
“Dairy farmers signed up for this study in good faith two decades ago, and they’ve been waiting ever since to find out what it would mean for their farms,” said Gregg Doud, President and CEO of the National Milk Producers Federation. “You can’t measure a handful of farms years ago and use those numbers to set expectations for thousands of other farms. We appreciate EPA following the data and giving farmers a clear, final answer.”
“Thank you to the EPA for providing Pennsylvania farmers with much-needed regulatory certainty. By protecting farmers from costly and burdensome air-emissions testing requirements on their barns, EPA is allowing our agricultural industry to focus on what It does best: feeding America,” said Chris Hoffman, Pennsylvania State Director for USDA Rural Development. “Supporting our farmers means supporting our food supply, our rural communities, and our nation's future. Well done!”
“EPA’s announcement that it will not establish emissions estimates for animal agriculture is one of several initiatives Pennsylvania agriculture has been advocating for. We are pleased with the decision from President Trump and EPA Administrator Zeldin to sideline an outdated initiative, irrelevant data-based policy that has plagued farmers for 20 years,” said PennAg Industries Association President Christian R. Herr. “Pennsylvania farmers have always been, and continue to be, stewards of the earth by upholding high standards of environmental and regulatory compliance. This is welcomed news and will help animal agriculture continue to grow in Pennsylvania.”
“The Delmarva Chicken Association (DCA) thanks the Environmental Protection Agency for ending the indecision of the 2005 Animal Feeding Operations Consent Agreement and Final Order,” said DCA Executive Director Holly Porter. “We have long shared our concerns with EPA that data from the National Air Emissions Monitoring Study (NAEMS) was too outdated to guide modern-day farm regulations. Our Delmarva chicken community is always moving forward with new technology and modernizing how we raise broiler chickens, making it difficult to use limited data from a study conducted more than 20 years ago.”
“Any time we can reduce regulatory burdens and provide some certainty and direction for our producers, it’s a win for rural communities,” said Beth Green, Virginia State Director for USDA Rural Development. “I’m grateful our friends at EPA have taken these steps so our farmers and ranchers don’t have to worry about the government moving the goalposts on them. That benefits everyone in rural Virginia.”
“America’s egg farmers applaud U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin and the Trump administration for taking long-awaited action on outdated air compliance measures...UEP advocated that the NAEMS data on bard design and egg production practices no longer represent how most egg farms operate today, and the EPA’s decision to terminate the agreement was welcome news to the egg industry,” said United Egg Producers (UEP).
Background
The 2005 agreement followed a National Academy of Sciences report that called for better ways to estimate emissions from Animal Feeding Operations, including livestock and poultry farms that raise animals in confinement. EPA offered farms the chance to sign a voluntary agreement and take part in the National Air Emissions Monitoring Study to help develop emissions estimation methods. The Trump EPA concluded that the data collected from 2005 to 2007 are too old and too limited to support reliable emissions methodologies. As a result, the agency will not finalize those methods under the 2005 Air Compliance Agreement
title: Mid-Atlantic Agriculture Leaders Praise EPA Action Bringing Closure to 20-Year-Old Agreement and Ending Decades of Uncertainty for American Farms

IR-2026-130, Nov. 4, 2026
WASHINGTON — The Internal Revenue Service today reminded paid tax return preparers to renew their preparer tax identification number for 2027.
Anyone who prepares or assists in preparing federal tax returns or claims for refund for compensation must have a valid preparer tax identification number (PTIN). PTINs must be renewed each year, and current PTINs expire Dec. 31, 2026.
“The PTIN program helps the IRS identify legitimate paid preparers and reinforces the responsibility that comes with preparing federal tax returns,” said IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano. “ IRS appreciates the time and effort that tax practitioners take each year to comply with the requirement to renew or obtain a PTIN.”
Renew PTINs online
The fastest way to renew a PTIN is online through the IRS PTIN System. Online renewal generally takes about 15 minutes.
To renew:
- Access the PTIN system on IRS.gov.
- Sign in to PTIN account and select “Renew my PTIN.”
- Review and update account information.
- Submit the application and pay the $18.75 fee, which is nonrefundable and nontransferable.
Once completed, applicants receive confirmation of their PTIN renewal.
Tax professionals who prefer to renew by mail can submit Form W-12, IRS Paid Preparer Tax Identification Number (PTIN) Application and Renewal. Paper applications can take about six weeks to process.
Other PTIN account features
The online PTIN system offers more than renewal. Tax professionals can use their accounts to:
- Check their completed continuing education.
- View the number of Form 1040 returns filed using their PTIN.
- Review communications from the IRS Tax Professional Management Office.
- Track their progress in the IRS Annual Filing Season Program.
Tax professionals should also keep their contact information current to ensure they receive important PTIN communications.
Annual Filing Season Program
Non-credentialed tax return preparers may also consider participating in the voluntary Annual Filing Season Program. Preparers who meet the program’s continuing education and other requirements receive a Record of Completion, are included in the IRS Directory of Federal Tax Return Preparers with Credentials and Select Qualifications and may have limited representation rights. More information is available through the Annual Filing Season Program on IRS.gov.
Reminder for enrolled agents
PTIN renewal is separate from enrolled agent renewal. Enrolled agents whose Social Security numbers end in 7, 8, or 9, as well as those without an SSN, are in the current enrollment renewal cycle, which runs through Jan. 31, 2027. Enrolled agents should also renew their PTINs for 2027.
title: IRS reminder: Tax professionals should renew their PTINs for 2027

A man who downloaded hundreds of photos and videos of child pornography was sentenced today to 12 years in federal prison.

Damon Wesley Powers, age 44, from Osage, Iowa, received the prison term after a July 1, 2026, guilty plea to one count of receipt of child pornography.

Evidence at a prior hearing showed that law enforcement officers searched Powers’s house in Osage in June 2025. Agents found child pornography on his phone, including depictions of prepubescent children. Powers had also stored hundreds of additional photos and videos of child pornography in a cloud‑based account. In an interview with law enforcement officers, Powers admitted that he had sent and received child pornography.

Powers was sentenced in Cedar Rapids by United States District Court Judge Leonard T. Strand. Powers was sentenced to 144 months’ imprisonment and was ordered to pay $24,350 in special assessments and restitution to victims. Powers must also serve a five-year term of supervised release after the prison term. There is no parole in the federal system.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and CEOS, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit Justice.gov/PSC .

Powers is being held in the United States Marshal’s custody until he can be transported to a federal prison.

The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Devra T. Hake and investigated by the Iowa Division of Criminal Investigation Cyber Crime Bureau, the Internet Crimes Against Children Taskforce, and the Osage Police Department.

Court file information at https://ecf.iand.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/login.pl .

The case file number is 26-CR-2015.

Follow us on X @USAO_NDIA.

INDIANAPOLIS- A former United States Postal Service letter carrier, Destinee Ruffin, 29, of Indianapolis, has been sentenced to six and a half years in federal prison, followed by two years of supervised release, after pleading guilty to Conspiracy to Commit Bank Fraud and Theft of Mail. This case was brought as part of the Trump Administration’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud.

According to court documents, Ruffin was employed as a letter carrier at the Bacon Station Post Office. Between April 2020 and May 2022, Ruffin used access to both incoming and outgoing mail to steal checks, which she then sold to co-conspirators.

In spring 2020, as the federal government issued Economic Impact Payment (EIP) checks to taxpayers, the USPS OIG received a complaint from a Bacon Station customer who never received theirs. Additional complaints soon followed. When agents reviewed the affected addresses and matched them to delivery routes, they discovered all missing checks were assigned to the same mail carrier, Destinee Ruffin.

In one example, Ruffin and McMullen exchanged 38 Cash App transactions totaling over $10,000 in payments from McMullen to Ruffin for stolen checks. Using the stolen checks, McMullen sought individuals on social media who were willing to deposit altered checks into their bank accounts. These individuals provided debit cards, PINs, or online banking credentials. McMullen altered the payee information on the stolen checks, deposited them, and later withdrew funds or demanded payment through Cash App or Zelle. In total, McMullen fraudulently negotiated 36 checks stolen from Bacon Station, worth approximately $235,632.

Ruffin sold even more stolen checks to Young. Young established trusted mid-level conspirators, primarily Eric Hollis (Hollis) and Kendall Thompson (Thompson), who deposited stolen checks into various accounts and recruited/ acquired account holders. Young would also list many of the stolen checks for sale on the internet-based application titled “Telegram.”

Investigators uncovered the scheme by mailing controlled Treasury checks with recorded serial numbers and tracing them back to Ruffin’s delivery route.

In April 2024, officers executed a search warrant on Ruffin’s vehicle, residence, person, and electronic devices. They discovered thousands of stolen checks valued at over $20 million that Ruffin had stolen but not yet sold. Stolen mail was found in her vehicle, on shelves, in closets, on the floor, stacked in corners, and even in the bathroom.

In total, Ruffin supplied Young with more than $12 million in stolen checks and provided McMullen with stolen checks worth more than $235,000.

For the intended recipients, the impact was severe. One victim explained that after mailing a $1,618 check to Sheet Metal Workers Local Union No. 20 Welfare and Benefit Fund—needed to maintain her retired husband’s health insurance—she learned the payment never arrived. She discovered the theft when she appeared for a scheduled surgery and was told her insurance had been terminated, forcing the procedure to be canceled. The United States Attorney’s Office estimates that approximately 6,500 victims were affected by this widespread fraud scheme.

Three of Ruffin’s co-conspirators have already been sentenced for their roles in the scheme. The final co-conspirator, John Young, is scheduled to be sentenced on December 3 rd , 2026.

“Destinee Ruffin’s crimes were not isolated acts of theft; they represented a sweeping scheme that touched thousands of households and eroded a fundamental public trust. By stealing millions of dollars’ worth of checks from the mail, Ruffin and her co-conspirators disrupted critical benefits, jeopardized family finances, and caused real harm to individuals who depended on timely delivery for essential needs,” said Tom Wheeler, United States Attorney for the Southern District of Indiana. “Today’s sentence reflects our commitment to protecting the integrity of the U.S. Postal Service and all government institutions, and to ensuring that those who exploit them for personal gain are held fully accountable.”

“The Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA) aggressively investigates individuals who attempt to exploit U.S Treasury refund checks meant for hard working taxpayers for their own private gain,” said TIGTA Special Agent in Charge Kelly Moening. TIGTA’s mission is to protect the integrity of our nation’s tax administration system. We are committed to working with our law enforcement partners to ensure that those who violate federal laws are prosecuted to the fullest extent possible.

The U.S. Postal Service – Office of Inspector General, the United States Postal Inspection Service, and the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration investigated this case. The sentences were imposed by U.S. District Court Judge Sarah Evans Barker.

U.S. Attorney Wheeler thanked Assistant U.S. Attorney Adam Eakman, who prosecuted this case.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

FORT BUCHANAN, Puerto Rico — Civilian employees and leaders from U.S. Army Garrison Fort Buchanan participated in a Building Strong and Ready Teams (BSRT) workshop Nov. 4 at the installation's Community Club to strengthen trust, improve teamwork and enhance organizational effectiveness in support of military readiness.
The workshop focused on the "speed of trust" concept, emphasizing how integrity, effective leadership and strong professional relationships help organizations operate more efficiently while reinforcing the Army's commitment to taking care of its people.
Col. David L. Brewer, Fort Buchanan garrison commander, opened the workshop by connecting trust directly to the installation's mission of supporting Soldiers and military formations.
"As you build trust in your organization, you're able to speed up your operations, and you're able to create more value for those individuals that we're serving," Brewer said.
Brewer explained that the installation workforce creates value by delivering services and resources that enable military readiness.
"We build value for the Soldiers, the formations that are operating and building readiness on our installation," Brewer said.
The commander also highlighted the importance of trust during leadership transitions, emphasizing that strong relationships help organizations adapt to change and achieve results faster.
He identified integrity as a fundamental leadership expectation, reminding employees that trust takes time to establish but can disappear in seconds.
"It's your integrity; you own it," Brewer said.
Installation Chaplain Farlin Reynoso facilitated the workshop, emphasizing the influence supervisors and directors have on organizational culture and employee development.
"You influence way more than you think," Reynoso said.
Reynoso also outlined plans to expand the training to employees throughout the installation, extending its benefits beyond senior leaders and supervisors.
For Eileen Santiago, an administrative assistant with the Directorate of Plans, Training, Mobilization and Security, the workshop offered an opportunity to reflect on trust and strengthen relationships with colleagues.
"It was motivating. It made me think about why we trust people, systems, family and friends," Santiago said.
She also valued the opportunity to interact with coworkers outside their daily work environment.
"Sharing time with coworkers outside the office was enriching. It allowed us to see other people's perspectives," Santiago said.
The workshop demonstrates how the Army in Puerto Rico takes care of its people by investing in professional development, strengthening workplace relationships and fostering an organizational culture built on trust and accountability.
With an annual budget exceeding $500 million, Fort Buchanan supports about 15,000 active-duty personnel, Soldiers of the Army Reserve and Puerto Rico National Guard, Marine Corps Reserve members and Navy Reserve personnel, providing infrastructure and services that enable forces to train, mobilize and deploy worldwide.
To stay connected with Fort Buchanan news and events, download the My Army Post app, select Fort Buchanan and activate notifications.
title: Fort Buchanan advances civilian employee readiness through trust-focused training

NEWARK, N.J. – A Bergen County, New Jersey man was sentenced to 20 years’ imprisonment for receipt and possession of multiple images of child sexual abuse, U.S. Attorney Robert Frazer announced.

Corey Hipscher, 55, of Lodi, New Jersey previously pleaded guilty yesterday before U.S. district Judge Wiliam J. Martini in Newark federal court to an Information charging him with receipt and possession of child pornography.

According to documents filed in this case and statements made in court:

From 2020 to August 2023, Hipscher communicated with a minor victim located outside of the United States using a social media platform. Hipscher encouraged the minor victim to send Hipscher images and videos of the minor victim engaging in sexually explicit conduct. Hipscher also began an online romantic relationship with the minor victim’s mother which he used to arrange for the minor victim and the minor victim’s family to visit him in New Jersey. During the visit, he sexually assaulted the minor victim and took sexually explicit photos of the minor victim and the minor victim’s sibling.

In addition to the prison term, Judge Martini sentenced Hipscher to 15 years of supervised release.

U.S. Attorney Frazer credited FBI Newark’s Child Exploitation and Human Trafficking Task Force, under the direction of Special Agent in Charge Stefanie Roddy in Newark, with the investigation leading to the charges. U.S. Attorney Frazer also thanked the Lodi Police Department and the Bergen County Prosecutor’s Office.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS) in the Justice Department’s Criminal Division, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.projectsafechildhood.gov

U.S. Attorney Frazer has announced proactive steps to connect with New Jersey’s families and communities, bringing training opportunities and resources through direct outreach. Organizations and community members interested in arranging prevention programming or learning more about available resources can contact the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of New Jersey at USANJ.CommunityOutreach@usdoj.gov . Moreover, prevention resources are available through the Department of Justice's Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section Prevention webpage and the Department of Homeland Security’s Know2Protect Campaign.

The government is represented by Assistant U.S. Attorney Sean Nadel of the Cybercrime Unit in Newark.

Fact Sheet

Office of the Spokesman

November 4, 2026

Today, the Department of State is designating two individuals and one entity that have been involved in efforts to help the Iranian regime obtain man-portable air-defense systems (MANPADS).

These designations continue a sustained U.S. campaign against Iran’s military procurement networks involving MANPADS. They follow actions on May 8, June 10, and July 15, 2026. Together, these actions close off more of the channels Tehran uses to try to rebuild its arsenal and raise the risk for third-country brokers and suppliers. Today’s action also supports enforcement of the UN arms embargo on Iran restored in September 2025. Those restrictions bar UN Member States from supplying such weapons to Iran.

The United States will keep exposing the networks that arm Iran’s military and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and will keep denying the regime the resources that sustain its destabilizing activities.

All three targets are being designated pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13949, which targets certain persons with respect to the conventional arms activities of Iran. Designations Pursuant to Section 1(a)(iii) of E.O. 13949

(U) MOHAMMED ALI TOLIBOV ( TOLIBOV ) is the Chief Executive Officer of Armory Alliance and has contributed to Armory Alliance’s efforts to procure weapons on behalf of Iran. Armory Alliance is a Belarus-based entity that has acted as an intermediary between China-based companies and Iran and has been involved in efforts to facilitate the purchase of hundreds of MANPADS. Armory Alliance was previously designated pursuant to E.O. 13382 and E.O. 13949. TOLIBOV was previously designated under E.O. 13382.

(U) VANGUARD TACTICAL SUPPLY LIMITED ( VANGUARD ) is a Nigeria-based entity that has been involved in efforts to facilitate the procurement of Chinese-origin MANPADS for Iran via false end-users. VANGUARD was previously designated under E.O. 13382.

(U) ALISHER DOMULLODZHANOV ( DOMULLODZHANOV ) is a Russia-based individual who has been involved in efforts to facilitate the procurement of MANPADS for Iran.

Sanctions Implications

As a result of today’s sanctions actions, and in accordance with E.O. 13949, all property and interests in property of the designated persons described above that are in the United States or in possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to the Department of Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). In addition, all entities that are owned, directly or indirectly, individually or in the aggregate, 50 percent or more by one or more blocked persons are also blocked.

All transactions by U.S. persons or within (or transiting) the United States that involve any property or interests in property of designated or otherwise blocked persons are prohibited unless authorized by a general or specific license issued by OFAC or exempt. These prohibitions include the making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit of any blocked person and the receipt of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services from any such person.

The power and integrity of U.S. government sanctions derive not only from the U.S. government’s ability to designate and add persons to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) List, but also from its willingness to remove persons from the SDN List consistent with the law.

Petitions for removal from the SDN List may be sent to: OFAC.Reconsideration@treasury.gov . Petitioners may also refer to the Department of State’s Delisting Guidance page.

WILMINGTON, N.C. — When disaster strikes, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers relies on trained personnel who can respond quickly, adapt to challenging conditions and provide critical support to affected communities. For one Wilmington District employee, a desire to contribute more to that mission led her to pursue an additional qualification that expands her ability to serve.
Amanda Henke, an emergency management specialist with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Wilmington District, recently earned her qualification as a Deployable Tactical Operations System (DTOS) operator, joining a specialized workforce responsible for delivering mobile operational capabilities to disaster-affected areas.
For Henke, the decision to pursue the qualification wasn't about recognition. It was about finding another way to put her skills to work.
"I wanted to be a part of something bigger and be able to assist and help where I was needed," Henke said.
DTOS vehicles provide mobile office space and operational capabilities that support USACE emergency response missions when existing facilities may be damaged, inaccessible or otherwise unavailable. The vehicles can be deployed throughout the United States and overseas, providing personnel with the resources necessary to establish and sustain field operations.
According to Jeff Harilson, an emergency management specialist supporting the DTOS program, there are currently 72 qualified DTOS operators across the USACE enterprise, only three of whom are women. Henke's qualification places her among that small group while expanding the pool of trained personnel available to support emergency response missions.
Henke's interest in becoming an operator developed through her experience supporting emergency response operations, including Hurricane Helene, where she observed the role DTOS teams play in establishing operational facilities.
Already holding a commercial driver's license through her work as a lacrosse coach at North Brunswick High School and an activity bus driver for Brunswick County Schools, Henke recognized an opportunity to apply an existing skill to her career with USACE.
"I figured why not put my qualifications as a bus driver towards my career and expand my capabilities," Henke said.
With encouragement from colleagues and leadership, Henke volunteered to pursue the additional training necessary to become a qualified DTOS operator.
Earning the qualification required more than possessing a commercial driver's license. DTOS operators must complete Civil Level I and DTOS Level II training and maintain a Class B CDL with an air brake endorsement.
The specialized DTOS course, typically conducted over two to four days depending on class size, familiarizes participants with the vehicle's mechanical, electrical and communications systems. Operators must demonstrate their ability to inspect, maintain, troubleshoot and operate the equipment while coordinating with the DTOS management team.
For Henke, the mechanical components presented the greatest learning curve.
"I know how to change my own oil and tire, but knowing what the actual parts are under the front of a diesel vehicle is something completely different," she said. "It's all about getting a method that works for you and following it."
During training, Henke participated in realistic deployment scenarios that included conducting vehicle inspections, preparing equipment for deployment and completing a 200-mile round-trip driving exercise.
Terrell Bosarge, a member of the USACE DTOS program, said Henke approached the training with attention to detail and a willingness to learn.
"She did very well," Bosarge said. "She was very attentive and thorough through the training."
Her qualification adds another trained operator to the enterprise-wide DTOS program, which relies on primary and backup two-person teams to support emergency response missions.
According to Bosarge, maintaining a sufficient number of qualified personnel provides flexibility when operators are unavailable and allows the program to sustain extended deployments through 30-day team rotations.
Henke's background in emergency management also provides an additional benefit. Beyond transporting and operating the DTOS vehicle, her familiarity with emergency response procedures and Planning and Response Team operations may allow her to assist with other mission requirements once her primary DTOS responsibilities are met.
"Not only can I assist by getting the office space there for others to work out of, but I can also support using my knowledge through EM when I get there," Henke said.
Although Henke has not yet deployed as a qualified DTOS operator, she has already returned for additional maintenance and familiarization activities. Maintaining her qualification requires continued proficiency with the vehicle and its systems, along with periodic maintenance and driving requirements.
For Henke, the accomplishment represents another step in an ongoing commitment to professional development and service.
"I don't think you should ever get comfortable enough to stop learning," Henke said. "The more tools you have the better member of a team you can be."
And while she looks forward to her first deployment as a DTOS operator, Henke hopes her experience encourages others to explore opportunities beyond their everyday responsibilities.
"Learn as much as you can and never stop learning," she said. "If you have a goal outside of your line of work pursue it even if that means giving up your own personal time. Nothing is too big or out of reach."
title: Driven to serve: Wilmington District employee expands emergency response capabilities

CLAY KASERNE, Germany — The U.S. Army Garrison Wiesbaden community came together in an installation-wide effort to keep service members fed when the Stronger Together Dining Facility temporarily closed on Sept. 30.
The dining facility, which has since reopened, had been undergoing phased modernization renovations since Sept. 14, operating in split halves separated by temporary partitions to maintain food services.
During the renovation, improperly handled insulation material in the construction zone released fiberglass dust into the dining area. Officials immediately ordered air testing by a certified host-nation laboratory, and when samples tested positive, the garrison ordered a precautionary closure to ensure safety and allow for thorough environmental decontamination.
The shutdown coincided directly with the launch of Avenger Triad 26, a major U.S. Army Europe and Africa exercise that brought thousands of additional U.S. service members and multinational NATO allies into the area of responsibility. (To read more about Avenger Triad 26 visit: https://www.army.mil/article/296123)
To mitigate the immediate disruption for service members relying on the DFAC, the installation quickly rolled out interim feeding plans.
The response was aimed first at meal cardholders, who are service members entitled to a meal or meal reimbursement; to members of the Security Assistance Group-Ukraine; and to NATO Security Assistance and Training for Ukraine personnel, who are on orders from other services; and Avenger Triad participants.
Every interim meal announcement was directed to those groups, but the effort reached further: for everyone else who wanted to eat at the DFAC, the community made sure there were other options.
The response quickly evolved into a comprehensive community effort across Clay Kaserne to keep the force fed and the mission going.
Garrison personnel erected large tents and set out additional picnic tables in the open area across from the DFAC. Essential personnel were immediately provided Meals Ready-to-Eat for rapid, on-demand pick-up, with the Wiesbaden Commissary distributing sack lunches outside the DFAC on Oct. 1.
“I gave a call to all of the Command Sergeants Major that are responsible for our tenant organizations, and they all came together. No questions asked,” said USAG Wiesbaden Command Sgt. Maj. Andre Brown. “They just wanted to know what needed to be done.”
The response moved quickly from MREs and sack lunches to hot-meal service. Garrison leaders personally took to the grill lines for two days, preparing and serving hot lunches and dinners on-site to keep morale high and ensure frontline personnel received warm meals.
“We are here to make sure that the Soldiers don’t lose morale and stay motivated,” said Sgt. Maj. Nina Alcedo, U.S. Army Europe and Africa Senior Culinary Management Sergeant Major. “Most importantly, we want them to know that the chain of command cares about them and about providing them with the proper meals they deserve.”
Beginning Oct. 3, a contracted food service took over hot meal service for the remainder of the closure.
Beyond dedicated dining options, the broader Clay Kaserne community mobilized to support everyone else impacted by the facility’s downtime:
AAFES positioned two food trucks outside the DFAC for everyone else who wanted a hot meal. Family and MWR extended operating hours at the Barbell Bistro to provide patrons with an expanded dining window. The American Red Cross and USO Wiesbaden set up stations outside the DFAC, serving complimentary hot coffee to diners waiting in line.
Morale received an extra boost from local talent. Cameron McBride, a student at Wiesbaden High School, teamed up with Spc. Jose Cruz of the 2nd Military Intelligence Battalion, 66th Military Intelligence Brigade, volunteering their time throughout the week to play trumpet outside the DFAC as troops picked up their daily food.
While the closure caused unexpected operational adjustments, garrison officials emphasized that this is exactly why precautionary testing and safety protocols exist.
The swift identification, immediate air testing and precautionary closure did what they were designed to do, and the rapid community mobilization highlighted the resilience, adaptability, and cohesion of the USAG Wiesbaden community.
Following comprehensive decontamination and air clearance tests validated by a certified service provider, the Stronger Together Dining Facility partially reopened its doors to service members on Oct. 11 with modified hours while renovation work safely continues.
The ongoing renovation project is designed to modernize the dining facility and improve quality of life across Clay Kaserne, offering a modern space for service members, civilians, and mission partners to recharge.
Meal cardholders who missed meals during the dining facility downtime may submit a claim for missed meal reimbursement. Guidance and paperwork instructions are outlined on the garrison reimbursement resource page: DFAC Closure Reimbursement Flyer.
title: USAG Wiesbaden community steps up to feed the force during precautionary DFAC closure

text:
WEST FALLS, N.Y. — For U.S. Army veteran Nathan Kalwicki, the journey to finding a place to call home began more than a decade ago, thousands of miles away in Afghanistan.
On Christmas Eve 2011, Kalwicki was wounded when a member of the Afghan forces his unit was training opened fire on American soldiers. The attack left him with a life-changing injury and led to more than a year of recovery and rehabilitation at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center.
Years later, Kalwicki and his wife, Veronica, received an opportunity that would change their lives once again: a new, accessible home built by a community of volunteers.
The opportunity came through A Soldier's Journey Home, a nonprofit organization that builds mortgage-free homes for wounded veterans.
The organization selected Kalwicki and his wife as recipients of a new home in West Falls, New York, bringing together more than 100 volunteers to complete the construction in just two weeks.
Among those volunteers was Eric Monkelbaan, a U.S. Air Force veteran and logistics manager with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Buffalo District.
Monkelbaan learned about the project through a local news report and immediately knew he wanted to get involved.
"Veterans giving back to veterans hits home for me," Monkelbaan said. "I've done some things with some other veteran organizations. So when I saw this organization locally on the news, it just hit home. And it was something I needed to be a part of."
With a background in carpentry and a passion for helping fellow veterans, Monkelbaan volunteered for the entire two-week construction period. From framing walls to installing exterior light fixtures and door handles, he worked alongside volunteers from across the community to bring the project to completion.
For Monkelbaan, the experience reflected many of the same principles he sees in his work at the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Buffalo District.
"Teamwork is a must, especially in a project like this," he said. "Similarly to the Army Corps projects. It doesn't take just one person, it takes a team. And without a full team effort, nothing like this could be accomplished."
The project also demonstrated how military service can continue to shape a person's life long after taking off the uniform. Although Monkelbaan volunteered in a personal capacity, his involvement reflected a commitment to service that extends beyond his military career and his work as an Army civilian.
After two weeks of construction, volunteers gathered to welcome Kalwicki and his wife to their completed home. American flags lined the driveway as the couple arrived, surrounded by the people who had helped make the project possible.
"Reveal day was very emotional," Monkelbaan recalled. "Not only for Nathan, as I can assume, but for the volunteers as well."
For Kalwicki, the experience was about more than receiving a house. It was seeing the generosity and dedication of people who came together to support a veteran and his family.
Now settled into their new home, Nathan and Veronica are looking toward the future with gratitude for the volunteers who helped make it possible.
"Since that time, we've sort of been making it our home. And it does feel like home now," Kalwicki said.
As the nation observes Veterans Day, their story serves as a reminder that the bonds formed through military service endure long after the uniform comes off. Whether through military service, civilian careers or community volunteerism, veterans like Kalwicki and Monkelbaan demonstrate the lasting impact of answering the call to serve.
The Buffalo District delivers world class engineering solutions to the Great Lakes Region, the Army and the Nation to ensure national security, environmental sustainability, water resource management, and emergency assistance during peace and war. Learn more at www.lrd.usace.army.mil/buffalo.
title: Service Beyond the Uniform

SANTA ANA, California – A federal grand jury today returned indictments against 10 noncitizens living in Los Angeles and Orange counties, alleging they illegally registered to vote in California by making false claims that they were United States citizens.

Today’s indictments are a part of “Operation Protect the Vote” – an ongoing, coordinated federal effort in California to root out fraud in U.S. elections and protect electoral integrity.

The 10 defendants indicted today are lawful permanent residents (LPRs), commonly known as having a “green card.” LPRs are not U.S. citizens and are not legally permitted to register to vote or vote in U.S. elections. The defendants previously were charged by federal criminal complaint last month.

The following nine defendants are charged with making false statements on their naturalization forms:

Omar Alexander Muñoz, 72, a Belizean national living in Commerce, fraudulently registered to vote in September 2019 by falsely claiming he was a U.S. citizen. He then illegally voted in U.S. elections in 2020, twice in 2022, and again in 2024. On his application to become a naturalized U.S. citizen Muñoz falsely stated under oath to have never claimed to be a U.S. citizen and that he never registered to vote in a U.S. election. His arraignment is scheduled for November 16.

Muhammad Khan, 50, a Pakistani national and Anaheim resident, submitted a provisional ballot in 2020 on which he falsely claimed to be a U.S. citizen. Five years later, on his naturalization paperwork, he falsely denied having done so. His arraignment is scheduled for November 16.

Ana Domínguez, 60, a Salvadoran national living in Long Beach, fraudulently registered to vote in July 2006 and lied in her naturalization paperwork in March 2026 about never having done so. Her arraignment is scheduled for November 16.

José Antonio Bañuelos-Díaz, 42, a Mexican national and West Adams resident, illegally registered to vote in 2007, falsely claimed U.S. citizenship. On his naturalization paperwork in March 2025, he falsely denied having done so. His arraignment is scheduled for November 16.

Jesús Narez-Madrigal, 52, a Mexican national living in Carson, fraudulently registered to vote in 2014 by falsely claiming to be a U.S. citizen, illegally voted in the 2024 U.S. general election. He made false statements about it in his naturalization paperwork in June 2024. His arraignment is scheduled for November 17.

Carlos Antonio Galeas, 54, a Honduran national and West Covina resident, fraudulently registered to vote in 2012 and 2016 by making false claims to being a U.S. citizen, then lied about it in his naturalization paperwork in September 2018. His arraignment is scheduled for November 17.

Flavio Alejandro Zúñiga, 43, a Mexico national and La Puente resident, illegally registered to vote in 2003 by falsely claiming to be a U.S. citizen then and then falsely denied having done so on his naturalization paperwork in February 2026. His arraignment is scheduled for November 17.

Amandeep Kaur, 30, an Indian national living in Rancho Palos Verdes, illegally registered to vote in December 2022 and unlawfully voted in the November 2024 U.S. election. In her application to become a naturalized U.S. citizen, she denied ever having claimed U.S. citizenship and further denied ever registering to vote. Her arraignment is scheduled for November 20.

Axel Giovani Prera García, 46, a Guatemalan national and Pico Rivera resident, fraudulently registered to vote in 2002 and 2005, and made false statements about it in his naturalization paperwork in June 2025. He is a fugitive.

The following defendant is charged with falsely claiming United States citizenship to register to vote:

Ernesto Gutiérrez Ruvalcaba, 57, a Mexican national living in Wilmington, illegally registered to vote in February 2024 by falsely claiming to be a U.S. citizen and then unlawfully voted one month later. He is a fugitive.

An indictment contains allegations that a defendant has committed a crime. Every defendant is presumed to be innocent until and unless proven guilty in court.

If convicted, each defendant would face a statutory maximum sentence of five years in federal prison.

Homeland Security Investigations is investigating these matters.

Assistant United States Attorneys Michael Wheat and Minjae Kim of the Orange County Office are prosecuting these cases.
title: Federal Grand Jury Indicts 10 Noncitizens Who Illegally Registered to Vote in California

ALBUQUERQUE – A federal grand jury has returned the first indictment in the ongoing DWI corruption investigation, charging former Bernalillo County Sheriff's Office deputy Paul Jessen, Jr., with using his official position to further a long-running scheme involving the dismissal of DWI cases in New Mexico.

According to court documents, between March 2018 and January 2024, Jessen , who was convicted earlier this year of obstructing a Drug Enforcement Administration investigation and making false statements to the FBI, conspired with attorney Thomas J. Clear III and his paralegal, Ricardo Mendez, to help DWI offenders avoid criminal and administrative penalties related to their DWI arrests. In exchange for items of value, Jessen allegedly failed to appear at required criminal settings for DWI offenders who retained Clear, knowing his absence would allow Clear to seek dismissal of the proceedings.

Court documents allege that after Jessen expressed concerns to a co-conspirator, a senior BCSO deputy, about accepting cash payments for his participation in the scheme, he agreed to receive gifts instead. These gifts allegedly included a Pit Boss grill and smoker, a Sharp large-screen television, Craftsman tools and a toolbox.

Jessen also allegedly received free legal services, including representation while he was under investigation for tipping off DEA targets, as well as alcohol, hotel rooms, and other benefits during the course of the scheme.

Jessen is charged with conspiracy to commit interference with commerce by extortion under color of official right. If convicted, Jessen faces up to 20 years imprisonment.

To date, thirteen people, including Clear and Mendez, have pleaded guilty to federal charges stemming from their involvement in the conspiracy.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison and Special Agent in Charge Justin A. Garris of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albuquerque Field Office made the announcement today.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albuquerque Field Office investigated this case with assistant from the Albuquerque Police Department. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of New Mexico is prosecuting the case.

An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
title: Former BCSO Officer Indicted in Federal DWI Corruption Investigation

The U.S. Department of Agriculture's (USDA's) Rural Development (RD) mission area supports projects that invest in rural communities in the United States. RD programs are administered through three USDA agencies: the Rural Business-Cooperative Service (RBCS), Rural Utilities Service (RUS), and Rural Housing Service (RHS).
RBCS administers a variety of programs that provide grants, loans, loan guarantees, and technical assistance to support rural businesses. RUS administers water and waste disposal programs and rural electric, telecommunications, and broadband programs. RUS programs provide grants, loans, loan guarantees, and technical assistance to ensure rural communities have safe and reliable drinking water and electric, telecommunications, and broadband infrastructure. RHS administers community facilities programs that offer grants, loans, loan guarantees, and technical assistance to help construct, repair, or modernize essential community facilities.
Many RD programs have been amended or codified through rural development titles of farm bills. Farm bills provide authorizations of appropriations for RD programs, and Congress funds most RD programs through annual appropriations acts. (This report does not discuss appropriations for rural housing programs that are not authorized in the farm bill.)
Congress appropriated funding for RD programs for FY2026 through the Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-37, Division B). For FY2027, the House passed the Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agency Appropriations Act, 2027 (H.R. 8646). To date, the Senate has not passed an Agriculture appropriations bill for FY2027.
Appropriations and loan authority for rural business programs administered by RBCS increased between FY2025 ($69.5 million with $1.8 billion in loan authority) and FY2026 ($81.6 million with $1.9 billion in loan authority). The President's FY2027 budget request does not include funding for RBCS programs. H.R. 8646 would increase total appropriations and loan authority ($93.8 billion and $2.1 billion, respectively) for rural business programs compared with FY2026. An issue Congress may consider regarding RBCS programs is whether any of them may duplicate the activities of Small Business Administration programs.
Appropriations for water and waste disposal programs administered by RUS decreased between FY2025 ($478.5 million) and FY2026 ($445.9 million). Loan authority for these programs increased from FY2025 ($910 million) to FY2026 ($1.1 billion). The President's FY2027 budget request proposes lower levels of appropriations and loan authority ($202.5 million and $866.9 million, respectively) than in FY2026. H.R. 8646 would decrease overall appropriations for rural water programs in FY2027 ($385.3 million) compared with FY2026 ($445.9 million) and keep loan authority at FY2026 levels. Some issues Congress may consider regarding RUS programs are the roles of Community Project Funding/Congressionally Directed Spending (CPF/CDS) in the selection of projects and cost-share requirements generally.
Appropriations for rural electric, telecommunications, and broadband programs administered by RUS decreased between FY2025 ($150 million) and FY2026 ($108.5 million). Loan authority for these programs increased from FY2025 ($7.6 billion) to FY2026 ($8.5 billion). The President's FY2027 budget requests lower levels of appropriations and loan authority ($30 million and $7.6 billion, respectively) than in FY2026. H.R. 8646 would decrease FY2027 appropriations for rural electric, telecommunications, and broadband programs ($88.2 million) compared with FY2026 levels and increase the loan authority ($8.9 billion). An issue Congress may consider regarding RUS programs is the range of technologies used to provide broadband services.
Appropriations and loan authority for community facilities programs administered by RHS increased between FY2025 ($29.1 million with $1.6 billion in loan authority) and FY2026 ($677.2 million with $1.9 billion in loan authority). The President's FY2027 budget request does not include appropriations for community facilities programs but requests $1.9 billion in loan authority. H.R. 8646 would decrease appropriations for rural community facilities programs ($423 million) compared with FY2026 levels and maintain FY2026 loan authority levels. An issue Congress may consider regarding RHS programs is the role of CPF/CDS in the selection of projects.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA's) Rural Development (RD) mission area supports projects that invest in rural communities and businesses in the United States. RD programs are administered by three agencies: the Rural Business-Cooperative Service (RBCS), Rural Housing Service (RHS), and Rural Utilities Service (RUS). The Under Secretary for RD leads and coordinates this mission area.1 RD programs are administered through a national office in Washington, DC, and field offices throughout the country.
Many RD programs are authorized, reauthorized, or amended through the rural development title of farm bills.2 In previous farm bills, the rural development title has focused on rural business programs administered by RBCS, community facilities programs administered by RHS, and rural utilities programs administered by RUS (referred to as RD farm bill programs in this report). Farm bills generally do not reauthorize or address rural housing programs, and those programs are not discussed in this report except for RHS community facilities programs.
Congress has passed farm bills about every five years for nearly a century.3 The most recent farm bill was the Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018 (2018 farm bill; P.L. 115-334).4 Farm bill reauthorization has been debated in the 119th Congress. The House passed the Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026 (H.R. 7567), and the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry reported the Agriculture Act of 2026 (S. 5526).5
The farm bill authorizes appropriations for RD programs. Congress funds most of these programs with discretionary appropriations through annual Agriculture appropriations acts. A limited number of RD programs receive mandatory funding through the farm bill.6
Most RD programs fund projects through a competitive process in which recipients are typically required to submit a series of documents to USDA, such as a project proposal, work plan, and budget. The agency then selects the projects that are to receive funds. In some cases, certain priorities, such as project characteristics or recipient circumstances, are considered in the competitive process.7
Funding for certain RD programs is allocated noncompetitively by Congress and benefits a specific entity or locality, which is sometimes referred to as a congressional earmark.8 The House Committee on Appropriations refers to congressional earmarks as Community Project Funding (CPF), and the Senate Committee on Appropriations refers to them as Congressionally Directed Spending (CDS). CPF/CDS can affect account funding differently. In some accounts, funding may remain relatively flat or at similar totals across multiple fiscal years, and CPF/CDS will be used to displace funding within that total.9 In other accounts, the amounts for CPF/CDS will be additive to the total funding for the account.10
The most recent Agriculture appropriations act was the Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agency Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-37, Division B). P.L. 119-37 funded RD agencies and selected programs in their jurisdictions for FY2026. In the 119th Congress, the House passed an FY2027 Agriculture appropriations bill (H.R. 8646). To date, an FY2027 Agriculture appropriations bill has not been introduced in the Senate.11
This report provides an overview of appropriations in FY2025 and FY2026. The report also discusses the FY2027 President's budget request for RD farm bill programs, and FY2027 appropriations for RD farm bill programs proposed in the House-passed Agriculture appropriations bill (H.R. 8646). Additionally, the report discusses policy issues pertaining to RD farm bill programs for consideration by Congress.
USDA RBCS administers a variety of programs that provide grants, loans, loan guarantees, and technical assistance to support rural businesses.12 Table 1 shows the nominal appropriations and loan authority for RBCS programs for FY2025 and FY2026. Table 1 also shows the appropriations and loan authority proposed in the President's request for FY2027 and in House-passed H.R. 8646.

Notes: Budget Authority includes grants, loan subsidies, and administrative expenses. Congress increased total appropriations and loan authority for USDA rural business programs between FY2025 and FY2026. Appropriations increased from $69.5 million in FY2025 to $81.6 million in FY2026. Loan authority increased from $1.8 billion in FY2025 to $1.9 billion in FY2026. In FY2025 and FY2026, the RBCS program that received the highest appropriation was the Rural Business Development Grant Program (over $20 million in each of FY2025 and FY2026). Congress increased the appropriation for the loan subsidy for the Business and Industry (B&I) Loan Guarantee Program from $3.3 million in FY2025 to $15.6 million in FY2026. The loan authority for the B&I Loan Guarantee Program increased from $1.7 billion in FY2025 to $1.8 billion in FY2026.
The President's FY2027 request would terminate or not fund many rural business programs.13 For example, the President recommends terminating the B&I Loan Guarantee Program because "applicants can access the private market to obtain financing for projects funded under this authority." In addition, the President's request proposes the termination of the Rural Business Development Grants program because "it is duplicative and overlaps with similar business development programs operated by other Federal agencies."14
The House-passed bill (H.R. 8646) proposes to increase appropriations for the rural business programs from $81.6 million in FY2026 to $93.8 million in FY2027. This increase in appropriations reflects the proposed increase in the loan subsidy for the B&I Loan Guarantee Program (from FY2026 levels of $15.6 million to $38.6 million in H.R. 8646). H.R. 8646 proposes to decrease appropriations for most other rural business programs (e.g., the Rural Business Development Grant Program from $25 million in FY2026 to $18 million in FY2027). The bill also proposes to increase the loan authority for rural business programs from $1.9 billion in FY2026 to $2.1 billion in FY2027. H.R. 8646 would increase the loan authority for the B&I Loan Guarantee Program, specifically, to $2 billion in FY2027.
As Congress continues to deliberate appropriations for rural business programs, Members may consider the distribution of funds across these programs and whether they would prioritize any efforts. Congress may consider whether USDA rural business programs are duplicative with other programs in the federal government that support businesses, such as those offered through the Small Business Administration. Alternatively, Congress may determine that rural businesses should have access to dedicated funding sources for business development or that the programs serve different intents and interests from other federal programs. Another consideration might be whether rural business programs should be consolidated; a reduction in the number of programs may ease some administrative requirements of the programs and require fewer federal staff.
USDA RUS administers a variety of water and waste disposal programs that provide grants, loans, loan guarantees, and technical assistance to ensure rural communities have safe and reliable drinking water.15 Table 2 shows the nominal appropriations and loan authority for RUS rural water and waste disposal programs for FY2025 and FY2026. Table 2 also shows the President's request for FY2027 and the proposed appropriations and loan authority in House-passed H.R. 8646.
Sources: Compiled by CRS from P.L. 119-4, P.L. 119-37, H.R. 8646, and associated explanatory statements and committee reports; and U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), 2027 USDA Explanatory Notes – Rural Utilities Service, https://www.usda.gov/sites/default/files/documents/FY-2027-Chapter-33-RUS.pdf.
Notes: Budget Authority includes grants, loan subsidies, and administrative expenses. Loan subsidies are the cost of making loans, including administrative expenses, interest rate subsidies, and anticipated losses from loan delinquencies. Loan Authority is the amount of loans that USDA is authorized to issue. CPF/CDS refers to Community Project Funding/Congressionally Directed Spending. Short descriptions on most of these programs can be found in the "Rural Utilities Service" section in CRS Report R46471, Federally Supported Projects and Programs for Wastewater, Drinking Water, and Water Supply Infrastructure.
a. Grants for Colonias, Tribes, Hawaiian Homelands, and Alaska Native Villages include funding for the Grants for Rural and Native Alaskan Villages Program, Water and Waste Facility Loans and Grants to Alleviate Health Risks on Tribal Lands Program, and Water and Waste Facility Loans and Grants to Alleviate Health Risks for Colonias Program.
b. Although the High Energy Cost Grant Program provides funding for electricity and is not a water and waste disposal program, it is in this table because its funding is included in water and waste disposal accounts.
c. The values in the column sum to $385.3 million, the amount in the committee-reported bill and report. An amendment subsequently passed on the House floor redirected $2 million from the Office of the Chief Information Officer to the Water and Waste Disposal Program account without further direction for its use.
Congress decreased total appropriations and increased total loan authority for USDA water and waste disposal programs between FY2025 and FY2026. Appropriations decreased to $445.9 million in FY2026 from FY2025 levels of $478.5 million. Loan authority increased from $910 million in FY2025 to $1.1 billion in FY2026. The grant funding in the Water and Waste Disposal Program received the highest appropriation in FY2025 and FY2026, and the total appropriation for this program increased from $238 million in FY2025 to $250.5 million in FY2026. In FY2025, all USDA water and waste disposal grant funding was for competitive grants; in FY2026, $110.5 million (approximately 44%) of the grants were distributed through CPF/CDS. The loan subsidy for the Water and Waste Disposal Program decreased to $47.6 million in FY2026 from FY2025 levels of $88 million. The loan authority for the program increased from $851.5 million in FY2025 to $1 billion in FY2026.
The President requests $202.5 million in appropriations and $866.9 million in loan authority for FY2027.16 The Administration proposes to provide a loan subsidy of $58.5 million for direct water and waste disposal loans with $816.9 million in loan authority.17 The Administration proposes $100 million for water and waste disposal grants. The Administration does not request funding for the Rural Decentralized Water Systems Grant Program.
The House-passed bill (H.R. 8646) proposes to decrease the overall appropriation for rural water programs to $387.3 million and maintain loan authority at $1.1 billion in FY2027. This overall decrease primarily reflects a decrease in appropriations for Grants for Colonias, Native American lands, and Alaska Native villages to $20 million from $60 million in FY2026 and a decrease in appropriations for water and waste disposal grants to $78 million from FY2026 levels of $140 million. H.R. 8646 proposes to increase appropriations for other water programs. These include increasing the loan subsidy for direct water and waste disposal loans from FY2026 levels of $47.6 million to $71.6 million in FY2027, though this amount is lower than FY2025 levels of $88 million.18 Additionally, H.R. 8646 proposes to increase the amount appropriated through CPF/CDS to water and waste disposal programs from FY2026 levels of $110.5 million to $135.5 million in FY2027.
As Congress continues to deliberate appropriations for rural water programs, Members may consider the distribution of funds across water programs and whether they prioritize any efforts. Additionally, Congress may consider the share of water and waste disposal projects that are to be funded through CPF/CDS. H.R. 8646 would increase from FY2026 levels the amount appropriated through CPF/CDS for water and waste disposal programs. The share of the total appropriation would also increase from the FY2026 share of 25% to 35% in FY2027. An increase in the share of CPF/CDS would lower the funding share for water and waste disposal projects funded through competitive grants. On the one hand, a lower funding share for competitive grants may lead to some projects not receiving funding. On the other hand, an increase in the share of CPF/CDS may allow Members of Congress to better identify projects that they believe would be most beneficial to their home districts or states. However, if appropriations occur through a continuing resolution, these earmarked projects may not receive funding.
Another potential consideration for Congress is the extent to which cost-share requirements for water and waste disposal projects may impact participation. Some programs, such as the Water and Waste Disposal Grant Program, set cost-share requirements on the basis of the income level of the rural community.19 Cost-share requirements are generally seen as a mechanism to encourage funding recipients to invest their own resources to leverage federal funding and establish long-term interest in the outcome of a project. Cost-share requirements may disincentivize grant recipients that do not have adequate resources to meet the requirements from applying for federal programs. In some cases, a rural community that has lower income may be less able than a community with higher income to afford a cost-share requirement. Congress may consider the effects of cost-share requirements, the ramifications of removing match requirements for certain communities, and the consequences of allowing for flexibility on what can qualify as a cost-share requirement. Congress may choose to leave cost-share requirements as they are or to expand them to ensure that recipients are investing their own resources into the success of the project.
RUS administers programs that provide loans, loan guarantees, and grants to support the development of rural electric, telecommunications, and broadband infrastructure.20 Table 3 shows the nominal appropriations for RUS rural electric, telecommunications, and broadband programs for FY2025 and FY2026. Table 3 also shows the President's request for FY2027 and the proposed appropriations and loan authority in House-passed H.R. 8646.
Table 3. Appropriations for USDA Rural Electric, Telecommunications, and Broadband Programs
dollars in millions
Congress decreased appropriations for rural electric, telecommunications, and broadband programs from $188.6 million in FY2025 to $149.7 million in FY2026 and increased the loan authority from FY2025 levels of $7.6 billion to $8.5 billion in FY2026. In FY2025 and FY2026, the ReConnect Program received the highest level of funds. Funding for this program decreased to $50 million in FY2026 from $90 million in FY2025. The Distance Learning and Telemedicine Grant Program also saw a decrease in appropriations in FY2026.
Loan authority increased for multiple rural electric, telecommunications, and broadband programs. For example, between FY2025 and FY2026, loan authority for the electric infrastructure program increased by $500 million, and total loan authority for the telecommunications infrastructure program increased by $395 million.
The President requests $63.3 million in appropriations and $7.6 billion in loan authority for rural electric, telecommunications, and broadband programs. The President's request is for the Distance Learning and Telemedicine Grant Program.
H.R. 8646 would decrease appropriations for distance learning, telemedicine, and broadband programs to $129.2 million from FY2026 levels of $149.7 million. The bill would increase the loan authority for these programs from FY2026 levels of $8.5 billion to $8.9 billion. CPF/CDS for distance learning and telemedicine programs would decrease from FY2026 levels of $10.8 million to $3.2 million. Additionally, H.R. 8646 proposes to decrease the appropriation for the ReConnect Program to $40 million from $50 million in FY2026. The bill would keep loan authority at FY2026 levels for most programs and increase the loan authority for the Electric Infrastructure Program to $7.4 billion in FY2027.
As Congress continues to debate appropriations for rural electric, telecommunications, and broadband programs, Members may consider the distribution of funds across programs and whether they would like to prioritize any efforts. Additionally, Congress may consider the range of technologies to deliver broadband services under USDA programs. For example, in some remote or rural areas, low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite technologies may better provide broadband service than other technologies (e.g., fiber or cable) due to cost or geographical limitations.21 Not all technologies provide equal reliability; for example, weather conditions or heavily forested terrain may cause interruptions in LEO service.
RHS administers programs that offer grants, loans, loan guarantees, and technical assistance to help construct, repair, or modernize essential community facilities (e.g., fire stations, community centers, senior centers, and health clinics).22 Other community facilities programs include the Rural Community Development Initiative and the Tribal College Grant Program. The Rural Community Development Initiative provides grants for certain qualified organizations to provide technical assistance to private, public, and nonprofit organizations working on housing, community facility, and RD improvement projects.23 The Tribal College Initiative provides grants to 1994 land-grant institutions (Tribal Colleges and Universities) to make capital improvements to their educational facilities and purchase equipment.24 Table 4 shows the actual nominal appropriations and loan authority for RHS rural community facilities programs for FY2025 and FY2026. Table 4 also shows the President's request for FY2027 and the proposed appropriations and loan authority in House-passed H.R. 8646.
Sources: Compiled by CRS from P.L. 119-4, P.L. 119-37, H.R. 8646, and associated explanatory statements and committee reports; and U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), 2027 USDA Explanatory Notes – Rural Housing Service, https://www.usda.gov/sites/default/files/documents/FY-2027-Chapter-31-RHS.pdf.
Congress increased total appropriations and loan authority for USDA community facilities programs between FY2025 and FY2026. Appropriations for community facilities programs increased from FY2025 levels of $29.1 million to $677.2 million in FY2026. Loan authority increased from FY2025 levels of $1.6 billion to $1.9 billion in FY2026. The increase in appropriations reflects the increase in CPF/CDS community facilities grants from no funding in FY2025 to $659.2 million in FY2026. The increase in loan authority reflects the increase for community facilities loans from $989.3 million in FY2025 to $1.3 billion in FY2026.
The President's budget for FY2027 does not request funding for the rural community facilities grant programs.25 In the case of community facilities grants, the Administration stated that funding "has been overtaken" by CPF/CDS.26 In FY2026, Congress allocated $5 million to community facilities competitive grants and $659.5 million to CPF/CDS. The Administration requested the same loan authorization levels for community facilities direct loans and community facilities guaranteed loans as FY2026.
H.R. 8646 would decrease the appropriation for rural community facilities programs from FY2026 levels of $677 million to $423 million. Most of the reduction in appropriations reflects a lower amount proposed for CPF/CDS spending for community facilities grants ($659 million to $399 million). H.R. 8646 would increase the level of funding for competitive community facilities grants from $5 million to $11.5 million. The bill would maintain FY2026 levels for the loan authorization for community facilities direct loans and guaranteed loans.
As Congress continues to deliberate funding levels for rural community facilities programs, Members may consider the distribution of funding levels across programs. Additionally, Congress may consider the role of CPF/CDS and the share of community facilities grants that are to be competitive. Although FY2027 proposals would decrease both appropriations and the share of CPF/CDS for community facilities programs, CPF/CDS remains the primary mechanism that would fund these programs. CPF/CDS provide opportunities for Members of Congress to identify the projects in their districts that they believe are most in need of funds. A reliance on this funding mechanism may indicate that the competitive grants process has not been as effective at identifying under-resourced projects. Community facilities grants might also be impacted by whether FY2027 appropriations take the form of an Agriculture appropriations act or a continuing resolution. In FY2025, for example, no CPF/CDS were included in continuing resolutions.

NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA – RAYNARD JAMES (“JAMES”) , age 23, pleaded guilty on November 4, 2026 before U.S. District Judge Jane T. Milazzo to one count of conspiracy to commit bank fraud, and three counts of bank fraud, in violation of 18 U.S.C. §§ 1344 and 1349, announced U.S. Attorney David I. Courcelle.

According to court documents, JAMES entered into a scheme with a mail carrier for the United States Postal Service to steal checks from the mail, fraudulently deposit them, and withdraw the proceeds. In furtherance of that scheme, in July of 2024, JAMES ’sco-conspirator stole three checks from the mail and provided them to JAMES . JAMES either fraudulently endorsed the stolen checks or reprinted them to make them payable to an entity other than the intended payee. JAMES then attempted to deposit each of the checks. JAMES and other co-conspirators were able to successfully withdraw over $18,000 from the stolen checks.

As to each of his convictions, JAMES faces up to 30 years in prison, up to a $1,000,000 fine, up to five years of supervised release, and a $100 mandatory special assessment fee.

The case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the United States Postal Inspection Service. Assistant United States Attorney David Berman of the Violent Crime Unit is in charge of the prosecution.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

WASHINGTON – Gilberto Paz Madrid, 41, a citizen of Mexico, was sentenced today in U.S. District Court to 97 months in federal prison for his role as a broker in a fentanyl and cocaine conspiracy while he was incarcerated in Texas for a previous heroin trafficking offense, announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro.

“This illegal alien was already behind bars for trafficking heroin, yet he used a smuggled cellphone to broker fentanyl and cocaine deals aimed at D.C. streets,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “Prison walls will not stop us from pursuing traffickers who endanger our communities, and when he finishes his sentence, he will face deportation.”

“This illegal alien was already behind bars for trafficking heroin, yet he used a smuggled cellphone to broker fentanyl and cocaine deals aimed at D.C. streets,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “Prison walls will not stop us from pursuing traffickers who endanger our communities, and when he finishes his sentence, he will face deportation.”

Paz Madrid, aka “Taco,” pleaded guilty on July 2 before Judge Timothy J. Kelly to conspiracy to distribute 40 grams or more of fentanyl and 500 grams or more of cocaine. The 97-month prison term will be served after he completes a 10-year sentence for heroin trafficking out of the Eastern District of Virginia. Madrid faces deportation after serving his time in federal prison.

According to court documents, Paz Madrid was incarcerated and serving a 120-month sentence at FCI Beaumont in Texas in February 2024 when an individual sent a WhatsApp message to a contraband cellphone Paz Madrid was using in prison.

The individual claimed to have received Paz Madrid’s number from a mutual acquaintance and explained that he was hoping Paz Madrid could broker an introduction to drug customers in the United States. In a later WhatsApp call, the individual stated that they could distribute both “F” (meaning fentanyl) and “blanco” (meaning cocaine).

During a subsequent call between the two, Paz Madrid added co-defendant Jermaine Horne to the conversation. Horne asked the price for a kilo of cocaine, which the individual indicated would be between $17,000 and $18,000. Paz Madrid also advised that individual that Horne and his associates could assist the individual with the “F” and “cuadros” (meaning fentanyl and kilograms, respectively).

On March 6, 2024, another person reached out to Horne via telephone. The person indicated that he was a courier working for the individual. The person asked, “So what you need?” Horne replied, “He told you right? He was saying you were bringing four.” The person asked, “four or five?” Horne said, “I thought he said four but five, that’s cool.” The person clarified that they were told to deliver fentanyl. Horne responded that he was expecting “up” (meaning cocaine). The person ended that call by telling Horne that they needed to make sure everyone was on the same page and would call Horne back.

Following the call with Horne, the person called Paz Madrid. The two discussed the type of drug to be delivered to Horne. Paz Madrid indicated it would be the “blanco” (meaning cocaine). The person indicated that he could deliver four kilograms to Horne. The person later spoke again with Horne. Horne made clear that he wanted four kilograms of cocaine and one kilogram of fentanyl. The two made plans to meet the following week.

The narcotics were slated to be delivered March 14, 2024, to Horne in the District. However, Horne apparently saw surveillance vehicles in the area, and he did not enter the pre-arranged location to purchase the narcotics. In later conversations, Horne later told Paz Madrid that he did not like the location because it was near a police station, a message that Paz Madrid conveyed to the would-be supplier.

Horne pleaded guilty on July 28 to conspiracy to distribute 40 grams or more of fentanyl and 500 grams or more of cocaine. Sentencing is pending.

This investigation was conducted by the FBI Washington Field Office with valuable assistance from the White County (Arkansas) Sheriff’s Office, Nash County (North Carolina) Sheriff’s Office, the Bureau of Prisons Office of Special Investigations, and the Metropolitan Police Department.

The matter is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nihar Mohanty of the Violent Crime and Narcotics Trafficking Section.
