David X. Sullivan, United States Attorney for the District of Connecticut, today announced that WINIFER ACOSTA JIMENEZ, 32, of the Bronx, New York, was sentenced yesterday by U.S. District Judge Vernon D. Oliver in Hartford to 72 months of imprisonment and two years of supervised release for a fentanyl trafficking offense.

According to court documents and statements made in court, in February 2023, the Drug Enforcement Administration arranged the controlled purchase of two kilograms of fentanyl from a wholesale supplier of narcotics with multiple distribution points in the northeastern U.S. Acosta Jimenez and her co-defendant, Ovidalis Jimenez Pujols, were arrested on February 22, 2023, after they transported the two kilograms of fentanyl from New York to a meeting location in Milford, Connecticut.

Acosta Jimenez, who was released on $100,000 bond after federal arrest on January 31, 2024, removed her GPS monitoring equipment on July 31, 2024, and absconded. She was located and arrested in New York on December 18, 2025.

Acosta Jimenez has been detained since her arrest. On February 3, 2026, she pleaded guilty to conspiracy to distribute and to possess with intent to distribute 40 grams or more of fentanyl.

Jimenez Pujols also pleaded guilty and, on February 19, 2025, was sentenced to 48 months of imprisonment .

This matter was investigated the Drug Enforcement Administration, with the assistance of the Connecticut State Police and the West Haven Police Department. The case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Stephanie T. Levick and Nathan J. Guevremont.
title: Bronx Woman Who Trafficked Fentanyl and Then Fled After Her Arrest Sentenced to 6 Years in Federal Prison

text:
Dear Mr. Secretary,
Since the TBAC last met in early August, Treasury markets have repriced toward a higher path for interest rates, reflecting stronger economic activity and associated financing needs, persistent energy-supply disruptions, and the Federal Reserve’s initial rate hike and projections for further increases. The selloff in rates was led by the front end of the yield curve, with two-year yields rising by roughly 50bps and ten-year yields by roughly 40bps. The move accelerated in September and early October, with ten-year yields peaking around 5.4% and thirty-year yields around 5.7% in early October. Some of that increase has since reversed.
A substantial part of the repricing reflected stronger U.S. economic activity through the summer despite higher energy prices and rising rates. Household spending remained resilient as gains in financial wealth and lower savings rates cushioned pressure on real incomes. Existing fixed-rate mortgages limited the increase in homeowners’ debt-service costs, even as higher rates on new borrowing weighed on housing activity. Meanwhile, strong investment in computing equipment, intellectual property, and data centers offset weakness in more rate-sensitive investment. The infrastructure buildout proved less sensitive to financing costs than traditional housing-led expansions. Related gains in construction and equipment manufacturing are becoming visible but have not yet generated a broad acceleration in employment.
This resilience gave the Federal Reserve greater scope to respond to persistent inflation risks exacerbated by the energy shock. Supply disruptions that began over the summer have proved more persistent than initially expected, keeping crude and refined-product prices elevated through the quarter and feeding into transportation and freight costs. Headline CPI accelerated to 3.7% in September, with gasoline alone accounting for more than half of the monthly increase. Core CPI ran at 2.6% as fuel and freight costs passed through to other categories.
The Federal Reserve responded in September by raising its target range by 25 basis points to 3.75%–4.00%. Chairman Warsh emphasized both the strengthening economy and insufficient progress on inflation, characterizing the decision as removing accommodation rather than making already restrictive financial conditions materially tighter. The September Summary of Economic Projections reinforced the higher-for-longer message: the median policy-rate projection rose to 4.1% for both year-end 2026 and year-end 2027, compared with 3.8% and 3.6%, respectively, in June. Markets continued to price approximately three additional rate increases over the coming year even as the Fed held rates steady in October. More recently, higher borrowing costs and emerging weakness in equity and credit markets have moderated expectations for the pace of tightening but not eliminated expectations for further increases.
Several cross-market and technical developments came into play over the quarter:
- Term premium has risen less than yields this year, though the ten-year term premium showed some strain in the early fall. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York’s ACM model estimate of the ten-year term premium rose approximately 20bps in September. Interest rate implied volatility rose sharply, reflecting greater priced uncertainty and raising the cost of option-based protection against further yield increases. As yields rose and refinancing incentives diminished, mortgage durations extended, prompting convexity hedgers to reduce duration. Collateralized mortgage obligation floaters with coupon caps added to hedging pressures as forward-implied coupons approached their caps, likely increasing demand for intermediate-dated rates volatility. These flows likely amplified the initial selloff and increase in volatility, although the scope for further mortgage-duration extension diminished as yields moved higher.
- Stronger economic activity was also driving expectations of higher interest rates outside the United States. The European Central Bank and Bank of Japan raised policy rates over the period as markets priced a broader tightening cycle across major developed economies. Developments in European sovereign markets were also relevant for Treasuries, as fiscal and political uncertainty produced a sharp widening in French government-bond spreads, adding to volatility across global fixed-income markets. Those linkages have not operated uniformly: the correlation between French and U.S. yield changes weakened in October, and more acute French stress subsequently supported safe-haven demand for Treasuries and German Bunds.
- Technology-related financing remained an additional influence on capital markets and financial conditions. Large debt offerings and prospective mega-IPOs reflected substantial private-sector financing needs. Heavy technology issuance and uncertainty over future financing needs contributed to wider spreads in the sector and increased competition for long-duration capital. Banks and asset managers also helped technology companies tap a broader pool of capital through GPU-backed loans, equipment leases, and data center project financing. Foreign investor demand to finance U.S. technology contributed to dollar strength, providing an additional channel of financial tightening alongside higher borrowing costs. Although large issuance windows may influence Treasury concessions and hedging flows at the margin, there is no evidence of a persistent deterioration in Treasury auction demand. Recent auctions remained generally resilient, though individual results varied.
- Technology news also contributed to weaker risk sentiment later in the period, helping restore demand for Treasuries. By late October, the Nasdaq 100 had fallen just over 7% from its early-October high amid greater scrutiny of the returns on increasingly debt-financed technology investment. Together with wider credit spreads, the equity pullback helped restore a safe-haven bid for Treasuries, partially reversing the earlier rise in yields.
Against that backdrop, the Committee convened for its quarterly refunding discussion. The outlook shows the funding gap widens over FY27 and increases further in FY28 and FY29. Consistent with Treasury’s cash management policy, Treasury recently published cash balance assumptions for the end of Q1 FY27 and Q2 FY27 at approximately $850 billion and $1 trillion, respectively.
The Committee next addressed the first of its two charges: Super Intelligence (SI)-related issuance. Members discussed recent trends in corporate bond issuance related to SI and associated businesses. Members noted the market is in the midst of a significant technology financing cycle. Financing is also expanding beyond long-dated corporate bonds, with secured and asset-backed structures increasingly bringing issuance inside 10 years. Taken as a whole, the technology ecosystem appears to have both the capacity and incentive to sustain borrowing and investment.
Foreign demand for U.S. fixed-income assets has accelerated this year, while the broader investor base retains significant capacity to absorb additional issuance. Insurers, pensions, households, and foreign investors provide diversified sources of demand, with households and private pensions still relatively under allocated to fixed income. Even modest reallocations from cash and equities could therefore absorb a meaningful share of projected borrowing.
Treasury auction results show no evidence that 2026 technology-related issuance has crowded out long-end Treasury demand. To the extent technology investment is affecting rates, the Committee viewed the transmission as stemming from stronger growth rather than through crowding out. Higher Treasury yields have primarily reflected growth, policy expectations, and energy prices rather than an issuance-driven supply shock. Members emphasized, however, that the financing cycle remains in its early stages and recommended that Treasury continue to monitor potential effects on Treasury market demand as SI-related issuance grows.
The Committee’s second charge focused on Treasury derivatives and their growing role in the market. Since the 2022 rise in yields, asset managers have increasingly used futures to gain synthetic Treasury exposure, while liability-driven investors, including pension funds and insurers, have used interest rate swaps to manage duration. The Committee emphasized that expressing duration through derivatives enhances demand for Treasuries by broadening market access and expanding intermediation capacity.
In the context of discussing derivatives, the Committee identified several policy options that could further improve demand for cash Treasuries. These include easing regulatory constraints on balance sheet capacity, including exempting Treasuries from leverage ratios and recognizing pre-positioned discount window collateral in liquidity metrics; expanding access to repo financing; improving the availability of term repo; and enabling new entrants in repo market making. The Committee also recommended evaluation of fund accounting treatment of repo interest, tax treatment, and operational challenges. Together, these steps could broaden and diversify the base of cash Treasury holders, strengthen market intermediation, and support durable demand for Treasuries.
The Committee discussed the efficacy of the liquidity support buyback program. There is a variety of evidence that the program has supported liquidity conditions since it was introduced in 2024, and buybacks remain an effective tool for that purpose. While an effective tool, the Committee believes that any management of Treasury’s maturity profile should be done via changes to auction sizes.
To further the goal of financing the government at the lowest cost over time, the Committee continues to endorse an issuance strategy that balances expected costs and volatility of interest expense, matches issuance patterns to market demand, encourages smooth market functioning, and is regular and predictable. As members look ahead, baseline fiscal projections suggest that current auction sizes are likely to shift Treasury’s debt profile toward an increasing share of bill and shorter-term funding. The Committee believes that the market has recently been absorbing Treasury issuance well and that the bulk of recent interest rate rises reflect strong economic conditions and the monetary policy outlook rather than weak investor demand for Treasuries. The Committee discussed that real money investors, including retail and some institutional investors, have grown their demand as rates have risen and as a hedge against downward moves in economic conditions. However, the Committee also noted that money market fund assets have leveled off and the bill market has started to show some signs of price sensitivity.
In light of that outlook, for the current quarter, the Committee recommended keeping nominal coupon, FRN, and TIPS auction sizes unchanged. However, the Committee believes that given current fiscal projections, increases in coupon auction sizes will be warranted later in FY27. Looking ahead, given the projected funding gaps in FY28 and FY29, members discussed different approaches to coupon increases over the horizon. While there is broad agreement across the Committee to increase coupon auction sizes, there was considerable debate around the pace and sizing specific to the long end of the curve.
Members recommended that Treasury change its forward-guidance language and emphasized that clear communication alongside a regular and predictable operating framework remains important to help market participants adjust to future changes.
In conclusion, consistent with its past messaging, the Committee encourages Congress to act to raise or suspend the debt limit to avoid disrupting Treasury market functioning, increasing costs to the taxpayer, and constraining economic growth.
Respectfully,
Jason S. Granet
Chair, Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee
E. Alexander Schiller
Vice Chair, Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee
title: Report to the Secretary of the Treasury from the Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee

Press Statement

Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, Spokesman Office of the Spokesman

November 4, 2026

Today, the United States is acting against a criminal network that sells fraudulent flags to the Iranian regime’s shadow fleet of ships. The United States is also targeting a Türkiye-based company that provides ground services to sanctioned Iranian airlines. The Department of the Treasury is taking these actions under Operation Economic Outcast, the Trump Administration’s campaign to cut off revenue the Iranian regime uses to fund terrorism, weapons proliferation, and its proxies across the Middle East.

For more than a decade, India-based Suniel Kumar Sharma and his wife, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid, have formed companies that pose as the flag registries and maritime service providers of countries and jurisdictions such as Guyana, Eswatini, Aruba, Mali, Mozambique, Malawi, Sint Maarten, and Timor-Leste. These companies have sold fraudulent registrations and certificates to vessels carrying illicit Iranian oil. Most of these governments have publicly disavowed the fraudulent registries.

Today’s action targets 13 individuals and companies in the Sharma network. We commend the governments that have exposed these schemes. We call on flag states, port authorities, and the maritime industry to verify vessel registrations and deny shadow fleet vessels access to their waters and ports.

The designations imposed today are being taken pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13902, which targets the Iranian petroleum, petrochemical, and aviation sectors, among other key sectors of the Iranian economy. For more information on today’s action, please see the Department of the Treasury’s press release .

Teneika Reynolds, 50, pleaded guilty before U.S. District Judge Greg Kays, to aiding and assisting in the preparation of false tax returns.

Reynolds was the owner and operator of TR Tax Service, a tax preparation business operating in Kansas City. Reynolds prepared and electronically filed returns claiming false items including Schedule C business expenses, false Forms 7202, Sick and Family Leave Credits, and fictitious Household Help income for client-taxpayers for the tax years 2019 to 2023. This resulted in refunds larger than what her clients were entitled to receive.

Reynolds assisted at least 15 individuals file at least 33 false and fraudulent income tax returns for tax years 2019 through 2023. Specifically, on Feb. 8, 2022, Reynolds aided and assisted in the filing of an IRS Form 1040, U.S. Individual Income Tax Return, with the Internal Revenue Service. On that form, Reynolds included false Sick and Family Leave credits, resulting in a fraudulent refund.

Under federal statutes, Reynolds is subject to a sentence of up to three years in federal prison without parole. The maximum statutory sentence is prescribed by Congress and is provided here for informational purposes, as the sentencing of Reynolds will be determined by the court based on the advisory sentencing guidelines and other statutory factors. A sentencing hearing will be scheduled after the completion of a presentence investigation by the United States Probation Office.

This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Rudolph R. Rhodes IV. It was investigated by Internal Revenue Service-Criminal Investigation.

The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

WASHINGTON —The U.S. Small Business Administration announced the opening of a Disaster Loan Outreach Centers in Cumberland and Madison Counties to assist businesses, private nonprofit organizations, and residents affected by severe storms, straight-line winds, tornadoes, and flooding occurring June 18 – 27.
Beginning Wednesday and Thursday, Nov. 4 and 5, SBA customer service representatives will be on hand at the Disaster Loan Outreach Centers in Cumberland and Madison Counties to answer questions about SBA’s disaster loan program, explain the application process, and help individuals complete their application. Walk-ins are welcome, and you can schedule an in-person appointment in advance at appointment.sba.gov.
The hours of operation are listed below:
CUMBERLAND COUNTY
Disaster Loan Outreach Center
Burkesville Fire Training Center
Burkesville, KY 42717
Opens at noon, Wednesday, Nov. 4
Hours: Monday – Friday, 9 a.m. – 6 p.m.
Saturday, 9 a.m. – 1 p.m.
Temporary closing: Wednesday, Nov. 11, in observance of Veterans Day
Closes permanently at 5 p.m. Wednesday, Nov. 18
MADISON COUNTY
Disaster Loan Outreach Center
Madison County Public Library
Richmond, KY 40475
Opens at noon, Thursday, Nov. 5
Hours: Monday – Friday, 9 a.m. – 6 p.m.
Saturday, 9 a.m. – 1 p.m.
Temporary closing: Wednesday, Nov. 11, in observance of Veterans Day
Closes permanently at 5 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 19
“When disasters strike, SBA’s Disaster Loan Outreach Centers perform an important role by assisting small businesses and their communities,” said Chris Stallings, Associate Administrator of the Office of Disaster Recovery at SBA. “At these centers, our specialists help business owners and residents apply for disaster loans and learn about the full range of programs available to support their recovery.”
Businesses and nonprofits are eligible to apply for business physical disaster loans and may borrow up to $2 million to repair or replace disaster-damaged or destroyed real estate, machinery and equipment, inventory, and other business assets.
The SBA’s Economic Injury Disaster Loan (EIDL) program is available to eligible small businesses, small agricultural cooperatives, and private nonprofits — including faith-based organizations — impacted by financial losses directly related to this disaster. The SBA is unable to provide disaster loans to agricultural producers, farmers, or ranchers, except for aquaculture enterprises.
EIDLs are for working capital needs caused by the disaster and are available even if the business or private nonprofit did not suffer any physical damage. The loans may be used to pay fixed debts, payroll, accounts payable, and other bills which could not be paid due to the disaster.
Homeowners and renters are eligible to apply for home and personal property loans and may borrow up to $100,000 to replace or repair personal property, such as clothing, furniture, cars, and appliances. Homeowners may apply for up to $500,000 to replace or repair their primary residence.
Interest rates are as low as 4% for small businesses, 3.625% for nonprofits, and 2.875% for homeowners and renters with terms of up to 30 years. Interest does not begin to accrue, and payments are not due until 12 months from the date of the first loan disbursement. The SBA determines eligibility and sets loan amounts and terms based on each applicant’s financial condition.
To apply online, visit sba.gov/disaster. Applicants may also call the National Support Network Center at (866) SBA-HELP or email disastercustomerservice@sba.gov for more information on SBA disaster assistance. For people who are deaf, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability, please dial 7-1-1 to access telecommunications relay services.
The filing deadline to return applications for physical property damage is Dec. 28. The deadline to return economic injury applications is July 26, 2027.
###
About the U.S. Small Business Administration
The U.S. Small Business Administration helps power the American dream of business ownership. As the only go-to resource and voice for small businesses backed by the strength of the federal government, SBA empowers entrepreneurs and small business owners with the resources and support they need to start, grow or expand their businesses, or recover from a declared disaster. It delivers services through an extensive network of SBA field offices and partnerships with public and private organizations. To learn more, visit www.sba.gov.
title: SBA Opens Disaster Loan Outreach Centers in Kentucky

Soldiers from the 121st Field Hospital “Legends,” part of the 549th Hospital Center and the 65th Medical Brigade “Pacific Medics,” packed up four critical clinical sections on a late August night and moved them into a nearby fixed Army medical facility here.
The hospital’s emergency treatment area, operating room, intensive care unit and intermediate care ward displaced under emissions control, limited visibility and a simulated drone threat as a signature event of Pacific Medic Forge 26-2, a 65th Medical Brigade exercise held in August 2026 that served as the 121st Field Hospital’s external evaluation.
The 121st Field Hospital has served in South Korea since 1950, arriving at the outset of the Korean War. Seventy-six years later, its planners are studying modern conflicts to make the hospital more maneuverable. Unit planners cited World Health Organization data recording more than 3,300 attacks on health care in Ukraine since February 2022 as a driving factor behind the displacement plan.
During the exercise, no simulated patient moved until an advance party confirmed the new site was secure. The emergency treatment area at the original site remained open until the last vehicle departed, and simulated patients rode in dedicated vehicles with a set limit on the number of patients per provider. Teams rehearsed patient loading, downed-vehicle drills and counter-drone procedures before the first tent came down.
According to Maj. Joshua Okoemu, executive officer of the 121st Field Hospital, the four sections moved within the unit’s established planning timeline, and the displacement was completed safely.
“We did not want leaders waiting on a phone call to make a decision about a patient,” Maj. Okoemu said. “The delegated authorities matrix told every leader what they could decide on their own, and that is what allowed us to run one hospital out of two locations.”
Designed to identify friction, the external evaluation yielded several unit recommendations to improve future operations. These include establishing a signed agreement that settles equipment rules with the receiving facility before a move, creating a ready-made “fall-in” package of ward procedures for every section and pushing radio updates directly to section noncommissioned officers in charge.
“Moving under drone threat means giving up some of the communication you are used to having,” said Warrant Officer 1 Norman M. Abrams, signal officer of the 121st Field Hospital, who supported communications planning for the exercise. “This move showed us how to adapt our primary and alternate radio plans in an air-contested environment.”
Leader assessments also emphasized clinician endurance. After the night crew completed the move and transitioned into day operations the next morning, the unit’s after-action review recommended building dedicated rest cycles into future displacement phases.
“Our Soldiers moved a hospital in the dark and then came right back to take care of patients, and that says a lot about who they are,” said Master Sgt. Miriam L. Reyes, senior enlisted advisor, 121st Field Hospital. “But fatigue is a patient safety issue. Protecting their rest must be part of the plan, not an afterthought.”
The Soldiers of the 121st Field Hospital showed that a hospital can pack up in the dark, move under a simulated threat and keep caring for patients. They will carry these lessons into the next iteration of Pacific Medic Forge.
title: 121st Field Hospital Moves Its Hospital in the Dark During Pacific Medic Forge 26-2

The Department of War announced today that this year, the Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Unmanned Systems (DRPM-UxS) has delivered a massive surge of combat-ready, mass-producible unmanned systems and counter-drone capabilities to U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), providing operational commanders with immediate, cost-effective tactical lethality across the theater.
Through an investment of approximately $782 million this year, DRPM-UxS has fielded:
Over 100 Unmanned Surface Vessels (USVs) and Unmanned Underwater Vessels (UUVs), expanding maritime reconnaissance and strike lethality; and
More than 24,000 Counter-Unmanned Aerial Systems (C-UAS), establishing a dense, multi-layered defensive shield to protect forward-deployed forces against adversary drone attacks through its counter unit, Joint Interagency Task Force 401 (JIATF-401).
These deliveries demonstrate the Department's rapid shift from multi-year developmental pipelines to an agile "Warfighting Acquisition" model. In the hands of American warfighters, these low-cost, attritable systems serve as high-volume alternatives to legacy, multi-million-dollar exquisite munitions—flipping the battlefield cost-exchange ratio firmly in favor of the United States.
"Under Secretary Hegseth's direction, we are moving at the speed of modern combat to equip our forces with decisive, affordable mass," said Owen West, CEO of Project Agincourt and DRPM-UxS. "DRPM-UxS was established to cut through red tape and put lethal technology directly into the hands of our frontline troops. The thousands of systems operating across CENTCOM this year are just the beginning. We will out-innovate, out-build, and out-adapt any adversary on the battlefield. The goal is to scale these capabilities across the Joint Force."
By scaling commercial production lines and deploying modular software baselines, DRPM-UxS is driving a fundamental restructuring of defense procurement. This effort serves as the operational foundation for the Autonomous Warfare Command (AUTOWARCOM), a planned four-star functional combatant command scheduled to stand up by October 1, 2027.
At Secretary Hegseth's direction, DRPM-UxS will sustain continuous deliveries of low-cost, mass-producible unmanned and autonomous systems to CENTCOM while rapidly expanding fielding pipelines to Pacific Command, European Command, and the broader Joint Force.
title: DRPM-UxS Deliver Over 25,000 Autonomous and Counter-Unmanned Systems to CENTCOM AOR

In March 2023, the United States and Japan signed a critical minerals agreement (CMA) covering five key minerals related to the production of batteries for clean vehicles (also commonly referred to as electric vehicles or "EVs"). The U.S.-Japan CMA entered into force immediately upon signature, without approval by Congress. The CMA partially addressed Japan's concerns regarding certain content requirements for the consumer tax credit for new EVs included in P.L. 117-169, the FY2022 reconciliation law. U.S. policymakers had crafted these EV tax credit requirements, in part, to reduce U.S. dependence on goods from the People's Republic of China (PRC, or China). Section 70502 of P.L. 119-21 terminated the EV tax credit from September 30, 2025. Since 2025, the Trump Administration has undertaken several cooperative initiatives with Japan. Congress may consider whether—and, if so, how—to exercise oversight of agreements like the CMA. Congress has constitutional authority over foreign commerce and tariffs and has played a role in approving and implementing trade agreements. Another issue for Congress is the outlook for U.S.-Japan supply chain cooperation and whether U.S. tariff actions, including current and potential tariffs on Japanese goods and critical minerals-related sectors, align with congressional priorities related to critical minerals supply chains.
Some Members of Congress have expressed concerns about ensuring reliable U.S. access to the mined, processed, and refined critical minerals, rare earth elements (REEs), and critical materials needed to produce key goods related to defense capabilities, energy generation and storage, and data centers and quantum computing, as well as mass consumer technologies such as smartphones and automobiles. China dominates the EV supply chain, including mining and processing of critical minerals, particularly REEs, and production of EVs and EV batteries. The PRC government has imposed export control measures on certain critical minerals since December 2023. Following November 2025 statements by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi related to Taiwan, the PRC government implemented Japan-specific export restrictions on certain goods containing REEs.
The FY2022 reconciliation law (P.L. 117-169) provided consumers a tax credit of up to $7,500 for new EVs. EVs could qualify for partial credit if they met requirements related to the sourcing of critical minerals in the EV battery. Specifically, a certain percentage of the EV battery's critical minerals had to be sourced from the United States or a U.S. free trade agreement (FTA) partner and could not be sourced from "foreign entities of concern" (FEOC), such as Russia and China. The U.S. Department of the Treasury and the U.S. Department of Energy defined FEOC to include all entities headquartered in or organized under the laws of an FEOC country.
According to the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, in 2025, Japan was the sixth-largest U.S. trading partner (goods and services). The automotive sector plays a major role in the U.S.-Japan economic relationship. In 2025, the United States imported $51.1 billion in vehicles and parts from Japan and exported $2.6 billion to Japan. As of 2025, Japanese automakers have reported $70 billion in U.S. manufacturing investments.
The U.S.-Japan CMA changed neither U.S. law nor existing tariffs and did not include other market access provisions. The CMA covers cobalt, graphite, lithium, manganese, and nickel—all key EV battery inputs. Japan is not a large source of mined critical minerals but has related capabilities, including mineral processing and manufacturing of EV batteries, semiconductors, semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and other goods.
Under the CMA, the United States and Japan agreed to, among other measures, (1) maintain the "current practice" of not imposing export duties on critical minerals trade between their countries; (2) confer on measures to address nonmarket policies and practices affecting critical minerals supply chains; (3) confer on best practices for review of foreign investments in their countries' critical minerals sectors; (4) coordinate on actions related to forced labor and other labor rights connected to critical minerals supply chains; and (5) promote employer neutrality related to unions. The two countries agreed to review the CMA periodically to determine whether to terminate or amend the CMA, including which critical minerals are covered.
In 2024, Treasury designated the CMA as an FTA for the purposes of the P.L. 117-169 EV tax credit. There is no statutory definition for an FTA, but under World Trade Organization (WTO) rules, a regional trade agreement such as an FTA generally must cover "substantially all trade" between trading partners. The United States has 14 such "comprehensive" FTAs—authorized and approved by Congress—with 20 countries, not including Japan. During the first Trump Administration, the United States and Japan signed the 2020 U.S.-Japan Trade Agreement (USJTA), which reduced tariffs on some goods, but not those in the automotive or critical minerals sectors.
Some Members of Congress raised concerns about the CMA's lack of binding or enforceable commitments, particularly related to labor and the environment. Some Members also criticized Treasury's designation of the CMA as an FTA for the purposes of the EV tax credit, describing this action as overriding congressional trade authorities.
During the second Trump Administration, the United States has imposed various tariffs on Japanese imports, with potential implications for U.S.-Japan cooperation on critical minerals supply chains. Under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 (19 U.S.C. §1862), President Trump imposed a 15% tariff on Japanese automotive products. Section 232 allows the President to impose trade restrictions if the Secretary of Commerce determines that imports of a good threaten U.S. national security. Under separate authorities, the United States has also imposed tariffs on most goods from nearly all trading partners. As of July 2026, there is a 12.5% tariff on most Japanese goods. At the same time, the U.S. and Japanese governments have signaled their intention to cooperate on critical minerals supply chains. As part of 2025 bilateral trade negotiations, the United States and Japan reached a framework agreement—among other things, the United States agreed to cap certain tariffs on Japan, and Japan pledged to invest $550 billion in the United States in key strategic sectors, including critical minerals.
Utilizing authorities under Section 232, President Trump directed the Secretary of Commerce and the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) to jointly negotiate agreements related to critical minerals; Trump did not implement any immediate trade restrictions related to critical minerals imports. In February 2026, USTR sought public comments on a potential plurilateral agreement on trade in critical minerals (ATCM) with "like-minded trading partners." The U.S. and Japanese governments signed a March 2026 action plan, which includes plans to develop a "plurilateral trade initiative in critical minerals supported by price floors or other measures." The two countries also signed an October 2025 framework for securing critical minerals and rare earth elements and a March 2026 memorandum of cooperation regarding deep-sea mineral resource development.
The United States and Japan have also collaborated with other partners in global forums related to critical minerals supply chains. The Biden Administration launched the Minerals Security Partnership in 2022 alongside global partners, including Japan, to collaborate on developing secure and sustainable critical minerals supply chains among like-minded partners through both public and private investments. In February 2026, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the creation of the Forum on Resource Geostrategic Engagement (FORGE) as the successor to the Minerals Security Partnership.
In December 2025, Japan was one of the first signatories to the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative, which focuses on global collaboration on artificial intelligence (AI) supply chains including software, network infrastructure, semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, critical minerals, and energy. Some Members have proposed legislation that would establish a program that may support initiatives including Pax Silica and express the sense of Congress that it is in the U.S. interest to "establish policies and procedures that streamline foreign government partners' ability to procure trusted and reliable technologies from the United States and United States allies and partners" (H.R. 10675, S. 4570).
Congressional trade authorities. Congress has approved all previous U.S. FTAs via legislation and typically set FTA procedures and requirements in Trade Promotion Authority (TPA), which expired in 2021. Some Members of Congress have asserted that the executive branch should engage in more substantive consultations with Congress and that Congress should authorize and approve sectoral agreements like those covering critical minerals (e.g., S. 429). Some analysts have argued that agreements approved by Congress and enacted into law are more durable than executive branch initiatives and could therefore provide greater certainty for critical minerals-related projects, which require large, sustained investments. Some Members of Congress have proposed legislation that would authorize the President to negotiate agreements related to critical minerals, establish negotiating objectives and congressional consultation requirements for such negotiations, and authorize the Secretary of State to lead U.S. participation in a "Minerals Security Partnership" (H.R. 7037). Another issue for Congress is the extent to which U.S. trade policy may promote or hinder U.S.-Japan cooperation on critical minerals and other related supply chains. Congress could consider whether to curb, bolster, or exercise oversight of the President's authority to negotiate an agreement with Japan, or impose, expand, or reduce U.S. tariffs on Japanese goods. For more information on congressional trade authorities, see CRS Report R47679, Congressional and Executive Authority Over Foreign Trade Agreements and CRS Report R48435, Congressional and Presidential Authority to Impose Import Tariffs.
Critical minerals supply chains. Members of Congress may evaluate whether current U.S. policies align with Members' expressed priorities related to critical minerals supply chains, which have included, for example, bolstering U.S. production, reducing reliance on PRC imports, and/or encouraging cooperation with trading partners. Some Members, for example, have proposed measures that would involve allies, including Japan, in efforts to reduce U.S. reliance on PRC critical minerals supply chains (e.g., S. 823, H.R. 3198). Additionally, Members may consider whether the FY2022 reconciliation law's EV tax credit requirements, such as sourcing requirements or prohibiting content from FEOCs, may be an appropriate model to be considered in any future federal incentives or U.S. trade negotiations, such as the potential ATCM or the ongoing review of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). Congress may also consider potential effects of the rescission of the P.L. 117-169 EV tax credits.
title: U.S.-Japan Critical Minerals Agreement

David X. Sullivan, United States Attorney for the District of Connecticut, and Jarod Forget, Special Agent in Charge of the Drug Enforcement Administration for New England, announced that CONROD DAVY, 41, a citizen of Jamaica last residing in Bridgeport, pleaded guilty today before U.S. District Judge Sarala V. Nagala in Hartford to fentanyl trafficking and false statement offenses.

According to court documents and statements made in court, a Drug Enforcement Administration Hartford Task Force investigation revealed that Davy was trafficking large quantities of fentanyl and was involved in the processing and packing of fentanyl. On April 24, 2026, investigators conducted a controlled purchase of approximately two kilograms of fentanyl from Davy.

Davy was arrested on April 30, 2026. After his arrest, Davy told investigators that he was a U.S. citizen named “Timothy Stater” and he provided a false date of birth. The investigation revealed that Davy was a Jamaican citizen and he had been removed from the U.S. in November 2019 as a result of a criminal conviction in Florida.

Davy pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to distribute and to possess with intent to distribute 400 grams or more of fentanyl, an offense that carries a mandatory minimum term of imprisonment of 10 years and a maximum term of imprisonment of life, and one count of making false statements and representations, an offense that carries a maximum term of imprisonment of five years.

Davy has been detained since his arrest.

This investigation is being conducted by the Drug Enforcement Administration’s Hartford Task Force, which includes personnel from the DEA Hartford Resident Office, the Connecticut State Police, and the Bristol, Hartford, East Hartford, Enfield, Manchester, New Britain, Rocky Hill, Wethersfield, and Windsor Locks Police Departments. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Geoffrey M. Stone.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America, a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.
title: Illegal Alien Pleads Guilty to Fentanyl Trafficking, False Statement Offenses

Pallone Celebrates Democrats Winning House Majority
Washington, D.C. – Energy and Commerce Committee Ranking Member Frank Pallone, Jr. (D-NJ) released the following statement on Democrats winning the House majority last night:
“Last night, the American people overwhelmingly rejected the failed policies of President Trump and Congressional Republicans that prioritized billionaires and corporate interests over everyday people. This victory is both a historic win and opportunity, which is why Democrats must be prepared to act quickly and decisively to deliver for the American people. In the days ahead, I will be asking my Democratic colleagues for their support to serve as Chairman of the Energy and Commerce Committee to help lead a bold agenda that prioritizes all those struggling to survive on Republicans’ watch.
“Democrats must relentlessly pursue an agenda that puts working people first and focuses on resolving the outrageous price increases that are making it impossible for families to make ends meet. Over the last two years, Republicans have driven up the cost of virtually everything and imposed the largest health care cuts in history – stripping health care from millions, forcing people to pay more for less, and shuttering hospitals. We will advance policies that lower costs, expand access to quality and affordable health care, protect consumers and the environment, prioritize clean energy, and rein in Big Tech.
“We must also rein in the most corrupt Administration in our nation’s history with an aggressive oversight agenda that holds them accountable for repeatedly breaking the law, violating our Constitution, and enriching Trump, his family and his friends at taxpayers’ expense. The days of Trump getting a free pass are over as Democrats will investigate the widespread and blatant corruption that’s ripping off the American people.
“There’s an abundance of great ideas across the Democratic Caucus, and I look forward to continuing to work with all my colleagues to advance a serious, robust agenda that will make a real difference in people’s lives.”

FORT LEE, Va. – Deputy Commanding Generals for Support as well as Sustainment Brigade Commanders from the active Army, Army National Guard and Army Reserve came to Fort Lee Oct. 27-28 to attend the U.S. Combined Arms Support Command-hosted DCG-S Course where they were updated on the sustainment warfighting functions.
CASCOM DCG-S Course empowers Division level leaders with the latest sustainment updates across the Doctrine, Organization, Training, Materiel, Leadership Development, Personnel, Facilities and Policy spectrum to strengthen relationships within the sustainment community and provide reach back capabilities that will help generate and build readiness across our sustainment formations.
“It's all about you; it's a chance for the DCG-S and the Sustainment Brigade Commander to come together and work together, strategize,” said CASCOM Commanding General, Maj. Gen. Sean Davis. “It’s an opportunity to familiarize how you want to get after instilling command discipline in your divisions, but also getting your divisions ready for combat and/or getting ready to pass on to someone so that they can continue to get on that road to war.
“DCG-S is a remarkable position because you have your sustainment brigade commander as your partner; you have an AFSB (Army Field Support Brigade) commander as your link to the enterprise; you have a Division G1, G4 and G8 who's got fire in his or her belly coming right out of battalion command and getting after it,” said Davis. “This (course) is all about how you can use those teams to your advantage to make your division the best it can be.”
The role of the DCG-S is to synchronize sustainment and protection warfighting functions to support the Division and control the rear area of operations.
“I recommend at your installations, you wrap your arms around your AMC enablers that bring to bear the power of the (sustainment) enterprise and work through your sustainment commanders and your senior staff at echelon,” said Army Materiel Command Commanding General, Lt. Gen. Gavin Lawrence. “Who are the AMC enablers that you should be wrapping your arms around?
“In terms of installation support, the garrison command team that act essentially as the mayors of your installations,” said Lawrence. “Each installation has either an AFSB headquarters or an AFSBn (Army Field Support Battalion) that act as the faces of the field in terms of integration of AMC equities; they absolutely should be a part of your Team Sustainment and involved in your sustainment-related algorithm of defense.
Lawrence also mentioned the importance of the Army contracting brigades and battalions delivering operational contracting support.
The first day of the course focused on the larger sustainment warfighting system as well as Lessons Learned panel from former DCG-S officers and a senior warrant officer panel. Day two contained overview briefs from Finance, Adjutant General, Transportation, Ordnance and Quartermaster commandants.
“With power comes responsibility, and you have to understand that command supply and maintenance discipline are not administrative functions; they are combat requirements,” said Davis. “You must maintain discipline, you must maintain proper accountability; it is not something we do because we're good government stewards, we need our equipment to be ready for combat.
“Each of the commandants will take you, as I said at the beginning, and they'll take you to their areas to show you again how to inspect an SSA (Supply Support Activity), how to inspect a motor pool, and how to run a command discipline program,” said the general.
Many of the attendees were not logisticians by trade but are now in a position where they oversee sustainment sections and units.
“The DCG-S course was phenomenal; this gave us an opportunity both to network with our peers and then also understand all of the different systems, offices, and capabilities within the sustainment warfighting function available to us,” said Col. Patrick Schuck, DCG-S, 2nd Infantry Division, Camp Humphreys, Republic of Korea. “I would absolutely recommend taking this course as soon as you could, or as soon as you are in position, because it has been a phenomenal experience.”
CASCOM hosts the DCG-S course one to two times a year.
title: CASCOM hosts DCG-S Course

PHILADELPHIA – United States Attorney David Metcalf announced that Seth S. Jones, 46, of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, was sentenced to 14 months in prison and three years of supervised release by United States District Judge Gerald J. Pappert for defrauding two Philadelphia-area non-profit companies out of $322,798. Judge Pappert also ordered Jones to pay $322,798 in restitution.

The defendant was charged by information in June and pleaded guilty in July to two counts of wire fraud.

As detailed in court filings and statements, Jones worked in the finance department of Non-Profit Company #1, which was a parent company to Non-Profit Company #2. From May 2021 to June 2025, the defendant defrauded the non-profit companies by using a company credit card to pay for approximately $291,023 in personal expenses, including travel, gambling debts, Amazon purchases, rent, utilities, and car payments, and diverting approximately $31,775 in funds from a bank account associated with Non-Profit Company #2 to bank accounts controlled by him. In order to carry out and conceal the fraud scheme, Jones falsified expense reports, failed to submit expense reports, and created fake invoices.

This case was investigated by the FBI and prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorneys Francis A. Weber and John G. Iannacone.
title: Philadelphia Man Who Defrauded Two Area Non-Profits Out of More Than $320,000 Sentenced to 14 Months in Prison

The second Trump Administration has proposed to develop a "next-generation missile defense shield" against nuclear and conventional attacks that it has called a "Golden Dome for America." Since the 1950s, Members of Congress have periodically debated the costs, feasibility, scope, and sufficiency of strategic defense systems that could limit damage to the U.S. homeland from a nuclear attack. In these debates, some Members have stated that some of these systems could adversely affect U.S. security by destabilizing nuclear deterrence relationships with adversaries and/or by contributing to a competition in nuclear-armed missiles. This Insight focuses on certain strategic stability issues that Congress may consider when providing oversight of or funding for Golden Dome. See the text box for a definition of strategic stability.
One of the major roles of U.S. strategic nuclear forces has been and remains the deterrence of a nuclear attack on the U.S. homeland through a threat of nuclear retaliation (a second strike). After the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, the United States and the Soviet Union gradually sought to improve strategic stability in their mutual deterrence relationship. The Johnson and Nixon Administrations concluded that deploying missile defenses (anti-ballistic missile, or ABM, systems) against a large-scale Soviet nuclear attack was infeasible and that U.S. interests would be better served by negotiating with the Soviet Union to reduce Soviet incentives for a nuclear first strike or an offensive nuclear missile buildup to overcome U.S. ABM systems. In 1972, after hearings, the Senate voted 88-2 to provide advice and consent to ratification of the ABM Treaty that restricted the development and deployment of ABM systems and approved an Interim Agreement that imposed numerical limits on strategic nuclear ballistic missiles.
As part of his 1983 Strategic Defense Initiative, President Ronald Reagan articulated a shift in U.S. strategy from threatening nuclear retaliation toward a defensive approach reliant on intercepting Soviet strategic ballistic missiles with space-based ABM systems. In negotiations that eventually led to the 1991 Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (START I), Soviet leaders sought to keep the United States in the ABM Treaty and limit U.S. space-based ABM systems.
After the end of the Cold War, Congress passed several Missile Defense Acts setting policy and providing funding for missile defenses to protect the U.S. homeland from threats posed by the regional proliferation of missile technologies. Russian concerns about these efforts complicated bilateral nuclear arms control during the 1990s. However, the United States and Russia concluded the 2002 Moscow Treaty that further reduced strategic nuclear forces despite the concomitant U.S. withdrawal from the ABM Treaty. During the Clinton, George W. Bush, and Obama Administrations, the two countries also attempted to cooperate bilaterally and within the NATO-Russia framework on elements of a collaborative missile defense system.
Russian officials express concern that U.S. missile defenses are not limited programs aimed at countering regional threats like North Korea or Iran but are instead an open-ended effort aimed at undermining Russia's ability to engage in nuclear retaliation. Russian negotiators unsuccessfully sought "legally binding guarantees" that U.S. missile defenses would not be aimed against Russian strategic nuclear forces. The 2010 New START Treaty's preamble included language, secured by Russian negotiators, regarding an "interrelationship" between strategic offenses and defenses. The Senate's resolution of advice and consent to New START ratification stated that the treaty did not restrict U.S. missile defenses.
The Russian military has some missile defense systems and capabilities to protect its nuclear deterrent, as well as to counter U.S. missile defenses beyond traditional countermeasures. In 2018, Russian President Vladimir Putin announced that Russia had novel nuclear weapons to counter U.S. missile defenses. During the Biden Administration, Russian officials focused on missile defense as one of the factors, in addition to nuclear weapons and conventional precision strike, affecting strategic stability.
U.S. missile defense policy has become an area of coordination for Russia and the People's Republic of China (PRC), whose growing nuclear arsenal now poses "a direct threat to the [U.S.] Homeland," according to U.S. intelligence estimates. In a May 2025 statement, Russia and the PRC stated that, through Golden Dome, the United States sought to undermine their ability to engage in nuclear retaliation.
As Congress assesses the Trump Administration's homeland missile defense plans and their strategic stability implications, it may consider the following issues:
title: Golden Dome: Potential Strategic Stability Considerations for Congress

ST. LOUIS – U.S. District Judge Zachary M. Bluestone on Wednesday sentenced a convicted felon who was repeatedly caught with firearms to 87 months in prison.

Darrion Boyd-Barnes, 29, was caught with guns on three occasions after traffic stops. On Sept. 22, 2022, he was stopped by St. Louis police in a vehicle with an expired temporary tag. After officers discovered that he had given them a false name and had an active arrest warrant, they arrested him and found a loaded Glock 29 10mm pistol.

On April 16, 2025, Boyd-Barnes was a passenger in a vehicle pulled over for having an improper license plate. He had an active arrest warrant and officers found a loaded Palmetto State Armory Dagger 9mm handgun.

On Nov. 12, 2025, St. Louis police pulled Boyd-Barnes over in a Jeep after he ran three stop signs. When officers asked him to get out of the Jeep, he sped off to his girlfriend’s house in St. Louis County, triggering a standoff involving multiple police agencies. Boyd-Barnes refused multiple times to leave the house and then escaped. Police found 29 firearms in the home, including AR-style pistols and rifles, a shotgun, multiple stolen pistols and five pistols that had been illegally converted into fully automatic weapons with a machinegun conversion device (MCD).

In court Wednesday, Assistant U.S. Attorney Paul D’Agrosa said that since the age of 18, Boyd-Barnes has been undeterred in his repeated unlawful possession of firearms and fleeing from police.

Boyd-Barnes pleaded guilty in August in U.S. District Court in St. Louis to three counts of being a felon in possession of a firearm.

The St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Paul D’Agrosa prosecuted the case.

This case is part of Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN), the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities.
title: St. Louis Felon Sentenced to 87 Months in Prison After Being Caught with Firearms Repeatedly

PLANO, Texas – An illegal alien from Honduras has been sentenced to federal prison as part of a Homeland Security Task Force investigation into fentanyl trafficking in the Eastern District of Texas, announced U.S. Attorney Jay R. Combs.

Argenis Alfredo Brizo-Mendoza, 31, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute fentanyl and was sentenced to 134 months in federal prison by U.S. District Judge Sean D. Jordan on October 30, 2026.

According to information presented in court, Brizo-Mendoza, a citizen of Honduras, was a drug courier for a drug trafficking organization that supplied various narcotics, mostly fentanyl and methamphetamine from Mexico. Brizo-Mendoza was responsible for storing and distributing large amounts of narcotics in the Austin area for the drug trafficking organization.

This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Dallas comprises agents and officers from the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Dallas Field Office; U.S. Department of Homeland Security, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Homeland Security Investigations - Dallas (ICE-HSI); Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Dallas Field Division; Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) Dallas Field Division; Internal Revenue Service, Criminal Investigations (IRS-CD; United States Postal Service, United States Postal Inspection Service (USPIS); and U.S. Marshals Service (USMS) Eastern District of Texas with the prosecution being led by Eastern District of Texas Assistant U.S. Attorney William R. Tatum.

###
title: Illegal alien receives lengthy federal prison sentence as part of Homeland Security Task Force investigation into fentanyl trafficking in the Eastern District of Texas

Vitter, after previously pleading guilty to reentry of a removed alien, in violation of Title 8, United States Code, Section 1326(a), announced United States Attorney David I. Courcelle.
