ASHEVILLE, N.C. – Shawnenna Caroline Roland, 41, of Cherokee, an enrolled member of the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians, appeared in federal court today and pleaded guilty to child abuse, child neglect, and assault in Indian Country, announced Russ Ferguson, U.S. Attorney for the Western District of North Carolina.

“There is no excuse for treating a helpless child this way,” said U.S. Attorney Russ Ferguson. “Roland relentlessly assaulted and abused a child entrusted in her care, causing the child serious and lasting harm. This is disgusting behavior that will land you in federal prison.”

According to plea documents, between May 6 and May 20, 2024, Roland repeatedly assaulted a child resulting in serious bodily injury, including permanent and protracted loss and impairment of the child’s mental and emotional function. Plea documents show that Roland assaulted the victim on multiple occasions, hitting the victim with “switches,” banging her fist on the victim’s fingers, and striking her multiple times. According to court documents, on May 20, 2024, Roland banged the victim’s head into a wooden couch frame. Roland did not seek immediate medical attention for the victim. First responders came to Roland’s residence where they found the victim unresponsive, after another minor in the home called 911. The victim was flown by helicopter to the hospital and received treatment for traumatic brain injury. Court documents show that a bone scan performed at the hospital revealed several healing fractures throughout the victim’s body, including on the victim’s right arm, pelvis, and both hands. The victim’s nose was also broken, and the victim had sustained multiple bruises and abrasions, in addition to having torn ligaments in the neck and a fractured sacrum.

Roland remains in federal custody. At sentencing, she faces a sentence of up to 395 months in prison. A sentencing date has not been set.

U.S. Attorney Ferguson thanked the FBI and the Cherokee Indian Police Department for their investigation of the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Alex M. Scott of the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Asheville is prosecuting the case.
title: Cherokee Woman Pleads Guilty to Inflicting Serious Bodily Injury on a Child in Indian Country

Tallahassee, Florida –Christy Cody Holgate, 49, and Kim Demetrius Benson, 53, both of Tallahassee, Florida, have been sentenced in federal court after pleading guilty to conspiracy to commit mail theft, and multiple counts of mail theft. Holgate was sentenced to over three and a half years in federal prison. Benson was sentenced to two years’ imprisonment. The sentences were announced by John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida.

U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “These defendants sought to enrich themselves by stealing the mail, but now they’ll see the inside of a federal prison cell. My office is committed to aggressively prosecuting anyone who tampers with, steals, or diverts the U.S. Mail to ensure our citizens can continue to rely upon the U.S. Postal Service to quickly, safely, and securely deliver the mail.”

Court documents reflect that between August 5, 2025, and December 5, 2025, the defendants broke into multiple apartment complex mailboxes through use of United States Postal Service (USPS) mail key that permitted access to the mail of complex residents. Through investigation, the U.S. Postal Inspection Service and Tallahassee Police Department documented multiple thefts of hundreds of pieces of mail. They also obtained video surveillance which captured the break-ins. Upon their arrest in December 2025, the two were found in a vehicle containing bags of stolen mail items along with stolen debit and credit cards, as well as a USPS mail key. Together, the defendants conspired to steal U.S. Mail, which, according to a confession by Holgate, was then sold to another individual for money to purchase illegal drugs.

This case was jointly investigated by the Tallahassee Police Department and the United States Postal Inspection Service. The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Eric K. Mountin.

The United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Florida is one of 94 offices that serve as the nation’s principal litigators under the direction of the Attorney General. To access public court documents online, please visit the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida website. For more information about the United States Attorney’s Office, Northern District of Florida, visit https://www.justice.gov/usao-ndfl .
title: Tallahassee Accomplices Sentenced for Mail Theft Conspiracy

CMS Finalizes CY 2027 Physician Fee Schedule to Shift from Sick Care to Healthcare and Curb Waste
WASHINGTON, D.C.—NOVEMBER 4, 2026—The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) is prioritizing prevention, strengthening primary care, cracking down on duplicate billing, and reinforcing fiscal stewardship across Medicare. A new final rule advancing payment policies under Medicare Part B modernizes physician payment structures to reward health maintenance and coordinated primary care rather than disjointed, volume-based intervention. Through targeted enhancements to the Medicare Shared Savings Program (Shared Savings Program) and fee schedule recalibrations, CMS is shifting the health system’s focus from reactive sick care to proactive healthcare.
“Medicare should reward clinicians for keeping people healthy,” said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “Under President Trump’s leadership, we are putting prevention and primary care at the center of Medicare, closing payment loopholes, and cracking down on waste. This rule directs resources toward coordinated care that puts patients first. We are changing what Medicare pays for to change what our health system delivers.”
“For too long, fee-for-service payment has rewarded volume over value, fueling a reactive system of sick care,” said CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz. “This final rule breaks from that status quo. By ending duplicate billing and closing costly loopholes, we are protecting taxpayers and directing Medicare dollars to clinicians doing the hard work of keeping patients healthy.”
Modernizing Quality Reporting and Statutory Mandates
Marking a decade of progress under the Quality Payment Program, CMS will officially sunset the traditional Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) reporting option beginning with the CY 2031 performance period. Clinicians will have through CY 2030 to transition to the MIPS Value Pathways (MVPs), which already cover approximately 98%of clinicians, or Advanced Alternative Payment Models. This reflects two additional years of transition time compared to the proposed rule. The rule also finalizes three new MVPs focused on diabetes, hypertension, and hospitalists, and requires clinicians to report at least one specialty-specific “Core Measure” starting in CY 2027.
Additionally, the Calendar Year (CY) 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule (PFS) rule finalizes two new billing codes dedicated to Advance Care Planning and codifies noncitizen Medicare eligibility criteria established by the Working Families Tax Cuts legislation.
Expanding and Strengthening Accountable Care Organizations
Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) are vital to improving primary care and helping beneficiaries live healthier lives. Data shows that patients aligned with an ACO are less likely to experience uncontrolled diabetes or hypertension and are more likely to receive recommended preventive care. In performance year 2024, 75% of the 476 participating ACOs earned shared savings totaling $4.1 billion, while generating net savings for the Medicare Trust Funds of approximately $2.5 billion compared to projected spending benchmarks.
The Shared Savings Program has generated savings for the Medicare Trust Funds for eight consecutive performance years, and to build on this progress, the final rule:
- Permits ACOs to Eliminate Patient Cost-Sharing: Starting April 1, 2027, approved ACOs may reduce or eliminate Part B cost-sharing for many items and services for assigned beneficiaries, directly lowering out-of-pocket costs for essential care.
- Incentivizes Growth: CMS increases shared savings rates for eligible ACOs, provides new incentives for first-time participants, and sets more predictable spending targets.
- Cuts Red Tape: The rule simplifies electronic health record reporting requirements, streamlines patient notice mandates, and removes outdated administrative hurdles.
Restoring Payment Integrity and Curbing Waste
CMS is recalibrating fee schedule valuations to reflect the true complexity and resources of modern care and closing loopholes that allow users to game the system:
- Ending Duplicate Billing: When an office visit and minor procedure occur on the same day, CMS will reduce payment by 20% for the lower-cost service, reducing duplication in payment by patients and the Medicare program for clinical work already covered in the procedure’s valuation.
- Closing Windfall Loopholes: The rule corrects an incentive payment loophole, preventing an estimated $2.38 billion in unintended windfall payments over the next decade.
- Improving Rate Accuracy: CMS is streamlining outdated steps from its rate-setting formula, leading to greater simplicity and transparency for clinicians and patients while allowing payment policy to adapt to changes in healthcare delivery.
CMS Expands Access to Preventive Care and Wellness in Support of MAHA Initiative
CMS is finalizing critical coding and payment expansions to strengthen preventive care and wellness across the nation. CMS is establishing national payment pathways for health and well-being coaching under general supervision, introducing dedicated billing for shared medical appointments with flexible time-based add-on codes, and boosting valuations for smoking cessation and behavioral health assessments.
Additionally, the agency is finalizing separate billing for the dedicated clinical time required to diagnose, treat, and counsel patients experiencing vaccine adverse effects, reinforcing our commitment to patient trust and robust clinical support. These pivotal updates ensure Medicare resources directly support proactive, patient-centered care and improve health outcomes for Americans.
Ambulatory Specialty Model
CMS is also finalizing refinements to the Ambulatory Specialty Model — a CMS Innovation Center model launching Jan. 1 that holds specialists accountable for the quality and cost of care associated with the longitudinal management of two common chronic conditions, heart failure and low back pain, to slow disease progression and reduce avoidable hospitalizations and low-value procedures.
For more information on the CY 2027 Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule, which is effective Jan. 1, 2027, visit the Fact Sheet for Calendar Year (CY) 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule.
For a fact sheet on the updates on the Shared Savings Program, visit: https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/calendar-year-cy-2027-medicare-physician-fee-schedule-final-rule-cms-1848-f-medicare-shared-savings.
To view the final rule on Federal Register, visit: https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2026-22743.

Washington D.C. — Today, Congressman Herb Conaway Jr., MD released the following statement on last night’s election results:
“I am absolutely honored, humbled, and deeply appreciative of the confidence and support of the people of New Jersey’s 3rd Congressional District. They have entrusted me with an incredible privilege and an enormous responsibility, one that I am proud to have worked so hard to earn: the opportunity to continue serving our home in Central and South Jersey and fighting for our shared values in Washington, D.C.
“Last night, the American people spoke, and their message was clear: enough is enough.
“The results of this election have made clear that the American people expect their elected representatives to deliver. We have a responsibility to meet that expectation: a responsibility to lower costs for working families, ensure that everyone has access to quality, affordable health care, and hold this Administration accountable for its actions.
“I will work every single day in the next Congress to make sure the will of the people is heard and their priorities are met. I will never forget the responsibility that my constituents have placed in my hands. The work ahead will not be easy, and there will undoubtedly be challenges along the way. But we will not back down, we will not give up, and we will never stop fighting for the people we represent.
“Last night was a victory, but tomorrow the work begins. And I am ready to get to work.”

OKLAHOMA CITY – Scott Maule, Civil Division Chief for the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Oklahoma, has been nationally recognized for excellence in leadership and management by the Executive Office for the United States Attorneys (EOUSA), announced U.S. Attorney Robert J. Troester.

Maule was formally recognized during the 2026 Director’s Awards ceremony on October 28, 2026, held at the Department of Justice in Washington D.C., where he received the Director’s Award for Excellence in a Managerial or Supervisory Role, an honor recognizing outstanding leadership, management, and service within the Department of Justice. Maule was one of just seven managers selected from U.S. Attorney’s Offices across the country to receive the award.

Civil Division Chief Scott Maule receives the Director’s Award for Excellence in a Managerial or Supervisory Role. Pictured from left to right are Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, Scott Maule, EOUSA Director Francey Hakes, and U.S. Attorney Robert J. Troester.

“Scott is an exceptional leader whose dedication, professionalism, intellect, and commitment to public service make our office stronger every day,” said U.S. Attorney Robert J. Troester. “His ability to lead by example and navigate complex legal matters reflects the best of the Department of Justice. The people of the Western District of Oklahoma are well served by Civil Chief Scott Maule.”

Maule is a 19-year veteran of the U.S. Attorney’s Office and has served as Chief of the Civil Division since 2019. He has also served as the healthcare fraud coordinator, civil rights coordinator, and the discovery coordinator for the Civil Division. From 2021-2026, Maule was selected to serve on a national Civil Chief’s Working Group where he was at the forefront of addressing the most difficult legal and policy issues facing the Department of Justice. From 2021-2026, he also served as a member of a national eLitigation Working Group helping lead the Department’s efforts to prepare for and address the ever-emerging technical, policy, and practice issues involving eLitigation. Over his 19-year career, Maule has represented the United States and its agencies, officials, employees, and agents in a wide range of both affirmative and defensive cases at the trial and appellate level in federal and state courts. Maule received his Bachelor of Arts degree from the University of the South (Sewanee) in 1999, and his J.D. from the William & Mary Law School in 2002.

The award was presented by the Director of EOUSA. EOUSA provides oversight, general executive assistance, and direction to the 94 United States Attorneys’ offices around the country. For more information on EOUSA and its mission, visit http://www.justice.gov/usao .
title: Western District of Oklahoma Civil Division Chief Honored with Prestigious Department of Justice Award

Seattle – A 40-year-old Pierce County, Washington man was sentenced late yesterday in U.S. District Court in Seattle to 15 years in prison for attempted enticement of a minor and production of images of child sexual abuse, announced Acting U.S. Attorney Charles Neil Floyd. Randy Lee Young came into federal custody April 24, 2025. He was arrested November 16, 2024, after allegedly communicating with someone he thought would provide her young daughters to him for sexual assaults. When Young arrived at the proposed meeting place in Marysville, Washington, he was arrested. Forensic review of his cell phone found images of child sexual abuse that he had produced.

At the sentencing hearing U.S. District Judge Lauren King praised the victim’s “truthfulness and assistance with law enforcement” and conveyed “hope todays sentencing brings you a sense of some closure” as “the only blame here lies with Mr. Young and Mr. Young alone.”

“The community is safer with this defendant off the street,” said Acting U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd. “Mr. Young made his intentions clear while communicating with the undercover officer. Then when he was arrested law enforcement discovered a 13-year-0ld had already been victimized. This lengthy sentence is the appropriate result.”

“Not only did Mr. Young demonstrate he was willing to travel across Washington state to exploit children, but his phone also contained videos of him actually abusing a child on multiple occasions,” said W. Mike Herrington, Special Agent in Charge of the FBI Seattle field office. “We hope this sentence will protect the youth of the Pacific Northwest from Mr. Young for a long time and sends a strong message to other would-be predators that they cannot hide behind supposed anonymity online. The FBI and our partners will pursue these offenders and hold them to account for the lifelong harm they have inflicted on our children.”

According to records filed in the case, Young began communicating with a law enforcement officer who was posing as the mother of 8 and 11-year-old daughters. Between November 8 and 15 2024, Young communicated with the law enforcement officer via text messaging multiple times. Ultimately Young drove from his residence in Pierce County to the location in Marysville where he was arrested. Young was held in the Snohomish County Jail until the federal charges were filed.

Young gave permission for law enforcement to review his cell phone. On the phone investigators found images of sexual abuse of a minor. The investigation revealed that in October and November 2024, Young met a minor online, traveled to her hometown in southwest Washington seven times and videotaped sex acts with the 13-year-old. Text messages reveal that the victim had told Young her age.

In her victim statement, the mother of the 13-year-old said, “He stole more than her innocence. He stole her sense of safety, her ability to trust, and parts of a childhood that she cannot get back…. As her mother, one of the hardest parts has been knowing that I cannot go back, that I cannot undo what happened, and that I cannot give her back the innocence and sense of security that were taken from her.”

In asking for the 15-year sentence, prosecutors wrote to the court, “The defendant chatted with the undercover officer about his intentions for eight days before showing up to act on his desires. He was provided opportunities to disengage and instead doubled down by informing the undercover he wanted to follow through with his ‘fetish’…. (T)here are simply too many individuals wired to abuse children to ever eliminate child exploitation, it is vitally important that these would-be offenders understand the steep cost of acting on their deviant desires. The law must send a clear and unmistakable message of specific and general deterrence – that society simply will not and cannot tolerate such perverted abuse – and those that engage in it, will be met with lengthy custodial sentences.”

Juge King ordered Young to be on supervised release for 20 years following his prison term. A separate hearing in February 2027 will determine the amount of restitution owed to Young’s victim.

The case is being investigated by the FBI Seattle’s Child Exploitation and Human Trafficking Task Force, with assistance from the Renton Police Department.

The case is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Cecelia Gregson.

The Justice Department is committed to combating child sexual exploitation. These cases were brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and CEOS, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, visit www.justice.gov/psc .
title: Pierce County man sentenced to 15 years in prison for sex crimes involving minors

Calendar Year (CY) 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule (CMS-1848-F) — Medicare Shared Savings Program
On November 4, 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) issued the calendar year (CY) 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule (PFS) final rule (CMS-1848-F), which includes changes to the Medicare Shared Savings Program (Shared Savings Program). These policies aim to accelerate accountable care service delivery, further CMS’ goal of aligning spending and value in Original Medicare, and support achieving other related strategic objectives. This fact sheet summarizes the major changes to the Shared Savings Program included in the CY 2027 PFS final rule.
We are finalizing changes to the Shared Savings Program’s benchmarking and financial methodology to strengthen financial incentives for ACOs to participate in the program while mitigating selection issues and benchmark rebasing concerns. The changes are projected to grow the program by adding up to 1 million assigned beneficiaries in an average year during the 10-year projection period, increase net federal savings by $5.5 billion over 10 years (range of uncertainty +/- $3.3 billion), and generate an overall increase in shared savings net of losses to ACOs by $1.1 billion over 10 years (+/- $3.6 billion).
Modifications to the Shared Savings Program Financial Methodology
Strengthen Financial Incentives to Participate and Encourage Additional Savings in Two-Sided Risk
We are finalizing the following changes to the Shared Savings Program’s financial methodology which, in combination, would balance incentives between Level E of the BASIC track and the ENHANCED track, mitigate selection issues and benchmark rebasing concerns, and encourage participation by ACOs with higher risk and higher cost populations.
Given the timing of CY 2027 PFS rulemaking and the Shared Savings Program application cycle for the Jan. 1, 2027 start date (occurring in CY 2026), we are providing additional flexibility to ACO applicants in making their final selection of track/level of participation. Accordingly, following the issuance of the CY 2027 PFS final rule, ACOs applying for an agreement period start date of Jan.1, 2027, will be able to change their final selection during Phase 2 RFI (Nov. 6-12, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. (noon) ET).
(1) Increase the shared savings rate (“sharing rate”) for Level E of the BASIC track from 50% to 60%. The Shared Savings Program is structured into risk tracks that financially reward ACOs that transform their care delivery practices by taking on higher levels of financial risk and reward on behalf of taxpayers. Currently, evidence suggests that ACOs in BASIC track Level E generate higher savings to the Trust Funds than ACOs in the ENHANCED track, and there are fewer ACOs participating in Level E of the BASIC track than the ENHANCED track. Increasing the sharing rate for BASIC track Level E could more properly balance this participation option relative to the ENHANCED track (with a 75% sharing rate). By reducing the savings percentage gap between BASIC track Level E and the ENHANCED track, we may increase the participation and long-term success of ACOs, particularly those with less experience with the Shared Savings Program, with unique patient and/or provider populations, and low revenue ACOs (which tend to be small, rural, and physician-only ACOs).
(2) Reduce the maximum weight used in calculating the positive regional adjustment for lower-spending ACOs participating under the ENHANCED track from 50% to 35%. Our analysis indicates that ENHANCED track ACOs on average, achieve higher gross savings than BASIC track Level E ACOs and have substantially larger positive regional adjustments. Moreover, the average size of the positive regional adjustment has gone up while the share of ACOs receiving such an adjustment has remained stable over the same period. This pattern suggests that, while the prevalence of regional adjustments has remained broadly unchanged, the financial impact of those adjustments has increased over time, amplifying the influence of regional cost variation adjustments on ACO benchmark calculations.
In the current structure, ENHANCED track ACOs with lower spending than their region are receiving both a higher shared savings rate and larger positive regional adjustment on average. Together, these advantages may incentivize selection into the ENHANCED track independent of an ACO’s capacity to achieve genuine cost savings to Medicare. The reduction in the positive regional adjustment weight for these ACOs, paired with an increase in the shared savings rate for BASIC track Level E, is designed to rebalance financial incentives across tracks and encourage ACOs to select their tracks based on their actual capacity to reduce costs rather than differences in financial advantages embedded in track design, thereby potentially improving Trust Funds net savings.
(3) Increase the prior savings adjustment’s scaling factor from 50% to 75%. Increased prior savings adjustment amounts could provide additional relief from the rebasing “ratchet effect,” in which the savings an ACO achieves in one agreement period can reduce its rebased benchmark for the subsequent period by lowering the historical spending that forms the basis for that benchmark. This change could incentivize ACOs to generate more savings in their initial agreement period and encourage long-term participation in the Shared Savings Program.
(4) Risk adjust the 5% cap on upward adjustments to the historical benchmark. ACOs with higher risk populations have expressed concern that the current 5% cap that applies to the three upward adjustments to the historical benchmark (regional adjustment, prior savings adjustment, and population adjustment) is too restrictive. Under the approach we are finalizing, we will account for the severity and case mix of the ACO’s assigned population in calculating the 5% cap, which is based on national per capita FFS expenditures for the assignable beneficiary population. This approach will result in potentially higher upward adjustments to the benchmark for ACOs whose assigned beneficiary populations have higher risk, and potentially higher costs, and thereby encourage such ACOs to enter and remain in the Shared Savings Program.
Growth Adjustment to the Historical Benchmark to Incentivize New Participation
We are finalizing a growth adjustment to the historical benchmark to reward ACOs for recruiting ACO professionals who are inexperienced with value-based care arrangements and serving beneficiaries new to value-based care. This growth adjustment will be applied on top of the highest existing benchmark adjustments for which an ACO is eligible, either a positive regional adjustment, prior savings adjustment, or population adjustment, and will not exceed the finalized risk adjusted 5% cap. Additionally, the growth incentive will be included in a subsequent agreement period’s prior savings adjustment (if applicable), if the ACO continued to maintain or increase the growth it achieved in the previous agreement period.
Reform ACPT Component of the Benchmark Update Factor
The Accountable Care Prospective Trend (ACPT) is part of a three-way blended benchmark update factor that projects an administrative growth target to partially insulate ACOs from a downward “ratchet effect” in benchmarks from both individual and collective success in lowering programmatic costs. However, the ACPT depends on cost growth projections that could be subject to potential projection errors. For agreement periods beginning on Jan. 1, 2027, and in subsequent years, we are finalizing an ACPT guardrail policy that limits the effect of under-projection or over-projection as compared to observed growth in expenditures for the national assignable FFS population such that the ACPT is no more than 1 percentage point below (or no more than 1.5 percentage points above) national growth. For ACOs within existing agreement periods with 2024, 2025, and 2026 start dates, we are retroactively applying the lower guardrail, which will limit the ACPT to no more than 1 percentage point below the national growth rate in determining financial reconciliation for PY 2025 and any subsequent performance year of the ACO’s agreement period. We are delaying PY 2025 financial reconciliation until November 2026, after the final rule is issued, so that we can implement this policy for PY 2025 reconciliation.
We also are finalizing the policy to calculate annualized growth rates used in determining the ACPT for each performance year for all ACOs in agreement periods beginning on or after Jan. 1, 2027, rather than calculating the annualized growth rates on an agreement period basis (under the existing policy). This approach will improve consistency in the calculations across agreement periods.
Changes to the Shared Savings Program Beneficiary Assignment Methodology
We are finalizing several changes to the Shared Savings Program’s beneficiary assignment methodology, applicable for the performance year starting on Jan. 1, 2028, and subsequent performance years, with the goal of increasing the number of Medicare beneficiaries involved in accountable care relationships.
First, we are excluding from assignment calculations allowed charges for primary care services billed through a non-ACO Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) by an ACO professional used in assignment. We would apply this approach in determining whether a beneficiary received the plurality of primary care services under the stepwise claims-based assignment methodology. This policy will be a tailored approach reducing the potential for ACO professionals’ billing patterns, inside and outside the ACO, for the care of the same beneficiaries, to result in differences in assignment outcomes that advantage the ACO’s financial performance.
Second, we are finalizing modifications to assignment eligibility criteria and prospective assignment exclusion criteria based on Medicare enrollment status. Currently, to be eligible for assignment to an ACO for a performance year or benchmark year, a beneficiary must meet criteria including having at least one month of Part A and Part B enrollment without any month of Part A only or Part B only enrollment, or Medicare group health plan enrollment (including Medicare Advantage (MA)), during the assignment window. For an ACO participating under prospective assignment, a beneficiary may be excluded later from the ACO’s prospective assignment list if they no longer meet these eligibility criteria. We are finalizing modifications to the assignment criteria based on Medicare enrollment status to align with our current operational approach to identifying the assignable beneficiary population. Under our new approach, we will consider as eligible for assignment beneficiaries who have at least one month of Part A and Part B enrollment and no Medicare group health plan enrollment (including MA) during that same month during the 12-month assignment window for the relevant performance year or benchmark year.
Third, we are finalizing updates to the definition of primary care services used for beneficiary assignment under the Shared Savings Program to align with payment policy proposals under the Medicare PFS. We are finalizing to include, among other services for determining beneficiary assignment for the performance year starting on Jan. 1, 2027, and subsequent performance years, new codes for Screening, Brief Intervention, and Referral to Treatment, Vaccine Adverse Effects Management, and Advance Care Planning.
Shared Savings Program ACOs and ACO participants may also be impacted by the replacement of HCPCS code G2211 (E/M Visit Complexity Add-On) with a modifier and should review the CY 2027 PFS Final Rule Fact Sheet for additional information.
Enhance Beneficiary Engagement — Allow ACOs to Reduce or Eliminate Part B Cost Sharing
Informed by experience in the ACO REACH model, we are finalizing a policy to allow ACOs to reduce or eliminate Part B cost sharing for many items and services for beneficiaries in accordance with an approved implementation plan starting April 1, 2027, which we believe will remove cost barriers for beneficiaries to receive services that will positively impact their health. Eligible ACOs could enter Part B cost-sharing support arrangements with ACO participants to reduce or eliminate cost sharing for certain categories of Part B items and services and eligible beneficiaries identified by the ACO. We will allow ACOs to reduce or eliminate beneficiary cost sharing for all Original Medicare Part B items and services except for durable medical equipment, prosthetics, orthotics, and supplies (DMEPOS), and prescription drugs. An ACO must apply to, and be approved by, CMS to enter Part B cost-sharing support arrangements with its ACO participants. To allow ACOs to participate as quickly as possible, we will be collecting initial applications in early 2027 to approve eligible ACOs and their ACO participants to begin eliminating or reducing Part B cost sharing for beneficiaries by the second quarter of CY 2027.
We also are removing the prepaid shared savings payment option from the Shared Savings Program in light of that option’s low uptake and because we believe the aims of that option could be more efficiently achieved for ACOs and beneficiaries through the proposal to offer ACOs the ability to reduce or eliminate Part B cost sharing and other Shared Savings Program policies. No additional cohorts of ACOs will be allowed to apply for the prepaid shared savings payment option after the application cycle for the Jan. 1, 2027, start date. Participating ACOs will receive prepaid shared savings payments through Dec. 31, 2027.
Modifications to the Shared Savings Program Quality and CEHRT Use Requirements to Advance ACO Use of dQMs
Extending the Availability of the MIPS CQMs Collection Type and the MIPS CQM Reporting Incentive for Shared Savings Program ACOs
We are extending the availability of the MIPS CQMs collection type for Shared Savings Program ACOs reporting the APP Plus quality measure set for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs. Maintaining the MIPS CQMs collection type for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs will eliminate the administrative burden associated with ACOs changing their current quality reporting collection type to another collection type after PY 2026. It will also allow ACOs to instead focus their resources and efforts on the transition to dQM reporting.
To continue to align the reporting incentive with the MIPS CQMs collection type, we are also extending the reporting incentive to ACOs reporting MIPS CQMs for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs. This will further support ACOs in meeting the Shared Savings Program quality performance standard to be eligible to share in savings at the maximum rate available for the ACO’s track/level of participation and for ACOs participating in the ENHANCED track to avoid maximum shared losses.
Extending the Use of Flat Benchmarks to Score Medicare CQMs
For PY 2027 and subsequent PYs, all measures of the Medicare CQMs collection type will be scored using flat benchmarks. In addition, the Diabetes: Glycemic Status Assessment Greater Than 9% (Quality ID: 001), Preventive Care and Screening: Screening for Depression and Follow-up Plan (Quality ID: 134), and Controlling High Blood Pressure (Quality ID: 236), if reported via the Medicare CQMs collection type for PY 2026 (and subsequent PYs), will be scored using flat benchmarks.
Addressing ACOs’ Challenges with Meeting the MIPS Data Completeness Requirement
Revising the Shared Savings Program Quality Reporting Requirements beginning in PY 2026
Given the concerns raised by ACOs about challenges meeting the Shared Savings Program quality reporting requirements, we are revising the quality reporting requirements. For PYs beginning on or after Jan. 1, 2026, ACOs may exclude one or more ACO participant TINs from an ACO’s submission of eCQM/MIPS CQM/Medicare CQM/Medicare eCQM data (as applicable) for each measure when certain exclusions apply. These exclusions include unforeseen circumstance(s) outside the ACO’s control (such as the unexpected closure of a group or individual practice that bills under the ACO’s participant TIN), an ACO participant TIN having CEHRT that is intended for specialty use and does not support the measure(s) included in the APP Plus quality measure set, or other circumstances as determined by CMS, so long as the ACO can report on ACO participant TINs that represent at least 95% of the beneficiaries assigned to the ACO before applying the measure specifications.
ACOs will still be required to meet the MIPS data completeness requirement (that is, the ACO must report on at least 75% of the APM Entity's applicable beneficiaries who meet the measure’s denominator criteria) for each eCQM/MIPS CQM/Medicare CQM/Medicare eCQM for which the ACO submits data.
Medicare eCQMs for Accountable Care Organizations Participating in the Medicare Shared Savings Program (Medicare eCQMs) Collection Type for Shared Savings Program ACOs
For PY 2027 and subsequent PYs, we are establishing Medicare eCQMs as a new collection type for Shared Savings Program ACOs reporting on the APP Plus quality measure set. A Medicare eCQM is essentially an eCQM that is part of the APP Plus quality measure set and reported by an ACO on only the ACO’s assigned beneficiaries, instead of its all payer/all patient population. We will not be providing separate Medicare eCQM measure specifications. ACOs should use the eCQM measure specifications, report data on their assigned beneficiaries, and use a different identifier that CMS will provide to distinguish that the submission is for a Medicare eCQM rather than for an eCQM. We believe the addition of Medicare eCQMs will help our efforts to transition to dQMs by supporting ACOs that want to report eCQMs but are unable to operationally report on all patient/all payer data due to data aggregation challenges.
In addition, measures of the Medicare eCQMs collection type would be scored using flat benchmarks beginning with the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year. We note that ACOs that choose to report Medicare eCQMs will not be eligible for the eCQM/MIPS reporting incentive or the Complex Organization Adjustment.
For PY 2027 and subsequent PYs, ACOs will have the option to report the five Medicare eCQMs, or a combination of eCQMs/MIPS CQMs/Medicare CQMs/Medicare eCQMs, to meet the Shared Savings Program quality reporting requirement and the quality performance standard.
Revising the Definition of a “Beneficiary Eligible for Medicare CQMs”
We are revising the definition of a “beneficiary eligible for Medicare CQMs” for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs, to align with the population of beneficiaries assigned to the ACO. Our revised definition will build on the revisions finalized in the CY 2026 PFS final rule and further align the definition of a "beneficiary eligible for Medicare CQMs" to correspond to an ACO’s assigned beneficiary list to continue to address ACO challenges with patient aggregation.
Revising the Shared Savings Program Scoring Policy for Excluded APP Plus Measures and APP Plus Measures That Lack a Benchmark
We are finalizing revisions to the scoring policy at § 425.512(a)(7) with respect to excluded APP Plus measures and APP Plus measures that lack a benchmark, such that for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs, it will apply only if the ACO’s MIPS quality performance category score is calculated on less than five measures for a PY. In other words, if four or more measures in the APP Plus quality measure set are excluded from MIPS, then we will apply our new scoring policy (§ 425.512(a)(7)(iii)). The previous scoring policy will no longer apply when at least one of the required measures in the APP Plus quality measure set does not have a benchmark for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs.
We believe that these revisions will ensure that ACOs are fairly assessed on their quality performance in our determination of whether they meet the quality performance standard.
Updating the APP Plus Quality Measure Set
For PY 2025 and subsequent PYs, Shared Savings Program ACOs are required to report the APP Plus quality measure set. We are finalizing several changes to the APP Plus quality measure set for Shared Savings Program ACOs, including the removal of Initiation and Engagement of Substance Use Disorder Treatment (Quality ID: 305) and Adult Immunization Status (Quality ID: 493) from the APP Plus quality measure set.
We are finalizing that the APP Plus quality measure set for Shared Savings Program ACOs will include eight measures (five eCQMs/MIPS CQMs/Medicare CQMs/Medicare eCQMs, two administrative claims-based measures, and the CAHPS for MIPS Survey measure) beginning with PY 2027.
Table 1 below displays the list of the quality measures that will be included in the APP Plus quality measure set for Shared Savings Program ACOs for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs with the removal of Initiation and Engagement of Substance Use Disorder Treatment (Quality ID: 305) and Adult Immunization Status (Quality ID: 493) from the APP Plus quality measure set.
Table 1: Quality Measures in the APP Plus Quality Measure Set for Shared Savings Program ACOs for PY 2027 and Subsequent PYs
Simplifying Shared Savings Program Requirements to Reduce Participant Burden — ACO CEHRT Use Requirements
To be considered an Advanced APM, in which qualifying participants are exempt from MIPS, an APM must require participants to meaningfully use CEHRT that meets specific requirements.
In response to the challenges we’ve heard from ACOs about existing Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements, and to support ACOs’ meaningful advancement toward the digital exchange of health information and digital quality measurement to improve care for ACO beneficiaries, we are replacing the existing requirements. For PY 2027 and subsequent years, ACOs will be required to meet Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements by choosing one of the following three activities:
- Completely report at least one of the five ACO-reported measures1 in the APP Plus quality measure set through the eCQMs or Medicare eCQMs collection type using CEHRT certified to ONC health IT certification criteria; or
- Completely report at least one of the five ACO-reported measures in the APP Plus quality measure set using CEHRT and attest to using data collected from an HL7® Fast Healthcare Interoperable Resources (FHIR®)-based API to support quality measurement using a Health IT Module certified to a certification criterion supporting standardized API access; or
- Select and attest to one of the Shared Savings Program ACO CEHRT use metrics from the list of metrics we establish for each performance year. Table 2 reflects the metrics we finalized for PY 2027. Unlike similar MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category measures, which are specified for clinicians and groups, these Shared Savings Program ACO CEHRT use metrics are specific to ACOs and have specific allowable exclusions.
Table 2: Shared Savings Program ACO CEHRT Use Metrics for PY 2027
ACOs attesting to one of the three above metrics will be permitted to apply, without filing a request to CMS, TIN-level exclusions similar to those that MIPS-eligible clinicians can request. ACOs will be permitted to exclude a TIN composed solely of providers and/or suppliers who: meet the Shared Savings Program definition of “special status” or meet hardship conditions detailed in the final rule preamble.
ACOs electing to report one of these three CEHRT use metrics will be required to maintain documentation on excluded TINs and produce it in the event of a CMS audit. ACOs could face compliance actions if they fail to meet Shared Savings Program CEHRT requirements, including the requirement to demonstrate that their TIN exclusions were appropriate.
We are also finalizing our proposal to replace the existing public reporting requirement with a requirement that ACOs publicly report which of the allowable CEHRT use activities they elected to complete, to promote transparency for beneficiaries or providers who want to make informed choices.
Revising Beneficiary Notification Requirements
We are finalizing changes to the beneficiary notification requirements to address concerns that beneficiary notices are burdensome for ACOs to distribute and potentially confusing for beneficiaries. Under previous requirements, an ACO or ACO participant must provide certain Original Medicare beneficiaries with a standardized written notice before or at a beneficiary’s first primary care service visit during the first performance year in which the beneficiary receives a primary care service from an ACO participant. We are removing the requirement that ties the timing of the notification to a beneficiary’s first primary care service visit and instead require the ACO or ACO participant to provide a beneficiary with a standardized written notice at least once during an agreement period in the form and manner specified by CMS. Under the approach we are finalizing, the notice must be furnished by May 30 unless CMS specifies a later date during the performance year. This better aligns with CMS Innovation Center ACO model policies. Further, we are removing the requirement, applicable to all ACOs, specifying the ACO or ACO participant must provide a verbal or written follow-up communication to a beneficiary, following the provision of the standardized written notice. These changes will be effective Jan. 1, 2027.
Advance Investment Payments Changes to Encourage Greater Rural Participation
We are changing the calculation methodology for setting quarterly advance investment payment amounts for eligible ACOs. We will no longer use a risk factors-based score, which includes consideration of a beneficiary’s Area Deprivation Index (ADI) national percentile rank, to determine the payment amount, as there have been methodological issues identified with the ADI metric. Instead, we will include a rural criterion and use a flat per-beneficiary payment amount in setting an ACO’s quarterly payments for PY 2028 and subsequent performance years. Specifically, ACOs will receive a quarterly payment of $45 for each beneficiary who meets one or more of the following criteria: is enrolled in Medicare Part D LIS, is dually eligible for Medicare and Medicaid, or is residing in a county with rural census status (either Micropolitan or Noncore as proposed). The ACO will receive a quarterly payment of $25 for each beneficiary who does not meet any of the criteria, capped at 10,000 beneficiaries.
Revising Approach to Determining an ACO’s Experience with Risk Based on Prior Participation of ACO Participants
CMS identifies whether an ACO is experienced or inexperienced with performance-based risk Medicare ACO initiatives as part of determining the ACO’s eligibility for participation options under the Shared Savings Program, including whether an ACO is eligible to enter the BASIC track’s glide path or is limited to participating under higher levels of risk and potential reward (either Level E of the BASIC track or the ENHANCED track). In determining the ACO’s experience or inexperience with performance-based risk, CMS considers ACO participant TINs’ prior participation in a performance-based risk Medicare ACO initiative, including CMS Innovation Center ACO models under which an ACO accepts risk for shared losses, among other factors. Effective Jan. 1, 2027, an ACO participant TIN that did not have a written agreement to participate in a performance-based risk Medicare ACO initiative will not be considered to have participated in such initiative, even if the TIN was or will be included in financial reconciliation for the initiative. Under this approach, a “Legacy” TIN participating under a CMS Innovation Center ACO model will not be considered to have participated in a performance-based risk Medicare ACO initiative for purposes of determining a Shared Savings Program ACO’s experience with risk, as we do not believe including these TINs aligns with the original intent of our policy.
###
- ^ This excludes administrative claims and CAHPS for MIPS Survey measures. For PY 2027, the reportable measures would be #001, #112, #113, #134, and #236.

JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. – A Columbia, Mo. man was sentenced in federal court today for possession of a machine gun conversion device.

Deshawn Anthony Harris, 21, was sentenced by U.S. District Judge Stephen R. Bough to 60 months in prison, to be followed by three years of supervised release. Harris had previously pleaded guilty to one count of illegally possessing a machine gun, admitting that he possessed a Glock-style machine gun conversion device in Boone County.

According to government filings, Harris was arrested after being pulled over in Columbia on April 4, 2025. During a search of the vehicle, officers located a firearm with a machine gun conversion device attached, which was loaded with a round in the chamber and 19 rounds in an extended magazine.

This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Lauren E. Kummerer. It was investigated by the Columbia Police Department and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives.

Project Safe Neighborhoods

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities .
title: Columbia Man Sentenced to 5 Years for Firearm Offense

BILLINGS – A Red Lodge man who kept an illegal stash of privately manufactured guns was sentenced today to five years and 10 months in prison, followed by three years of supervised release, U.S. Attorney Scott Twito said. He was also ordered to pay a $25,000 fine.

James Faddis Kennedy, 76, pleaded guilty in July 2026 to unlawfully possessing a firearm.

U.S. District Judge Kathleen S. Lane presided.

The government alleged in court documents that Kennedy had possibly violated the terms of his release after having been previously convicted of possessing an unregistered firearm . Law enforcement searched Kennedy’s Red Lodge home on Jan. 14, 2026, where they found “numerous firearms, suppressors, and rounds of ammunition.” The firearms appeared to be privately made. During the search, law enforcement also found tools associated with the production of privately made firearms.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Zeno Baucus is prosecuting the case. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives conducted the investigation.

Nov. 4, 2026
Help create holiday joy for those in need
WASHINGTON — USPS Operation Santa adoption registration is officially open!
Groups and individuals interested in adopting letters for this year’s program should visit USPSOperationSanta.com, click on the registration link and follow the prompts. For security reasons, all prospective adopters must be vetted through a short registration and ID verification process before they can participate. If someone has adopted letters in the past, they must still be verified each year.
“Every year we receive thousands of letters filled with holiday wishes — often outnumbering available adopters — many letters come from entire households,” said Sheila Holman, vice president of marketing for the Postal Service. “To help these families, we encourage companies and organizations to form teams to adopt a household together, ensuring everyone in the home can share in the joy of the holidays.”
Letter Adoption Opens Nov. 16
Beginning Monday, Nov. 16, approved adopters can begin selecting letters and shopping for gifts. The deadline to send gifts is Saturday, Dec. 12. Interested adopters can follow a few easy steps to start granting wishes:
The Postal Service is once again working with Toys“R”Us to provide Santa’s Gift Shoppe. This online gift catalog gives adopters an easy way to shop for and ship gifts directly to recipients. Of course, for those who prefer to shop for gifts in person and send them from a Post Office location, that option is still available.
“USPS Operation Santa has been an enduring holiday program for more than a century. Through the generosity of others, the holiday season has been made extra special for thousands of children and families in need,” Holman said.
The U.S. Postal Service began accepting letters for the 114-year-old holiday program Sept. 14. Letters are available on USPSOperationSanta.com, and they’re ready to be read and adopted*.
For more information on the USPS Operation Santa program, history, important dates and how to participate as either a letter writer or adopter, visit USPSOperationSanta.com.
*There is no guarantee every letter will be posted, and if posted, there is no guarantee it will be adopted and fulfilled.

WASHINGTON — The U.S. Department of the Treasury is offering $125 billion of Treasury securities to refund approximately $97 billion of privately-held Treasury notes and bonds maturing on November 15, 2026. This issuance will raise new cash from private investors of approximately $28 billion. The securities are:
- A 3-year note in the amount of $58 billion, maturing November 15, 2029;
- A 10-year note in the amount of $42 billion, maturing November 15, 2036;
- A 30-year bond in the amount of $25 billion, maturing November 15, 2056.
The 3-year note will be auctioned at 1:00 p.m. ET on Monday, November 9, 2026. The 10-year note will be auctioned at 1:00 p.m. ET on Tuesday, November 10, 2026. The 30-year bond will be auctioned at 1:00 p.m. ET on Thursday, November 12, 2026. All these auctions will take place on a yield basis and will settle on Monday, November 16, 2026.
The balance of Treasury financing requirements over the quarter will be met with regular weekly bill auctions, cash management bills (CMBs), and monthly note, bond, Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS), and 2-year Floating Rate Note (FRN) auctions.
NOMINAL COUPON AND FRN FINANCING
Treasury believes its current auction sizes leave it well positioned to address potential changes to the fiscal outlook and to the size and composition of the SOMA portfolio. Based on current projected borrowing needs, Treasury anticipates maintaining nominal coupon and FRN auction sizes for the next several quarters. Treasury is monitoring SOMA purchases of Treasury bills and growing demand for Treasury bills from the private sector. Looking ahead, Treasury continues to evaluate potential future changes to nominal coupon and FRN auction sizes, with a focus on trends in structural demand and potential costs and risks of various issuance profiles. As part of that process, Treasury will engage with a variety of market participants to better understand evolving Treasury supply and demand dynamics. In considering any changes, Treasury will be guided by the objective of financing the government at the lowest cost over time.
The table below presents, in billions of dollars, the actual auction sizes for the August to October 2026 quarter and the anticipated auction sizes for the November 2026 to January 2027 quarter:
Treasury plans to address any seasonal or unexpected variations in borrowing needs over the next quarter through changes in regular bill auction sizes and/or CMBs.
TIPS FINANCING
Over the November 2026 to January 2027 quarter, Treasury plans to maintain TIPS auction sizes at current levels: the November 10-year TIPS reopening auction size at $19 billion, the December 5-year TIPS reopening auction size at $24 billion, and the January 10-year TIPS new issue auction size at $21 billion.
BILL ISSUANCE
Treasury continues to see strong demand for bill securities from a broad range of market participants. Based on current forecasts, Treasury expects to maintain current auction sizes of benchmark bills into late November and anticipates potentially issuing a short-dated CMB to meet its cash management needs around the end of November. Given projections for receipts associated with the mid-December corporate and non-withheld tax date, Treasury expects to implement reductions to shorter-dated bill auction sizes during the month of December. In January, Treasury anticipates increasing auction sizes across the bill curve based on expected seasonal fiscal outflows. As always, Treasury will continue to evaluate near-term borrowing needs and assess additional adjustments to bill auction sizes as appropriate.
CONVERSION OF 7-YEAR NOTE TO QUARTERLY NEW ISSUE
Treasury plans to convert the 7-year note from a monthly new issue to a quarterly new issue with two reopenings (similar to the 10-year note). The 7-year note will continue to be auctioned towards the end of each month and issue and mature at month end. Treasury will auction new issues in March, June, September, and December and conduct reopening auctions in the subsequent two months of each cycle. This conversion will go into effect beginning with the March 2027 new issue, which will be reopened in April and May.
CASH BALANCE
Treasury is assuming an $850 billion cash balance at the end of December. However, based on current projections for the upcoming refunding quarter, Treasury estimates that the size of the Treasury General Account (TGA) could peak at $1.025 trillion (plus or minus $50 billion) in late November and late January. These figures are consistent with Treasury’s long-standing cash balance policy and are driven by the large outflows expected to occur at those times.
BUYBACKS
Treasury is releasing a tentative buyback schedule for the upcoming refunding quarter. Treasury anticipates that, over the course of the upcoming quarter, it will purchase up to $70 billion in off-the-run securities across buckets for liquidity support and up to $25 billion in the 1-month to 2-year maturity bucket for cash management purposes. Treasury will continue to evaluate possible enhancements to buyback operations such as changes to maximum purchase amounts, buyback operation scheduling and frequency, security eligibility, and execution process.
Please send comments or suggestions on these subjects or other subjects related to debt management to debt.management@treasury.gov.
The next quarterly refunding announcement will take place on Wednesday, February 3, 2027.

Article I, Section 8, of the Constitution stipulates, "The Congress shall have Power To ... raise and support Armies ... make Rules for the Government and Regulation of the land and naval Forces ... for calling forth the Militia to execute the Laws of the Union, suppress Insurrections and repel Invasions." The Army's purpose is described in 10 U.S.C. §7062:
It is the intent of Congress to provide an Army that is capable, in conjunction with the other armed forces, of—
(1) preserving the peace and security, and providing for the defense, of the United States, the Commonwealths and possessions, and any areas occupied by the United States;
(2) supporting the national policies;
(3) implementing the national objectives; and
(4) overcoming any nations responsible for aggressive acts that imperil the peace and security of the United States.
The Department of the Army (DA) is one of three military departments, along with the Navy and the Air Force, reporting to the Department of Defense (DOD), which is "using a secondary Department of War designation" under Executive Order (EO) 14347 of September 5, 2025.
The Army is composed of two distinct components: the active component (AC) and the reserve component (RC). RCs are the United States Army Reserve (USAR) and the Army National Guard (ARNG). The department's Army Civilians (DAC) also play a significant supporting role. See Table 1
Source: Defense Manpower Data Center, as of August 31, 2026, accessed November 2, 2026. Numbers are updated quarterly.
Note: CONUS = Continental United States and OCONUS = Outside of the Continental United States (overseas).
The DA is led by a civilian Secretary of the Army appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate. The Secretary of the Army reports to the Secretary of Defense, who is using "Secretary of War" as a "secondary title" under EO 14347 of September 5, 2025, and serves as civilian oversight for the Army as an institution and the Chief of Staff of the Army (CSA). The CSA is an administrative position held by a four-star Army general and is a statutory office (10 U.S.C. §7033). The CSA is the chief military advisor and deputy to the Secretary of the Army and, by statute (10 U.S.C. §151), serves as a member of the Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS). The JCS is composed of DOD's senior uniformed leaders who advise the President, Secretary of Defense, and Cabinet officials on military issues.
The authorities of the Secretary of the Army and the CSA are prescribed by law: 10 U.S.C. §7013 and 10 U.S.C. §7033, respectively. The CSA does not have operational command authority over deployed Army units. Under 10 U.S.C. §162, the operational chain of command runs from the President to the Secretary of Defense and then to the commanders of the unified combatant commands, with the Chairman of the JCS (CJCS) serving as the principal military advisor rather than a commander of forces. The CSA does, however, exercise supervision of Army units and organizations as designated by the Secretary of the Army. Under 10 U.S.C. §7074, the Secretary of the Army has authority to divide the Army into subordinate commands and organizations to accomplish the Army's mission.
[t]he operational Army consists of numbered armies, corps, divisions, brigades, and battalions that conduct full-spectrum operations around the world. The institutional Army supports the operational Army. Institutional organizations provide the infrastructure necessary to raise, train, equip, deploy, and ensure the readiness of all Army forces.
The operational Army, known as the Operational Force, consists of
units that are trained, equipped, and ready to deploy. These forces make up about two-thirds of the Regular Army and three-fourths of the Total Army.
The institutional Army supports the operational Army by
generating, preparing, and sustaining the Army operating forces. Institutional forces do not normally deploy, but they perform other critical tasks like recruiting, servicing, educating, mobilizing, and constructing.
There are three types of commands: Army Commands, Army Service Component Commands (ASCCs), and Direct Reporting Units (DRUs).
Army commands perform many Title 10 functions across multiple disciplines. At present, the two Army Commands include the Army Material Command (AMC), which provides technology, acquisition, and logistics support to the Army, and the U.S. Army Transformation and Training Command (T2COM), which generates, develops, designs, and trains Army forces.
On October 1, 2026, the Acting Secretary of the Army directed the establishment of FASCOM. FASCOM is to be a three-star headquarters and expected to focus on autonomy in the areas of aviation, armor, fires, sustainment, engineering, and training.

text:
DETROIT ARSENAL, Mich. – Five careers. Decades of impact. One enduring legacy.
Meet the former Army Civilians whose achievements, leadership and commitment to excellence earned them a spot in the U.S. Army Tank-automotive and Armaments Command Hall of Fame.
AGNES E. HOLLEY-SMITH
From depot intern to Integrated Logistics Support Center leader, Agnes E. Holley-Smith broke barriers and enhanced Soldier readiness.
“Support to Soldiers was always the No. 1 priority, regardless of what else was going on around you,” she said.
Holley-Smith’s 35-year career began in 1971 as an intern at Red River Army Depot. She moved the next year to TACOM, where her expertise and leadership skills catapulted her from an entry-level job writing descriptions of spare parts for catalogs to high-profile, strategically important leadership roles.
Holley-Smith served as chief of the Special Vehicles Division, senior budget representative, director of both the Logistics Integration Office and the Heavy Combat Commodity Business Unit, deputy director of the Integrated Materiel Management Center (now the ILSC) and director of Operations and Security Assistance for the ILSC.
A strong advocate for TACOM’s logistics programs, Holley-Smith drove modernization and strengthened cross-functional collaboration. She championed the transition toward multidisciplinary, multifunctional and multiskilled teams, which helped position the command to respond more effectively to increasingly complex operational requirements.
At the time, Holley-Smith was among the youngest people to ascend to senior executive leadership, inspiring future generations of Civilian leaders. She retired in 2006.
Keith Berman, retired deputy chief of staff, Resource Management, met Holley-Smith while working in the Army Working Capital Fund Office. In a Hall of Fame nomination letter, he said her professionalism, integrity, dedication and selfless service shaped his career.
“From the beginning,” he said, “she made me feel seen, valued and capable.”
DAVID W. HORTON
David W. Horton proudly served the U.S. Army for nearly four decades, first in uniform and then as a highly respected Civilian leader.
His favorite assignment was also one of the most impactful: Logistics Development Chief for Program Management Office Abrams.
“At that time, we were still in the stages of developing the M1A2 tank,” he said. “My organization was responsible for developing all the logistics products. … It was a very fulfilling job for me. It was new; it was exciting.”
Horton became a Soldier in 1983. He entered the Civil Service three years later, working his way up from supply management intern to acting executive director of the ILSC.
Horton drove modernization and critical logistics initiatives throughout his career. He served two years in Kuwait executing the sale of the Abrams tank, the cornerstone of Kuwait’s effort to modernize its army. His other assignments included chief of logistics engineering for Program Management Office Stryker; director of logistics integration for Future Combat Systems, where he managed the Army’s primary efforts to modernize the Brigade Combat Teams; and director, Ground Combat Support, Readiness and Sustainment Directorate.
At the ILSC, Horton oversaw more than 3,000 personnel and most of the Army’s maintenance, fielding, new equipment training, supply chain management and system readiness. He retired in 2023.
Mark Granger, ILSC staff action officer, described Horton as a steadfast leader who provided stability in times of both peace and conflict.
“Mr. Horton epitomized the Army values of loyalty, duty, respect, selfless service, honor, integrity and personal courage and fostered a cohesive team environment wherever he went,” he said.
MICHELE M. MOORE
From the devastating ashes of an attack on a federal building to high-stakes logistical operations, Michele M. Moore was a force multiplier.
A single question fueled her 35-year career: “How can I best serve Soldiers?”
Moore worked in multiple fields on several military installations, including at the Pentagon in the Army Public Affairs Office. One poignant assignment involved returning to her hometown to help rebuild the Army’s Oklahoma City Recruiting Battalion command information program after the 1995 federal building bombing.
Leveraging her communications and logistics expertise, Moore led TACOM’s efforts to document and train personnel on wartime operational processes after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. She also oversaw 23 diverse mission areas as TACOM’s Life Cycle Logistics director. Before retiring in 2024, she coordinated the command’s support to Army computer system transformation.
At the apex of her career, Moore served as the final director of the Army Force Generation Integration Directorate, which managed the complex effort of repairing war-torn, TACOM-managed weapon systems that were used in Afghanistan and Iraq.
“I loved that time (as director),” she said. “You’re on the cutting edge, you’re part of a team, and you’re doing good work for Soldiers.
“Every morning, no matter how tired I was or how stressful it was, I told myself, ‘Michele, you’re doing this for God and country.’ And that’s what matters.”
Nicole Kurz and Tina Travis, Moore’s former staff action officer and former administrative assistant, described her in a nomination letter as a kind and collaborative leader who believed learning never stops.
“She quickly became more than just a supervisor,” they said. “She was a guiding light and a wonderful influence.”
JAMES PATTON TIDWELL
James “Patton” Tidwell walked in as a production controller and walked out as deputy commander, shaping Red River Army Depot history along the way.
Tidwell’s 44-year career began in 1978 in U.S. Army Materiel Command’s Maintenance Management intern program. He joined RRAD in 1979 as the first production controller for the Bradley fighting vehicle.
A commitment to excellence infused every role that followed. Tidwell spent the core of his career in RRAD’s Production/Maintenance and Logistics directorates. In 1990, he helped transform the maintenance shop floor through automated supply ordering, inventory and storage. Other roles included contracting officer in the Business Management Office and deputy director and director for Production, Logistics and Contracting.
As deputy commander under six different commanders, Tidwell steered the depot’s transition to the Logistics Modernization Program and the Complex Automated Manufacturing System. He was instrumental in launching the maintenance programs for the Armored HMMWV and the MRAP.
“My style was to make sure that we were doing the right thing for the right reason,” Tidwell said. “It was really important that we understood what the mission and the goal and the requirements were, and that we publicized and supported that all the way down the line.”
Tidwell retired in 2021. One of his former employees, James E. Bass, said his legacy still reverberates throughout the depot.
“Mr. Tidwell’s dedication extended beyond modernization; he fostered a lasting legacy of leadership and mentorship that continues to positively impact the organization today,” he said.
DAVID L. VAN AGTMAEL
David L. Van Agtmael’s introduction to TACOM as an Army private in Vietnam sparked a decades-long career of preparing warfighters.
“Whatever it takes for that Soldier to be successful, that’s the ultimate goal,” he said. “It doesn’t matter if it’s a three-star, a two-star or a private, we supported them.”
Van Agtmael enlisted in the U.S. Army in 1967, working his way up from a heavy equipment operator to Chief Warrant Officer 3. He retired from active duty in 1988 and joined TACOM as a Civilian – a transition influenced by his appreciation of the command’s rapid support when he was a young Soldier.
Van Agtmael helped shape the future of Army logistics while serving as an equipment specialist, provisioning specialist, logistics assistance representative, logistics management specialist and Senior Command Representative. He was at the forefront of force modernization efforts and a key architect of the logistics support structure for the Stryker Brigade, playing a significant role in the platform's effectiveness during Operation Iraqi Freedom.
Van Agtmael spearheaded other life-saving initiatives, as well, from fielding a mobile tire wheel assembly site in Afghanistan to facilitating support for Small Arms Readiness and Evaluation Teams (SARET) to improve weapons readiness.
Colleagues respected Van Agtmael’s fiscal stewardship, hands-on leadership and talent for building collaborative relationships. He deployed once to Bosnia, twice to Iraq and twice to Afghanistan in support of U.S. forces before retiring in 2015.
Logistics Assistance Directorate Director Travis Spurrier said Van Agtmael’s career is a powerful story of service and impact.
“He has been a pioneer who shaped modern logistics support concepts, a leader who solved critical readiness challenges on the battlefield and a mentor who invested in the next generation of logisticians,” he said.
title: Fantastic Five: Introducing the TACOM Hall of Fame Class of 2026

SAVANNAH, Georgia: An illegal alien from Honduras has been sentenced in federal court for receiving and shipping firearms and firearms parts.

The sentence was imposed by U.S. District Court Chief Judge R. Stan Baker and was announced by Margaret E. “Meg” Heap, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Georgia.

Jefferson Flores-Padilla , 31, a citizen of Honduras, was sentenced to 46 months in prison followed by immediate deportation after pleading guilty to Receipt of a Firearm by an Illegal Alien and Shipping Firearms by an Illegal Alien.

There is no parole in the federal system.

As described in court documents and testimony, Flores-Padilla and his co-defendant, Sindi Mencias-Escobar , 38, a citizen of Honduras, entered the United States illegally and took up residence in Savannah. As illegal aliens, they were prohibited by law from purchasing firearms. On multiple occasions in 2023, Flores-Padilla solicited an acquaintance to purchase numerous firearms for him, including AR-15s and Glock pistols. Some of these firearms were later recovered by Honduran authorities during law enforcement operations in that country.

Additionally, in early 2024, law enforcement authorities in Miami seized and searched a suspicious package that was outbound for Honduras and discovered hidden firearms and firearms parts. Flores-Padilla’s fingerprints were lifted from the packaging materials. Additional investigation revealed that Flores-Padilla and Mencias-Escobar had shipped the package from the Savannah area.

Mencias-Escobar was previously sentenced in the case after pleading guilty to Misprision of a Felony and was referred to Immigration and Customs Enforcement for immediate deportation.

Under federal law, it is illegal for any person who is illegally or unlawfully in the United States to ship, transport, receive, or possess any firearm or ammunition.

"The illegal acquisition and trafficking of firearms poses a direct threat to public safety, both at home and abroad," said U.S. Attorney Heap. "By intercepting these dangerous weapons before they could be smuggled out of our country, law enforcement successfully disrupted a dangerous pipeline. This sentence serves as a clear reminder that our office, along with our federal partners, will continue to vigorously enforce laws that keep firearms out of the hands of those who are unlawfully present in the United States."

This case was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives, Homeland Security Investigations, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection.

“Firearms trafficking endangers communities and undermines the rule of law,” said Jose R. Figueroa, Special Agent in Charge of HSI Miami. “HSI and our law enforcement partners in the United States and abroad will continue to identify and investigate those who illegally acquire and move weapons across borders. This sentence reflects our shared commitment to protecting the public, enforcing federal firearms laws, and ensuring that those who threaten the safety of our communities are held accountable.”

This case was prosecuted for the United States by Southern District of Georgia Assistant U.S. Attorney Timothy P. Dean.
title: Illegal alien sentenced to federal prison for firearms-related charges

text:
On Wednesday, NASA unveiled its newest experimental aircraft, the X-70 Fractal, during the UP.Summit at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. This high-performance, highly adaptable research platform is designed to accelerate the development and testing of advanced aviation technologies.
The crewed X-70 features advanced, rapidly reconfigurable flight-control technology that will allow NASA to explore aircraft maneuverability in ways never before demonstrated in crewed flight. The aircraft can also accommodate up to 2,000 pounds of experimental payloads in internal and external locations, enabling a wide range of research and flight-testing opportunities.
“The X-70 Fractal gives NASA a crewed, high-performance platform to test advanced flight-control, maneuverability, and other cutting-edge technologies in real flight,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Its modular design and ability to rapidly swap internal and external payloads will keep our teams flying, learning, and moving quickly from one experiment to the next. We expect her first flight under the NASA banner within the next two years, and X-70 is just one part of this new beginning for aeronautics. This is why people come to NASA: to build, to learn, and most importantly, to fly.”
The X-70 Fractal has a takeoff weight of 10,000 pounds and is designed to cruise at Mach .75, reach altitudes of up to 45,000 feet, and provide an operational range exceeding about 1,726 miles (1,500 nautical miles). These capabilities will enable NASA to conduct demanding flight research across a broad range of operating conditions.
“For decades, NASA Aeronautics has used X-planes to develop technologies that advance aviation,” said Laurie Grindle, director of the Aeronautics Division within NASA’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate. “It’s exciting to bring on another X-plane to accelerate and drive aeronautics research.”
The X-70 joins a storied legacy of experimental aircraft that have helped establish America’s leadership in aviation. From the Bell X-1, which first broke the sound barrier in 1947, to the X-15 hypersonic research aircraft and today’s X-59 quiet supersonic demonstrator, NASA has spent decades pushing the boundaries of flight.
With the X-70, NASA will expand its capacity to conduct experimental flight research, accelerate the testing of emerging technologies, and advance the next generation of American aviation.
