DETROIT – Roland Chatmon, 37, of Detroit, Michigan; Leica Lopez Martinez, 33, of Lake Orion, Michigan; Ieasha Stroman, 38, of Pontiac, Michigan; and Dneiqua Stroman, 43, of Pontiac, Michigan, have all pled guilty to kidnapping conspiracy and federal firearms offenses; and Kenneth Anderson, 54, of Pontiac, Michigan, previously pled guilty to money laundering for his role, United States Attorney Jerome F. Gorgon Jr. announced today.

Gorgon was joined in the announcement by James Deir, Special Agent in Charge of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), Detroit Field Division.

According to court filings and admissions by the defendants during the plea hearings, the conspiracy began in August 2025 after Chatmon’s uncle had gone “viral” on social media after offering to help someone in need. To reward him for his good deed, a social media influencer raised money for the uncle and gave him over $100,000, a new car, and other gifts, all of which were highly publicized. On August 24, 2025, Chatmon talked to his brother, who was in jail, and told him about the uncle. On a recorded jail call, Chatmon and his brother hatched a plan to take the money from the uncle and laughed about it. The plan included several other conspirators.

On September 1, 2025, Chatmon and his co-conspirators put their plan into action. One conspirator lured the victim by pretending to need a ride. While the victim drove, Chatmon gave directions by cell phone. After the victim parked, Chatmon and the remaining conspirators carjacked the victim at gunpoint, hog-tied him, and kept him hostage in his own truck. They drove the victim around trying to get money out of his bank accounts, repeatedly pistol whipping and beating him. After successfully making cash withdrawals, the conspirators wanted more money, and the victim offered up a safe at his house with some cash. The conspirators drove to the victim’s house and, with the victim still tied up in his truck, Chatmon and Dneiqua Stroman broke into his house and stole the safe. They also tied up Chatmon’s aunt and left her in a bathtub. Then, the conspirators left the victim on the ground next to his truck and set his truck on fire before fleeing. Later, they met up with Anderson, who helped them move money from the victim’s Cash App account into their own.

The ATF and United States Attorney’s Office led the investigation. On September 25, 2025, the ATF executed search warrants at five residences in Detroit, Rochester Hills, and Pontiac, and arrested all the suspects.

With their guilty pleas, Chatmon, Lopez Martinez, Ieasha Stroman, and Dneiqua Stroman all face a mandatory minimum sentences of 7 years in federal prison and maximum possible sentences of life imprisonment. Anderson was previously sentenced to probation and ordered to pay restitution. Sentencing for the rest are scheduled as follows:

Leica Lopez Martinez – February 3, 2027

Dneiqua Stroman – February 9, 2027

Roland Chatmon – February 25, 2027

Ieasha Stroman – March 15, 2027

This case was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. It is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Andrew R. Picek and Diane N. Princ.
title: Five Defendants Convicted in Kidnapping Conspiracy Targeting Family Member

Los Angeles Woman Charged for $18M COVID-19 Relief Fraud Scheme
A federal grand jury in the Central District of California returned an indictment yesterday charging Marisela Nuno, 53, of Los Angeles, California, with an $18 million scheme to defraud the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) and the Economic Injury Disaster Loan (EIDL) program, federal stimulus programs authorized as part of the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act.
According to court documents, the defendant allegedly obtained funds under the PPP and EIDL program by submitting false and fraudulent loan applications that collectively sought over $15.7 million in PPP funds and over $2.6 million in EIDL funds. The defendant is alleged to have submitted applications on behalf of businesses and entities she purportedly owned, knowing that the applications contained materially false statements and misrepresentations concerning, among other things, the purported entities’ number of employees, average monthly payroll, gross revenues, and eligibility for funding.
The defendant also is alleged to have submitted materially false supporting tax documentation with the applications. The defendant then allegedly used the loan funds for purposes not authorized by the PPP or the EIDL program, including for the purchase of private property, business startup costs, and payments to family members.
Nuno is charged with three counts of wire fraud and one count of money laundering. If convicted, she faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison on each count of wire fraud, and 10 years in prison on the count of money laundering.
Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division (Fraud Division); Special Agent in Charge Robert Molvar of the FBI’s Criminal Division; Special Agent in Charge Darren Lian of the Internal Revenue Service, Criminal Investigation Division (IRS CI) Los Angeles Field Office, Special Agent in Charge Timothy Larson of the U.S. Small Business Administration Office of Inspector General (SBA OIG) made the announcement.
The FBI Los Angeles Field Office, IRS CI, and SBA OIG investigated the case.
Trial Attorney Ariel Glasner of the Fraud Division’s Public Trust and Financial Integrity Section and Trial Attorney Edward Emokpae of the Criminal Division’s White Collar and Corporate Enforcement Section are prosecuting the case.
On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
An indictment is merely an allegation, and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
title: Los Angeles Woman Charged for $18M COVID-19 Relief Fraud Scheme

Baltimore, Maryland – A Baltimore man pled guilty to a federal firearm-possession charge stemming from a domestic-violence incident.

Marquis Thomas, 34, is charged with possession of a firearm and ammunition by a prohibited person. Thomas is prohibited from possessing a firearm and ammunition due to a prior felony conviction.

Kelly O. Hayes, U.S. Attorney for the District of Maryland, announced the guilty plea with Special Agent in Charge Charles Doerrer, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives (ATF), and Commissioner Richard Worley, Baltimore Police Department (BPD).

According to the plea agreement, on October 30, 2025, BPD received a call about a domestic-assault involving a firearm. Upon law enforcement’s arrival at the residence, the victim opened the door and told officers that Thomas left the premises. The victim then led law enforcement into the living room and pointed to a handgun on the couch. Additionally, the victim reported that Thomas hit her in the face three times before pointing a gun at her, saying, “I should kill you right now.”

Thomas faces a maximum of 15 years in prison for possession of a firearm by a prohibited person. U.S. District Court Judge Adam B. Abelson set sentencing for Wednesday, Jan. 28, 2027, at 2 p.m.

Actual sentences for federal crimes are typically less than the maximum penalties. A federal district judge determines sentencing after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

This prosecution is part of Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) and Project Safe Home. These programs bring together all levels of law enforcement and the communities they serve to reduce violent crime and gun violence, and to make our neighborhoods safer for everyone. On May 26, 2021, the Department launched a violent crime reduction strategy strengthening PSN based on these core principles: fostering trust and legitimacy in our communities, supporting community-based organizations that help prevent violence from occurring in the first place, setting focused and strategic enforcement priorities, and measuring the results. Project Safe Home is an initiative under the Violence Against Women Act (VAWA) through the Office on Violence Against Women (OVW) to reduce domestic violence and prevent escalation to lethal violence by targeting offenders who use or possess handguns with a history of Domestic Violence.

In response, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Maryland is working closely with its federal, local, and state partners — along with Baltimore City community organizations — to reduce violent crime and enhance public safety. This partnership and coordination between the U.S. Attorney’s Office and the City of Baltimore ensures that federal resources are leveraged effectively to address intimidate-partner firearm violence.

U.S. Attorney Hayes commended the ATF and BPD for their collaborative efforts in this investigation. Ms. Hayes also thanked Special Assistant U.S. Attorney Kathleen Godwin who is prosecuting this federal case.

For more information about the Maryland U.S. Attorney’s Office, its priorities, and resources available to help the community, visit justice.gov/usao-md .

text:
The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), formerly called the Food Stamp Program, is designed primarily to increase the food purchasing power of eligible low-income households to help them afford a nutritionally adequate low-cost diet. This report describes the rules related to eligibility for SNAP benefits as well as the rules for benefits and their redemption. SNAP is administered by the U.S. Department of Agriculture's (USDA's) Food and Nutrition Administration (FNA, formerly Food and Nutrition Service [FNS]), in partnership with state SNAP agencies. SNAP is authorized by the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008. This law, formerly the Food Stamp Act of 1977, has since 1973 been periodically reauthorized by the farm bill—omnibus legislation that also typically includes the authorization of other federal agricultural policies and programs. The program was last reauthorized by the 2018 farm bill (P.L. 115-334), though other laws have amended SNAP policy since then. Many farm bill provisions expired in 2023 but were then extended through September 30, 2025. In a period of farm bill expiration, SNAP operations continue with the provision of appropriations. As of the date of this report, the 119th Congress has begun work on a 2026 farm bill but has not completed it.
This report focuses on SNAP. For an overview of SNAP along with other nutrition programs in the 2018 farm bill, see CRS In Focus IF11087, 2018 Farm Bill Primer: SNAP and Nutrition Title Programs. The FY2025 budget reconciliation law, P.L. 119-21, also made a number of changes to SNAP law. Many of these policies are mentioned in this report. For further detail on the law's SNAP provisions, see CRS Report R48552, Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and Related Nutrition Programs in P.L. 119-21: An Overview.
SNAP eligibility and benefits are calculated on a household basis. Financial eligibility is determined through either a traditional or a categorical eligibility path. Under traditional eligibility, applicant households must meet gross income, net income, and asset tests. Specifically, household gross monthly income (all income as defined by SNAP law) must be at or below 130% of the federal poverty level (FPL), and household net monthly income (i.e., minus SNAP-specified deductions) must be at 100% FPL. The traditional (inflation-adjusted) asset limit is set for FY2027 at $3,000 per household. Households that contain elderly or disabled members have a higher asset limit and do not have to meet the gross income test.
Under categorical eligibility, SNAP eligibility is automatically conveyed based upon the applicant's participation in other means-tested programs, namely Supplemental Security Income (SSI), Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), or General Assistance (GA). States have the option to offer SNAP program eligibility under different rules (known as broad-based categorical eligibility), including elimination of the asset test and a state-set gross income limit of up to 200% FPL. This practice stems from state flexibility in determining what constitutes TANF-funded benefits and who may receive them. Applicants and beneficiaries are also subject to nonfinancial rules, which include work requirements such as a three-month time limit for certain nondisabled adults.
In FY2025, an average of 42.4 million individuals in 22.6 million households participated in SNAP each month. Monthly benefits averaged $188.30 per person and $353.43 per household. Of the $102.6 billion in federal spending for the SNAP program, about 93% ($95.8 billion) was spent on benefits themselves.
If eligible for SNAP, an applicant household also undergoes a calculation of its monthly benefit amount (or allotment). This calculation uses the household's net income as well as the maximum allotment, a figure that equals the current value of the USDA-calculated Thrifty Food Plan (TFP).
Benefits are issued on an electronic benefits transfer (EBT) card, which operates with a declining balance like a debit card. Benefits are not cash, may not be accessed at an automatic teller machine, and are redeemable only for foods. Benefits may be redeemed for foods at licensed retailers, which may include a wide variety of retailers so long as retailers meet licensing requirements.
SNAP operates in the 50 states, the District of Columbia, Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands. In lieu of SNAP, Nutrition Assistance Program (NAP) block grant funding is provided to Puerto Rico, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, and American Samoa. Additionally, the Food Distribution Program on Indian Reservations provides, in lieu of SNAP benefits, food commodities to low-income households on reservations and to Native American families residing in Oklahoma or in designated areas near Oklahoma.
The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), formerly called the Food Stamp Program, is designed primarily to increase the food purchasing power of eligible low-income households to a point where they can afford a nutritionally adequate low-cost diet. This report describes the rules related to eligibility for SNAP benefits and the rules related to the issuance and use of benefits.
SNAP is authorized by the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008. This law, formerly the Food Stamp Act of 1977, has since 1973 been periodically reauthorized by the farm bill—omnibus legislation that also typically includes the reauthorization of other federal agricultural policies and programs. SNAP was most recently authorized by the 2018 farm bill (Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018; P.L. 115-334). See CRS In Focus IF11087, 2018 Farm Bill Primer: SNAP and Nutrition Title Programs, for further discussion of the nutrition program policy changes. As of the date of this report, the 119th Congress has begun work on a 2026 farm bill but has not completed it.1
Though reauthorized through the farm bills, SNAP's authorizing law has at times been amended by other bills, including most recently the FY2025 budget reconciliation law (P.L. 119-21/H.R. 1, enacted July 4, 2025). See CRS Report R48552, Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and Related Nutrition Programs in P.L. 119-21: An Overview. As of the date of this report, the U.S. Department of Agriculture's (USDA's) Food and Nutrition Administration (FNA, formerly Food and Nutrition Service [FNS])2 is in the process of issuing guidance and otherwise implementing the policy changes associated with P.L. 119-21's SNAP provisions. Consider references to P.L. 119-21 in this report (e.g., work requirements, state funding, immigrant eligibility) subject to additional detail in agency guidance and rulemaking.3
The Food, Conservation, and Energy Act of 2008 (2008 farm bill; P.L. 110-246) changed the name of the program from the Food Stamp Program to SNAP and revised the name of the governing law from the Food Stamp Act to the Food and Nutrition Act. State names for the program may vary; some states continue to name their programs "food stamps," while others have switched to SNAP or maintain other names.4
SNAP benefits are available for households that meet financial eligibility tests for limited monthly income and (in some states) liquid assets. To be eligible for SNAP, household members must fulfill requirements related to work effort and must meet citizenship and legal permanent residence tests.
In general, the maximum SNAP benefit is based upon the level of USDA's lowest cost food plan (the Thrifty Food Plan or TFP) and varies by household size.
Monthly SNAP benefit amounts are calculated as the difference between the household's expected contribution to its food costs and the maximum benefit. (Participating households are expected to devote 30% of their net monthly cash income to food purchases.) Thus, a recipient household with no net cash income receives the maximum monthly SNAP allotment for its size, while a household with some counted income receives a lesser allotment—the maximum benefit minus 30% of the net income. Net income is the gross income with certain SNAP-law-specified deductions subtracted.
This report provides current participation, benefit amount, and spending figures. For a historical table of such information (dating back to 1990), see Table A-1.
FNS administers SNAP in partnership with SNAP state agencies. States are responsible for certifying household eligibility and issuing benefits to households, while FNS administers retailer authorization and oversight functions. SNAP operates in the 50 states, the District of Columbia, Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands. (References to "state" or "SNAP state agency" in this report refer to these jurisdictions.)
The federal government currently funds 100% of benefit costs and—newly effective October 1, 2026—25% of the state's SNAP administrative costs. The benefit cost-share policy is to change in future years according to P.L. 119-21 provisions. In FY2028, with the possibility of later implementation for some states, a state may be required to share part of the cost of SNAP benefits, depending on the state's payment accuracy, measured by the Payment Error Rate (PER).6
A detailed framework of federal law and regulation exists, as does a robust framework of state options and waivers. Thus, while universal concepts of benefit eligibility and administration exist among the states, there are also many policies that vary among the states.7 One variation is that some states delegate their administration of SNAP even further to county, regional, or municipal governments. This report focuses on the federal framework but will at times discuss state options that may cause state and local programs to vary.
In lieu of SNAP, Nutrition Assistance Program (NAP) block grant funding is provided to Puerto Rico, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, and American Samoa.8 Additionally, the Food Distribution Program on Indian Reservations provides, in lieu of SNAP benefits, food commodities to low-income households on Indian reservations and to Native American families residing in Oklahoma or in designated areas near Oklahoma.9
SNAP has financial, work-related, and categorical tests for eligibility:
In addition to eligibility rules, there are also disqualifications of eligibility to specific groups (e.g., workers on strike, many noncitizens and postsecondary students, people living in institutional settings, many drug felons). However, applications cannot be denied because of the length of a household's residence in a SNAP agency's jurisdiction, because the household has no fixed mailing address or does not reside in a permanent dwelling, or because the applicant does not provide a driver's license or photograph identification.
The basic SNAP beneficiary unit is the household. A household can be either a person living alone or a group of individuals living together. There is no requirement for cooking facilities. Generally speaking, individuals living together constitute a single household if they customarily purchase food and prepare meals together. Members of the same household must apply together, and their income, expenses, and assets are normally aggregated in determining SNAP eligibility and benefits. However, persons who live together can sometimes be considered separate households for program purposes.
Persons who live together, but purchase food and prepare meals separately, may apply for SNAP benefits separately, except for (1) spouses; (2) parents and their children (21 years old or younger); and (3) minors 18 years old or younger who live under the parental control of caretakers (excluding foster children and, in some cases, citizen children of noncitizen parents, who may be treated separately). In addition, persons 60 years old or older who live with others and cannot purchase food and prepare meals separately because of substantial disability may apply separately from their co-residents so long as their co-residents' income is below 165% of the federal poverty level (FPL).10
Although those living in institutional settings are generally barred from SNAP, individuals in certain types of group living arrangements may be eligible and are automatically treated as separate households regardless of how food is purchased and meals are prepared. These arrangements must be approved by state or local agencies and include residential drug addiction or alcoholic treatment programs, small group homes for the disabled, shelters for battered women and children, and shelters for the homeless.
If a household includes an elderly or disabled member, the household is entitled to different SNAP deduction rules as well as some different financial eligibility rules (discussed in the next section). Financially eligible one- and two-person households (in the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia) are also ensured (for FY2027) a minimum monthly benefit of $25.11 Without the minimum benefit it may be possible that these smaller households would be eligible for SNAP but for an arguably negligible amount. It is possible that different SNAP households can live together, and recipients can reside with nonrecipients. In the case of recipients residing with nonrecipients, the eligibility and benefit level of the household is based on a household size that excludes the nonrecipients. Whether the nonrecipients' income or assets are included depends upon the specific circumstances.
The SNAP definition of household is different than that used in other means-tested programs (e.g., TANF families with dependent children, elderly or disabled individuals or couples in the SSI program). However, it is close to those used by some other programs such as the National School Lunch Program; the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC); and the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP).
There are two pathways to eligibility for SNAP. The first is the traditional pathway to eligibility with financial eligibility thresholds stated in the Food and Nutrition Act (7 U.S.C. §2011 et seq.). Federal law sets income and asset eligibility thresholds as well as the rules for what types of income and assets are counted or disregarded. Also, the act lists what types of expenses can be deducted in determining income eligibility and, if eligible, determining the benefit amount.
The second pathway is known as categorical eligibility. The basis of categorical eligibility is a rule that makes households composed entirely of recipients of benefits funded from the TANF block grant, SSI cash assistance, or state GA automatically eligible for SNAP. Recipients of benefits from these programs bypass financial eligibility rules and automatically go to the next step, determining SNAP benefits. However, states have the option of interpreting categorical eligibility broadly. Below is a discussion of the traditional pathway to SNAP eligibility, followed by a discussion of categorical eligibility.
For households without elderly or disabled members, SNAP uses both the household's basic (or gross) monthly income and its counted (or net) monthly income. Eligible households' gross income must be at or below gross income standards, and their counted income must meet net income eligibility thresholds. When judging eligibility for a household with elderly or disabled members, only the household's counted net monthly income is considered. In effect, this procedure applies a somewhat less strict income test to the elderly and disabled.
In general, gross monthly income includes all of a household's cash income. When a type of income is not explicitly excluded by law, it is counted or included. This is the case with, for example, the military basic allowance for housing, which is counted because it is not excluded in current law. The Food and Nutrition Act and regulation specifically excludes from gross income12 (1) most payments made to third parties (rather than directly to the household); (2) unanticipated, irregular, or infrequent income, up to $30 a quarter; (3) loans13; (4) income received for the care of someone outside the household; (5) nonrecurring lump sum payments such as income tax refunds, retroactive lump sum Social Security payments, and certain charitable donations14; (6) federal energy assistance (e.g., LIHEAP); (7) reimbursement for expenses15; (8) income earned by schoolchildren 17 or younger; (9) the cost of producing self-employment income; (10) federal postsecondary student aid (e.g., Pell grants, student loans); (11) "on the job" training earnings of dependent children under 19 in the Workforce Investment and Opportunity Act programs; (12) income set aside by disabled SSI recipients under an approved "plan for achieving self-support"; and (13) combat-related military pay. Gross income also excludes types of income disregarded by other federal laws. For example, the Internal Revenue Code bars federal income tax refunded—including those resulting from refundable tax credits such as the Earned Income Tax Credit and the Child Tax Credit—from being counted in need-tested programs, including SNAP.16 These refunds are also excluded from being counted as a liquid asset for a period of 12 months. Other examples of payments disregarded by federal law other than the Food and Nutrition Act include training allowances under the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act, various payments under laws relating to Indians, and payments under Older Americans Act employment programs for the elderly.
States have the option to exclude from gross income child support payments made by a nonresident parent for a child living outside the household. In addition, states may, within certain limits, choose to exclude other types of income that they disregard in their TANF or Medicaid programs.
Net monthly income is computed by subtracting certain deductions from a household's basic (or gross) monthly income. This calculation is based on the recognition that not all of a household's income is available for food purchases. Thus, a standard portion of income, plus amounts representing costs such as work expenses or high nonfood living expenses, is deducted from the gross income.
For households without elderly or disabled members, net monthly income equals gross monthly income minus the following deductions, if applicable:
The amount of the standard deduction depends upon household size and statutorily set parameters (amounts shown in Table 118 In the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia, the FY2027 minimum standard deduction is $217 a month. Because of different living costs, different standard deductions apply in Alaska, Hawaii, Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands.
The excess shelter deduction is restricted to annually indexed monthly limits. For FY2027, these are $769 for the 48 states and the District of Columbia, $1,229 for Alaska, $1,036 for Hawaii, $903 for Guam, and $606 for the U.S. Virgin Islands. (This deduction is a way to further account for the variability of shelter costs across the country.)
For households with elderly or disabled members, net monthly income equals gross monthly income minus:
The calculation of net income discussed in this section is pertinent not just for determining eligibility but also for calculating the SNAP benefit amount to which the household is entitled (discussed below).
Under the traditional path to SNAP eligibility, households must have net monthly income that does not exceed 100% FPL. Households without elderly or disabled members must also have gross monthly income that does not exceed 130% FPL. Both these income eligibility limits are uniform for the 48 contiguous states, the District of Columbia, Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands. Somewhat higher income eligibility limits (because of higher poverty guidelines) are applied in Alaska and Hawaii. Net and gross income eligibility limits (which are adjusted for inflation each October) are summarized in Table 2.
Under the traditional pathway to eligibility, households cannot have counted liquid assets that exceed federally prescribed limits. In FY2027, a household without an elderly or disabled member cannot have counted liquid assets above $3,000. In that year, a household with an elderly or disabled member cannot have counted liquid assets above $4,750. These dollar limits are to be annually indexed for overall inflation (and rounded down to the nearest $250).19
Counted liquid assets include cash on hand, checking and savings accounts, savings certificates, stocks and bonds, and nonrecurring lump sum payments such as insurance settlements and lump sum payments that have been disregarded as income (e.g., some tax refunds) but have not been spent. Certain assets are also counted: a portion of the value of vehicles (in some cases) and the equity value of property not producing income consistent with its value (e.g., recreational property).
Counted assets do not include the value of the household's primary residence (home and surrounding property); business assets; personal property (household goods and personal effects); lump sum earned income tax credit and other nonrecurring payments; burial plots; the cash value of life insurance policies; the value of all tax-recognized pension savings/plans and education savings; and certain other resources whose value is not accessible to the household, that would not yield more than $1,000 if sold (e.g., a car with a small equity value), or that are required to be disregarded by other federal laws.
Some special rules apply when counting allowable assets. Although the general rule is that the fair market value of a vehicle in excess of $4,650 is to be counted as an asset, states may (and most often do) count vehicles as assets only to the extent they do under their TANF programs or disregard them entirely. Moreover, states may generally exclude additional assets to the extent they do so under their TANF or Medicaid programs.
SNAP also conveys eligibility to households that already participate in specific means-tested programs. Households composed entirely of recipients of public assistance funded from the TANF block grant, SSI, or state General Assistance programs are automatically (or categorically) eligible for SNAP. These applicants bypass the income eligibility and asset eligibility rules of the traditional pathway to SNAP eligibility discussed above.
In addition, states have the option to grant SNAP eligibility to those who receive, or are authorized to receive, any TANF-funded benefit. TANF is a broad-purpose block grant that funds a wide range of allowable expenditures in addition to traditional public assistance for families with children. Some such TANF-funded benefits are not restricted to families with children and may serve any individual. A state may extend this broad-based categorical eligibility to any type of household (with or without children) in the state and may determine the gross income limit for SNAP that applies in the state, though it cannot set a gross income limit above 200% FPL. Broad-based categorical eligibility also permits states to not use an asset test for SNAP.20
Categorical eligibility does not automatically entitle a household to a SNAP benefit. Households must still have net income below a level that results in a nonzero SNAP benefit.
Current SNAP law has rules on employment or work-related activities for able-bodied, nonelderly adult participants. Some rules apply in all states that operate SNAP. However, because each state designs its own SNAP Employment and Training Program (E&T), certain requirements can vary by state.
To gain or retain eligibility, most adults who are not elderly or disabled must do the following:
Individuals are disqualified from SNAP for failure to comply with work requirements for periods of time that differ based upon whether the violation is the first, second, or third. Minimum periods of disqualification, which may be increased by the state SNAP agency, range from one to six months. In addition, states have the option to disqualify the entire household for up to 180 days if the household head fails to comply with work requirements.
The law exempts certain individuals from the above requirements.21
SNAP agencies must operate Employment and Training (E&T) programs of their own design for work registrants. SNAP agencies may require all work registrants to participate in one or more components of their programs or limit participation by further exempting additional categories and individuals for whom participation is judged impracticable or not cost effective.23 States may also make E&T activities open only to those who volunteer to participate.
Program components can include any or all of the following: supervised job search or training for job search, workfare (work-for-benefits), work experience or training programs, education programs to improve basic skills, or any other employment or training activity approved by FNS.24
SNAP also imposes a special time limit, requiring work for able-bodied adults. This requirement—historically referred to as the Able-Bodied Adults Without Dependents (ABAWD) rule—was added by the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 (P.L. 104-193). It was amended by the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 (P.L. 118-5) and then most recently by the FY2025 budget reconciliation law (P.L. 119-21, enacted July 4, 2025).26 In FY2025, prior to P.L. 119-21, this rule applied to ABAWDs ages 18-55. Currently, under P.L. 119-21, the time limit is expanded to apply to able-bodied adults ages 18-65 and includes any adult with a youngest dependent of 14 years of age or older.
SNAP law limits benefits for this population to three months out of a 36-month period, unless the participant:
Certain individuals are exempt from the time limit. As indicated earlier, adults 65 or older and adults with dependents under age 14 are exempt. Adults "medically certified as physically or mentally unfit for employment" are exempt. Also exempt are those who are pregnant, exempt from the general work requirements,28 or "Indian" (as defined by the law).29 The Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 had exempted veterans, homeless individuals, and former foster children age 24 or younger from the time limit; P.L. 119-21 struck those exemptions.
States have the option to offer anyone subject to the time limit a slot in an E&T program or a workfare program. Some states pledge to serve all of them in such programs; others do not. States that pledge to serve all subject to the time limit in these programs receive extra federal funding for that purpose. If a state does not offer a slot in an E&T or workfare program, benefits can be terminated for an individual without at least a half-time job once the three-month limit is reached unless he or she is covered by an exemption or a waiver of the time limit for able-bodied adults.
Those who lose benefits under this rule are able to reenter the program if, during a 30-day period, they work or participate in work/training activity for at least 20 hours per week.30
SNAP law also makes available waivers and discretionary exemptions from the time limit. A state, under P.L. 119-21's stricter terms, may request a waiver for an area with an unemployment rate of over 10%, with added flexibilities for Alaska and Hawaii.31 Prior to the change, a state could apply for waivers for all or part of the state using the more permissive grounds of "lack of sufficient jobs," as defined in regulation. States may also, at their discretion, exempt some individuals per month from the rule based on a formula set in the law.32
In addition to exemptions and waivers, enacted emergency legislation has, in several instances, suspended the ABAWD rule nationwide.33
Eligibility is sometimes denied for reasons other than financial need or compliance with work requirements.
Many noncitizens are barred, and P.L. 119-21 further reduced the types of lawfully present immigrants that may be eligible for SNAP. Under the amended law, eligibility is extended only to lawful permanent residents,34 the elderly and disabled who were lawfully residing before August 1996, Cuban-Haitian entrants, and Compact of Free Association migrants lawfully residing in the United States.<del> </del>
SNAP benefits are denied to those who intentionally violate program rules, for specific time periods ranging from one year (on a first violation) to permanently (on a third violation or other serious infraction). A state may disqualify an individual from SNAP if he or she is disqualified from another public assistance program. Those who transfer assets for the purpose of qualifying for benefits are also barred.
For the most part, college students (attending higher education courses half-time or more) between ages 18 and 50 are ineligible for SNAP. A student enrolled in an institution of higher education more than half-time is eligible for SNAP benefits only if the individual is (1) under age 18 or age 50 or older, (2) disabled, (3) enrolled in school because of participation in certain programs,35 (4) employed at least 20 hours per week or participating in a work-study program during the school year, (5) a parent (in some circumstances),36 or (6) receiving TANF cash assistance benefits.37
Other ineligibility rules include the following:
There are circumstances where SNAP benefits are offered separately and distinctly from the standard SNAP application and eligibility process. These situations include the issuance of transitional and disaster benefits.
States are allowed to provide transitional benefits. States have the option to offer up to five months' transitional SNAP benefits to someone leaving TANF or a similar state-financed program (for reasons other than a sanction) without requiring that the household apply for SNAP. The transitional benefit is the amount received prior to leaving TANF (or a similar state program), adjusted to account for the loss of TANF/state cash income. Transitional benefit households may reapply during the five-month period to have their benefits adjusted based on changed circumstances, and a state may opt to adjust benefits based on information received from another program (such as Medicaid) in which the household participates. At the end of the transitional period, a household may reapply for continued benefits under regular SNAP rules. According to the most recent SNAP State Options Report, as of October 1, 2024, 24 SNAP state agencies provide transitional benefits.39
For areas affected by natural or other disasters, states may request that USDA operate the Disaster Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (D-SNAP).40 SNAP benefits are provided to already-participating SNAP households who qualify for replacement or additional benefits as well as to non-SNAP households that become temporarily eligible under D-SNAP rules. If a disaster results in households' ongoing loss of income, households may be eligible to apply for SNAP under regular program rules after the D-SNAP benefit period has ended.
Until the implementation of Section 10105 of P.L. 119-21, SNAP benefits are 100% federally financed and constitute the vast majority of federal spending for the SNAP program. This section discusses how SNAP benefit amounts are determined, how the benefits are issued, what benefits may and may not be used for, and the redemption of benefits.
Once a household is eligible for SNAP, it is also subject to a benefit calculation process, which determines the household's monthly benefit amount or allotment. The calculation of SNAP benefits takes into account the size of the household, the maximum benefit for the fiscal year, and the household's net income. For one- and two-person households, the minimum benefit may also play a role.
Maximum monthly benefit allotments are tied to the cost of a nutritionally adequate low-cost diet, as measured by the Thrifty Food Plan (TFP), created and calculated by USDA.42 The TFP is the cheapest of four diet plans meeting minimal nutrition requirements devised by USDA, specifically USDA's Center for Nutrition Policy and Promotion. Maximum allotments are set at the monthly cost of the TFP for a four-person family consisting of a couple between ages 20 and 50 and two school-age children, adjusted for family size (using a formula reflecting economies of scale developed by the Human Nutrition Information Service) and rounded down to the nearest whole dollar.
Allotments are adjusted for food price inflation each October to reflect the cost of the TFP in the immediately previous June. Although USDA calculates the cost of the TFP each year to account for food price inflation, the contents of the TFP—often thought of as its own market basket of goods—was last revised in 2021. Under a provision of the 2018 farm bill, the TFP was scheduled to be revised every five years. After P.L. 119-21 amendments to this provision, the TFP is expected to be revised less frequently and be recalculated under additional constraints. Maximum allotments are standard across the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia, but they are higher—reflecting substantially different food costs—in Alaska, Hawaii, Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands.
Table 3. Maximum Possible Monthly SNAP Allotments, FY2027
Effective October 1, 2026, through September 30, 2027

Note:
a. Maximum allotment levels in rural Alaska are 27% to 55% higher than the urban Alaska allotments noted in this table. See FNA, "SNAP—Fiscal Year 2027 Cost-of-Living Adjustments."
SNAP benefits are a function of a household's size, its net (counted) monthly income, and inflation-indexed maximum monthly benefit levels (in some cases, adjusted for geographic location). An eligible household's net income is determined (i.e., the deductions noted earlier for judging eligibility are subtracted from gross income), its maximum benefit level is established, and a benefit is calculated by subtracting its expected contribution (by law, 30% of its net income) from its maximum allotment. Thus, as shown in Figure 1, a three-person household in one of the 48 states with $400 in counted net income (after deductions) would receive a monthly allotment of $688 in FY2027.44 A three-person household with no counted income would receive the maximum monthly benefit.
Benefits are not taxable, and purchases made with SNAP benefits may not be charged sales taxes. Receipt of SNAP benefits does not affect eligibility for, or benefits provided by, other public assistance programs, although some programs use SNAP participation as a trigger for eligibility, and others take into account the general availability of SNAP benefits in deciding what level of benefits to provide.
Eligible one- or two-person households are guaranteed a minimum monthly benefit allotment equal to 8% of the maximum benefit for a one-person household. This 2008 change replaced an older rule stipulating a minimum benefit of $10 a month only for one- and two-person households.45 For FY2027, the minimum benefit is $25 a month for a household in the 48 states and the District of Columbia. This means that if the benefit calculation for a one- or two-person household yields a result of less than $25, that household is guaranteed to receive $25 a month.
In FY2024, 9.1% of SNAP households received the minimum benefit.46
Benefit issuance is a state responsibility, and states contract with private vendors to carry out most of their issuance activities. Benefits are provided through electronic benefits transfer (EBT) systems under which recipients are issued EBT cards loaded with benefits, which are then used to make food purchases. At the point of sale, the retailer debits the recipient's SNAP account and credits its own account. EBT cards can include both SNAP benefits (usable only to buy food items) and cash benefits (e.g., TANF payments, unemployment payments, child support payments). Only cash benefits can be accessed using the card at ATMs.47 The majority of SNAP state agencies issue benefits on EBT cards with magnetic stripes, but some states have transitioned to or are planning a transition to chip cards to prevent theft of benefits.48
SNAP benefits are normally issued monthly. The state SNAP agency must either deny eligibility or make benefits available within 30 days of initial application and must provide allotments without interruption if an eligible household reapplies and fulfills recertification requirements in a timely manner. Households in immediate need because of little or no income and limited cash assets, as well as the homeless and those with extraordinarily high shelter expenses, must be given expedited service (provision of benefits within seven days of initial application). A household's calculated monthly allotment can be prorated (reduced) for one month. On application, a household's first month's benefit is reduced to reflect the date of application. If a previously participating household does not meet eligibility recertification requirements in a timely fashion, but does subsequently become certified for eligibility, benefits for the first month of its new certification period are normally prorated to reflect the date when recertification requirements were met.
SNAP benefits are not the same as cash. Although SNAP benefits have a dollar value, they may be spent only on eligible food at authorized retailers equipped with EBT point-of-sale systems.50
In general, SNAP benefits may be redeemed for any foods in approved retailers for home preparation and consumption.51 SNAP benefits may not be redeemed for alcohol, tobacco, or hot foods intended for immediate consumption.
SNAP may also be redeemed for seeds and plants to produce food for personal consumption. Elderly and disabled recipients and their spouses may redeem SNAP benefits for meals prepared and served through approved communal dining programs or home-delivered meal providers. SNAP may also be redeemed for meals prepared and served to residents of drug addiction and alcoholic treatment programs, small group homes for the disabled, shelters for battered women and children, and shelters or other establishments serving the homeless. In the case of certain remote areas of Alaska, benefits may be redeemed for items used to procure food by hunting and fishing (e.g., nets, hooks, fishing rods, and knives).52
According to annual benefit redemption data, in FY2025 nearly 100% of SNAP benefits were redeemed in markets and stores, and the remaining share (approximately 0.4%) were redeemed at meal services and delivery routes.53 Superstores and supermarkets made up 15% of retailers authorized, but 72% of SNAP benefits were redeemed at these stores. Convenience stores made up 44% of retailers authorized, but 5% of benefits were redeemed at them (see Table 4 for this FY2025 redemption data by retailer type).54
Under SNAP law's demonstration authorities,55 the Trump Administration has solicited and approved state requests to limit the foods SNAP recipients can buy.56 As of September 25, 2026, requests from 18 states have been approved to limit a variety of foods, including sugar-sweetened beverages and candy. The exact food restrictions vary by state. Some of the approved projects are currently operating, and others are expected to begin later this year or in 2027. Additionally, USDA had previously approved five states' waivers, though these waivers are now paused in response to ongoing litigation.57 In past years, some jurisdictions had requested to pilot similar policies, but past Administrations denied such requests.58

HONOLULU – United States Attorney Ken Sorenson announced that Eric Lee Boltz, 52, most recently residing in Montana, pled guilty on November 4, 2026 to one count of cyberstalking. Boltz was remanded into custody following his plea, and sentencing is scheduled for March 4, 2027, before Senior United States District Judge J. Michael Seabright.

According to court records, in December 2025, Boltz left a series of threatening and antisemitic voicemails with Hawaii Governor Josh Green’s office. Disguising his voice, Boltz threatened to kill the Governor and his family and sexually assault his daughter. When interviewed by law enforcement, Boltz said he left the voicemails to “shake [Governor Green] up.”

In his plea agreement, Boltz admitted that he was motivated to engage in his cyberstalking campaign due to Governor Green’s official government position and religion.

At sentencing, Boltz faces up to 5 years in prison, a fine of up to $250,000, plus a term of supervised release.

The FBI investigated the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Barbara Eucker is prosecuting the case.
title: Man Pleads Guilty to Cyberstalking After Sending Repeated Antisemitic Threats to Kill Governor of Hawaii and His Family

Ranking Member Scott to Trump Administration: “Save Everything”
“Any agency employee who ‘willfully and unlawfully conceals, removes, mutilates, obliterates, falsifies, or destroys’ or attempts any such action against a federal record is subject to fine and/or imprisonment for up to three years.”
WASHINGTON – Today, House Education and Workforce Committee Ranking Member Robert C. “Bobby” Scott (VA-03) issued notices to heads of ten federal departments and agencies under the Committee’s jurisdiction, reminding them of their obligation under the Federal Records Act of 1950 (FRA) to preserve all records that may be in the public interest.
“As you are aware, the FRA requires all departments and agencies in the Executive Branch to collect, retain, and preserve records that document ‘the transaction of public business’ or contain ‘informational value.’ The FRA’s regulations require the head of each federal agency to ‘make and preserve records containing adequate and proper documentation of the organization, functions, policies, decisions, procedures, and essential transactions of the agency,’” wrote Ranking Member Scott.
In his letters, the Ranking Member emphasized the importance of full compliance with the law that allows Congress to conduct oversight on behalf of the American people, noting that federal officials and employees who violate the FRA face criminal penalties, including up to three years in prison. In addition, any federal officeholder convicted of violating the FRA can lose their position and be disqualified from holding future federal office.
“The American people have given Congress a clear mandate to root out waste, fraud, and abuse within the Administration. I request an assurance, in writing, by November 18, 2026, that records, documents, data, or information have not been and will not be concealed, modified, removed, transferred, destroyed, or otherwise rendered inaccessible,” concluded Ranking Member Scott.

American coins are produced by the U.S. Mint. The U.S. Mint was established by the Coinage Act of 1792 (1 Stat. 246) to produce coins. This In Focus discusses types of coins produced by the U.S. Mint, a bureau of the Department of the Treasury. These include circulating coins, bullion coins, and numismatic coins.
The U.S. Mint strikes circulating coins—coins produced for everyday transactions. Most design aspects of circulating coins are required by law. Pursuant to statute (31 U.S.C. §5112), Congress instructs the Secretary of the Treasury, through the U.S. Mint, to issue specific denominations of circulating coins and specifies the coins' size, weight, and metallic content. For example, the U.S. Mint may issue "a quarter dollar that is 0.955 inch in diameter and weights 5.67 grams" and that is made of a copper and nickel alloy (31 U.S.C. §5112(a)(3) and (b)).
In addition to specific denominations, size, and metallic content, Congress also requires that specified design elements be present on certain coinage. For example, this includes the inscriptions "In God We Trust" and "Liberty" on a coin's obverse, and "United States of America" and "E Pluribus Unum" on a coin's reverse ((31 U.S.C. §5112(d)(1)). Additionally, for some coins, the law specifies the obverse's image—for example, Thomas Jefferson on the nickel's obverse.
For other aspects of coin design not specified by Congress, the Secretary of the Treasury is authorized to change the design or die of a coin only once within 25 years of the first adoption of the design features for that coin (31 U.S.C. §5112(d)(2)). Figure 1 shows the 2025 circulating nickel, dime, and quarter coins.
For more information on circulating coins, see CRS In Focus IF10533, Congressional Involvement in the Design of Circulating Coins; CRS In Focus IF12293, Penny: History and Current Status; CRS In Focus IF12593, Nickels and Dimes: History and Current Status; CRS In Focus IF11394, Quarter and Half Dollar Coins: History and Current Status; and CRS In Focus IF11190, U.S. Dollar Coins: History and Current Status.
The U.S. Mint produces bullion coins as "investment-grade" products purchased by "investors seeking a simple and tangible means to own and invest in the gold, silver, platinum, and palladium markets." Bullion coins are not sold directly to the public. The U.S. Mint sells bullion coins to a "network of official distributors called 'authorized purchasers,'" who sell the bullion coins to the public.
Bullion coins can be struck in gold, silver, platinum, and palladium. Recent bullion coins all include an eagle on the reverse. On the obverse, the 2026 gold and silver bullion coins feature an image of Liberty. In 2025, the U.S. Mint produced platinum and palladium coins. The 2025 platinum coin featured the First Amendment's "Right to Petition," with an image of an oak tree on the obverse and an eagle on the reverse. The palladium coin featured Liberty on the obverse and an eagle on the reverse. Figure 2 shows recent designs of bullion coins.
The U.S. Mint also produces numismatic coins designed for collectors. Numismatic coins are sometimes minted to commemorate a historical occurrence or event and are sometimes made of precious metals.
Numismatic coins specifically authorized by Congress generally include two types of coins: commemorative coins and other congressionally authorized coins.
Commemorative Coins
Congress authorizes commemorative coins to celebrate and honor American people, places, events, and institutions. Considered legal tender, commemorative coins are not minted for general circulation. Instead, they are designed to be collected and to assist groups designated by statute ("statutorily designated groups") raise money to support the group's activities through authorized surcharges added to the coin's cost.
Commemorative coin authorization legislation generally specifies certain aspects of the coins, which have included requirements for inscriptions, metallic content, and design. For example, the 2026 commemorative coins for the FIFA World Cup were required to list the year (2026) and "inscriptions of the words 'Liberty,' 'In God We Trust,' 'United States of America,' and 'E Pluribus Unum.'" Figure 3 shows the 2026 FIFA World Cup commemorative coins.
For more information on commemorative coins, see CRS In Focus IF10262, Commemorative Coins: An Overview, by Jacob R. Straus, and CRS Report R44623, Commemorative Coins: Background, Legislative Process, and Issues for Congress, by Jacob R. Straus.
Other Numismatic Coins
In addition to commemorative coins, Congress has directly authorized other numismatic coins. These include authorizations for specific coins (the Buffalo $50 coin (31 U.S.C. §5112(q)) and the reissuance of the Morgan Dollar and Peace Dollar coins (P.L. 116-286)); and the authorization to redesign a coin, but without specific design instructions (the semiquincentennial $1 coin for 2026 that featured President Donald J. Trump on the obverse (31 U.S.C. §5112(y)(1)(C)).
Additionally, Congress has also authorized the Mint to issue silver versions of circulating coins (31 U.S.C. §5132(a)(2)).
The U.S. Mint also produces numismatic precious metal coins for which Congress has not directly specified a design. For example, in 2020, the U.S. Mint issued gold $10 coins to honor the 400th anniversary of the Mayflower (see Figure 4).
For 2026, the U.S. Mint issued several numismatic coins. These include a nonround "Freedom Ringing" Liberty Bell gold coin (and accompanying silver medal). The U.S. Mint also issued a "Best of the Mint" series that honors five historic coins with gold coins that feature each of the five coins' original design (accompanied by silver medals that feature a modernized version inspired by the original design). For more information on the semiquincentennial coins, see CRS In Focus IF13165, Commemoration of the 250th Anniversary of the Declaration of Independence: Coins and Medals, by Jacob R. Straus.
title: Types of Coins Produced by the U.S. Mint

The Committee convened in a closed session at the Department of the Treasury at 10:45 a.m. All members were present. Denise Rosenhaft Gray from BNY was also present to assist the Committee Chair. Assistant Secretary for Financial Markets Hunter McMaster, Deputy Assistant Secretary for Federal Finance Brian Smith, Director of the Office of Debt Management Fred Pietrangeli, and Deputy Director of the Office of Debt Management Tom Katzenbach welcomed the Committee. Other members of Treasury staff present were Abigail Brown, Chris Cameron, Dave Chung, Gabriella Csepe, Robert Dunsky, Chandler Elwyn, Gary Grippo, Salar Moghadam, Gavin Ross, Renee Tang, and Spencer Woodruff. Federal Reserve Bank of New York staff members Ellen Correia Golay, Peggy Kauh, and Kyle Watson were also present.
Director Pietrangeli highlighted changes in receipts and outlays through Q4 FY2026. Within receipts, Pietrangeli cited a $159 billion (5%) increase in withheld and a $103 billion (9%) increase in non-withheld taxes. These increases were offset by a $22 billion decrease in customs deposits, adjusting for tariff refunds, as well as a $43 billion (-9%) decrease in gross corporate taxes and a $27 billion increase (79%) in corporate refunds, the latter two attributed to provisions from the One Big Beautiful Bill. In terms of outlays, Pietrangeli noted that the largest increases occurred at the Department of the Treasury, which rose by $122 billion (8%) due to higher gross interest resulting from higher levels of debt, and at the Department of Health and Human Services, which rose by $120 billion (6%) because of higher Medicare and Medicaid spending.
Pietrangeli then turned to deficit and privately-held net marketable borrowing projections, noting that the median primary dealer’s aggregate FY2027-28 privately-held net marketable borrowing estimate was nearly unchanged since last quarter’s Committee meeting. He noted that current issuance sizes would result in a modest funding shortfall in FY2027 relative to projected borrowing needs, but that the gap could likely be managed using bills. However, looking ahead to FY2028-2029, the median primary dealer forecast for privately-held net marketable borrowing implies a $2.14 trillion funding shortfall based on current coupon auction sizes and privately-held bill supply.
Debt Manager Dunsky next reviewed primary dealers’ feedback on whether Treasury should avoid scheduling Treasury bill and floating rate note (FRN) auctions on days when the Federal Open Market Committee is expected to release a statement (i.e., “FOMC days”), which would be consistent with its existing scheduling practices for nominal coupons and TIPS. Almost all primary dealers favored no change to the auction schedule. Primary dealers pointed to operational complexities associated with conducting more auctions on the surrounding days as generating a greater cost than any benefit associated with avoiding bill and FRN auctions on FOMC days. Overall, dealers do not currently see bill and FRN auctions on FOMC days as a problem.
Debt Manager Elwyn then summarized primary dealers’ views on the effects of the larger liquidity-support buyback operations announced on August 19 for the 10- to 20-year and 20- to 30-year sectors, as well as potential enhancements to the buyback program. Most dealers reported at least modest improvements in liquidity and market functioning, citing a more dependable outlet for off-the-run securities, less risk of price dislocations, and more stable relative-value relationships, although the effect on dealers’ ability to intermediate client flows was mixed. Recommendations from primary dealers included clearer and earlier communication, broader distribution of purchases through per-CUSIP limits, and smaller, more frequent operations. Some dealers noted that concentrated purchases increased the risk of “missing” the buyback and having to manage the associated duration exposure. Dealers also discussed spread-based pricing and switch transactions, both of which have been discussed previously and would require further exploration and significant time and effort to implement.
Deputy Director Katzenbach next recapped primary dealers’ thoughts on trends in structural demand for Treasuries. Money market mutual funds, stablecoins, and the Federal Reserve System Open Market Account (SOMA) were identified as potential sources of growing demand for bills, while respondents pointed to increased bank demand in the belly of the curve. Conversely, primary dealers had mixed views about market demand for longer-dated securities from liability-driven investors.
Katzenbach then reviewed primary dealers’ expectations for coupon issuance. Respondents generally expected Treasury to begin increasing nominal coupon and FRN auction sizes by the end of FY2027, and overwhelmingly expected Treasury to focus the eventual increases in short- and intermediate-dated tenors. Katzenbach noted that several primary dealers reiterated their view that Treasury should consider issuing a 1-year SOFR-indexed FRN. The Committee agreed that exploring potential issuance of SOFR-indexed FRNs would be worthwhile and suggested that multiple tenors be considered in light of potential interest from different investor types.
The Committee adjourned at 11:50 a.m. for lunch.
The Committee reconvened at 1:00 p.m.
The Committee then discussed the first charge, which addressed the recent trends in corporate borrowing related to super intelligence (SI) and associated businesses. The presenter stressed that borrowing in the SI sector is constantly evolving as new issues are announced nearly every week. Additionally, the sector is expected to continue to ramp up borrowing in 2027 as the demand for computing capacity outstrips supply into 2028. The presenter asserted that competition for capital currently appears to be contained within the tech credit ecosystem, and that there is no clear evidence that SI-related issuance is crowding out Treasuries or non-tech credit. Lastly, the presenter attributed the rise seen in the 10-year Treasury yield primarily to capex-driven economic growth that has pushed real yields higher, with additional upward pressure from energy price shocks.
The Committee next discussed the second charge, which evaluated the growth in the use of Treasury derivatives, in particular swaps and futures. The presenter noted that certain types of investors prefer to obtain leveraged duration exposure through derivatives for liquidity and operational reasons. Compared to buying cash Treasuries and obtaining leverage through repo markets, derivatives typically provide more favorable accounting treatment, have implicit financing costs that are not reported as explicit expenses, and reduce rollover risk for financing. Tax considerations were highlighted as another relevant factor for some investors. To increase the attractiveness of using cash Treasuries, the presenter suggested that policymakers could consider options to lessen balance sheet constraints of holding cash Treasuries, evaluate potential changes to expense, accounting and tax treatment, incentivize institutions to build repo infrastructure, reduce operational frictions associated with Treasury settlement, and minimize legal and regulatory challenges associated with onboarding as a repo transaction counterparty.
The Committee adjourned at 2:45 p.m.
The Committee reconvened at 3:00 p.m.
The Chair summarized key elements of the Committee report for Secretary Bessent and followed with a discussion of recent market developments.
Finally, the Committee turned to its financing recommendation for the current quarter and unanimously recommended that Treasury maintain nominal coupon, FRN, and TIPS auction sizes at current levels but also consider adjusting its forward guidance language. The Committee agreed that in light of projected borrowing needs, increases in coupon auction sizes would likely be appropriate in the second half of FY2027. Members generally agreed that additional issuance should be concentrated in the 2- to 10-year sector, and had a meaningful discussion about potential future changes to 20-year and 30-year issuance.
The Committee adjourned at 4:05 p.m.

Please also provide perspectives regarding market expectations for Treasury issuance, the effects of changes in SOMA holdings, the evolution of Treasury holdings by different types of investors, as well as auction calendar construction.

SEMBACH, Germany — Under bright blue skies and near-perfect flying conditions, the 68th Theater Medical Command dedicated its headquarters building as the Lt. Col. Paul A. Bloomquist Medical Hall during a ceremony at Sembach Kaserne, Germany, Oct. 30, 2026.
The building honors the late U.S. Army Lt. Col. Paul A. Bloomquist, a distinguished Medical Service Corps officer, combat aviator, and pioneer of aeromedical evacuation. His courage and dedication to wounded service members embodied the DUSTOFF spirit.
Born Oct. 30, 1932, in Utah, Bloomquist was killed in a terrorist bombing at V Corps headquarters in Frankfurt, Germany, on May 11, 1972, as he approached a nearby officers’ club.
Bloomquist was inducted posthumously into the DUSTOFF Hall of Fame on Feb. 22, 2003. His induction recognized a career defined by courage and commitment to the aeromedical evacuation mission. During nearly 35 months in Vietnam, he earned four Distinguished Flying Crosses, 37 Air Medals, and three Purple Hearts.
One Distinguished Flying Cross citation notes that, although wounded himself, Bloomquist continued flying for nearly 13 hours while rescuing numerous casualties under heavy enemy fire. He was named Army Aviator of the Year in 1964, and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce recognized him as an Outstanding Young American.
In addition to the DUSTOFF Hall of Fame, Bloomquist was inducted into the Utah Aviation Hall of Fame in 2010 and the Army Aviation Hall of Fame in 2015. In June 1980, the U.S. Army installation at Ziegenberg, West Germany, which served as headquarters for the 68th Medical Group, was named Camp Paul Bloomquist in his honor.
Although Bloomquist was not assigned to the 68th Medical Group, the naming connected his legacy permanently to the organization and recognized his extraordinary contributions to Army Medicine.
“We stand on the shoulders of giants, and knowing our history and the people who came before us can inspire us,” said Command Sgt. Maj. Kyle Brunell, 68th Theater Medical Command command sergeant major. “Going through the old photos of World War II, Vietnam, and the Cold War was enlightening and inspiring. I hope it shows current members of the organization that we have an amazing history filled with courage and sacrifice, that they have joined an organization with a rich history, and that serving in this organization matters and is bigger than themselves.”
Brunell added that he hopes the dedication fills current and future members of the 68th Theater Medical Command with pride and reinforces that their work matters.
Bloomquist was known for his fearlessness. He often flew missions without wearing a flak vest and, during his time as a battalion commander, confronted the drug, racial, and social challenges affecting the Army during that period. His leadership helped redirect Soldiers’ efforts toward productive goals while maintaining discipline, cohesion, and operational readiness.
“As you enter or pass through these halls that now bear the Bloomquist name, take the time to recognize his actions, his character, and his example,” said Brig. Gen. Lance C. Raney, commanding general of the 68th Theater Medical Command and command surgeon for U.S. Army Europe and Africa. “When you face a hard decision, when the mission is demanding and the path forward is unclear, remember Paul and his peers who faced uncertainty with courage and compassion.”
Bloomquist remains an enduring example of mission-first leadership and an officer who placed the lives of others above his own.
“To every Soldier and civilian in the 68th and on Sembach, this building is now a reminder of the standard,” Raney said. “Live up to it. Paul, happy rebirthday, and welcome back to the 68th team.”
Although his life and career ended far too soon, Bloomquist left an enduring legacy of courage, selfless service, and dedication to the aeromedical evacuation mission.
title: 68th Theater Medical Command dedicates building in honor of Army medevac pilot

Coast Guard, partner agencies respond to downed helicopter off Miami
Southeast Public Affairs - SoutheastPublicAffairs@uscg.mil
MIAMI – Coast Station Miami Beach and partner agency crews responded to a downed aircraft, Wednesday, off Biscayne Bay.
One person was reported deceased and two people were transported to emergency medical services for a higher level of care.
“Our hearts go out to everyone affected by this sudden and devastating event,” said Petty Officer Adrian Guttierez, search and rescue operations unit, Sector Miami.
A good Samaritan reported to Sector Miami watchstanders, at approximately 11:30 a.m., that a helicopter crashed. Marine units from Customs and Border Protection Air and Marine Operations and Miami-Dade Sheriff’s office arrived on scene also.
A safety zone is in place, and mariners are asked to use caution while transiting the area.
The National Transportation Safety board is investigating the cause of the crash and coordinating salvage.
Visit our Newsroom for Coast Guard Southeast District press releases. Visit our DVIDS account for Coast Guard Southeast District imagery.
For breaking news, follow us on X. For additional information, find us on Facebook and follow us on Instagram.

SEC Adopts Amendments to Update Definitions of Small Entity for Investment Companies and Investment Advisers
Washington D.C., Nov. 4, 2026 —
The Securities and Exchange Commission today adopted amendments to the rules that define which registered investment companies, investment advisers, and business development companies qualify as small entities for purposes of the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA).
The Commission has a longstanding commitment to understanding and addressing the concerns of small entities. The adopted amendments recognize the substantial growth in the asset management industry over the decades since the asset-based thresholds for identifying “small entities” were initially set. By helping to ensure the Commission’s RFA analyses capture a more meaningful population of investment companies, investment advisers, and business development companies that are considered “small entities,” the adopted amendments are therefore intended to minimize the significant economic impact of the Commission’s rules on these market participants.
“Updating the SEC’s definition of small entities for investment companies and investment advisers – which has not been done in nearly 30 years – is an important step to eliminate unnecessary regulatory burdens and modernize our rulebook,” said SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins. “These amendments more accurately capture the types of registered investment companies, investment advisers, and business development companies that are considered small relative to today’s market and will help ensure the Commission’s rulemaking is reflective of that reality.”
The RFA seeks to, in part, promote the effectiveness and efficiency of regulations, including through consideration of alternative regulatory approaches, with the goal of minimizing the significant economic impact of federal rulemaking on small entities. The Commission tailors its regulations to the relevant characteristics of regulated entities and weighs the impact of its rules on small entities, including through performing regulatory flexibility analysis under the RFA.
Specifically, the amendments:
- Increase the asset-based thresholds under which investment companies, investment advisers, and business development companies are deemed small entities.
- Update the way that related funds’ assets are aggregated for purposes of defining small entities.
- Eliminate the investment adviser total assets threshold.
- Provide for inflation adjustments to the asset-based thresholds by order every 10 years.
The adopting release is published on the SEC website and will be published in the Federal Register.
###
Last Reviewed or Updated: Nov. 4, 2026
title: SEC Adopts Amendments to Update Definitions of Small Entity for Investment Companies and Investment Advisers

WASHINGTON, D.C. -- House Armed Services Committee Ranking Member Adam Smith (D-Wash.) released the following statement outlining the priorities of the HASC Democrats in the coming Congress.
“My Democratic colleagues on the House Armed Services Committee and I are ready to hit the ground running in the 120th Congress and the top priority will be to conduct vigorous oversight of the Department of Defense and the Trump Administration. As a start, we must demand public transparency and accountability from senior Pentagon officials through increased public testimony. I also believe it is important to reestablish an Oversight & Investigations Subcommittee to help support the committee’s work. 
“The list of potential oversight topics is long, but the illegal war against Iran is top of mind for me and the American people. So too are sweetheart deals and favoritism to certain entities and individuals. We must dive into any waste, fraud, and abuse by examining contracts and other financial support awarded to private companies. The list continues with the unauthorized military strikes in the Caribbean and Latin America, the deployment of the military to U.S. cities, and the blatant and corrosive politicization of our Armed Forces and purging of the ranks based on loyalty and ideology are high on the list.
“I continue to listen to voters regarding costs.We must push for the development of a more realistic and sustainable approach to our national security—one that does not require a defense budget in excess of $1 trillion or one paid for with draconian cuts to critical domestic programs.  We also need to reform the way resources are spent and accounted for. Investment in new weapon systems must take lessons learned from recent conflicts and provide relevant capabilities in a more cost-effective manner. I also believe the bipartisan efforts on acquisition reform should continue.
“Finally, another cornerstone for this committee has focused on the people who are the heart of our national defense—service members, civilian personnel, and their families. We need to ensure we are recruiting, developing, and retaining the military and civilian talent we need by providing the benefits and standard of living they need. And we need to address the Trump Administration’s sustained assault on the federal workforce and his promotion of loyalty to a political ideology over competence for key senior military and civilian positions, and the erosion of the apolitical foundation of the armed forces.
“I am confident that we can address these issues and many more in the coming Congress. I also look forward to working with my colleagues on both sides of the aisle to ensure a return to our duty of oversight as a coequal branch of government that is responsible for providing for the common defense and our national security.” 
###
title: Smith Statement on HASC Democrats' Priorities for the 120th Congress

WASHINGTON – Wilbert Whitaker, 77, of Washington, D.C., was found guilty today in the Superior Court for the District of Columbia, on charges stemming from the murder of 30-year-old Leo Hackett, his daughter’s boyfriend on April 30, 2016, in Northeast, announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro.

Whitaker was found guilty of second-degree murder while armed and possession of a firearm during a crime of violence on November 4, 2026. The second-degree murder while armed offense carries a mandatory minimum of five years in prison when committed with a firearm. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman scheduled sentencing for January 8, 2027.

According to the government’s evidence, on April 30, 2016, in the 800 block of 21st Street Northeast, Fifth District Officers responded to a 911 call for a family disturbance at 811 21st Street Northeast. There they found that Whitaker and the victim, Leo Hackett, had been in an argument. Officers observed no injuries and heard no reports of an assault, so they left the scene without making any arrests.

A short time later, the defendant retrieved a .38 special revolver from his bedroom and loaded it. Mr. Hackett left the house to go to work. The defendant followed him out of the house. As the victim was walking away, the defendant called out to him. As Mr. Hackett turned, the defendant fired two shots with his revolver, striking the victim once in the left side of his chest and killing him.

Whitaker was arrested on April 30, 2016, on the scene of the offense and was released on May 16, 2016, following his preliminary hearing.

Joining the announcement was Interim Chief Jeffery Carroll of the Metropolitan Police Department.

This case was investigated by the Metropolitan Police Department.

The case is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorneys Kathleen Gibbons and Michael Roberts.

2016 CF1 006574
title: Jury Finds D.C. Man Guilty of the 2016 Murder of His Daughter’s Boyfriend
