Since the British withdrawal from the Persian Gulf in the early 1970s, successive U.S. presidential Administrations have considered Oman important to the promotion of regional stability and peace in the Middle East. Over the past two decades, Oman has played the role of discreet mediator, having served as an intermediary in seeking to resolve conflict in Yemen and nuclear negotiations with Iran. Oman's strategic location at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important maritime chokepoints, and along the Arabian Sea approaches to East Africa and the Red Sea provide it with some regional and global influence.
Since the February 2026 start of the U.S.-Iran conflict and the ensuing contest for control over the Strait of Hormuz, Oman's long-standing tradition of serving as a quiet diplomatic interlocutor has been challenged. Iran and the United States have sought Oman's support for their contrasting proposals over future control of the strait. Oman's attempts to balance competing demands from Washington and Tehran have, at times, drawn criticism from Iranian and U.S. officials.
In the early months of the conflict, Iran struck several Omani ports and coastal facilities. Since then, Iran has not targeted the Sultanate directly but has continued to strike commercial tankers in Oman's territorial waters. Oman has provided navigational guidance and search and rescue aid to tankers transiting the strait.
As the U.S.-Iran conflict continues and as fighting between neighboring Saudi Arabia and the Yemen-based Houthis has intensified, Oman has found itself diplomatically wedged between warring parties in a region beset by war. Oman's geographic position has helped insulate its economy from some of the effects of disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. For 2026, the International Monetary Fund projects that Oman will be the only Gulf state with positive economic growth, with gross domestic product forecast to grow by over 4%.
In January 2020, Oman's long-time leader, Sultan Qaboos bin Sa'id Al Said, passed away and was succeeded by his cousin Haythim bin Tariq Al Said (born 1955). Sultan Haythim leads a stable, high-income nation, though Oman faces challenges in maintaining its decades-long social contract, in which oil has brought prosperity to its citizens in exchange for their apparent acceptance of the Sultan's absolute rule. Like the other Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states—Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Bahrain, and Kuwait—Oman derives most of its state income from hydrocarbon production and export; however, Oman's hydrocarbon-focused economy is smaller than those of most of the others. To curb government spending, attract foreign investment, and diversify the economy, Sultan Haythim has launched "Vision 2040," a strategic plan similar to those of other GCC states.
Oman and the United States maintain strong defense ties, whereby Oman permits the U.S. military to use its military facilities. However, when compared with other Gulf Arab states, such as Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Kuwait, U.S.-Omani defense relations are smaller in scale. The United States has provided minimal foreign assistance to Oman, mainly for border security. From 1946 to 2025, the United States provided Oman with $1.6 billion in total economic and military assistance.
The U.S.-Oman Free Trade Agreement was signed on January 19, 2006, and ratified by Congress (P.L. 109-283, signed by the President September 26, 2006). Today, the United States is one of Oman's largest trading partners and foreign investors. In 2025, the total volume of bilateral trade was $3.3 billion. In July 2026, the Trump Administration imposed a 12.5% tariff on most U.S. imports from Oman as a result of an investigation that found Oman and various economies failed to impose and effectively enforce bans on imports made with forced labor. Certain categories of goods are subject to higher tariffs globally, including aluminum, of which Oman is an exporter.
Oman is positioned astride the southeastern corner of the Arabian Peninsula, bordering the Arabian Sea, Indian Ocean, and the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's key maritime choke points (see Figure 1
Since the start of the U.S.-Iran conflict and the ensuing contest over reopening the Strait of Hormuz, Oman's long-standing tradition of serving as a quiet diplomatic interlocutor has been challenged. Iran and the United States have sought Oman's support for their contrasting proposals to reopen the strait. Oman's attempts to balance competing demands from Washington and Tehran have, at times, drawn criticism from Iranian and U.S. officials; in 2026, President Donald Trump twice threatened military action against Oman if it opposed U.S. efforts to reopen the strait fully and freely.
In the early months of the conflict, Iran struck several Omani ports and coastal facilities. Since then, Iran has not targeted the Sultanate directly but has continued to strike commercial tankers off Oman's territorial waters. Oman has provided navigational guidance and search and rescue aid to tankers transiting the strait. U.S. forces have reportedly been offering air-based defense to ships transiting the strait along Oman's coast.1
As the U.S.-Iran conflict continues and as fighting between neighboring Saudi Arabia and the Yemen-based Houthis has intensified, Oman has increased its regional diplomatic efforts independent of U.S. policy. In October 2026, Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi called on the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) members to reach a nonaggression pact with Iran, saying that the GCC can "no longer rely upon the co-operation of external partners."2
Although Oman has found itself diplomatically wedged between combatants in a region beset by war, Oman's geographic position has helped insulate its economy from some of the effects of restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.3 In contrast to the economic downturns all other GCC members appear to be experiencing this year, Oman's gross domestic product (GDP) for 2026 is projected by the International Monetary Fund to grow by over 4%.4
Since becoming sultan in 2020, Sultan Haythim bin Tariq Al Said has pursued economic diversification aimed at expanding the private sector and reducing Oman's dependence on hydrocarbon revenues. Like other oil-producing Gulf monarchies, Oman is pursuing a plan ("Vision 2040") to boost non-oil sectors, such as logistics, manufacturing, tourism, mining, space, and the digital economy. While Oman's decades-long social contract has brought it prosperity, Oman lacks the hydrocarbon reserves of most other GCC states. The gradual transition away from hydrocarbon extraction and toward human capital-driven growth is arguably the biggest challenge facing the Sultanate over the long term.
Before the launch of Operation Epic Fury in February 2026, Oman attempted to prevent a possible conflict by offering to serve as an intermediary between Iran and the United States. However, compared with previous instances of Omani mediation, such as its backchannel role in facilitating negotiations leading to the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), the rapid buildup of U.S. military forces in the Gulf, escalatory rhetoric by both U.S. and Iranian officials, and unbridgeable U.S.-Iranian gaps over the scope of issues to be discussed made Oman's role far more challenging.5
U.S. and Omani differences over Iran were apparent both immediately before and after the start of Operation Epic Fury. A day before the launch of hostilities, Omani Foreign Minister Albusaidi stated, "I am confident, and in my assessment of the way the talks are going, I think there is, really I can see that the peace deal is within our reach."6 That statement apparently sowed distrust with some Trump Administration officials.7 Once Israeli and U.S. forces launched airstrikes and Iran retaliated, Omani officials expressed rare public displeasure with U.S. policy.8
As the conflict continued, Oman, like all other GCC states, was subject to Iranian retaliatory strikes. Between February and October 2026, Iran launched an estimated 66 strikes against Oman, leading to over two dozen casualties (including 14 fatalities).9
Throughout the conflict, U.S.-Omani relations have fluctuated over the issue of freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. When the United States has sought Oman's support, both sides have cooperated; however, when Oman has engaged Iran in dialogue over the possibility of charging service fees for ships to transit the strait, such conversations have met U.S. criticism (see below).
When President Trump announced in May 2026 the start of "Project Freedom," a U.S. campaign to help ships safely transit the Strait of Hormuz, the United States instructed tankers to exit via Omani territorial waters while the Coast Guard Command of the Royal Oman Police provided traffic control.10 Project Freedom was suspended shortly after its launch because Saudi Arabia reportedly denied U.S. forces the use of its territory and airspace.11 Also in May 2026, Iran and Oman conducted bilateral talks over possibly charging tolls or service fees to commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz. In response, President Trump warned, "Oman will behave just like everybody else, or we'll have to blow them up…. They understand that. They'll be fine."12
A month later, the June 2026 U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding (MOU) called for, among other things, an Iranian commitment to "make arrangements using its best efforts for the safe passage of commercial vessels, with no charge for 60 days only," through the Strait of Hormuz, and to subsequently work with Oman and other Gulf states "to define the future administration and maritime services in the Strait."13 In response to the MOU, Oman established safe passage routes through shipping lanes (see Figure 214 After commercial tankers began using the southern route near Omani territorial waters to transit the strait, Iran began attacking commercial vessels. In response, the United States launched its first post-MOU strikes against Iran in late June 2026. Several weeks later, President Trump declared the MOU "over." Reportedly, Iranian hardliners saw the potential success of the southern route along Oman's coast as a threat to Iranian control over the strait.15
Despite the collapse of the MOU, Oman and Iran continued to discuss ways to jointly manage the operation of the Strait of Hormuz and potentially collect payments from transiting vessels. While Oman officially maintained that it recognized international conventions banning maritime tolls (including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea or UNCLOS), Omani officials worked with their Iranian counterparts to develop alternative arrangements to collect "service fees" based on other international models governing key waterways, such as the Dardanelles and the Strait of Malacca.16 Oman has proposed that such fees be voluntary, whereas Iran has sought to make them mandatory.17
By the end of July 2026, Omani media reported that Iran had rejected Oman's proposal to jointly manage the strait and collect voluntary service fees.18 Though Oman had based its proposal partially on Article 26 of UNCLOS (which allows countries to levy some fees on ships "for specific services rendered"), Iran rejected the proposal because the arrangement did not recognize the extent of Iranian control over the strait that Tehran sought to assert. The United States opposed Oman's initiative on freedom of navigation grounds. According to one analysis, "This leaves Oman in a tricky position: aiming to use international law to negotiate a way out of a crisis, but with opposition coming from all sides."19
In August 2026, President Trump again threatened to bomb Oman, as U.S. officials expressed frustration with Oman's proposals concerning the collection of voluntary fees from vessels transiting the strait.20 In September 2026, Senators Tim Kaine and Adam Schiff introduced S.J.Res. 215 (119th Congress), a joint war powers resolution to direct the removal of U.S. forces from hostilities within or against the Sultanate of Oman that have not been authorized by Congress.
As of November 2026, U.S.-Omani relations in the context of the Iran conflict are uncertain. Reports continue to suggest that Oman's diplomatic engagement with Iran, particularly over the Strait of Hormuz, has heightened U.S. distrust of Oman among some Trump Administration officials, while others see Oman's role as potentially valuable.21 As of November 2026, countries that have been serving as lead interlocutors with Iran include Qatar, Turkey, and Pakistan—not Oman. In a September 2026 phone call between U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Omani Foreign Minister Albusaidi, Secretary Rubio "acknowledged Oman's important role in deescalation in the region."22
Though Oman's diplomatic role on matters involving Iran may be less central than in the past, high volumes of shipping have been transiting Oman's coastal waters inside and outside the strait. Also, the Royal Navy of Oman has been responding to distress calls from ships that have been attacked by Iran.23 According to one report, Oman's navy has requested U.S. assistance in monitoring maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.24 Press accounts suggest that the increase of oil traffic through the Strait of Hormuz toward prewar levels is due in part to U.S. military protection of vessels transiting along the southern edge of the Strait of Hormuz alongside the Omani coast. 25
Oman has attempted to mediate resolutions to the conflict in Yemen, which has been mired in a civil war since 2014. Unlike Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, Oman has not played an active military role there.26 Instead, over the past decade, it has brokered cease-fire negotiations and prisoner releases. Oman has long hosted Mohammad Abdul Salam, the official spokesman of the Yemen-based, Iran-backed Ansarallah/Houthi movement and one of the group's lead negotiators.27
The resumption of conflict and deadly attacks on Saudi infrastructure and energy facilities by the Houthis since July 2026 have prompted Omani officials to condemn attacks against Saudi Arabia while calling for a political solution to the conflict that "preserves the unity, stability, and territorial integrity" of Yemen.28 Oman, like Saudi Arabia, is opposed to Yemeni secession movements like the Southern Transition Council. From 1965 to 1975, Oman endured a rebellion in its Dhofar province adjacent to Yemen that had been partially supported by the southern Yemeni state known as the People's Democratic Republic of Yemen (PDRY). The PDRY unified with North Yemen in 1990 to form the present-day Republic of Yemen.
Oman's territory reportedly has served as a conduit for the smuggling of weapons and weapons components to the Houthis.29 Smuggled materiel allegedly included anti-ship missiles,30 surface-to-surface short-range missiles, anti-tank guided missiles, small arms, explosives, and unmanned aerial vehicles.31 At times, the United States has obligated funds (relatively small grants) under the Nonproliferation, Anti-Terrorism, Demining and Related Programs (NADR) account for counterterrorism programming, some of which is used for the Oman Border Security Enhancement Program.32
Beyond its close ties to fellow GCC states and the West, Oman also is cultivating ties to the People's Republic of China (PRC). As of the beginning of the U.S.-Iran conflict, Oman had exported the vast majority of its oil to the PRC.33 The PRC government also has financed an industrial park in the port of Duqm (Figure 134 Additionally, Chinese companies have invested in Omani state enterprises that were privatized, such as the Oman Electricity Transmission Company and the Oman Cement Company.35 In 2025, China's Central New Energy Holding Group committed to investing in solar power projects in Oman.36 In 2026, a Chinese company began construction of a facility to manufacture anode materials for lithium-ion batteries in Oman.37
The Chinese telecommunications firm Huawei has an extensive presence in Oman. Oman Airports have partnered with Huawei to install WiFi networks in Oman's airports,38 and in 2025 Huawei signed an offset agreement with the Omani Ministry of Finance to train thousands of Omani students and workers in information and communication technology.39
Beyond economic relations, Omani-PRC military ties are being closely followed by U.S. policymakers. According to one report, in November 2023, U.S. officials briefed then-President Joe Biden on a PRC plan to build a military facility in Oman.40 PRC naval taskforces conduct goodwill visits and joint exercises with the Royal Navy of Oman.41 The Royal Army of Oman has purchased 122 mm multiple rocket launch systems from PRC producers.42
In November 2026, Sultan Haythim conducted a two-day state visit to China, the first by an Omani Sultan since Omani-Chinese diplomatic relations began in 1978 (see Figure 3). During the visit, both sides agreed to a five-year bilateral currency swap agreement for $4.50 billion.43 They also signed nearly two dozen investment partnership agreements. Prior to the state visit, Oman and China reportedly have been discussing the possible Omani procurement of the PRC-Pakistani jointly developed JF-17 fighter jet; the Royal Air Force of Oman currently possesses only Western fighter aircraft (U.S. F-16s and Eurofighter Typhoons).44
Since the mid-eighteenth century, the Al Said (or Busaid) dynasty has ruled Oman. The Sultanate of Oman is a hereditary monarchy, and the sultan has sole authority to enact laws through royal decree.45 In January 2020, Oman's long-time leader, Sultan Qaboos bin Sa'id Al Said, passed away without children and was succeeded by Haythim bin Tariq Al Said (b. 1955), a cousin selected by Oman's royal family immediately upon Qaboos's death.
In late January 2021, Sultan Haythim appointed his son, Theyazin bin Haythim, who was born in August 1990, as Crown Prince. The appointment represented a contrast with the Qaboos era in which the succession was unclear. Theyazin first served in the government as Minister of Culture, Youth, and Sports. In 2026, he was promoted to deputy prime minister for economic affairs, a portfolio in which he may focus on promoting Oman as a regional financial center.46
Oman has a bicameral parliament with limited legislative powers; members may question ministers, select their own leadership, and review government-drafted legislation, but law-making powers rest firmly in the hands of the sultan. Members of the Consultative Council (Majlis As Shura) are directly elected by Omani citizens, male and female, over 21 years of age.47 In order to boost the number of female Omani lawmakers, in 2026 Sultan Haythim allocated a total of 11 Consultative Council seats for women across the governorates. The sultan appoints all members of the upper house or State Council (Majlis Ad Dawla). Appointees are usually former high-ranking government officials, military officials, tribal leaders, and other notables.
Oman is an absolute monarchy in which, according to international human rights groups, state authorities often target individuals and entities that are critical of the sultan or state.48 Freedom House's annual survey of political rights and civil liberties globally ranks Oman as "not free." In 2026, Sultan Haythim issued a new Royal Decree making it illegal to publish online content that violates morals or public order (e.g., sedition, sectarianism, social division).49 The Oman Human Rights Commission is a government entity that monitors human rights cases in the Sultanate.
Sultan Haythim leads a stable, high-income nation (as categorized by the World Bank), though Oman faces challenges in maintaining its decades-long social contract, in which oil has brought prosperity to Omani citizens in exchange for their apparent acceptance of the sultan's absolute rule. Like the other GCC states—Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Bahrain, and Kuwait—Oman derives most of its state income (over 70%) from hydrocarbon production and export.50 However, Oman has the lowest per capita GDP in the GCC owing to its modest levels of oil and gas production relative to its GCC neighbors.51
Although higher global prices stemming from the conflict with Iran and various attempts to circumvent the Strait of Hormuz using Omani ports have boosted the economy, the Omani government had begun to explore other options to generate revenue and cut spending—including on development expenditures—well before the outbreak of the current conflict.52 Oman introduced a Value Added Tax in 2021. In June 2025, Oman became the first GCC country to impose a personal income tax.53 Though the new tax only affects a small number of high-earning Omanis, it could, according to one report, "lead to a recalibration of the relationship between citizens and their government."54
Economists note that while Oman's economy has been boosted by its neighbors' maneuvers to circumvent the Strait of Hormuz through proposed pipeline, rail, and port connections to Oman, this growth will likely moderate should oil prices begin to decline as a result of greater stability in the Gulf. However, according to the Economist Intelligence Unit, "A prolonged regional conflict could sustain elevated hydrocarbon prices for an extended period, further strengthening Omani fiscal and current-account surpluses."55
To date, the Sultanate has used its relatively limited oil-generated wealth to provide citizens with subsidized goods, low taxes, housing support, and public sector salaries. Nevertheless, at current oil production rates (estimated at a million barrels per day or bpd),56 and barring any new discoveries or major technological innovations, Oman could exhaust its proven oil reserves (around 5 billion barrels-ranked 21st globally)57 in around 20 years.
Given the possibility of declining production, the Sultanate has embarked upon a diversification strategy called "Vision 2040." Under that whole-of-government approach, domestic and foreign investment is being channeled into other sectors, such as tourism, software, manufacturing, green hydrogen, renewable energy, and mineral-processing. With 64% of the population under 30, the Sultan has directed the Omani government to monitor the implementation of Vision 2040 on a regular basis.58 According to Bloomberg, "Just a few years ago, Oman's ratings were placed in junk territory by all three major rating companies and concerns mounted that it could require financial support from wealthier neighbors. Fiscal reforms, higher oil prices and privatizations have since helped Oman cut debt and restore its investment-grade ratings."59
As other Gulf Arab monarchies attempt to enact their own economic diversification plans, it remains to be seen what comparative advantages the Sultanate can capitalize on relative to its Gulf neighbors. Though the non-oil sectors of the economy (e.g., transportation, financial services, construction) have experienced recent growth, manufacturing has remained flat and the bulk of foreign investment in Oman through 2025 was in the oil and natural gas sector.60
In January 2026, the United States and Oman held their third Strategic Dialogue in Muscat (see Figure 4
[w]elcomed advancements in building relationships between U.S. states and Oman, including our mutual intention to finalize a Sister Port MOU between the State of Louisiana and the Port of Duqm…. The delegations also recognized the growing ties between Oman and the U.S. state of Arizona, through the State Partnership Program, and agreed to continue to foster this subnational relationship. 61
Oman was the first Persian Gulf state to sign a formal accord permitting the U.S. military to use its facilities (1980) as part of the two countries' long-standing strategic partnership. In 2019, Oman and the United States signed a "Strategic Framework Agreement" that expands the U.S.-Oman facilities access agreements by allowing U.S. forces to use the ports of Salalah and Duqm; the latter is large enough to handle U.S. aircraft carriers.62
U.S.-Omani security cooperation is ongoing. Through the U.S. Department of Defense's63 National Guard Bureau State Partnership Program, the Arizona National Guard has partnered with the Sultan of Oman's Armed Forces. U.S. arms sales to Oman are modest when compared with U.S. sales to Oman's neighbors, such as Saudi Arabia and the UAE. From 1950 to 2024, the United States completed nearly $3.4 billion worth of Foreign Military Sales cases with Oman.64 In 2026, the State Department notified Congress of a potential $188 million sale to Oman of equipment to sustain its fleet of F-16 fighters.65
From 1946 to 2025, the United States provided Oman with $1.6 billion in total economic and military assistance. Oman has received a small amount of annual foreign assistance to support specific U.S. programs. The United States provides Oman with annual International Military Education and Training (IMET) grants to support Omani participation in the IMET program, which provides professional military education and training to foreign military students and seeks to establish lasting relationships with future leaders. As previously mentioned, the United States has provided small funding grants (estimated $1 million)—much of it through NADR—to help Oman counter terrorist and related threats. Congress also has authorized Oman to receive U.S. military aid for border security through DOD-managed accounts, such as Section 1226 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2016 (22 U.S.C. 2151).
Though national defense spending in the Sultanate remains opaque, according to one source, Oman's overall defense budget (est. $6.6 billion) accounts for a quarter of the overall national budget.66 Jane's Defence Budget noted in 2025 that "while the UK and US will remain key providers of defence and security equipment in the future, Oman is likely to continue expanding its horizons as third-party suppliers are able to deliver more capable equipment at lower costs."67
The United States is one of the largest foreign direct investors in Oman after the United Kingdom and has registered a cumulative trade surplus of $6.3 billion since 2006.68 The U.S.-Oman Free Trade Agreement was signed on January 19, 2006, and ratified by Congress (P.L. 109-283, signed by the President September 26, 2006). It was intended to facilitate Oman's access to the U.S. economy and accelerate Oman's efforts to diversify its economy. The United States is one of Oman's largest trading partners. In 2025, the total volume of bilateral trade was $3.3 billion. According to the U.S. Department of Commerce, total U.S. investment in Oman stood at $20 billion as of late 2025, and principal U.S. merchandise exports to Oman included vehicles, aircraft, petroleum products, chemicals, plastics, and industrial engines.69 In July 2026, the Trump Administration imposed a 12.5% tariff on most U.S. imports from Oman as a result of an investigation that found Oman and various economies failed to impose and effectively enforce bans on imports made with forced labor. Certain categories of goods are subject to higher tariffs globally, including aluminum, of which Oman is an exporter.70
title: Oman: Politics, Security, and U.S. Policy

DORAL, Fla. — U.S. and Colombian armies officially launched Exercise Southern Vanguard 2027 on Nov. 2, bringing together approximately 800 military personnel to strengthen interoperability, readiness, and bilateral security cooperation.
The 41st iteration of the annual exercise is hosted by the Colombian Army, sponsored by U.S. Southern Command and led by U.S. Army Western Hemisphere Command, with approximately 350 U.S. military personnel and more than 400 Colombian Army soldiers participating.
The exercise aims to strengthen soldiers’ skills, improve their ability to operate together in challenging environments, and enhance mutual readiness. Colombia’s role as host underscores the importance of the U.S.-Colombia security partnership and regional military cooperation.
“American and Colombian soldiers operating with shared purpose, mutual trust, and professional discipline,” said Brig. Gen. Peter L. Gilbert, USAWHC G-4 deputy chief of staff. “You will sweat together, you will learn together, and you will build bonds that can only be forged through shared hardships and shared accomplishment.”
Following the opening ceremony, U.S. and Colombian soldiers will conduct combined training focused on jungle exercises and counter-improvised explosive device tactics. The exercise also includes a command post and field training exercise, with broader training objectives spanning maritime interdiction, ground security, cyber defense and interagency cooperation. These activities will promote knowledge-sharing, strengthen interoperability and improve combined readiness.
“I extend a warm and fraternal greeting to all officers, non-commissioned officers, soldiers and international partners participating in the Southern Vanguard 2027 exercise,” said Brig. Gen. Edilberto Cortés, chief of the Force Generation Staff of the Colombian National Army. “This presence demonstrates the shared commitment of our nations to strengthen collective readiness and consolidate the ties of cooperation that support our strategic and historical relationship.”
Building on more than 200 years of diplomatic relations, the United States and Colombia continue to strengthen their military partnership through combined training and professional knowledge-sharing. Southern Vanguard 2027 aims to improve readiness, reinforce interoperability, and support peace, stability and security across the Western Hemisphere.
title: US, Colombia launch joint exercise to strengthen readiness, regional security

Today, General Counsel Crystal S. Carey announced the appointment of Jessica Foley to Regional Director of the NLRB Region 1-Boston office. In this capacity, she will lead the Region in its administration of elections, investigation of unfair labor practice charges, mentoring of staff, and partnership with headquarters to advance Agency initiatives and strengthen service to the public. Region 1 is responsible for administration of the National Labor Relations Act in most of New England, with offices in Boston, MA and Hartford, CT.

“Jessica is an exemplary public servant with a deep commitment to the National Labor Relations Act,” said General Counsel Carey. “Her excellence and skill in navigating complex matters have earned her the confidence of both regional and headquarters’ leadership. I am equally impressed with her ability to build and maintain relationships with local bar associations and practitioners, which has greatly helped the Region fulfill its mission in Region 1. I am confident that Region 1 is in capable hands with Jessica, and I look forward to working with her to effectuate the mission of the Agency.”

A native of Central New York, Ms. Foley earned a Bachelor of Arts in Psychology from St. Bonaventure University and a Master of Industrial Relations from Cornell University’s School of Industrial and Labor Relations. She began her career with the National Labor Relations Board in 2003 as a Field Examiner in its Co Op program in Buffalo, NY (Region 3). The following year, she joined Region 31 in Los Angeles as a Field Examiner, where she further developed her expertise in representation and unfair labor practice casework.

In 2008, Ms. Foley transferred to Region 1. Over the next decade, she served as a key contributor to the Region’s case investigations, election processes, and compliance operations. Her leadership and mentorship were formally recognized in 2019 when she was promoted to Supervisory Examiner.

Since 2021, Jessica served as Assistant Regional Director of Region 1, where she played a central role in overseeing casehandling quality, managing supervisory staff, and guiding the Region through significant operational transitions.

Established in 1935, the National Labor Relations Board is an independent federal agency that protects employees from unfair labor practices and protects the right of private sector employees to join together, with or without a union, to improve wages, benefits and working conditions. The NLRB conducts hundreds of workplace elections and investigates thousands of unfair labor practice charges each year.
title: Jessica Foley Named Regional Director for Region 1-Boston and Hartford

The Department of War's Office of Strategic Capital (OSC) announced today a $150 million conditional loan commitment with LeoLabs, Inc., a leading provider of Space Domain Awareness (SDA) and Space Traffic Management (STM) solutions. This financing would accelerate the deployment of critical radar infrastructure and advanced decision science software, helping sustain American leadership in the increasingly contested space domain.
In alignment with OSC's mission to attract private capital to national security priorities, the conditional loan is matched dollar-for-dollar with co-investment, resulting in a capital infusion of $300 million. The financing would scale production and deployment of multi-mission phased array radars, significantly expanding U.S. radar manufacturing capacity and sensing infrastructure.
This financing would directly support Department of War priorities by expanding LeoLabs' global footprint and accelerating the production and deployment of advanced sensor hardware, including the company's mobile "Scout" radar units.
"To maintain our strategic advantage, we must leverage the innovation and agility of the American commercial sector," said David A. Lorch, Director of the Office of Strategic Capital and Senior Advisor to Deputy Secretary of War Steve Feinberg. "This financing equips the Department of War with unparalleled Space Domain Awareness capabilities and demonstrates our commitment to unleashing private capital to solve our most pressing national security challenges. By supporting the expansion of a globally distributed, wholly domestic space radar architecture, this transaction bolsters U.S. resilience against geopolitical disruptions in orbit and ensures that next-gen technologies are powered by secure, domestically sourced data."
As the only commercially available provider of ground-based radar space domain awareness in the United States, LeoLabs is uniquely positioned to deliver this critical infrastructure and enhance space monitoring capabilities. LeoLabs' globally distributed radar network allows for rapid, continuous cloud-based data updates and unclassified information sharing, making it a critical commercial capability for national defense and for allied partners.
"High-precision orbital tracking is integral to the U.S. economy and the defense industrial base, and its importance is only going to grow on account of the rapid commercialization of space," said Jordan B. Sebold, Senior Managing Director (Investments) at OSC. "OSC's investment in LeoLabs will help ensure we maintain persistent custody of the objects that matter most."
The conditional loan commitment specifies additional steps LeoLabs must complete before financial close, including satisfying various financial, legal, technical, investment, due diligence, and other requirements.
"I applaud OSC for another strategic investment in the important space domain sector," said Emil Michael, Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering. "Maintaining American space superiority means we must scale commercial capabilities that enhance decision-making for the Joint Force. This OSC financing ensures the United States and our allies control the data needed to maintain our decision advantage in orbit."
title: Department of War's Office of Strategic Capital Signs $150 Million Conditional Loan Commitment With LeoLabs, Inc.

PORTLAND, Maine: A Cornish man was sentenced today in U.S. District Court in Portland for transmitting a threatening interstate communication.

Chief U.S. District Judge Lance E. Walker sentenced Blake Tibbetts , 25, to 10 months in prison to be followed by three years of supervised release. Tibbetts pleaded guilty on April 27, 2026.

According to court records, Tibbetts made a post on the social platform X in which he used a racial epithet in an angry exchange with another X user and threatened to pay “a visit VERY soon” to the user’s “kind,” sending “them” his “condolences.”

The FBI, the Maine State Police, and the Office of the Maine State Fire Marshal investigated the case.
title: Cornish Man Sentenced for Making Interstate Threats

text:
Network Circumvented Maritime Law to Enable Iran’s Shadow Fleet
WASHINGTON—Today, as part of Operation Economic Outcast, the U.S. Department of the Treasury targeted the vast criminal network of India-based Suniel Kumar Sharma and his spouse, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid, who have supported Iran’s shadow fleet through a web maritime fraud. Their schemes have provided false flags and certifications to sanctioned vessels involved in transporting Iranian petroleum, including vessels operating on behalf of the Iranian military and its proxies.
“As we have said many times, under Operation Economic Outcast, you are either with us or against us,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent. “We know where you are, and we will sanction those who continue supporting the Iranian regime, whether by land, sea, or air.”
False flags and fake maritime certifications allow vessels engaging in illicit activity to evade international regulations aimed at ensuring crew safety and safeguarding against environmental harm. Falsely flagged vessels carry no valid protection and indemnity insurance, meaning that Iranian shadow fleet vessels operating under false flags could potentially cause billions of dollars in damages to the economies of the countries in whose territorial waters they operate.
OFAC today also sanctioned Türkiye-based Fugo Ground Services Inc for its ongoing services in support of Iran’s aviation sector. Treasury has repeatedly warned that it will take action against those who continue to support Iran’s aviation industry, a key enabler of the regime’s destabilizing proliferation and terrorist activity.
Concurrently with these designations, OFAC is issuing a new alert to industry to warn of the sanctions risks of dealing with potentially falsely flagged vessels, reemphasizing previous warnings from Treasury to the maritime industry to screen against unscrupulous actors such as Sharma and the vessels his network supports. OFAC’s action also follows through on Treasury’s previous warning that any foreign firm or individual enabling sanctioned Iranian airlines—including through aircraft transfers, cargo services, or general sales agent support—will face serious consequences for supporting the world’s leading state sponsor of terrorism. The designations imposed today are being taken pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13902, which targets the Iranian petroleum, petrochemical, and aviation sectors, among other key sectors of the Iranian economy.
OPERATION ECONOMIC OUTCAST IS ISOLATING THE IRANIAN REGIME
Announced by Secretary Bessent on August 24, 2026 and dubbed Economic D-Day, Operation Economic Outcast is severing the remaining economic lifelines that sustain the Iranian regime. Treasury has mapped the networks, facilitators, and financial channels that Iran uses to smuggle oil, evade sanctions, and fund terror. Working with partners across the U.S. government, the European Union, United Kingdom, Gulf partners, and others, Treasury is targeting any source of the regime’s illicit revenue, as well as its sanctions evasion schemes to move funds.
Operation Economic Outcast significantly expanded sanctions risk for those who continue to choose to do business with Iran. Treasury warned that any entity facilitating money laundering or sanctions evasion on behalf of Iran risks being cut off from the U.S. financial system. Operation Economic Outcast also expanded sanctions exposure for non-U.S. persons who continue doing business with the Iranian regime and will accelerate the pace of U.S. enforcement. More information on Operation Economic Outcast is available here.
SHARMA CRIMINAL NETWORK
For years, Suniel Kumar Sharma (Sharma) and his wife, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid (Shahid), have, through their base in Chandigarh, India, defrauded maritime regulatory administrations in multiple jurisdictions in order to establish false flagging authorities and maritime classification societies. Purporting to represent nations from nearly every continent, from Guyana to Eswatini and Laos, Sharma and Shahid have allowed the Iranian shadow fleet, including those operating on behalf of the Iranian military and its proxies, to evade international restrictions on their operation.
Sharma and Shahid’s operations began as early as 2014, when the couple sought to impersonate the flagging authority of the Caribbean nation of Dominica. In 2023, Sharma established the Singapore-based Eswatini Maritime Affairs and International Ship Registry PTE. Ltd. (Eswatini Maritime), which, despite being publicly disavowed by Eswatini authorities, continues to provide flagging services for vessels transporting Iranian petroleum, including the sanctioned vessel PING SHUN (IMO 9231901), which at the time of its sanctioning had engaged in multiple shipments of Iranian oil.
Many of Sharma and Shahid’s false flagging registries are not tied to registered companies, however. In each case, the Sharma network purchases web domains, creating websites that claim to offer a variety of services on behalf of a country that has not authorized it to provide any of those services. The services often include flagging, seafarer training and certification, and vessel classification, all of which are traditionally handled by legitimate organizations that hold vessels to strict international standards.
Sharma’s network can be tied to multiple active websites that purport to belong to legitimate flagging registries. Among these false representations are websites purporting to provide flagging services on behalf of Aruba, Guyana, Mali, Mozambique, Malawi, Sint Maarten, and Timor-Leste, among others. Sanctioned shadow fleet vessels have since gravitated towards these registries despite widespread awareness that they are not endorsed by the relevant governments. For example, on April 22, 2026, the U.S. Department of War seized the false Guyana-flagged MAJESTIC X, formerly known as the PHONIX (IMO 9198317), which was carrying Iranian oil at the time of its boarding.
Sharma and Shahid additionally manage a network of primarily India-based entities, some of which are used to establish fraudulent flagging registries. Sharma is the managing director of India-based Oceaniek Technologies India, a company he has used to establish duplicitous flag registries, including those purporting to belong to Aruba, Nicaragua, and Sint Maarten. Through these fraudulent registries Sharma has provided false flags to numerous sanctioned vessels that transport Iranian petroleum products, including LATTAFA (IMO 9245794), BINARY STAR (IMO 9380570), and VERA (IMO 9304655).
As Sharma’s activities have garnered greater attention, Shahid has stepped in to manage—at least on paper—the pair’s business empire, which includes companies ranging from financial services businesses to media streaming platforms. Following press coverage of his activities, Sharma has closed down multiple deceitful registries, including the Laos Ship Registry and Maritime Safety Administration, previously known as the International Maritime Safety Agency of Guyana, a company that served as a false flagging agency for Guyana and was likely intended to similarly impersonate the Laotian government.
In addition to Shahid, Indian nationals Ashwani Kumar Dhiman and Ishwinder Singh nominally serve as directors of Sharma’s businesses, including India-based Aryavart Ship Management Private Limited.
Suniel Kumar Sharma is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the petroleum sector of the Iranian economy. Jaspreet Preeti Shahid is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, Suniel Kumar Sharma.
Eswatini Maritime Affairs and International Ship Registry PTE. Ltd. is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for being owned or controlled by, or having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid.
Oceaniek Technologies India is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for being owned or controlled by, or having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Suniel Kumar Sharma.
Aryavart Ship Management Private Limited is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for being owned or controlled by, or having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid. Ashwani Kumar Dhiman and Ishwinder Singh are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Aryavart Ship Management Private Limited.
In addition, the following India-based companies are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for being owned or controlled by, or having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid:
- Precept Trends Private Limited;
- Polynesia Maritime Private Limited;
- Alexarya Finserv Private Limited;
- Alexarya Media and Entertainment Private Limited;
- Viharaboating Private Limited; and
- Aryavart Maritime and Educational Trust.
GROUND HANDLING COMPANY SUPPORTING IRANIAN AIRLINES
On August 24, 2026, Treasury issued determinations pursuant to E.O. 13902 against critical sectors––including aviation––that the Iranian regime uses to try to prop up its economy. As Treasury has repeatedly highlighted, Iran uses its supposed “commercial” airlines, many of which are controlled by the regime and its military, to ferry fighters, ship weapons and sensitive technologies, and move gold and cash to its proxies. Today, OFAC is taking action against a Türkiye-based ground handling company that continues to service sanctioned Iranian airlines, despite Treasury’s warnings of the sanctions risks associated with supporting Iran’s aviation sector.
Türkiye-based Fugo Ground Services Inc provides ground handling and other services to several U.S.-designated Iranian airlines that continue to fly to Türkiye. Fugo Ground Services Inc has direct service agreements with U.S.-sanctioned Iranian carriers including Iran Air Tour, Saha Airlines, Sepehran Airlines, Varesh Airlines, Taban Airlines, and Ata Airlines Company, and began providing services to several of these carriers in the weeks after their September 8, 2026 designations.
OFAC is designating Fugo Ground Services Inc pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the aviation sector of the Iranian economy.
SANCTIONS IMPLICATIONS
As a result of today’s action, all property and interests in property of the designated or blocked persons described above that are in the United States or in the possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to OFAC. In addition, any entities that are owned, directly or indirectly, individually or in the aggregate, 50 percent or more by one or more blocked persons are also blocked. OFAC’s regulations generally prohibit all transactions, unless authorized by a general or specific license issued by OFAC, or exempt, by U.S. persons or within (or transiting) the United States that involve any property or interests in property of blocked persons.
Violations of U.S. sanctions may result in the imposition of civil or criminal penalties on U.S. and foreign persons. OFAC may impose civil penalties for sanctions violations on a strict liability basis. OFAC’s Economic Sanctions Enforcement Guidelines provide more information regarding OFAC’s enforcement of U.S. economic sanctions. The prohibitions include the making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit of any designated or blocked person, or the receipt of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services from any such person. Non-U.S. persons are also prohibited from causing U.S. persons to wittingly or unwittingly violate U.S. sanctions, as well as engaging in conduct that evades or conspires to violate U.S. sanctions. Individuals located in the U.S. or abroad who provide information about sanctions violations to FinCEN’s whistleblower incentive program may be eligible for awards if the information they provide leads to a successful enforcement action that results in monetary penalties exceeding $1,000,000. Financial institutions and other persons may risk exposure to sanctions for engaging in certain transactions or activities with designated or otherwise blocked persons, including the persons designated today. This includes, in addition to blocking prohibitions, that OFAC can prohibit or impose strict conditions on opening or maintaining, in the United States, a correspondent account or a payable-through account of a foreign financial institution that knowingly conducts or facilitates any significant transaction on behalf of a person who is designated pursuant to the relevant authority.
The power and integrity of OFAC sanctions derive not only from OFAC’s ability to designate and add persons to the SDN List, but also from its willingness to remove persons from the SDN List, when consistent with relevant statutes and other authorities. The ultimate goal of sanctions is to bring about a positive change in behavior. What constitutes a sufficient change in circumstance will vary based on context, including the status of the broader geopolitical circumstances affecting the national security and foreign policy interests implicated by the declared national emergency. In the case of sanctions related to Iran, OFAC is employing all available statutory, regulatory, and policy tools to resolve the persistent national emergencies posed by Iran, which has not changed its behavior to align with U.S. national security and foreign policy objectives. OFAC sanctions determinations, including removal determinations, are made consistent with Administration foreign policy and national security policies and priorities. For more information concerning the process for seeking removal from an OFAC list, including the SDN List, or to submit a request, please refer to OFAC’s guidance on How to Request Removal from an OFAC List.
###
title: Operation Economic Outcast Targets Global Maritime Fraud Network Supporting Iranian Regime

Democratic House Majority Means Oversight, Accountability and Results for Veterans
Press Contact
Mike Lavigne (Communications Director)
Elain Shubat (Deputy Communications Director/Digital Director)
WASHINGTON–Today, the House Veterans’ Affairs Committee Ranking Member Mark Takano (CA-39) released the following statement after Democrats won the House majority:
“This election gives veterans a Congress that will check the executive branch and write good laws at the same time. Committee Democrats spent the 119th Congress doing both from the minority. We gathered 218 signatures on the Major Richard Star Act discharge petition. We flipped Republican votes on a benefits-cutting package until leadership pulled it from the floor. We forced a unanimous vote to authorize subpoenas of Oracle’s leadership. We held 18 shadow hearings and sent hundreds of oversight letters to VA. Imagine what this team can do with a gavel.”
Ranking Member Takano noted that the last time Democrats held the majority, in the 117th Congress, 60 House veterans’ bills became law, including the PACT Act.
Committee Democrats’ priorities for the 120th Congress include:
- Corruption and Contracts. Investigate VA Secretary Doug Collins and political appointee decisions at VA, hold VA contractors accountable, and follow the money, including Electronic Health Record Modernization and Community Care.
- Protect Earned Benefits. Defend the VA home loan program, go after claims sharks who prey on veterans, and strengthen the benefits veterans have earned.
- Healthcare. Expose delays, denials, and network failures in Community Care, and strengthen VA’s direct care system while protecting it from privatization.
- Workforce and Capacity. Scrutinize DOGE actions, staffing cuts, and vacancies that weaken VA’s ability to serve veterans or push care outside the department.
- Honor the Promise. Improve benefits, strengthen the PACT Act, hold VA accountable for the administration’s homelessness commitments, and ensure minority veterans receive equitable care and benefits.
“Veterans have a right to a VA that works, a Congress that checks the executive branch, and leaders who answer when it doesn’t. Beginning in January, they will have a House that fights for that right,” Takano said.

MARTINSBURG, WEST VIRGINIA – Six drug traffickers were sentenced today to a combined 37 years in federal prison for selling fentanyl, cocaine, and methamphetamine in the Eastern Panhandle of West Virginia, announced U.S. Attorney Matthew L. Harvey.

The separate cases are a part of a collaborative effort by multiple states and jurisdictions to arrest offenders and remove deadly drugs from our communities. Those sentenced are:

Kenneth Robert Eversole, 48, of Keyser, West Virginia, was sentenced to 168 months in federal prison for having more than 400 grams of fentanyl in Mineral County. Eversole was a source of supply for other drug traffickers in the Keyser area, distributing large quantities of pressed fentanyl pills and methamphetamine. Investigators determined Eversole distributed hundreds of fentanyl pills and executed a search warrant at the duplex where he resided. Officers seized nearly three pounds of fentanyl, almost two pounds of methamphetamine, 150 pounds of marijuana, and a small amount of cocaine. Along with the drugs, officers seized five firearms, cash, body armor, and drug paraphernalia.

Brenton Daniel Berens, 38, was sentenced to 60 months in prison and Shannon Lynn Smith, 40, was sentenced to 60 months for their roles in a drug trafficking operation selling fentanyl and cocaine in Berkeley County. Berens and Smith, both of Martinsburg, West Virginia, maintained a residence to store and package the drugs to serve as a distribution hub for the operation. Officers searched the home and seized nearly one pound of fentanyl. Investigators traced the drugs back to a Baltimore, Maryland man, Rodney Harry Augustine. Augustine was convicted for his role in this case and will be sentenced in 2027.

Malachi Brian Maurice Younger, 23, was sentenced to 41 months in prison for trafficking fentanyl and cocaine in Berkeley County. Younger was selling fentanyl and cocaine in West Virginia and Maryland, crossing state lines to continue his drug operation. During a traffic stop, officers seized more than a half a pound of cocaine, more than 50 grams of fentanyl, and a quarter pound of marijuana from his vehicle.

Shawn Douglas Kile, 29, of Keyser, West Virginia, was sentenced to 120 months in federal prison for distributing 50 grams or more of methamphetamine. Kile was selling methamphetamine, sometimes using his social media to communicate with customers. Investigators determined he sold a little more than 93 grams of methamphetamine in Mineral County.

“These sentences reflect the commitment of our federal, state, and local law enforcement partners who work tirelessly to protect our communities. Thanks to their exceptional teamwork, these dangerous traffickers have been removed from our streets, and our community is safer as a result. But our work does not end here. My office will continue to aggressively pursue those who choose to traffic deadly drugs into West Virginia and will remain relentless in our efforts to eliminate drug networks wherever they operate,” said U.S. Attorney Matthew L. Harvey.

“These sentences reflect the commitment of our federal, state, and local law enforcement partners who work tirelessly to protect our communities. Thanks to their exceptional teamwork, these dangerous traffickers have been removed from our streets, and our community is safer as a result. But our work does not end here. My office will continue to aggressively pursue those who choose to traffic deadly drugs into West Virginia and will remain relentless in our efforts to eliminate drug networks wherever they operate,” said U.S. Attorney Matthew L. Harvey.

Criminal Division Chief Lara Omps-Botteicher prosecuted the cases on behalf of the government. Investigative agencies include the Drug Enforcement Administration; the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives; the Washington County, Maryland Narcotics Task Force; the Eastern Panhandle Drug Task Force, a HIDTA-funded initiative; the Potomac Highlands Drug Task Force, a HIDTA-funded initiative; the Maryland State Police; the Hagerstown, MD Police Department; and the Washington County, MD Sheriff’s Department.

The prosecution of these cases directly advances a core priority of our office’s Four Corners of Public Safety initiative: stopping the flow of illegal drugs into the Northern District of West Virginia. Drug trafficking poses a serious threat to public safety, fueling addiction, harming families, and endangering communities. By focusing on dismantling drug trafficking activity, this effort reinforces our commitment to keeping dangerous drugs off the streets and safeguarding the people of Northern District of West Virginia. To learn more about the Four Corners of Public Safety, click here .

Fentanyl has been designated by President Donald Trump as a weapon of mass destruction due to its extreme lethality which poses a grave threat to public safety, even in trace amounts. This case is part of Operation Take Back America , a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime, and repel the invasion of illegal immigration.

U.S. District Judge Gina M. Groh presided.

text:
CMS Finalizes CY 2027 Physician Fee Schedule to Shift from Sick Care to Healthcare and Curb Waste
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) is prioritizing prevention, strengthening primary care, cracking down on duplicate billing, and reinforcing fiscal stewardship across Medicare. A new final rule advancing payment policies under Medicare Part B modernizes physician payment structures to reward health maintenance and coordinated primary care rather than disjointed, volume-based intervention. Through targeted enhancements to the Medicare Shared Savings Program (Shared Savings Program) and fee schedule recalibrations, CMS is shifting the health system’s focus from reactive sick care to proactive healthcare.
“Medicare should reward clinicians for keeping people healthy,” said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “Under President Trump’s leadership, we are putting prevention and primary care at the center of Medicare, closing payment loopholes, and cracking down on waste. This rule directs resources toward coordinated care that puts patients first. We are changing what Medicare pays for to change what our health system delivers.”
“For too long, fee-for-service payment has rewarded volume over value, fueling a reactive system of sick care,” said CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz. “This final rule breaks from that status quo. By ending duplicate billing and closing costly loopholes, we are protecting taxpayers and directing Medicare dollars to clinicians doing the hard work of keeping patients healthy.”
Modernizing Quality Reporting and Statutory Mandates
Marking a decade of progress under the Quality Payment Program, CMS will officially sunset the traditional Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) reporting option beginning with the CY 2031 performance period. Clinicians will have through CY 2030 to transition to the MIPS Value Pathways (MVPs), which already cover approximately 98%of clinicians, or Advanced Alternative Payment Models. This reflects two additional years of transition time compared to the proposed rule. The rule also finalizes three new MVPs focused on diabetes, hypertension, and hospitalists, and requires clinicians to report at least one specialty-specific “Core Measure” starting in CY 2027.
Additionally, the Calendar Year (CY) 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule (PFS) rule finalizes two new billing codes dedicated to Advance Care Planning and codifies noncitizen Medicare eligibility criteria established by the Working Families Tax Cuts legislation.
Expanding and Strengthening Accountable Care Organizations
Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) are vital to improving primary care and helping beneficiaries live healthier lives. Data shows that patients aligned with an ACO are less likely to experience uncontrolled diabetes or hypertension and are more likely to receive recommended preventive care. In performance year 2024, 75% of the 476 participating ACOs earned shared savings totaling $4.1 billion, while generating net savings for the Medicare Trust Funds of approximately $2.5 billion compared to projected spending benchmarks.
The Shared Savings Program has generated savings for the Medicare Trust Funds for eight consecutive performance years, and to build on this progress, the final rule:
- Permits ACOs to Eliminate Patient Cost-Sharing: Starting April 1, 2027, approved ACOs may reduce or eliminate Part B cost-sharing for many items and services for assigned beneficiaries, directly lowering out-of-pocket costs for essential care.
- Incentivizes Growth: CMS increases shared savings rates for eligible ACOs, provides new incentives for first-time participants, and sets more predictable spending targets.
- Cuts Red Tape: The rule simplifies electronic health record reporting requirements, streamlines patient notice mandates, and removes outdated administrative hurdles.
Restoring Payment Integrity and Curbing Waste
CMS is recalibrating fee schedule valuations to reflect the true complexity and resources of modern care and closing loopholes that allow users to game the system:
- Ending Duplicate Billing: When an office visit and minor procedure occur on the same day, CMS will reduce payment by 20% for the lower-cost service, reducing duplication in payment by patients and the Medicare program for clinical work already covered in the procedure’s valuation.
- Closing Windfall Loopholes: The rule corrects an incentive payment loophole, preventing an estimated $2.38 billion in unintended windfall payments over the next decade.
- Improving Rate Accuracy: CMS is streamlining outdated steps from its rate-setting formula, leading to greater simplicity and transparency for clinicians and patients while allowing payment policy to adapt to changes in healthcare delivery.
CMS Expands Access to Preventive Care and Wellness in Support of MAHA Initiative
CMS is finalizing critical coding and payment expansions to strengthen preventive care and wellness across the nation. CMS is establishing national payment pathways for health and well-being coaching under general supervision, introducing dedicated billing for shared medical appointments with flexible time-based add-on codes, and boosting valuations for smoking cessation and behavioral health assessments.
Additionally, the agency is finalizing separate billing for the dedicated clinical time required to diagnose, treat, and counsel patients experiencing vaccine adverse effects, reinforcing our commitment to patient trust and robust clinical support. These pivotal updates ensure Medicare resources directly support proactive, patient-centered care and improve health outcomes for Americans.
Ambulatory Specialty Model
CMS is also finalizing refinements to the Ambulatory Specialty Model — a CMS Innovation Center model launching Jan. 1 that holds specialists accountable for the quality and cost of care associated with the longitudinal management of two common chronic conditions, heart failure and low back pain, to slow disease progression and reduce avoidable hospitalizations and low-value procedures.
For more information on the CY 2027 Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule, which is effective Jan. 1, 2027, visit the Fact Sheet for Calendar Year (CY) 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule.
###

title: CMS Finalizes CY 2027 Physician Fee Schedule to Shift from Sick Care to Healthcare and Curb Waste

ROCHESTER, N.Y.-U.S. Attorney Michael DiGiacomo announced today that Robert Tantalo, 43 of Greece, NY, was charged by criminal complaint with wire fraud and the transportation and sale of stolen goods in interstate commerce, which carry a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison and a fine of $250,000.

According to the criminal complaint, Tantalo was the controller for a group of companies that operated under common management (Victim Company). As controller, he oversaw accounting, auditing, financial reporting, and budget preparation, as well as bank accounts, credit cards, and assets and was responsible for disbursing funds to pay expenses and payroll. As a result, Tantalo had access to the personal information of every employee and member of the Victim Company, some of whom were issued credit cards for the payment of business expenses. Tantalo was responsible for obtaining those credit cards and distributing them, giving him access to each of the Victim Company’s bank account numbers, credit card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes.

In March 2026, Tantalo resigned from the Victim Company. After his departure, the Victim Company discovered that between February 2025 and April 2026, he used a company credit card to make approximately 248 personal, unauthorized purchases totaling approximately $492,996.96. These purchases included residential property tax payments, gift cards and electronics from Target, and electronics from Amazon, which Tantalo then resold on eBay. He masked the purchases by using multiple Victim Company bank accounts to make structured payments towards the balance of the card and by making false entries in the Victim Company’s books and records. According to the Victim Company, Tantalo was the only person with access to all of the bank accounts and therefore was the only person who could have made credit card payments.

Tantalo made an initial appearance before U.S. Magistrate Judge Mark W. Pedersen and was released on conditions.

The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Meghan K. McGuire. The complaint is the result of an investigation by the Monroe County Sheriff's Office, under the direction of Sheriff Todd Baxter and Homeland Security Investigations, under the direction of Special Agent-in-Charge Anthony Patrone.

The fact that a defendant has been charged with a crime is merely an accusation and the defendant is presumed innocent until and unless proven guilty.

ALBUQUERQUE – A Shiprock man pleaded guilty to federal firearms offenses for shooting multiple rounds into an occupied residence.

According to court documents, on January 21, 2026, Navajo Police Department dispatch received a call reporting that Taylon Keeswood , 20, an enrolled member of the Navajo Nation, was shooting at a house in Shiprock, New Mexico. Responding officers located and detained Keeswood near the house shortly after the call. Investigators recovered shell casings and confirmed that the residence, which was occupied by an adult and three children, had been struck numerous times by gunfire. No one inside the home was injured.

Keeswood later admitted to investigators that he fired an AK-style rifle from his hip, emptying a 30-round magazine at the residence, which he believed belonged to an individual with whom he had prior disputes. After the shooting, Keeswood fled the area and hid the firearm, which law enforcement later recovered at a location he identified.

Keeswood pleaded guilty to using and carrying a firearm during and in relation to a crime of violence. At sentencing Keeswood faces up to 10 years in prison.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison and Special Agent in Charge Justin A. Garris of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albuquerque Field Office made the announcement today.

The Farmington Resident Agency of the FBI’s Albuquerque Field Office investigated this case with assistance from the Navajo Police Department and Navajo Department of Criminal Investigations. Assistant U.S. Attorney Amy Mondragon is prosecuting the case.
title: Shiprock Man Pleads Guilty After Shooting into Residence

Two officers from the Polish armed forces visited the U.S. Army Test, Measurement and Diagnostic Equipment Activity, known as USATA, Oct. 20 and 21 to establish bilateral cooperation on the calibration and maintenance of key military systems.
Polish army Lt. Col. Przemysław Piróg and Maj. Sławomir Dąbrowski toured the U.S. Army Primary Standards Laboratory and a secondary reference calibration laboratory to observe standard operating procedures and exchange metrology best practices.
The engagement, initiated at Poland’s request through the Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Agile Sustainment and Ammunition, focused on sustaining U.S.-manufactured weapon systems currently fielded by the Polish military, including the M1A1 Abrams main battle tank, the M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket System and the Patriot air defense system.
"Poland has purchased advanced land-force weapon systems in recent years," Piróg said. "To keep these systems reliable and usable throughout their entire life cycle, proper maintenance is essential, and metrology sits at the top of that maintenance hierarchy. Our role is to adapt the existing Polish infrastructure to support the new platforms."
While foreign military sales often spotlight major combat platforms, USATA officials and the visiting delegation emphasized that test, measurement and diagnostic equipment, or TMDE, and calibration infrastructure are equally vital to preventing immediate readiness degradation for allied partners.
"These platforms are complex systems that represent true engineering marvels," Dąbrowski said. "To reap their combat advantages, careful maintenance is required. The silent service of calibration labs and TMDE support operates from the start to the finish line, ensuring accurate shots and successful mission outcomes. This is a critical factor for states like Poland, which faces a real threat on its eastern borders."
"Calibration is an integral part of maintenance, as it ensures the measurements and tests are accurate," said Ronald Binkowski, chief of the S-3 Management and Operations Directorate at USATA.
John Schneider, an equipment specialist with the portfolio acquisition executive office, agreed, noting the direct impact precision has on the warfighter.
"This helps ensure soldiers’ safety, as they can prove that all the maintenance tests performed with properly calibrated equipment are correct and traceable to Army and industry standards," Schneider said.
During the two-day visit, the Polish delegation received a comprehensive view of the traceability and processes underpinning the U.S. Army's metrology program. The tour highlighted the primary laboratory’s ongoing collaboration with the National Institute of Standards and Technology to deliver cutting-edge metrology capabilities to the warfighter.
For the visiting officers, the opportunity to tour the facilities and coordinate in person was crucial for building a functioning, long-term program.
"Equipment and standards are one thing, but building a fully functional system around them is a real challenge," Piróg said. "When you have direct contact with engineers who have been working on these systems for years, there is no need to reinvent the wheel when you can simply ask. That is why this contact is so valuable to us."
Although conducted outside the direct Foreign Military Sales transaction pipeline, bilateral engagements with NATO allies like Poland directly support U.S. Army security assistance priorities. The face-to-face coordination builds mutual technical trust, establishes direct lines of communication for overseas support and baselines requirements for future metrology interoperability.
"In one word, it is a matter of trust," Dąbrowski said. "In metrology, this is called mutual recognition; we trust our partner’s calibration methods and expect the same in return. We often use the same standards and technical documentation, so interoperability is not an empty term."
By aligning calibration standards and technical requirements now, officials noted that higher-level calibration work could eventually be performed with complete confidence at geographical locations closer to Polish forces, returning mission-critical equipment to soldiers' hands much faster.
title: U.S. Army Test, Measurement and Diagnostic Equipment Activity hosts Polish delegation to bolster allied readiness, interoperability

U.S. Marshals Arrest Texas Murder Suspect in Aberdeen
For immediate release
Gary Bunt, Supervisory Deputy U.S. Marshal
ABERDEEN, S.D. - On Monday evening the U.S. Marshals Service – Dakota Territory Fugitive Task Force located and arrested a fugitive wanted for Murder.
The fugitive, a juvenile, was wanted for a shooting that took place in the early morning hours of October 25, 2026, in Arlington, TX, a suburb of Dallas. The juvenile allegedly shot and killed the victim during an argument at a party.
On October 30, 2026, a Murder warrant was issued for the juvenile in Tarrant County, Texas. Investigators learned the juvenile likely fled the state of Texas to stay with relatives in Aberdeen.
On the evening of Monday November 2, 2026, U.S. Marshals, with the assistance of the Aberdeen Police Department and Brown County Sheriff’s Office, located and arrested the juvenile at an apartment in the 600 block of South Park Avenue.
The juvenile was placed in the Brown County Juvenile Detention Center and is currently awaiting juvenile court proceedings and extradition to Texas.
Due to the suspect’s status as a juvenile, the U.S. Marshals Service cannot release their name.

From a childhood spent moving with a Coast Guard family to a career focused on occupational health and safety, Ashlyn Schmitt brings both technical expertise and a people-first mindset to the Buffalo District. As an Industrial Hygienist, she helps identify and evaluate workplace health hazards while supporting safe operations across the district.
Q: Where are you from?
Ashlyn: I was born at Cherry Point Marine Corps Air Station in Havelock, North Carolina, and moved frequently growing up because my father served in the U.S. Coast Guard. My family lived in California and Iowa before eventually settling in Northeast Ohio, where we moved to be closer to extended family after my father accepted a position at the Coast Guard station in Cleveland.
Q: What did you study, and where did you attend college?
Ashlyn: I attended The University of Akron, where I majored in chemical engineering and earned my bachelor’s degree in 2020.
Q: What is your position with the Buffalo District?
Ashlyn: I serve as an Industrial Hygienist with the Buffalo District, specializing in occupational health hazards. My work includes conducting air and noise sampling at project sites to help evaluate employee exposure levels and ensure conditions remain within appropriate limits.
Q: How did you learn about the position with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers?
Ashlyn: I was already living in the same city as the field office where I worked, so I knew the Buffalo District had a local presence. When I saw the Industrial Hygienist vacancy, I viewed it as a great opportunity because it was closer to home and allowed me to remain in Ohio.
Q: What motivated you to join the Buffalo District?
Ashlyn: Before joining the Buffalo District, I worked for the Occupational Safety and Health Administration as a Safety Engineer, conducting onsite inspections and issuing citations throughout Northeast Ohio. I was interested in transitioning into a more proactive role that focused less on enforcement and more on helping prevent workplace hazards.
Q: What do you enjoy doing outside of work?
Ashlyn: Outside of work, my husband and I spend a lot of time with our four shepherd-mix dogs. I also compete with two of them in an Akron-area frisbee league that I have participated in for the past five years. In addition, I enjoy bouldering, scuba diving, and playing trivia. One of the most memorable places I have gone scuba diving was Taiwan, and I am National Association of Underwater Instructors (NAUI)-certified with additional diving experience in quarries throughout Ohio.
With a background in engineering, safety, and field-based hazard assessment, Ashlyn plays an important role in helping protect the Buffalo District workforce. Her proactive approach to occupational health supports safe, effective mission execution across the district.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Buffalo District delivers world-class engineering solutions to the Great Lakes Region, the Army and the Nation to ensure national security, environmental sustainability, water resource management, and emergency assistance during peace and war.
For 250 years, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers has been at the forefront of the nation’s engineering excellence, responding when called. From constructing fortifications during the Revolutionary War, to building the infrastructure that saw America’s strength grow militarily and economically, USACE’s mission has always been to deliver engineering solutions for our nation’s toughest challenges.
title: Meet the Team: Buffalo District Industrial Hygienist Brings Proactive Safety Focus to the Mission

Rep. Panetta’s Statement on His 2026 Reelection
Monterey, CA – United States Representative Jimmy Panetta (CA-19) released the following statement on the results of his 2026 reelection:
“I am deeply honored and humbled that the people of California’s 19th Congressional District again elected me to represent them in the United States Congress. My work in Congress has always been guided by the principle that good governing is good politics. Tonight’s overwhelming results reaffirm that belief, bolster my work, and strengthen my commitment to delivering for the people that I proudly serve.
“Over the past two years, the division and dysfunction in Washington could lead many across the nation to be disillusioned and disengage from the responsibilities of living in our democracy. However, tonight’s results demonstrate that Americans don’t cower during dark times. Instead, we face our challenges, stand together, and embrace our obligations through the democratic process of voting. By giving us robust Democratic majorities in the House and Senate, the American voters also gave us a mandate to govern in the 120th Congress.
“With our agency, we must now set the agenda and provide answers for Americans when it comes to the issues of affordability and accountability.  Living up to our Constitutional responsibilities and our system of checks and balances, we will legislate to bring down the cost of living, and, at the same time, we will investigate any and all misdeeds by this Administration.  I look forward to upholding my Constitutional oath through my service in the 120th Congress, my willingness to work with anybody who helps me govern, and my will to fight anybody who threatens our democratic values.”
