DALLAS — U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Texas Ryan Raybould announced that Nikolay Sapov, also known as Nikolay Georgiyevitch Sapov, was indicted by a federal grand jury on felony stalking charges after allegedly tracking a former coworker from Canada to North Texas.

The two-count indictment charges Sapov with stalking through interstate travel and stalking through electronic communications. Sapov was previously arrested by U.S. Customs and Border Protection on an Amtrak train entering the United States.

“No individual has the right to terrorize another human being or shatter their sense of safety inside their own home,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould. “From relentless digital harassment to an international stalking campaign that spanned across the globe, this defendant went to chilling lengths to hunt down, disguise himself, and intimidate this victim. This indictment makes our position clear: predatory behavior across borders will be met with swift, uncompromising federal justice.”

“Stalking and targeted harassment can have a profound impact, disrupting victims’ lives and leaving them feeling vulnerable,” said FBI Dallas Special Agent in Charge R. Joseph Rothrock. “The FBI remains committed to identifying and holding accountable those who use threats and intimidation to instill fear. We will continue working with our law enforcement partners to protect the members of our communities and pursue justice for victims.”

According to court filings, Sapov first met the victim several years ago while both were seasonal player services employees at the Miami Open tennis tournament. Over several years, Sapov allegedly developed an obsession with the victim, repeatedly contacting the victim outside of work hours, tracking down personal and family social media profiles, and sending unwanted gifts and correspondence to the victim’s residences.

Sapov traveled to Orlando and Plantation, Florida, to stalk her in 2023 and 2025. Court documents allege the conduct escalated in June 2026, when Sapov traveled from Toronto, Canada, to Dallas, Texas, where the victim was residing. After renting a vehicle at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, Sapov allegedly located the victim’s gated residential complex. On June 22, 2026, the victim observed Sapov loitering near their apartment building. Local law enforcement and property security responded, locating Sapov and issuing a criminal trespass warning.

Two days later, on June 24, 2026, a neighbor’s video doorbell captured an individual matching Sapov’s physical build, clothing, and footwear approaching the victim's front door while wearing a full rubber mask to conceal his face.

When confronted via the doorbell intercom, the masked suspect fled the premises. Fearing for their safety, the victim and their partner temporarily relocated to emergency hotel lodging and purchased security measures.

Despite the Dallas incident and subsequent police reports, Sapov allegedly continued to send unwanted electronic messages to the victim through August 2026, including an artificial intelligence-generated image depicting the victim posing alongside him.

On Aug. 22, Customs and Border Protection officers arrested Sapov pursuant to a Texas stalking warrant as he was traveling on an Amtrak train from Canada to into the US. Law enforcement recovered electronic equipment and two cellular devices containing maps and street names surrounding the victim’s neighborhood, photographs of women’s shoes exhibited in an apparent sexual way, and screenshots of key copying/locksmith companies. There were also explicit AI-generated photographs and videos of the adult victim.

If convicted, Sapov faces a statutory maximum penalty of five years in federal prison on each count, followed by a period of supervised release and potential financial penalties.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Dallas Field Office (Violent Crimes Task Force) investigated the case, with substantial assistance from U.S. Customs and Border Protection, the Dallas Police Department, and the Tyler Police Department. Assistant U.S. Attorney Nadin-Sarah Salkić from the is prosecuting the case.

Advancing Cooperative Federalism: EPA Awards Cooperative Agreement to the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials to Support States and Territories on Environmental Health
Contact Information
EPA Press Office (press@epa.gov) 
WASHINGTON — Today, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) announced a new agencywide cooperative agreement with the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials (ASTHO) to support their efforts to address environmental health challenges.
“Protecting public and environmental health works best when federal, state, and territorial partners work together. This collaboration between EPA and ASTHO puts cooperative federalism into action by bringing public health and environmental expertise to the same table, delivering impactful and timely results to improve environmental outcomes for communities across the country.” said Associate Deputy Administrator Travis Voyles.
“This cooperative agreement strengthens the partnership between ASTHO and EPA and supports state and territorial health agencies in addressing environmental health challenges and protecting the health of their communities,” said Dr. Meredith Allen, Vice President of Health Security, ASTHO.
Under the agreement, EPA and ASTHO will continue collaboration on shared environmental health priorities, including water safety, wildfire smoke, data centers, PFAS, lead, and indoor air quality.
Through this cooperative agreement, EPA scientists and engineers will provide critical technical assistance to enhance state and territorial capacity to address environmental health challenges through activities to support knowledge sharing and capacity building including webinars, in-person meetings, and technical training.
The agreement also supports a recently signed Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) between EPA, ASTHO, and the Environmental Council of the States (ECOS) to collaborate on environmental health projects, protect public health from environmental threats and hazards, and strengthen environmental health systems nationwide.
These types of agreements help advance cooperative federalism and cross-agency partnerships and continue cooperative progress toward providing clean air, land, and water for all Americans.
This work also supports EPA’s contributions to the Federal Lead Action Plan and President Trump’s Make America Healthy Again initiative by taking an integrated approach to addressing human health and environmental challenges.
For more information on EPA’s collaborations with ASTHO and ECOS, visit the Collaborative Projects with State Environmental Health Experts page.

ST. PAUL – United States Attorney Daniel N. Rosen announced that Tyler Maxon Avalos, 30, was found guilty by a federal jury of interstate transmission of a threat to injure the person of another. The guilty verdict was returned on November 4, 2026, following a federal jury trial before U.S. District Judge Susan Richard Nelson.

“The jury’s guilty verdict today is the result of the continuing campaign by my office and federal law enforcement to target those that threaten violence in the political arena,” said United States Attorney Daniel N. Rosen. “As American society continues to be more politically polarized, those that threaten, commit, or induce others to commit acts of political violence are becoming more numerous, more brazen, and more dangerous.

“Just this year, this office has won the convictions of individuals that have threatened a total of eight federal judges, one United States Supreme Court justice, four members of the United States House of Representatives, and two members of the United States Senate.

“And it’s more than threats: this year we won the conviction of an individual who assaulted a member of the United States House of Representatives from Minnesota; we charged three individuals with assaulting a journalist that they singled out for the journalist’s assumed political views; we charged fifteen individuals with plotting and carrying out acts of violence in order to impede law enforcement; we charged an individual with plotting a mass-casualty attack at the Mall of America, motivated by the religion of the owners and of those he intended to shoot; and we obtained the guilty plea and sentence to consecutive life terms in prison for the assassin of the former Speaker of the Minnesota House of Representatives and her husband.

“In our current polarized environment in which bitter and violent speech has become commonplace, our society is becoming increasingly callous. That callousness is breeding increased threats, attempted violence, and deadly violence.

“Politically motivated threats and violence are a plague on our society. Rest assured, however, that federal law enforcement agencies are on high alert, at all times, for such threats and violence, and the United States Attorney’s Office remains committed to prosecuting all perpetrators.”

According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, on October 9, 2025, a Michigan user of an internet-based social media platform observed a post that the user believed threatened then-United States Attorney General Pamela Bondi. The user reported the post to the FBI, stating that the post was “[i]mposing a hit on Pam bondi for $45,000 posting it on [the social media platform] his user name is @liminalvoidslip.” The threatening post featured a photograph of then-Attorney General Pamela Bondi with a sniper-scope-style red-dot crosshair imposed on her forehead, and words stating that she was “wanted” “dead or alive,” “preferably dead.” The person who made the post also included a comment below the post that read, “when they don’t serve us then what?”

The FBI traced the threatening post to Avalos. Avalos’s social media profile page contained various symbols associated with anarchists, including a link to an “Anarchist FAQ.” Avalos had a criminal history that includes a felony stalking conviction in 2022 in Dakota County, Minnesota, and a felony domestic battery conviction in 2016 in Polk County, Florida. Avalos additionally had several misdemeanor domestic-assault convictions.

Avalos used several social media platforms to engage with, promote, or post content that celebrated the killing of Charlie Kirk. His accounts also made references to Luigi Mangione, the alleged assassin of the United Healthcare CEO, including one post featuring an image of a sticker reading “be the Luigi you want to see in the world,” followed by an anarchist symbol.

Post made by Avalos depicting a sticker reading, “BE THE LUIGI YOU WANT TO SEE IN THE WORLD,” followed by an anarchist symbol

Avalos’s social media accounts posted other comments, including, “I bet if politicians got kirked they’d start acting right,” “do you expect to remove fascists from power without bloodshed,” “feds need it next,” and “the whole administrations needs to be put on a wall.”

A review of Avalos’s phone seized during a search of his residence uncovered other materials including a video narrated by Avalos stating that he believed he knew where a CEO of a technology company lived with his wife and child. In the video, Avalos said, “Since we got the brave souls that are targeting CEOs, I think that he should be next on the list, because obvious reason. Don’t disappoint please…”

This case was the result of an investigation by the FBI, with assistance from other law enforcement partners.

First Assistant United States Attorney Joseph S. Teirab and Assistant United States Attorneys David Green and Benjamin Bejar are prosecuting this case.
title: Federal Jury Finds Minnesota Man Guilty of Transmitting Threat to Injure Former United States Attorney General

FORT SMITH – Assistant United States Attorney Dustin Roberts and Assistant United States Attorney Kevin Eaton of the United States Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Arkansas were among 183 Department of Justice employees recognized by Attorney General Todd Blanche and Executive Office for U.S. Attorneys (EOUSA) Director Francey Hakes at the 2026 Director’s Awards Ceremony held October 28 in the Great Hall of the Robert F. Kennedy Department of Justice Building in Washington, D.C. The awards recognize outstanding achievements by employees of the United States Attorney’s Offices.

“I am incredibly proud of Assistant United States Attorneys Dustin Roberts and Kevin Eaton. Their dedication, integrity, and genuine commitment to protecting the people of the Western District of Arkansas shine through in everything they do,” said Kevin R. Holmes, United States Attorney for the Western District of Arkansas. “This recognition from the Attorney General is a truly deserved honor, and I’m grateful to serve alongside them.”

Excellence in a Managerial Role

This award recognizes an employee who has accomplished superior managerial and supervisory achievements over at least the last three years.

In 2025, Western Arkansas experienced a 7 year high in prosecutions, with Assistant United States Attorney Dustin Roberts serving as Criminal Chief over 13 AUSAs, often serving as second chair in trials. In addition to his supervisory duties, he maintained a full load of criminal cases as lead prosecutor, to include United States vs. Joshua Duggar, which drew national attention.

Excellence as an Appellate Assistant United States Attorney

This award recognizes AUSAs who perform appellate work for their USAO and who have distinguished themselves through the outstanding performance of their duties.

In 2025 Assistant United States Attorney Kevin Eaton handled several high-profile cases, four of which he argued at the Eighth Circuit within a ten-month period. The oral arguments involved defending the constitutionality of the federal ban on machineguns, resisting a defendant’s attempts to import the requirements of Apprendi into supervised release hearings, and defending a denial of a suppression motion raising unique issues involving the interplay between Arkansas law and the Fourth Amendment.

LITTLE ROCK—A federal jury has convicted Kyle Keith Robinson of conspiracy to possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine and possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine. The trial, which spanned two days, ended on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, with guilty verdicts on all counts he was charged with in the Indictment. Jonathan D. Ross, United States Attorney for the Eastern District of Arkansas, announced the verdict.

Robinson, 43, of Conway, was indicted by a federal grand jury on August 5, 2025, and went to trial facing two charges, conspiracy to possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine and possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine.

Evidence at trial proved that on August 15, 2024, investigators from the North Little Rock Police Department executed a search warrant at a residence of an individual suspected of selling methamphetamine. When officers arrived to execute the warrant, Robinson was observed sitting in the driver’s seat of his vehicle parked in the driveway, with another individual, co-defendant Bryan Matthews, sitting in the passenger seat. Robinson fled on foot from officers. While fleeing, Robinson became entangled in a briar patch, enabling officers to apprehend Robinson and place him into custody. During a search of Robinson’s vehicle, officers located 83 grams of methamphetamine in the driver’s side door pocket. Robinson also had more than $1,500 in cash, most of that in $20s, on his person. Robinson has five prior felonies for distribution of controlled substances.

After deliberating for approximately 30 minutes, the jury found Robinson guilty of all counts he was charged with in the Indictment. Following the guilty verdicts on the charges, Robinson was taken into custody to await sentencing. On each of the charges, Robinson faces a sentence of five years to 40 years in prison, with at least four years of supervised release to follow. There is no parole in the federal system.

Robinson’s criminal history includes four felony state convictions for possession with intent to distribute marijuana, and two separate federal felony convictions for conspiracy to distribute marijuana, heroin, cocaine, and oxycodone, and two counts of possession with intent to distribute cocaine.

The investigation was conducted by the North Little Rock Police Department with assistance from the Drug Enforcement Administration. The case was prosecuted and tried by Assistant United States Attorneys Bart Dickinson and Michael Gordon.

ALBUQUERQUE – A Morgan Lake man was sentenced to 17 days in custody for striking and injuring a Navajo Nation Police officer with his car.

According to court documents, on September 28, 2025, officers from the Navajo Nation Police Department responded to a report of a suspected drunk driver traveling at a high rate of speed and throwing containers from his vehicle. Officers located Kendall Benally , 43, an enrolled member of the Navajo Nation, sitting behind the wheel of a van near Morgan Lake. Benally , who had been convicted twice previously of driving while intoxicated, refused repeated commands to exit the vehicle. When officers deployed pepper spray, Benally accelerated, striking an officer and a civilian and pinning them between his vehicle and a police cruiser before fleeing the scene.

The officer suffered injuries to his elbow, knee and hip that required hospital treatment, while the civilian reported pain and injuries to multiple parts of his body. Benally was located and arrested later that morning. A subsequent breath alcohol test registered a blood alcohol concentration of 0.11. Benally admitted to investigators that he had consumed six beers and a double shot of liquor before driving.

Benally pleaded guilty to assault with intent to commit a felony. Upon his release from prison, Benally will be subject to two years of supervised release.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison and Special Agent in Charge Justin A. Garris of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albuquerque Field Office made the announcement today.

The Farmington Resident Agency of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albuquerque Field Office investigated this case with assistance from the Navajo Nation Police Department and Navajo Department of Criminal Investigations. Assistant U.S. Attorney Jack E. Burkhead is prosecuting the case.
title: Morgan Lake Man Sentenced for Assaulting a Police Officer

OAKLAND – Carson Fries was sentenced today to 72 months in federal prison for drug trafficking. U.S. District Judge Haywood S. Gilliam, Jr. handed down the sentence.

Fries, 34, of Bay Point, California, was charged by Criminal Complaint on September 22, 2025, and charged by Information on May 12, 2026. Fries pleaded guilty on July 29, 2026, to Possession with Intent to Distribute 50 Grams or More of a Mixture or Substance Containing a Detectable Amount of Methamphetamine, in violation of 21 U.S.C. § 841(a)(1) and (b)(1)(B)(viii)). Fries was a significant drug supplier in Contra Costa County. According to the plea agreement, Fries admitted to selling large quantities of meth on at least three instances between August 29, 2025, and September 9, 2025, in Bay Point. On August 29, 2025, he sold approximately 478 gross grams of methamphetamine. On September 3, 2025, Fries sold approximately 518 gross grams of methamphetamine. And on September 9, 2025, Fries sold approximately 506 gross grams of methamphetamine. Additionally, 160 grams of methamphetamine and 33 firearms and a stockpile of ammunition were found at Fries’ residence during a search conducted pursuant to a search warrant.

United States Attorney Craig H. Missakian and Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Special Agent in Charge Bob P. Beris made the announcement. In addition to the prison term, Judge Gilliam also sentenced the defendant to four years of supervised release.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Ivana Djak is prosecuting the case with the assistance of Jessie Chelsea and Amala James. The prosecution is the result of an investigation by the DEA and the Concord Police Department.

Washington, DC — Representative Gregory W. Meeks, Ranking Member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Senator Jeanne Shaheen, Ranking Member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, released the following statement on the Trump administration’s intent to terminate South Africa from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) trade program:
“The Trump administration’s policy toward South Africa has prioritized political spectacle and disputed narratives over substantive diplomatic engagement and longstanding U.S. strategic interests. The U.S. Trade Representative’s announcement that South Africa will soon lose its benefits under the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) risks further undermining American economic interests while handing China a strategic advantage. At a time when the United States should be encouraging manufacturers to diversify their supply chains away from China, trade preference programs like AGOA are critical tools for strengthening commercial ties with alternative markets. Rather than advancing this objective, the administration’s decision threatens to disrupt established supply chains, weaken opportunities for American manufacturers, and cede economic influence to China.
“AGOA has long been a valuable tool for U.S. economic relationships across Africa that both promote African prosperity and create opportunities for American businesses. Walking away from that partnership is shortsighted and ultimately undermines our own interests. We call on USTR and the White House to engage with the South African government in good faith during the 60-day notification period to explore remediation efforts that could address any eligibility concerns and protect this important relationship.”
###
title: Meeks, Shaheen Issue Statement on Trump Admin’s Decision to Remove South Africa from AGOA

OKLAHOMA CITY – HOWARD RAYMOND GIMMEY , 47, of Midwest City, Oklahoma, has pleaded guilty to communicating a threat in interstate commerce, announced U.S. Attorney Robert J. Troester.

According to public records, on May 5, 2026, Gimmey posted a message on social media stating, “I’m going to kill the President….” Court records allege that Gimmey posted the statement online, knowing that the communication would be viewed as a threat by others.

On October 6, 2026, a federal grand jury charged Gimmey with communicating a threat. Gimmey pleaded guilty on November 3, 2026, and admitted he made a comment online threatening to kill the President. At sentencing, Gimmey faces up to five years in federal prison, and a fine of up to $250,000.

This case is the result of an investigation by FBI Oklahoma City’s Joint Terrorism Task Force, the United States Secret Service, and the Midwest City Police Department. Assistant U.S. Attorney Matt Dillon is prosecuting the case.

This case is part of the nationwide National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 initiative, which is a White House directed, interagency effort to integrate federal, state, and local partners in protecting First Amendment rights while targeting individuals and organizations engaged in political violence.

Reference is made to public filings for additional information.

TUCSON, Ariz. – Sebastian Higuera-Fuentes, 23, of Nogales, Sonora, Mexico, was sentenced on Oct. 27, by United States District Judge Raner C. Collins to 60 months in prison, followed by four years of supervised release. Higuera-Fuentes previously pleaded guilty to Conspiracy to Distribute Methamphetamine.

As part of the conspiracy, Higuera-Fuentes was involved in the distribution of approximately 20 kilograms of pure methamphetamine. Higuera-Fuentes acted as a leader in the conspiracy, negotiating pricing, arranging meeting times and locations, and directing his co-conspirators to deliver the drugs. As a direct result of law enforcement’s efforts in this case, the methamphetamine never made it into Arizona communities.

This prosecution is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. This HSTF Tucson investigation involved agents and officers from the Drug Enforcement Administration in Detroit, Michigan and Tucson, Arizona, Homeland Security Investigations, Federal Bureau of Investigation, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, United States Marshals Service, Internal Revenue Service-Criminal Investigation, ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations, United States Customs and Border Protection, United States Border Patrol, United States Postal Inspection Service, United States Secret Service, and the Bureau of Land Management. The prosecution is being by the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Arizona. Assistant U.S. Attorney David Petermann, District of Arizona, Tucson, handled the prosecution.

ABERDEEN PROVING GROUND, Md. - Military-connected youth ages six and older gathered at Fanshaw Field on Nov. 3 to participate in Aberdeen Proving Ground’s first Presidential Fitness Test.
The inaugural event was organized by APG Child and Youth Services (CYS), a program under the installation's Directorate of Family and Morale, Welfare, and Recreation (MWR). The initiative brought school-age children from the Youth Center via CYS buses for a morning of friendly competition and personal goal setting. Following a 10 a.m. warmup, participants rotated through three measured components: 60 seconds of sit-ups to test core abdominal strength, 60 seconds of push-ups for upper body endurance, and a one-mile walk or run to measure cardio-respiratory fitness.
The event aligns with a Department of War initiative and Executive Order 14327, which supports the President’s Council on Sports, Fitness, and Nutrition and the reestablishment of the Presidential Fitness Test. The nationwide effort aims to encourage regular physical activity, recognize achievement, and build a broader culture of health and readiness.
For Bill Kegley, the APG CYS sports director, leading the installation’s inaugural assessment under the reestablished standard was both nostalgic and purposeful.
“I think it’s great that we brought back the test that we did 20 years ago,” Kegley said. “I feel it’s a great responsibility to make this a great experience for the kids so they will want to improve and set goals—not just to be fit, but to get outside and get moving.”
Rather than throwing the youth straight into a formal assessment, CYS and school-age sports staff spent weeks preparing the children through after-school activities. To prevent the test from feeling intimidating, staff integrated strength and cardio conditioning into recreational gym games.
“The staff started slow and encouraged the kids to do their best each time out,” Kegley said. “They played gym games that are fun, so the kids do not think about running, but are playing as they run.”
During preparation, staff also explained the broader concept behind the assessment, noting that the children were establishing benchmarks not only for themselves, but for the APG community compared to other military installations.
For many participants, the event was a chance to test themselves alongside their peers and mentors. Kegley highlighted one middle school athlete who participates in multiple APG sports and was especially eager to tackle the test because his soccer coach—who also works at the Youth Center—served as one of the event's scorekeepers.
“He tries hard at everything he does,” Kegley said. “He wanted to perform well for himself and his soccer coach.”
Beyond physical metrics, the initiative focuses heavily on character development, personal discipline, and resilience—traits critical to military-connected youth.
Kegley emphasized that teaching goal setting and perseverance at the school-age level directly supports military families and the installation's mission readiness.
“The ‘readiness’ culture allows our soldiers to know we are encouraging their kids to do their best—not just by participating in the event, but by practicing leading up to it,” Kegley said. “This provides the kids confidence not just in sports and fitness, but they can take pride in themselves in daily life skills where they deal with adversity.”
He added that the atmosphere on the field was designed to foster camaraderie as much as individual effort.
“The kids will develop good character by giving their best when their best is asked of them,” Kegley said. “This is a great age to start setting goals and understand the importance of trying your best and cheering on your friends to do well and give the support they need.”
To recognize their hard work, participants receive Presidential Fitness Test certificates to display at home—a tangible reminder of their baseline achievement and a motivator for future growth.
Moving forward, APG Family and MWR plans to make the Presidential Fitness Test a biannual tradition held every spring and fall, expanding participation to CYS sports teams and all local youth who wish to test their limits.
As the children boarded the buses to head back to the Youth Center, Kegley’s hope for their takeaway was simple: “That they gave it their best, took the event seriously, and are motivated to do even better the next time.”
title: APG youth build readiness, resilience during inaugural Presidential Fitness Test

FORT CHAFFEE, Ark. - As the U.S. Army shifts its operational focus to multi-domain operations under the newly released "How the Army Fights" warfighting guidance, the 100th Brigade Support Battalion, 75th Field Artillery Brigade, took decisive steps to prepare combat sustainers for a highly contested, transparent battlespace. During a multi-day field training exercise at the Fort Chaffee Joint Maneuver Training Center from Oct. 20-29, 2026, the battalion focused on hardening what is often described as the Army's "glass backbone," its logistics networks.
To test their readiness under realistic conditions, the battalion executed a tactical convoy movement across state lines from Fort Sill, Oklahoma, to Fort Chaffee, Arkansas. This long-distance movement served as an exhaustive evaluation of operational readiness at the lowest level, testing systems that begin long before rubber meets the road. In alignment with the "Swiss cheese model," of organizational readiness, weekly preventative checks and administrative validations served as overlapping layers of defense, preventing minor individual discrepancies from aligning into major logistical bottlenecks for the battalion. This collective attention to detail verified the unit's baseline readiness, resulting in the entire convoy arriving at Fort Chaffee with no major incidents.
"Fort Chaffee provided the operational depth and realistic friction necessary to train on tasks we simply cannot replicate at home station. Logistical excellence is meaningless if sustainers cannot survive to deliver it." said Lt. Col. Michael D. Bennett, the battalion commander. "In Large-Scale Combat Operations, rear areas are contested from day one. This exercise forced our formation to integrate basic field craft, dispersion, and perimeter defense directly into our sustainment tempo, ensuring our Soldiers depart not just as capable technicians, but as resilient combat sustainers ready to protect our footprint and extend the brigade's operational reach wherever called."
Upon arrival, the battalion immediately established its support area and initiated range training, including crew-served and small-arms qualification. This range density built immediate individual lethality before the unit transitioned into its main field training exercise. To meet the battalion's overall objectives, while being evaluated by outside observers, both the staff and the companies tested their respective systems under realistic field conditions. Companies focused heavily on validating their specific mission-essential task list (METL). At the same time, the staff elements synchronized and tested their operations, proving that organizational readiness is a collective, multi-echelon effort.
"Right now, my company needs to focus on basic Soldier tasks and battle drills," said Capt. Alana Humason, commander of the Headquarters and Services Company. "Once we build proficiency at the basics, then they will have increased lethality for all other operations. Going to the field is definitely going to be a test of physical and mental resilience while they're out there."
Recognizing that communication failures are historically the primary catalyst for operational collapse, especially in modern, contested electromagnetic environments where peer adversaries can jam digital signals, the staff placed special emphasis on command reporting. To make this reporting resilient, the staff integrated both digital systems and traditional analog backups to transmit critical tactical data, such as SITREPs and casualty reports, up the chain of command. This dual-method approach synchronized communication channels between subordinate companies and the staff, successfully closing reporting gaps identified during previous operations.
"From an administrative and reporting perspective, it's not necessarily just maintaining numbers; it is strength management," said Capt. Alexandria Lacy Holden, a battalion staff officer who oversaw the tracking and database systems. "Understanding our military occupational specialties across the unit, and what they are capable of, allows the commander to make decisive choices. We work collectively across all elements to maintain clear and mirrored reporting, so the battalion is fully aligned during large-scale operations."
To further evaluate their tactical mobility and adaptability during the field phase, the entire battalion and its subordinate companies successfully executed multiple tactical jumps, displacing their entire footprint to new training areas while remaining under contested conditions. This constant movement proved the unit's ability to maintain continuous command, control, and sustainment in a fast-paced environment. Following the successful field evaluation, the entire battalion redeployed across state lines to Fort Sill, with all equipment accounted for and once again, no major incident.
By mastering continuous displacement, securing their own footprint, and maintaining flawless baseline readiness across state lines, the 100th Brigade Support Battalion proved that tactical endurance is built from the ground up, and that victory remains a human contest of wills. This rigorous training ensures that when "America's Hammer" is called to strike, its sustainment forces stand ready to project, sustain, and endure anytime, anywhere.
title: 100th Brigade Support Battalion Validates Multi-State Mobility during Fort Chaffee Field Training

The Army Office of Small Business Programs hosted its 14th Annual Small Business Seminar and Matchmaking Event on October 13-14, 2026, during the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Annual Meeting and Exposition. The two-day event brought small businesses together with federal agency and industry representatives. The seminar focused on Army priorities and contracting resources, while the matchmaking event gave businesses an opportunity to meet directly with buyers.
Small Business Seminar
During the Small Business Seminar, Acting Director Ms. Pamela Callicutt highlighted the Army's fiscal year 2026 small business contracting achievements. As of October 2026, the Army has awarded $25.1 billion in prime contracts to small businesses across 730 NAICS codes. Ms. Callicutt also discussed the Army's industrial base priorities and the capabilities needed to support future requirements. These include advanced manufacturing, critical materials, batteries, electronics and components for unmanned systems. During the Small Business Seminar, Acting Director Ms. Pamela Callicutt highlighted the Army's fiscal year 2026 small business contracting achievements. As of October 2026, the Army has awarded $25.1 billion in prime contracts to small businesses across 730 NAICS codes. Ms. Callicutt also discussed the Army's industrial base priorities and the capabilities needed to support future requirements. These include advanced manufacturing, critical materials, batteries, electronics and components for unmanned systems.
Throughout the seminar, Army and federal agency leaders discussed how small businesses can support Army priorities. Mr. James Mismash, Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for Industrial Base Growth, provided an overview of the Section 1260H list, APEX Accelerators support, the Civil Reserve Manufacturing Network (CRMN), and LYNX.
Mr. Ryan Lambert, Associate Administrator for the Office of Government Contracting & Business Development, addressed the 8(a) Business Development Program, including recent changes, audits, identified fraud, and anticipated updates to size standards. The conversation continued during a fireside chat with the Army Portfolio Acquisition Executives (PAEs), who shared insights into their new organizational structure, priorities, and focus areas. They also offered advice to small businesses seeking to establish or strengthen relationships with their organizations and support acquisition priorities across their portfolios.
Attendees also learned about programs and resources available to support their businesses. Sessions covered cybersecurity requirements, recent changes, and free compliance assistance through Project Spectrum. Representatives from the Army’s enterprise innovation teams—Army FUZE and the Pathway for Innovation and Technology (PIT) and their forward-deployed acquisition leaders explained their roles in validating technology within the modernized acquisition enterprise.
To conclude the day, representatives from the Small Business Administration and the Defense Contract Audit Agency shared best practices, key Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) requirements, potential consequences of noncompliance, and helpful websites and guides.
Small Business Matchmaking
The following day, the Army Office of Small Business Programs hosted its Small Business Matchmaking Event, bringing together 36 buyers and more than 400 small businesses. Small businesses met one-on-one with federal agencies and industry partners to discuss their capabilities and learn about procurement opportunities. Each appointment lasted 10 minutes and a standby list was available to fill open appointments.
The annual two-day event supports AOSBP's mission to maximize small business participation in Army contracting. It also provides businesses with information to help them identify where their capabilities align with Army requirements.

Khanna, Moolenaar Seek Answers on Air Force Changes to China Aerospace Studies Institute
WASHINGTON – Ranking Member Ro Khanna (D-CA) and Chairman John Moolenaar (R-MI) of the House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party today requested a briefing from the Department of the Air Force on changes to the China Aerospace Studies Institute (CASI) at Air University, raising concerns that decisions affecting the Institute’s resources and personnel could weaken the United States’ ability to understand and counter the People’s Republic of China’s rapidly advancing aerospace capabilities.
In a letter to Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink, the lawmakers emphasized CASI’s critical role in providing the U.S. government, military, Congress, and the public with research and analysis on the PRC’s aerospace strategy, military modernization, and strategic thinking.
“Under-resourcing CASI’s mission could risk undermining the ability of military leaders and civilian policymakers to understand the PRC’s aerospace strategy and capabilities and, by extension, deter Beijing from using them in a military conflict,” Ranking Member Khanna and Chairman Moolenaar wrote in the letter. “Any potential loss of such expertise is particularly worrisome given the PRC’s continued efforts to rapidly modernize its aerospace forces while expanding its aggressive activities in the Indo-Pacific region.”
The lawmakers further warn that reductions in CASI’s resources or in-house expertise could leave the Air Force and other government agencies less equipped to assess the PRC’s military capabilities, potentially forcing them to rely on costly outside contractors to fill critical knowledge gaps. As the PRC continues to advance its military technology, access to reliable, specialized research will remain essential to informing defense planning and national security policy, the lawmakers added.
“Understanding the PLA’s capabilities in these domains is critical for deterring conflict and, as stated in CASI’s charter, for ‘improving [the U.S.] ability to be successful in strategic competition,’” the Members concluded. “As the PLA continues to expand its aerospace capabilities, our need to understand these advancements will continue to grow.”
The Ranking Member and Chairman have requested a briefing from the Department of the Air Force on its resourcing and personnel decisions concerning CASI by November 20, 2026.
Read the full letter HERE.
###
title: Khanna, Moolenaar Seek Answers on Air Force Changes to China Aerospace Studies Institute

TOLEDO, Ohio - The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Ohio endorsed a consent decree entered between the United States and the owner of R & R Chinchilla Inc. to surrender over 300 remaining chinchillas at a breeding facility in Jenera, Ohio. The court order follows R & R Chinchilla’s voluntary surrender of roughly 800 additional chinchillas to animal welfare organizations pursuant to a modified temporary restraining order.

“Animal breeders and caretakers that are federally licensed have an obligation to comply with basic standards Congress established to provide clean water, adequate food and housing, and sufficient veterinary care to their animals,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General Adam Gustafson of the Justice Department’s Energy and Natural Resources Division (ENRD). “We appreciate that the settlement agreement we reached in this matter has led to the safe relocation of all the animals involved. The heart of the Animal Welfare Act is to make sure animals are receiving good care, and that is what happened here. We highlight this case to show that we will enforce the law and hold violators accountable.”

“Federally licensed pet breeders must adhere to the Animal Welfare Act. Animals cannot be abused, kept in dirty cages, and neglected so badly that they suffer or die. We will hold those violating these federal laws accountable,” said U.S. Attorney David M. Toepfer for the Northern District of Ohio. “We are thankful for the great work of the USDA investigators which has resulted in the surrender of the animals that were in the breeding facility involved in this matter.”

“Federally licensed pet breeders must adhere to the Animal Welfare Act. Animals cannot be abused, kept in dirty cages, and neglected so badly that they suffer or die. We will hold those violating these federal laws accountable,” said U.S. Attorney David M. Toepfer for the Northern District of Ohio. “We are thankful for the great work of the USDA investigators which has resulted in the surrender of the animals that were in the breeding facility involved in this matter.”

“Over multiple inspections, APHIS inspectors documented deeply troubling conditions at this facility, including animals with untreated medical conditions, excessive fecal accumulation, and the concealment of approximately 800 additional chinchillas in a second structure that had been withheld from inspection for years,” said Deputy Administrator Bernadette Juarez of USDA’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS)’s Animal Care program. “USDA has a responsibility to ensure that licensed facilities meet the standards required under the Animal Welfare Act, and the conditions identified at this facility reflected a prolonged failure to provide basic animal care. After issuing an official warning in 2024 and taking multiple enforcement actions, including two summary suspensions, USDA worked closely with the Department of Justice to advance this case. We are grateful for the court's action, which enabled the safe removal of approximately 800 chinchillas from the facility and gives these animals the opportunity to receive the care they urgently need. We also welcome the revocation of the facility's Animal Welfare Act license, which reflects the seriousness of the violations documented by our inspectors. APHIS will continue to take strong enforcement action when serious or repeated noncompliance threatens animal welfare and undermines public trust in licensed operations.”

After receiving a referral from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) that animals were in serious danger, the Justice Department in August filed a complaint against R & R Chinchilla and its president, James. F. Ritterspach. The complaint alleged failures on multiple occasions to comply with the Animal Welfare Act (AWA) and its regulations and standards for the humane care, handling, and treatment of around 1,100 chinchillas at the R & R Chinchilla’s Hancock County facility. R & R Chinchilla has bred chinchillas for over 40 years. Chinchillas are small animals with dense, soft fur, weighing one to two pounds, and are typically categorized as exotic pets.

According to the complaint, since September 2022 the USDA conducted 18 inspections of R & R Chinchilla’s facility. In nearly every inspection, multiple violations of the AWA were identified, with 59 violations occurring within the past four years. For example, inspectors observed Ritterspach ripping a four-by-six-inch mat of hair off a chinchilla while holding the animal by the tail. The complaint alleged that R & R Chinchilla, through Ritterspach, falsely represented to USDA inspectors that it had between 300 to 450 animals at its facility. In reality, Ritterspach for years allegedly concealed about 800 additional animals in a separate building to avoid inspection of those animals.

On Aug. 5, USDA inspectors gained access to evaluate this previously undisclosed building and found hundreds of animals in dire conditions. The inspectors noted that the building was in worse condition than any facility they had ever inspected. Inspectors also observed multiple dead animals in the facility. Alleged AWA violations include:

Animals found with eyes so swollen and oozing with discharge that they could not open them;

Fecal material covering the entire floor of hundreds of enclosures;

Ammonia levels that were so high it caused USDA inspectors to cough to the point of having to leave the building;

Open packets of rat poison kept right next to enclosures housing chinchillas; and

A metal collar becoming tightly embedded in the neck of an animal.

ENRD and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Ohio filed a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction motion on Aug. 20. The court granted the temporary restraining order on Aug. 21 and later issued a modified order agreed to by the parties, adding to the measures already in place to address some of the alleged chronic issues at the facility. Furthermore, the order required R & R Chinchilla and Ritterspach to work with the United States to surrender approximately 800 of the animals at their facility. Under the terms of the consent decree, Ritterspach agreed to relinquish the remaining chinchillas and permanently cease any further AWA-regulated activity. Ritterspach also entered into a consent decree and order with USDA that permanently revokes Ritterspach’s AWA license.

Attorneys Kamela A. Caschette, Bonnie M. Ballard, and Davis A. Backer of ENRD’s Wildlife and Marine Resources Section, and Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Rojas for the Northern District of Ohio are handling this matter.

To report animal welfare violations, you can file a complaint on the USDA’s website .
title: Ohio Pet Breeder Agrees to Surrender Over 1,100 Chinchillas

BOSTON – The former Director of the City of Boston’s Municipal Protective Services pleaded guilty yesterday in federal court in Boston to obtaining federal pandemic funds through fraud.

Reuben Taylor, 40, of Boston, pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud. U.S. District Court Judge Angel Kelley scheduled sentencing for Feb. 12, 2027. Taylor was charged in October 2026 .

Taylor worked for the Municipal Protective Services, an unarmed, non-sworn security division within the City of Boston’s Property Management Department, since 2008. In April 2021 Taylor submitted an application for a $20,804 Paycheck Protection Program loan in which he falsely claimed that he had worked as an auto mechanic in 2019. Taylor supported his application with a fabricated Form 1040 and Schedule C, claiming that he received no wages in 2019 and instead received $99,863 as an independent contractor working as a mechanic. In the 2019 Form 1040 that Taylor actually submitted to the IRS, he reported earning $97,561 in wages as a municipal police officer and attached a Form W-2 from the City of Boston. In August 2021 Taylor submitted an application seeking forgiveness of the loan, claiming that he had spent the loan proceeds on payroll for his auto mechanic business. The Small Business Administration forgave Taylor’s loan in September 2021.

The charge of wire fraud provides for a sentence of up to 20 years in prison, up to three years of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley and Ted E. Docks, Special Agent in Charge of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Boston Division made the announcement today. Valuable assistance was provided by Internal Revenue Service’s Criminal Investigation in Boston and the Boston Police Department. Assistant U.S. Attorney Christine Wichers in the Public Corruption & Special Prosecutions Unit is prosecuting the case.

On March 26, 2026 , United States Attorney Leah B. Foley announced the creation of the Benefit & Voter Fraud Team, a district-wide initiative established in response to the rampant fraud being uncovered across Massachusetts. Members of the public are encouraged to report suspected benefit fraud in Massachusetts by calling 1-855-SCAM-MA-1 (855-722-6621).

On April 7, 2026, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division . The Fraud Division is investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
title: Former Boston City Official Pleads Guilty to Pandemic Fraud

OSAN AIR BASE, Republic of Korea — Soldiers assigned to Eighth Army’s Theater Gateway Center received incoming service members and families arriving on the Patriot Express, a military charter flight to South Korea, Oct. 15, 2026.
Theater Gateway Center staff received approximately 250 personnel and coordinated their movement to U.S. Army Garrison Humphreys for in-processing.
The flight was the first under a revised Patriot Express schedule and required extensive coordination for Soldiers, families, pets and other travel needs.
The mission relied on Soldiers who volunteered their time to support a central principle: Putting people first builds readiness.
“Our job is to receive, integrate and continue onward movement for all newly arriving permanent change-of-station personnel and their families,” said U.S. Army Capt. Beiling Liu, a human resources officer and commander of the Theater Gateway Center. “We are the first faces new Soldiers see when they arrive in Korea.”
For many arrivals, that first interaction helps make an unfamiliar environment more manageable. Personnel often arrive in Korea for the first time with questions about transportation, lodging and in-processing procedures.
U.S. Army Staff Sgt. Craig Pence, a human resources specialist assigned to the Theater Gateway Center, said the center provides incoming personnel with the resources they need to focus on integration rather than navigating a new country alone.
“The overall goal is to get personnel integrated and in-processed through Camp Humphreys,” Pence said.
Theater Gateway Center personnel coordinate transportation, track arrivals and arrange lodging, reducing uncertainty associated with overseas moves and helping Soldiers prepare for their assignments.
“We receive all incoming personnel, track them and coordinate lodging on their behalf,” Pence said. “We give them all the tools they need to ‘fight tonight’ and uphold the Eighth Army standard.”
The work requires flexibility. Passenger manifests for Patriot Express and commercial flights can change daily because of medical holds, leave adjustments and administrative delays.
U.S. Army Sgt. Devonte Nwaneri, a human resources specialist assigned to the Theater Gateway Center, said the team prepared extensively for the arrival while training newer personnel to minimize errors.
“As one of the subject matter experts in our unit, I wanted to be present to train personnel who are new and unfamiliar with the process to minimize mistakes,” Nwaneri said.
The reception mission continues after buses depart Osan. Incoming personnel attend briefings and complete in-processing requirements while Theater Gateway Center staff assist with equipment, transportation to gaining units and connections with unit leadership.
The work can extend late into the night when flights are delayed or arrival requirements change. Although much of it happens outside public view, it shapes the experience of every Soldier and family moving through the reception process.
Liu said the Theater Gateway Center’s success depends on Soldiers and noncommissioned officers who solve problems as they arise.
“There are a lot of last-minute problems that my team and I have to solve on the fly,” Liu said. “Whatever issue arises, we have to make a decision on the spot.”
As Soldiers and families continue arriving in Korea, the Theater Gateway Center remains a critical link between arrival and integration, demonstrating that readiness begins with ensuring people arrive safely, receive support and understand their next steps.
title: Theater Gateway Command welcomes South Korea's newest Soldiers and their Families

text:
Governments engage formally through international organizations and less formally through international forums to coordinate economic and foreign policies. International organizations, such as the United Nations (UN) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), are governed by official international agreements and have permanent offices with staff implementing and managing such agreements.
The Group of 7 (G7) and the Group of 20 (G20), in contrast, are informal forums for advancing international cooperation and coordination about economic and foreign policy issues. The G7 comprises seven economically developed democracies—Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom (UK), and the United States—as well as the European Union (EU). G20 membership includes a mix of economically developed and emerging-market countries: the G7 members as well as Argentina, Australia, Brazil, China, India, Indonesia, Mexico, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, South Korea, Turkey (Türkiye), and the African Union (AU) (Figure 1).1
Leaders of the G7 and G20 countries generally meet annually at summits, and lower-level officials meet throughout the year. The forums initially focused on international economic and financial issues and over time have expanded to include a range of foreign policy issues. The G7 and G20 do not have permanent headquarters or staff and have at times worked in conjunction with formal international organizations. For example, G7 and G20 leaders have invited the heads of international organizations to participate in meetings, requested international organizations to examine specific policy issues, negotiated reforms of international organizations, and reiterated support for the policy goals of international organizations.
France holds the rotating G7 presidency in 2026 and hosted the annual summit on June 16-17, 2026, in Évian-les-Bains, a town in southeastern France. The summit focused on reducing global economic imbalances and rebuilding international solidarity.2 The United States holds the G20 presidency in 2026, and the summit is scheduled for December 14-15, 2026, at Trump National Doral Resort in Miami, FL. U.S. priorities for the summit include refocusing the forum on its "core" mission of driving economic growth and prosperity.3 In 2027, the United States and the UK are hosting the G7 and G20, respectively.
The G7 has roots back to the 1970s, and the G20 rose to prominence during the global financial crisis of 2008-2009.4 Both forums run in parallel today.
In the mid-1970s, leaders from a group of five developed countries—France, Germany, Japan, the UK, and the United States (known then as the Group of Five, or G5)—began meeting annually to discuss international economic issues, including the oil price shocks in the 1970s and changes in exchange rate policies. In the 1980s, G5 leaders broadened their discussions to include Canada and Italy, forming the G7. The EU began participating in the G5 meetings in the late 1970s and is a permanent member of the G7, although it does not host or chair G7 meetings.
G7 discussions originally focused on macroeconomic policies, including exchange rates, balance of payments, globalization, trade, and economic relations with developing countries. Over time, the G7's focus on macroeconomic policies expanded to include a variety of other global and transnational issues, including the environment, crime, drugs, AIDS, and terrorism.
In 1998, Russia joined the G7, creating the Group of Eight (G8). Russia participated in discussions about foreign policy issues; it did not usually participate in discussions on international economic policy, which continued to occur mainly at the G7 level. The G7 leaders of the G8 disinvited Russia in 2014, following Russia's illegal annexation of the Crimean region of Ukraine, and the group reverted to the G7.
Starting in the early 1990s, emerging markets became more active in the international markets, and the Asian financial crisis of 1997-1998 demonstrated that problems in emerging-market countries can have spillover effects on developed economies. In 1999, finance ministers and central bank governors of the G7 partnered with their counterparts from 12 major emerging economies and the European Union to establish the G20, aimed at encouraging coordination between advanced and emerging economies.5 Over the next decade, the highest-level G20 meetings were held among finance ministers and central bank governors.
At the behest of the G7 leaders, the G20 leaders met for the first time in November 2008 in Washington, DC, to discuss the global financial crisis. Emerging markets' economies had grown rapidly over the previous decade (Figure 2), and the decision to convene G20 leaders reflected recognition that emerging markets needed to be included in the discussions about the global response to the financial crisis at the highest levels. Emerging markets also began organizing their own summits in 2009 (see text box below).
At the third G20 summit, held in September 2009 in Pittsburgh, PA, the G20 leaders decided that going forward, the G20 would be the premier forum for international economic cooperation, implicitly supplanting the G7's role as such.6 In practice, both forums have continued and it is not clear whether the G7's stature has changed. Former Treasury officials have attributed the G7's staying power to diplomatic inertia, a loss of the G20's momentum after the global financial crisis, and more like-minded economic and political structures among the G7 countries relative to the G20.7 Over time, G20 discussions have broadened from economic issues to include foreign policy issues such as health, refugees, terrorism, and climate change. In 2010, the G20 leaders made Spain a "permanent guest invitee" in the G20, which enables Spain to participate in the meetings,8 and the AU joined in the forum in 2023 at the invitation of the G20 leaders.
The president of the G7 and the G20 rotates annually among members (Table 1). The rotating president sets the agenda, date, and location of the annual summit, and manages the group's secretarial, clerical, and administrative affairs. The rotating president also organizes meetings among lower-level officials before and after the summit. The leaders' personal representatives for the G7 and the G20, known as "sherpas," meet regularly, as do the G7 and G20 finance ministers, central bank governors, and foreign affairs ministers.16
G20 presidents have also convened cabinet-level officials focused on nonfinance issues, such as energy, labor, and trade. The rotating president also has discretion to invite additional countries and international organizations to summits and meetings. In addition, the G7 and G20 parliamentary speakers usually meet annually, and the G20 president at times convenes meetings among businesses, think tanks, and civil society groups from member countries to inform G20 discussions.
The forums have led to the creation of a complex set of interactions among officials at many different levels of government. The interactions open communication channels, which can be particularly useful during crises. At the same time, it takes time and resources for the national agencies tasked with managing their countries' preparations for and participation in these meetings to execute their responsibilities.
Source: Compiled by CRS using data from the University of Toronto's G7 and G20 Information Centres.
After meeting, the groups usually release a statement summarizing the discussions and any commitments pledged by members. All agreements, comments, recommendations, and policy reforms reached by the G7 and G20 ministers, central bankers, and leaders are done so by consensus. There is no formal voting system and commitments are nonbinding; the G7 and G20 do not have a way to enforce implementation of the agreements at the national level beyond moral suasion.
Notable G7 outcomes have included, for example, calling for the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) Initiative, a debt-relief program for low-income countries in the late 1990s; proposing the creation of the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria in 2000; supporting the COVID-19 vaccine rollout to low-income countries in 2021; and coordinating sanctions in response to Russia's war against Ukraine in 2022. For the G20, examples of outcomes have included organizing the international response to the global financial crisis of 2008-2009, coordinating debt relief initiatives during the COVID-19 pandemic, and strengthening the lending capacity of the multilateral development banks in the early 2020s, among other initiatives. At the same time, not all G7 and G20 meetings result in significant policy commitments or outcomes. The joint statements are sometimes vague, emphasizing platitudes and repeating language from previous meetings. In some cases, participants have not reached consensus, and meetings have ended without a joint statement.17
The executive branch largely manages U.S. participation in the G7 and G20. The G7 and G20 work streams have generally evolved to each have a finance track and a foreign affairs track. Within the executive branch, the Department of the Treasury (the Treasury) manages the finance track, and the Department of State (State) manages the foreign affairs track. Depending on the topics on the forums' agendas, Treasury and State might coordinate with other federal agencies, such as the Departments of Energy and Labor and the U.S. Trade Representative. The White House, particularly through the National Security Council, is also involved in the G7 and G20 process.
Congress has tools for shaping U.S. participation in the G7 and the G20. The implementation of some U.S. commitments made by the executive branch in the G7 and G20 require legislation to implement, such as increasing funding to an international organization or reforming financial regulations. Members can support such legislation, oppose it, or condition their support on specific policy objectives. Congress also controls the funding of agencies involved in the G7 and G20 process. Members can also use hearings and reporting requirements to exercise oversight of the executive branch's engagement in the G7 and G20. Additionally, Members can use public statements to support or oppose an Administration's policy positions in the G7 and G20.
Congress has enacted a variety of legislation relevant to the G7 and the G20, including funding summits hosted by the United States, specifying which officials in the State Department are responsible for coordinating with G7 members, and directing the Administration to advance specific policy priorities in the G7 and G20. Table 2 provides specific examples enacted since 2016.
At the conclusion of the G7 summit in June 2026, the leaders released several joint statements.18 The statement on economic growth focused on the need to reduce global imbalances, in which certain countries run large, persistent current account deficits while others have large surpluses. Global imbalances can create financial vulnerabilities and economic distortions. The United States, the UK, Australia, and Brazil are among the countries that run current account deficits; examples of major current account surplus countries include China, Germany, Japan, and Norway.19
An additional statement on geopolitical issues reiterated leaders' support for Ukraine and the resumption of maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and expressed concerns about North Korea's nuclear and ballistic missile programs, among other issues. The leaders also issued statements calling for a coordinated response to the Ebola outbreak, secure supply chains for critical materials, safer digital spaces for minors, and an accelerated fight against cancer.20 In his G7 presidency role, French President Emmanuel Macron invited leaders from outside the G7 (Egypt, India, Qatar, Ukraine, and the United Arab Emirates) to the summit.21
The G7 leaders also held an emergency virtual meeting on October 2, 2026, to coordinate responses to high energy prices. The leaders agreed to release, through the International Energy Agency, 100 million barrels of crude oil and diesel from reserves over four months.22
As president of the G20 in 2026, the United States set the agenda and meetings for the year. Some key details about the December 2026 summit follow.
Core themes. The Trump Administration seeks to "return the G20 to focusing on its core mission of driving economic growth and prosperity" through "three core themes: unleashing economic prosperity by limiting regulatory burdens, unlocking affordable and secure energy supply chains, and pioneering innovations" in artificial intelligence (AI) and emerging technologies.23 Some in Congress have suggested additional focus areas. In March 2026, for example, the Tom Lantos Human Rights Commission held a hearing on how the G20 could be used as a vehicle to promote human rights issues, including freedom of religion.24
Attendees. The Trump Administration invited Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov to the Finance Ministerial in North Carolina in August 2026 and Russian President Vladimir Putin to the December 2026 summit. Neither official has attended a G20 meeting in person since Russia launched a full-scale war on Ukraine in 2022, and both are subject to U.S. sanctions. Under U.S. law, it is the policy of the U.S. government to exclude government officials of the Russian Federation, to the maximum extent practicable, from participation in specific international organizations, including the G20.25 Some Members of Congress have opposed G20 invitations to Russian officials,26 and European finance ministers objected to the participation of Russia's finance minister in August 2026.27
The Trump Administration has also invited to the summit several countries that are not members of the G20, including Azerbaijan, Finland, Ireland, Kazakhstan, the Netherlands, Norway, Qatar, Singapore, Spain, the United Arab Emirates, Uzbekistan, and Vietnam.28 As noted above, in June 2026 French President Macron similarly invited non-G7 countries to the G7 summit in Évian-les-Bains.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced in December 2025 that the United States would not invite the South African government to participate in the G20 in 2026 due to that government's "racism and tolerance for violence against its Afrikaner citizens," among other reasons.29 Such statements by the Administration have been refuted by South African officials and some policy experts.30 The United States boycotted the G20 in 2025, when the rotating presidency was held by South Africa.
Location. The summit is scheduled to be held at the Trump National Doral Resort in Florida. The Administration has pledged that the resort will host the summit "at-cost" and "will receive no profit from either the State Department or a foreign government."31 In March 2026, the Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW) sued the State Department and the U.S. Secret Service for failing to produce records in response to its Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests regarding the evaluation of prospective venues to host the G20 summit and how the State Department plans to address payments to a company owned by the President.32 In 2019, President Trump canceled plans to host the G7 summit at the same resort in response to broad criticism.33
Lower-level meetings. Over the course of its 2026 G20 presidency, the United States has held or plans to hold four sherpa meetings, two finance minister and central bank governor meetings, and two deputy finance minister and central bank governor meetings.34 Additionally, it has hosted or is scheduled to host a foreign affairs minister meeting, an energy minister meeting, a trade minister meeting, and an innovation minister meeting.
If Members of Congress are interested in shaping U.S. participation in the G7 and/or the G20, they have several options, depending on their policy goals. Some examples follow.
title: U.S. Participation in the G7 and the G20

Baltimore, Maryland – A Baltimore man is facing federal indictment, today, stemming from a counterfeit currency scheme.

Clifton Monroe, Jr., 49, is charged with four counts of passing or possessing counterfeit obligations or securities, along with one count of possessing counterfeit obligations or securities and one count of counterfeiting and forging obligations or securities of the United States after he manufactured counterfeit money and used it in an attempt to pay for goods. Monroe was previously charged by criminal complaint and made his initial appearance on Oct. 29, 2026.

Kelly O. Hayes, U.S. Attorney for the District of Maryland, announced the indictment with Special Agent in Charge Brian McDonough, United States Secret Service (USSS) – Baltimore Field Office.

According to court documents, in April 2025, Monroe offered counterfeit money as payment for goods at a Catonsville pizza shop, along with a convenience store. As part of the scheme, Monroe provided counterfeit money as payment at the pizza shop, and received $45 in real U.S. currency in change. Then in January 2026, Monroe attempted a similar scheme at a Glen Burnie retail store in which he expected to receive $36.15 in change. But an employee recognized the counterfeit bills and contacted store police who then apprehended Monroe. In April 2026, investigators executed a search warrant at Monroe’s home and discovered evidence of the production of counterfeit currency.

An indictment is not a finding of guilt. Individuals charged by indictment are presumed innocent until proven guilty at a later criminal proceeding.

If convicted, Monroe is facing a maximum of 20 years in federal prison for each count of passing or possessing counterfeit obligations or securities, a maximum of 25 years for possession of counterfeit obligations or securities, and a maximum of 20 years for forging obligations or securities of the United States.

Actual sentences for federal crimes are typically less than the maximum penalties. A federal district court judge determines sentencing after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

U.S. Attorney Hayes commended the USSS, for its work in the investigation, along with the Anne Arundel County Police Department and Baltimore County Police Department, for their valuable assistance. Ms. Hayes also thanked Assistant U.S. Attorney Elliot Higgins who is prosecuting this federal case.

For more information about the Maryland U.S. Attorney’s Office, its priorities, and resources available to help the community, visit justice.gov/usao-md .

# # #
title: Baltimore Man Indicted in Connection With Counterfeit Money Scheme

FORT LEONARD WOOD, Mo. — Traditional roast turkey is on top of the menu as Fort Leonard Wood plans to host its Thanksgiving Day celebration Nov. 26, 2026, in Army Warrior Restaurants across the installation, with meals for thousands of service members, as well as a specific time and location for Department of War ID cardholders, Gold Star families, veterans and their families.
“Thanksgiving reminds us that sometimes home is not a place, it's the people sitting around the table with you. For many of our Soldiers, this may be the first holiday they've ever spent away from family,” said Beverly Leggett, Installation Food Program manager. “We can't replace home, but we can make sure they know they're part of a military family that is grateful for their service and proud of what they're doing.”
Maneuver Support Center of Excellence Chief of Staff Col. Jeremy Kerfoot fondly remembers his first Thanksgiving away from family while deployed.
“Spending the time with my platoon was memorable since we all shared stories of what we were thankful for and our Thanksgiving meal traditions,” he said. “It put a pause, for a moment, at where we were and let us relax and share camaraderie.”
Kerfoot said the importance of the event is twofold.
“For many, Thanksgiving dinner is one of the biggest feasts that families share in and providing it at our (warrior restaurants) helps to create an environment for that continued tradition,” he said. “Another reason, and probably most important, is the celebration of thankfulness for the Soldiers who are gathered together — for a moment — to fellowship as a team, an Army Family. No matter blood or duty, family is forged in many ways. Thanksgiving gives us an opportunity to remember and experience that.”
According to Leggett, plans are set to serve approximately 12,000 Thanksgiving meals during the lunchtime celebrations, and 28,000-plus meals throughout the day — using 4,700 pounds of turkey, 4,200 pounds of shrimp cocktail, 6,300 pounds of prime rib and 15 different kinds of assorted cakes and pies with all the accompaniments.
“From the first turkey placed in the oven to the final dessert served, months of planning and coordination ensure every guest enjoys a memorable Thanksgiving meal,” Leggett said. “The menu includes herb-crusted salmon, oven-roasted strip loin steak or prime rib with au jus, baked ham with cranberry glaze, and a vegetable lasagna option.”
Guests will also enjoy an array of classic holiday sides, including mashed potatoes; baked macaroni and cheese; savory bread dressing; cornbread dressing; candied sweet potatoes; roasted asparagus; herb green beans; and corn.
“From traditional favorites to premium entrée selections, this year's meal is designed to deliver a true Thanksgiving experience,” she added.
According to Leggett, about 850 food-service employees are scheduled to prepare the feast and serve it alongside senior leadership.
Adding to the Thanksgiving experience, food-service employees from each warrior restaurant will be decorating their dining areas.
“Dining facility teams are already planning festive holiday decorations to help create a welcoming and memorable Thanksgiving atmosphere,” she said. “From seasonal decor to carefully prepared serving displays, every effort is made to transform the warrior restaurants into a place where Soldiers, families, veterans, and guests can gather and enjoy the spirit of the holiday.”
Leggett said her team understands that providing a Thanksgiving meal is much more than just serving food.
“It’s about creating a sense of belonging and reminding Soldiers that they are part of a community that cares about them,” she said.
According to Leggett, the Thanksgiving Day meal for DOW ID cardholders, retirees, Gold Star families and veterans with access to the installation will be served from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. at Celiz Hall Army Warrior Restaurant, Bldg. 6111, located on Indiana Avenue.
“The Army serves as a family, and Thanksgiving provides an opportunity to bring that family together,” Leggett said. “By welcoming veterans, retirees, Gold Star families, military dependents, and other members of our community, we recognize that military service is supported by countless individuals beyond those currently wearing the uniform.”
The Thanksgiving holiday meal rate is $11.85 for all visitors, except spouses and other dependents of service members E-4 and below, who pay the discounted holiday meal rate of $8.75.
“Years from now, they may not remember every item on the menu, but I hope they remember how this community made them feel,” Leggett said. “That's what Thanksgiving is really about.”
The Bldg. 3223 Army Warrior Restaurant near the Maneuver Support Center of Excellence Noncommissioned Officer’s Academy, commonly referred to as Tony’s, and Bldg. 1784 serving the Air Force, Navy and Marines, plan to serve their Thanksgiving meals Nov. 25, 2026.
