ST. LOUIS – U.S. District Judge Zachary M. Bluestone on Tuesday sentenced a former City of St. Louis building inspector to six years in prison and ordered him to repay the $1.64 million he stole from programs meant to repair decrepit buildings in St. Louis.

Adebanjo “Banjo” Popoola, 58, was a building division inspector with the City of St. Louis and was responsible for managing important aspects of two programs designed to help stabilize and rehabilitate city properties, Stable Communities STL and Prop NS.

In in a sentencing memo, Assistant U.S. Attorney Hal Goldsmith wrote, “This is a case of greed, plain and simple." Popoola “abused his longstanding and substantial position of trust with the City of St. Louis in order to enrich himself and his family members.” Popoola “destroyed two well-intentioned local and federal funded programs meant to stabilize decaying and debilitating properties within the City,” Goldsmith said.

Stable Communities STL was funded through federal American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funds and intended for privately-owned properties. Prop NS was intended for residential properties owned by the City’s Land Reutilization Authority (LRA) and was funded through general obligation bonds. Popoola was primarily responsible for identifying properties for rehab or stabilization; developing the scope of work; seeking, reviewing and awarding bids; inspecting the work that had purportedly been completed on each property and certifying that the work had been completed so funds could be disbursed to the contractors.

Popoola steered 41 contracts to Farst Construction LLC, a company he helped organize with his sister, a nurse living in Texas with no background or experience in construction. He directed 50 contracts to Premier Finish Contractors LLC, a company he helped his fiancée organize. Popoola “was so bold as to give 42% of the total funds disbursed under the City’s Stable Communities STL program to his sister’s and his wife’s companies,” Goldsmith wrote. Popoola concealed his role in the companies from the city and his sister and his fiancée (later wife) concealed their connection to Popoola. On multiple projects, Farst and Premier failed to perform the rehabilitation and stabilization work for which the companies were paid but Popoola falsely certified that the work had been performed completely and properly.

Popoola and his family members reaped $1,642,908 from the scheme. Popoola spent the stolen money on residential mortgage payments, multiple vehicle purchases and repairs, travel expenses, his September 2023 wedding in Hawaii, casino gambling and other dining and entertainment expenses.

The owner of a building on Rowan Avenue in the Hamilton heights neighborhood wrote in a victim impact statement to the court that Popoola’s theft of $48,500 in repair funds left a building “with severe, unaddressed structural decay that was actively masked by fraudulent building inspection reports… imposing an immense, unexpected financial burden on me as an independent developer.”

St. Louis Mayor Cara Spencer said in her own statement that the city may have to return millions of dollars in ARPA funds because of Popoola’s crimes. Innocent contractors were harmed when the city froze payments during the investigation, which also halted other stabilization work, including buildings damaged by the May 2025 tornado.

Popoola, 57, pleaded guilty in June in U.S. District Court in St. Louis to three counts of wire fraud.

“As a building inspector, Banjo Popoola stole more than $1.64 million in taxpayer dollars intended to stabilize and rebuild St. Louis neighborhoods. While families were left living next to deteriorating and unsafe buildings, he diverted those funds to finance his Hawaiian wedding, pay his mortgage, and cover personal expenses,” said Special Agent in Charge Chris Crocker of the FBI St. Louis Division. “The damage caused by this kind of corruption extends far beyond the theft of taxpayer money. When building inspectors compromise their responsibility to enforce safety standards for personal financial gain, they put entire communities and the lives of those residents at risk.”

The FBI investigated the case, with substantial cooperation from the City of St. Louis Comptroller’s Office. Assistant U.S. Attorney Hal Goldsmith prosecuted the case.
title: Former St. Louis Building Inspector Sentenced to 6 Years in Prison for $1.6 Million Fraud

Today, the U.S. Department of Justice and the U.S. Equal Employment Commission (EEOC) announced a two-part settlement against Lockheed Martin Corporation, headquartered in Bethesda, Maryland. Lockheed has agreed to pay a total of approximately $29.5 million to resolve allegations relating to employment discrimination and related false certifications of compliance with federal civil rights laws while serving as a federal contractor.

This includes $22 million to be paid to the United States pursuant to an agreement with the Justice Department to resolve allegations that Lockheed violated the False Claims Act arising from failures to comply with anti-discrimination requirements in its federal contracts and by discriminating against employees and applicants on the basis of their race or sex. It also includes approximately $7.5 million to be paid to over 1,000 affected Lockheed employees pursuant to a negotiated settlement agreement with the EEOC resolving a 2025 Commissioner’s Charge filed by EEOC Chair Andrea Lucas, which alleged Lockheed violated Title VII of the Civil Rights Act by engaging in race discrimination against white employees, including in performance assessments and in bonus and other compensation decisions. This is the largest class of workers to publicly recover under an EEOC settlement on account of alleged Title VII violations arising from or relating to a DEI program or practices.

Most federal contracts contain a provision that requires contractors to provide equal opportunity to employees and applicants for employment. As a condition to being a federal contractor, the company must certify that it will not discriminate against an employee or applicant for employment because of race or sex and must further certify that it will take steps to ensure that applicants are employed, and employees are treated during employment, “without regard to” race or sex. The Justice Department’s settlement under the False Claims Act resolves allegations that from 2019 to the present, Lockheed falsely certified compliance with these conditions, while engaging in discriminatory race and sex-based employment practices. This resolution follows other recent settlements secured under the Civil Rights Fraud Initiative, which was launched by the Justice Department in May 2025.

“Companies, especially those that do business with the federal government, should not make DEI compensation decisions that prioritize an employee's race over the merit of their work,” said Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward Jr. “This is the Department’s fourth False Claims Act settlement resolving allegations of racial discrimination against employees. The Department remains steadfast in its commitment to eliminating woke, unconstitutional practices from workplaces of companies that receive federal taxpayer funds.”

“Companies that receive taxpayer money from government contracts must play by the rules,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould for the Northern District of Texas. “It’s as simple as that, and this settlement is further proof of this Administration’s commitment to ensuring that employees of government contractors always get a fair shake when it comes to hiring, pay, and promotion decisions.”

“Companies that receive taxpayer money from government contracts must play by the rules,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould for the Northern District of Texas. “It’s as simple as that, and this settlement is further proof of this Administration’s commitment to ensuring that employees of government contractors always get a fair shake when it comes to hiring, pay, and promotion decisions.”

“Federal contractors must certify that they will make employment decisions—including decisions on how to compensate their hard-working employees—without regard to race or sex, and putting a thumb on the scale in hiring, promotion, and compensation decisions based on race flies in the face of that requirement,” said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. “Today’s resolution, just like the other recent settlements, protects the employees of federal contractors from unlawful discrimination and will hold federal contractors accountable for not following the law.”

The United States alleged that Lockheed took race into account when making compensation decisions for Lockheed employees. Starting in 2021, Lockheed operated an incentive program called “Compensation Adder” or “Comp Adder” that awarded the top 20% of Lockheed’s employees within each business area of the company with an additional pay increase over the annual company-wide increase each year. Managers were initially instructed to use merit-based performance criteria to make their Comp Adder nominations and higher-level leaders reviewed and revised the nominations to ensure that the 20% cap was not exceeded. The United States alleged that prior to finalizing the Comp Adder selections, Lockheed performed a statistical analysis to “flag” statistical outliers based on the race and sex composition of the Comp Adder list. When a business group’s selections were flagged, human resource personnel were supposed to reach out to business group leaders and ask them to re-review their selections and the merit-based basis for the selections, without asking them to take any protected characteristic into account.

In practice, the United States alleged that some Lockheed HR personnel exerted pressure on leaders in their business group to resolve race-related “flags” by directing them to add or remove particular employees based on race. Those Lockheed HR personnel encouraged their business group leaders to remove certain non-minority employees from the Comp Adder selections while adding minority employees who had not been initially nominated for Comp Adder. One HR employee explained to business group leaders that “increasing POC [People of Color] for Comp Adder will result in removing equal count of non-minority.” When an initial re-review failed to identify sufficient minority employees for selection to Comp Adder, certain business group leaders were instructed to perform additional re-reviews (in one example, a business unit leader was instructed “again to reevaluate POC and their performance”) until enough changes were made to resolve the “flags.” A Director of Global Diversity & Inclusion informed HR personnel that “we will identify at least 11 additional PoC adds from other functions” to add to the Comp Adder list “and the level 2 Race flag will clear (assuming everything else remains static). Let’s goooooooooo 😊.”

The United States also alleged that Lockheed took race or sex into account when making hiring and promotion decisions, including, to achieve progress towards non-public race and sex-based workforce composition goals for business units (closely held within the company). The goals were intended to impact Lockheed’s promotion and hiring decisions.

The United States alleged that Lockheed developed a Management Incentive Compensation Plan that contained “quantitative measures called Performance Metrics that are developed and tracked throughout the year.” One Performance Metric was based on achievement of specified goals for preferred demographics. Business units within Lockheed received quarterly summaries tracking the demographic goals within the unit for “women” and “minorities,” where representation or advancement towards the goal was highlighted in green, yellow, or red depending on whether the goal was “met,” “not met but w/in 1,” or “not met.” In addition, the United States alleged that in 2023, Lockheed’s Global Diversity & Inclusion, and Equity & Compliance offices set additional company-wide hiring goals characterized as “aspirational plus” goals that “stretch[] beyond what’s potentially achievable.” In certain business units, Lockheed achieved these “aspirational plus” goals for people of color.

Finally, the United States alleged that Lockheed offered certain training, mentoring, and leadership development programs, and/or similar opportunities to eligible employees on the basis of race or sex, for example, an Executive Leadership Diversity Mentoring program. These programs were designed to boost the career prospects of these individuals over others through sponsorship and networking.

The Justice Department’s civil settlement also includes the resolution of claims brought under the qui tam or whistleblower provisions of the False Claims Act by Tim Booher, a former Vice President at Lockheed. Under those provisions, a private party can file an action on behalf of the United States and receive a portion of any recovery. The qui tam case is captioned United States ex rel. Tim Booher v. Lockheed Martin Corporation (No. 4:25-cv-00769-P). Under this resolution, Mr. Booher will receive $4,400,000.

The resolution announced today also includes a settlement between the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and Lockheed of claims under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, arising from similar alleged conduct as asserted by the Department of Justice in its False Claims Act investigation. Title VII bars employers from taking any employment action motivated, in whole or in part, by race. Under its statutory authorities, the EEOC can recover monetary relief for individual employees and applicants who have been harmed by violations, including compensatory damages, backpay, front pay, and punitive damages, where warranted, in addition to equitable relief. Lockheed is settling with EEOC to resolve a Commissioner’s Charge alleging that Lockheed discriminated based on race against employees in performance assessments and in bonus and other compensation decisions, including via the Compensation Adder program. EEOC’s settlement provides over $7.5 million of monetary relief for over 1,000 Lockheed employees. As part of the resolution here, in addition to monetary relief, the EEOC’s agreement requires Lockheed Martin to comply with Title VII and Executive Order 14151 and to maintain a merit-based workplace in which race and sex are not considered in hiring, compensation, bonus, or promotion decisions. The EEOC may review the company’s compliance over the term of the agreement.

“Title VII requires employers to treat employees as individuals, ensuring that workplace opportunities, compensation, and rewards are not allocated based on race or sex. The resolution reflects a core EEOC enforcement priority: identifying and remedying unlawful race and sex discrimination carried out by employers under the euphemism of diversity, equity, and inclusion. Title VII protects every worker from employment discrimination on the basis of race — and that protection does not yield when discriminatory decisions are framed as diversity initiatives,” said EEOC Chair Andrea Lucas. “This settlement doesn’t just reinforce that principle, it delivers meaningful monetary relief to more than a thousand workers allegedly affected.”

The EEOC is the sole federal agency authorized to investigate and litigate against businesses and other private sector employers for violations of federal laws prohibiting employment discrimination, including Title VII. To pursue a Title VII claim, employees and applicants first must file a charge of discrimination with the EEOC. The Justice Department’s Civil Division is responsible for enforcing the False Claims Act, which is the government’s primary enforcement tool for recovering losses due to fraud or false statements, including from a failure to comply with anti-discrimination laws and requirements.

Lockheed cooperated in the resolution of these matters.

This year the Administration launched the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud and the National Fraud Enforcement Division to enhance the Administration’s war on fraud, waste and abuse in federal programs. When unscrupulous actors exploit these programs for their own financial gain, they defraud the government, harm the people these programs are designed to aid and protect, and undermine American businesses that play by the rules. The Justice Department Civil Division’s FCA enforcement plays a critical role in combatting such fraudulent schemes, recovering billions of dollars for American taxpayers, and holding wrongdoers accountable. FCA matters will continue to be on the forefront of the battle against fraud, and the Civil Division’s FCA work will support and advance the mission of the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud and the National Fraud Enforcement Division.

The two-part resolution obtained in this matter was the result of a coordinated effort between the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, the Justice Department’s Civil Division, Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section, and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Texas with investigative assistance from the Department of War, Office of Inspector General.

The claims resolved by the United States Department of Justice and United States Equal Employment Opportunity Commission in the settlement are allegations only and there has been no determination of liability.

###
title: Lockheed Martin agrees to pay $29.5m to resolve alleged employment discrimination violations

DALLAS — United States Attorney for the Northern District of Texas Ryan Raybould today announced that a federal grand jury indicted fourteen defendants, including allegedly corrupt insiders at major banking and telecommunication institutions, for allegedly orchestrating a sweeping nationwide bank‑account‑takeover conspiracy that targeted victims across the U.S.

Muhamed Dieye, 35, of Dallas, known to associates by several aliases including “MJ,” “JayJay,” “Medici,” and “Lambomotion Tony,” is the leader and chief architect of the alleged conspiracy. Dieye and the thirteen co-defendants are charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud and bank fraud, bank fraud, wire fraud and aggravated identity theft.

A federal grand jury returned the 22-count indictment on Aug. 26. It was unsealed today after the arrest of Terrence Dudley a/k/a Willy Watkins, Brian Faceman in Florida, a key co-conspirator in the case.

In addition to Dieye and Dudley, the indictment also charges:

Maurice Rashad McDuffie, a/k/a Heavvvy Motion

Saad Nashat Botros, a/k/a Felix Saucedo , Wesley Swipes , Wesley Swipes

Sammed Kweku Okyne, a/k/a OKC , Paris Jawn

Renaldo Santez Gaines, a/k/a BlackMigo , OsamaCapone , OsamaBin57

Alphonso Brndon Seke‑Horton, a/k/a The Wizard 302

Terry Leon Daniels Jr., a/k/a onedayrealsoon , Teazy Daniels

Jamel Allen Small, a/k/a Paypawerk

Kemar Fitzroy Needham, a/k/a Swap King Fx , kingzmanfx

Kevin Brandon Flores Cazares, a/k/a John First B , First B (Call)

Dylon Amari Ruby, a/k/a slimeyluhdude , AT&T

Courtney Jane Sutton

C.S.

“North Texas is the financial services hub of America, and protecting Main Street families and investors is a top priority of this office,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould. “These defendants are charged with targeting the life savings of thousands of Americans, and the ringleader was stopped at the gate before he could flee. Target Main Street and we will pursue you with every tool available."

“North Texas is the financial services hub of America, and protecting Main Street families and investors is a top priority of this office,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould. “These defendants are charged with targeting the life savings of thousands of Americans, and the ringleader was stopped at the gate before he could flee. Target Main Street and we will pursue you with every tool available."

A sophisticated, multi‑state identity‑theft ring

According to the indictment, Dieye possessed a spreadsheet that contained detailed personal and business information for nearly 3,000 individual victims who collectively held over $373,000,000 across their bank accounts.

From July 2023 through November 2024, the defendants allegedly conspired to obtain personal identifying information, produced and trafficked counterfeit identification documents, impersonated victims, manipulated victims’ phone lines by spoofing and SIM swapping, intercepted security codes and used corrupt insiders within banks and telecommunications companies to bypass authentication measures.

Among the plays detailed in the indictment, the conspirators allegedly:

Accessed or withdrew funds from victim accounts at Truist Bank, Bank of America, First Bank, Woodforest National Bank, JPMorgan Chase Bank, and Charles Schwab

Conducted or attempted numerous fraudulent financial transactions, including an attempted $2,000,000 wire to the Emirates Islamic Bank

Leveraged aliases referencing violent extremists and organized‑crime figures—such as OsamaCapone and OsamaBin57 —while executing and coordinating complex fraud plays

Ringleader attempted to flee the United States

Federal law enforcement, working closely with the U.S. Attorney’s Office, arrested Dieye after he allegedly attempted to flee the country.

According to the government’s motion to revoke release:

Dieye and his family vacated his Dallas residence, shipped most of his possessions to Kenya and traveled with his family to New York to board a one-way flight to Malaysia.

Within hours of his flight, the U.S. Attorney’s Office and Diplomatic Security Service secured an arrest warrant.

After scanning his boarding pass, Dieye allegedly physically resisted arrest, attempted to destroy one of his cell phones containing evidence that he was researching how to buy a home in Malaysia, and had to be subdued by multiple federal agents.

While a Magistrate Court in the Eastern District of New York initially ordered Dieye released on bond, the United States immediately sought and obtained an emergency stay of his release. Dieye has since been transported to the Northern District of Texas, where he and several of his co-defendants remain in federal custody pending trial.

If convicted, the defendants face a maximum penalty of 30 years in federal prison on the bank fraud conspiracy charge and 20 years in federal prison on the wire fraud conspiracy charge. Aggravated identity theft carries a mandatory sentence of two years’ imprisonment, consecutive to any other sentence imposed.

The Diplomatic Security Service conducted the investigation with substantial assistance from the U.S. Secret Service, U.S. Postal Inspection Service, Homeland Security Investigations, Drug Enforcement Administration, Customs and Border Protection, Social Security Administration Office of Inspector General, Federal Bureau of Investigation, National Insurance Crime Bureau, U.S. Embassy Dakar Senegal Office of Overseas Criminal Investigations, the Dallas Police Department, the Plano Police Department and the Collin County Sheriff’s Office.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Michael J. Murtha from the Major Crimes Section is prosecuting the case.

An indictment is merely an allegation of criminal conduct, and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law.

CHATANOOGA — ICE’s Homeland Security Investigations agents arrested Frederic Jean Rene Sicard, a French national, and Mark Adwar Odisho, an Iraqi national, in Cleveland Oct. 29. Under President Trump, Secretary Mullin and acting ICE Director David J. Venturella’s leadership, ICE is once again focused on enforcing the law, protecting the public and removing dangerous individuals from our communities.
HSI Chattanooga undertook the arrest as part of a joint investigation with the FBI and with assistance from the Cleveland Police Department. The Eastern District of Tennessee issued a criminal complaint and arrest warrant against the subjects Oct. 23.

A man who stole government funds intended to aid unemployed workers during the COVID-19 pandemic was sentenced on October 28, 2026, to more than two years in federal prison. Jacob Michael Laufenberg, age 36, from Dubuque, Iowa, received the prison term after a February 23, 2026, guilty plea to wire fraud.

Information from the guilty plea and sentencing hearings showed that in May 2020, Laufenberg applied for unemployment benefits in Iowa. He subsequently received unemployment benefits until April 2021. While he was receiving unemployment benefits, he concealed his employment with two employers and the fact that he was incarcerated in a county jail for nearly two months. Laufenberg’s false statements about his employment and custody status caused him to receive unemployment funds to which he was not entitled.

Laufenberg was sentenced in Cedar Rapids by United States District Court Chief Judge C.J. Williams. Laufenberg was sentenced to 33 months’ imprisonment. He was ordered to make $17,102 in restitution to Iowa Workforce Development. He must also serve a five-year term of supervised release after the prison term. There is no parole in the federal system.

Laufenberg is being held in the United States Marshal’s custody until he can be transported to a federal prison.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division. The core mission of the Fraud Division is to zealously investigate and prosecute those who steal or fraudulently misuse taxpayer dollars. Department of Justice efforts to combat fraud support President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Kyndra Lundquist and investigated by the United States Department of Labor, Office of Inspector General.

Court file information at https://ecf.iand.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/login.pl . The case file number is 25-CR-1040.

Follow us on X @USAO_NDIA.
title: Dubuque Man Sentenced to Federal Prison for COVID-19 Related Unemployment Fraud

Stakeholders Are Encouraged to Review Notice of Proposed Rulemaking and Submit Comments
Alexandria, VA (November 03, 2026) ― The National Credit Union Administration today announced two final rules and a proposed rule as part of the fourteenth round of proposed regulatory changes associated with NCUA’s Deregulation Project. The project is an ongoing review of NCUA’s regulations to ensure they are focused on credit unions’ safety, soundness, and resilience. With today’s announcement, NCUA is requesting comments on one proposal that would eliminate an obsolete regulation in the Code of Federal Regulations.
The proposal includes:
NPRM Summary
The NCUA Board (Board) is seeking public comments on an interim final rule that removes 12 CFR 723.9, an outdated transitional provision in the commercial lending regulation. The provision was adopted as part of the 2016 commercial lending rule to address credit unions operating under certain NCUA-approved waivers or supervisory actions during the transition to a principles-based regulatory framework. The Board has determined that the provision has served its purpose and is no longer necessary. Removing it would reduce regulatory complexity and improve the clarity of NCUA's regulations.
The two final rules NCUA announced are:
The Board adopted a final rule that makes permanent the regulatory treatment of Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loans that have been in place since April 27, 2020. These provisions were originally adopted during the COVID-19 pandemic to implement the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act (CARES Act).
The Board also amended 12 CFR 701.39 by removing paragraph (a)(1), which defined the phrase "except as otherwise provided by law or except as otherwise provided by federal law." The Board determined that the definition was unnecessary because credit unions are already responsible for identifying and complying with applicable laws when exercising their statutory lien authority. This change does not affect a credit union's statutory lien authority or existing legal obligations.
Find a detailed summary for each proposal at https://ncua.gov/news/deregulation-project/.
To submit comments, type or paste the docket numbers into the search on the Federal Rulemaking Portal.
title: NCUA Announces Fourteenth Round of Deregulation Proposals

Failed to Appear, Found in Maine, U.S. Marshals Arrest New Hampshire Fugitive
For immediate release
Ryan Guay, Supervisory Deputy U.S. Marshal
PORTLAND, Maine - The United States Marshals Service (USMS), District of Maine, announces the arrest of Andrew D. Secord, 24, in Rockland, Maine, on an outstanding arrest warrant issued by the Merrimack County Superior Court in New Hampshire for failure to appear for an arraignment/bail hearing. Secord was wanted on charges of Aggravated Felonious Sexual Assault (AFSA), Second Degree Assault, two counts of Criminal Threatening, and Domestic Violence Assault.
On October 20, 2026, investigators with the U.S. Marshals Service, District of New Hampshire, received an arrest warrant for Secord. Investigators developed information indicating that Secord had fled New Hampshire and was believed to be residing at a residence in Rockland, Maine. The USMS, New Hampshire Joint Fugitive Task Force subsequently forwarded an investigative lead to the U.S. Marshals Service, District of Maine, Maine Violent Offender Task Force requesting assistance in locating and apprehending Secord.
Through coordinated investigative efforts, on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, U.S. Marshals Service fugitive investigators, working in close coordination with the Rockland Police Department, located Secord in Rockland, Maine. Investigators successfully apprehended Secord without incident. Secord is charged as a fugitive from justice pending his extradition back to New Hampshire.
The U.S. Marshals Service remains committed to its mission of locating and apprehending fugitives who attempt to evade the judicial process. Through strong interagency partnerships, coordinated investigative efforts, and the dedication of its personnel, the USMS works to ensure that individuals wanted on outstanding warrants are located and brought before the appropriate court to answer for the charges against them.
The USMS Maine Violent Offender Task Force is comprised of personnel from the U.S. Marshals Service, Maine Department of Corrections, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and the Maine National Guard Counterdrug Task Force.
Anyone with information regarding the whereabouts of a state or federal fugitive is encouraged to contact the U.S. Marshals Service at MED.TIPLINE@usdoj.gov.

text:
DOJ To Monitor Elections in All 50 States for First Time
One of the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) most important missions is ensuring election integrity, supporting free and fair elections, and protecting the right to vote for U.S. citizens across the United States. The DOJ has sent election monitors in support of this mission since the enactment of the Voting Rights Act in 1965 across all Administrations.
Today, the DOJ will further this mission by engaging in its largest monitoring effort in history—with approximately 1,000 election monitors and observers deployed, and, for the first time, in all 50 states. The effort is coordinated by the Civil Rights Division. Monitors will include personnel from the Division, other DOJ divisions/components, U.S. Attorney’s Offices and federal observers from the Office of Personnel Management. Throughout Election Day, Division personnel will maintain contact with state and local election officials.
“Election integrity has been one of the top priorities for this Administration and this Division,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Civil Rights Division at the Department of Justice. “I am very proud we are deploying the largest monitoring effort in DOJ history, and pursuing transparency for elections in an assertive and nondiscriminatory manner.”
Election monitors will be checking for compliance with the federal voting rights statutes that fall within the jurisdiction of the Division. The Division’s Voting Section enforces the civil provisions of federal statutes that protect the right to vote, including the Voting Rights Act, National Voter Registration Act, Help America Vote Act, Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act, and Civil Rights Acts.
The Division’s Disability Rights Section enforces the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) to ensure that persons with disabilities have a full and equal opportunity to vote. The Division’s Criminal Section enforces federal criminal statutes that prohibit voter intimidation and voter suppression based on race, color, national origin, or religion.
Throughout the day and week, Division personnel will be available to receive questions and complaints from the public related to federal voting rights laws. If you have a question or complaint, please call our election issues hotline at 1-800-253-3931, email us at VEM@usdoj.gov, or submit a complaint through our website at www.civilrights.justice.gov/report.
Individuals with questions or complaints related to the ADA may call the Division’s toll-free ADA information hotline at 1-800-514-0301 or 1-833-610-1264 (TTY) or submit a complaint through our ADA website at www.ada.gov.
Complaints related to any disruptions at a polling place should always be reported to local election officials (including officials based in the polling place). Complaints related to violence, threats of violence or intimidation at a polling place should be reported immediately to local police authorities by calling 911. These complaints should also be reported to the department after local authorities have been contacted.
To learn more about what the DOJ and the Civil Rights Division has done historically to protect the vote and ensure free and fair elections, go to www.civilrights.justice.gov/electionintegrity.

text:
BOSTON – A Dominican man unlawfully residing in Lynn was indicted by a federal grand jury for unlawfully reentering the United States after deportation.

Cesar Fernando Guerrero-Casado, 41, was indicted for illegally reentering the United States after deportation. The defendant is currently detained in state custody on unrelated charges and appeared in federal court on Nov. 2, 2026.

According to the indictment, Guerrero-Casado was previously removed from the United States on Feb. 24, 2015. It is alleged that sometime after his February 2015 removal, Guerrero-Casado illegally reentered the United States without permission.

Guerrero-Casado was previously convicted of unlawful reentry in 2014. He is currently serving state prison sentences for drug offenses.

The charge of unlawful reentry of a deported alien provides for a sentence of up to 10 years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. The defendant is subject to deportation upon completion of any sentence imposed. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley and David T. Wesling, Acting Field Office Director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Enforcement and Removal Operations in Boston made the announcement. Assistant U.S. Attorney Catherine Conroy of the Major Crimes Unit is prosecuting the case.

The details contained in the charging document are allegations. The defendant is presumed to be innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in the court of law.
title: Illegal Alien from Dominican Republic Indicted for Unlawful Reentry

PORTLAND, Ore.— U.S. Attorney Scott E. Bradford announced today that Rithy Ham, 45, of Vancouver, Washington, has pleaded guilty to wire fraud and money laundering for orchestrating a yearslong scheme that defrauded a Portland resident of more than $333,000.

According to court documents, between September 2020 and May 2024, Ham created fictitious personas of two women and used them to deceive an adult victim. Ham falsely told the victim that the women needed financial assistance for living expenses, nursing school tuition and to escape prostitution and sex trafficking. Believing the women were real and in danger, the victim sent money on multiple occasions.

Ham communicated with the victim both directly and through the fabricated identities to maintain the deception. In November 2022, he falsely claimed one of the fictitious women urgently needed funds to escape sex trafficking, leading the victim to transfer $36,872.35. Ham later used part of those proceeds to write an $18,500 check to his wife. In March 2023, additional misrepresentations led the victim to transfer $20,922 from a retirement account, which was then deposited into accounts controlled by Ham and his wife.

In total, Ham stole $333,249.52 from the victim, much of it from the victim’s retirement savings.

Ham pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud and one count of money laundering. Under the plea agreement, he acknowledged the factual basis of the charges and agreed to pay full restitution.

Wire fraud carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison. Money laundering carries a maximum sentence of 10 years. Both charges also carry potential fines, up to three years of supervised release and mandatory fee assessments. Ham additionally agreed to a forfeiture money judgment of $333,249.52.

The FBI is investigating the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Meredith Bateman is prosecuting the case.
title: Washington Man Pleads Guilty to Wire Fraud and Money Laundering After Defrauding Victim of More Than $330,000 in Romance Scam

text:
While weather caused a greater loss of ozone this year, long-term recovery still on track 
Atypical weather conditions caused the Antarctic ozone hole to grow to an unusually large size in 2026, NOAA and NASA scientists reported today, though they said the protective ozone layer is still on track to recover by later this century.
Fueled by a powerful polar vortex, the 2026 ozone hole became the seventh-largest in 48 years of monitoring, based on NOAA and NASA analysis of the seasonal mean area. However, scientists noted that this year’s hole would have been larger still if levels of ozone-destroying chemicals in the atmosphere had not been reduced through international cooperation.
During peak ozone depletion season between September 7 and October 13, 2026, the average extent of the hole covered about 9.6 million square miles (25 million square kilometers) — more than twice the area of the United States. Scientists continually track the amount of ozone in the stratosphere because it acts as Earth’s “sunscreen,” helping shield life from harmful solar radiation. This is distinct from ground level ozone, which is an air pollutant commonly resulting from human activities.
“The annual ozone hole has been forming later in the season in recent years, which tells us the ozone layer is healing,” said Paul Newman, a senior scientist at the University of Maryland and longtime leader of NASA’s ozone research team at the agency’s Goddard Space Flight Center. “But an unusually powerful polar vortex has extended ozone depletion in the Antarctic this season, allowing the hole to grow to proportions we haven’t seen in a decade.”
The hole reached its greatest extent for the year on September 18 at 10.5 million square miles (27.1 million square kilometers). That’s about 90% as large as the largest ozone hole ever observed, which occurred on September 9, 2000.
“The 2026 ozone hole is large but could have been 1 to 2 million square miles (3.5 million square kilometers) larger if ozone-depleting substances were as prevalent in the atmosphere today as they were at their year 2000 peak,” Newman said.
How does ozone loss occur?
The ozone depletion process begins when human-made compounds containing chlorine and bromine are released into the environment. Air currents carry the gases up into the stratosphere, where they’re broken down by ultraviolet radiation. The freed chlorine and bromine atoms interact with cloud particles in the Antarctic stratosphere to enable ozone destruction. The stratospheric polar vortex, a seasonal stream of wind encircling Antarctica, plays a key role by corralling the frigid air necessary to produce polar stratospheric clouds.
“The polar vortex was unusually large this year in part because planetary-scale weather systems that typically well up from the lower atmosphere and break up the vortex were especially weak in August and September,” said Amy Butler, a research scientist at the NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory. “That weak wave action kept the strongest polar vortex winds further from the South Pole by several degrees of latitude, creating a larger area for conditions ideal for ozone depletion to occur.”
How do scientists measure and monitor the ozone hole?
The depletion of ozone within the hole was not as severe as record-breaking holes that occurred 10 or 20 years ago. Deploying balloon-borne instruments from the South Pole Baseline Atmospheric Observatory, and using an optical instrument called the Dobson Ozone Spectrophotometer, NOAA scientists found that ozone concentrations directly overhead reached their lowest value for the year — 105 Dobson units — on October 17.
The Dobson unit is the commonly used standard of measurement for expressing ozone concentration. One hundred Dobson Units represents a column of ozone that would be 1 millimeter deep – about as thick as a dime – if compressed under standard temperature and pressure conditions at sea level. The lowest value ever recorded over the South Pole was 92 Dobson units in October 2006.
Since 1979, satellites have also been integral to monitoring the health of the ozone layer. Instruments aboard NASA’s Aura satellite, the NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 satellites, and the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership satellite, jointly operated by NASA and NOAA, all contributed to the annual monitoring.
NOAA and NASA scientists said that the ongoing monitoring shows that controls established by the Montreal Protocol in 1987 continue to drive long-term recovery of stratospheric ozone.
As part of the Montreal Protocol, the international community committed to replacing ozone-depleting substances like chlorofluorocarbons with less-harmful alternatives. Since their peak, chlorine levels in the Antarctic stratosphere derived from ozone-depleting substances have declined by about a third relative to levels reached in the 1980s, said Stephen Montzka, senior scientist at NOAA’s Global Monitoring Laboratory.
What chemicals can cause the loss of ozone?
Chlorofluorocarbons and other ozone-depleting compounds were once widely used in consumer goods such as refrigerators, air conditioners, and building insulation. They can linger in the atmosphere or leach out of old products and landfills for many decades. As those older compounds break down, scientists estimate that the ozone hole will recover by the 2070s.
More: View the latest status of the ozone layer over the Antarctic by visiting NOAA’s South Pole Ozone website and NASA’s Ozone Watch.
title: NOAA, NASA release measurements of 2026 ozone hole

A man who illegally possessed a gun was sentenced on November 2, 2026, to more than five years in federal prison.

Leonard Craig Landt, Jr., age 39, from Cedar Rapids, Iowa, received the prison term after a May 29, 2026, guilty plea to possession of a firearm by a felon.

Evidence during the case showed that in 2015, Landt was convicted in federal court of conspiracy to commit robbery. After his release from federal prison, in September 2025, Landt was found in possession of a Glock 19 pistol.

Landt was sentenced in Cedar Rapids by United States District Court Chief Judge C.J. Williams. Landt was sentenced to 63 months’ imprisonment. He must also serve a three-year term of supervised release after the prison term. There is no parole in the federal system.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

Landt is being held in the United States Marshal’s custody until he can be transported to a federal prison.

The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Lisa C. Williams and investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. Court file information at https://ecf.iand.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/login.pl .

The case file number is 25-CR-0084.

Follow us on X @USAO_NDIA.
title: Felon Sent Back to Federal Prison for Illegally Possessing Gun

EPA Enforcement Leadership Helps Promote Military Readiness and Participates in Training During Swing Through Wyoming and Colorado
WASHINGTON – U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Assistant Administrator for Enforcement and Compliance Assurance Jeffrey A. Hall and Principal Deputy Craig Pritzlaff recently visited Wyoming and Colorado to promote military readiness and focus criminal environmental enforcement on major federal cases. In Wyoming, they visited a Minuteman launch control center and missile silo to understand the challenges the Air Force Global Strike Command faces in keeping missileers safe in aging missile facilities and to provide assistance in achieving compliance with indoor environmental standards. In Colorado, they participated in EPA’s criminal enforcement attorneys’ biannual training program, speaking on this Administration’s focus on federal priorities, including using the environmental laws to protect against foreign toxins.
“We are keeping the airmen stationed in missile alert facilities safe by helping the Air Force comply with toxic substances regulations, and that allows our warfighters to focus on defending our country,” said Assistant Administrator Hall.
Assistant Administrator Hall visited F.E. Warren Air Force Base, home of the Twentieth Air Force, which is responsible for U.S. intercontinental ballistic missiles, as part of EPA’s commitment to partner with the Department of War (DoW). The visit was focused on the Air Force’s ongoing efforts to comply with the nation’s environmental laws, address environmental hazards, and protect the homeland.
“Our highest priority for our criminal program is that it holds the worst environmental criminals accountable while being true to the Constitution and the rule of law,” said Assistant Administrator Hall. “EPA’s criminal enforcement attorneys ensure that our criminal program can investigate and prosecute cases effectively and lawfully.”
In support of Administrator Zeldin’s Powering the Great American Comeback initiative, the biannual training conference highlighted EPA’s effort to protect Americans by pursuing those who intentionally pollute or profit from sending harmful products and chemicals into the United States. The training program teaches EPA’s criminal enforcement attorneys about new developments in the investigation and prosecution of environmental crimes and fosters a collaborative working relationship. The training program focused on enforcement initiatives, civil and criminal coordination, 4th Amendment issues, trial strategies, and significant appellate decisions.
title: EPA Enforcement Leadership Helps Promote Military Readiness and Participates in Training During Swing Through Wyoming and Colorado

ROCHESTER, N.Y.-U.S. Attorney Michael DiGiacomo announced today that Kevin Dangerfield, 39, of Rochester, NY, who was convicted of possession with intent to distribute cocaine and being a felon in possession of a firearm, was sentenced to serve 156 months in prison by U.S. District Court Judge Charles J. Siragusa.

In November 2024, a United States Probation Officer conducted a home visit at Dangerfield’s Otis Street residence. During the visit, the officer recovered approximately 19 grams of cocaine, approximately $946 in cash, and a loaded 9mm semiautomatic pistol with a defaced serial number. Dangerfield was on probation following two previous federal convictions in the Western District of New York in July 2009 and May 2023. As a result, he is legally prohibited from possessing a firearm.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America, a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

The case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Matthew T. McGrath. The sentencing is the result of an investigation by the U.S Probation Office, under the direction of Chief Probation Officer Clifford Jackson, the Rochester Police Department, under the direction of Chief David Smith, and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, under the direction of Special Agent-in-Charge Bryan DiGirolamo, New York Field Division.

text:
TULSA, Okla. – A federal criminal complaint charges Dakota Horn, 25, and Willie Joseph Horn III, 28, with federal child exploitation offenses related to the production, receipt, distribution, and possession of child sexual abuse material.

Following a years-long international investigation into a previously unidentified child sexual abuse material (CSAM) series known as "SpiralTattoo," federal authorities have charged two Oklahoma residents after investigators identified both subjects depicted in the material and confirmed the identity of a child victim.

According to court documents, investigators determined that Dakota Horn and Willie Horn had access to the child victim while providing childcare and were able to connect the defendants to the material through a combination of witness statements, social media evidence, CyberTipline records, physical identifiers, and statements made during the investigation.

The investigation began in 2022 when an international law enforcement partner provided information to the Federal Bureau of Investigation regarding a CSAM series depicting the sexual abuse of a very young child. Despite extensive efforts, investigators were initially unable to identify the victim or the adults responsible for creating the material.

Through years of investigative work involving FBI personnel, victim identification specialists, digital forensic analysis, open-source intelligence, CyberTipline reports from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and coordinated law enforcement efforts, investigators ultimately identified the child victim and the two adults allegedly responsible for producing the abuse material.

Federal authorities are also seeking information about any additional victims who may have had contact with Dakota Horn or Willie Horn during the relevant time period.

Investigators believe the defendants had regular access to multiple children between approximately 2020 and 2023 while residing in the Tulsa-area. Anyone with information concerning potential victims, suspicious conduct involving either defendant, or other relevant information is encouraged to contact the FBI.

Anyone with information is asked to contact the FBI Oklahoma City Field Office at (405) 290-7770 or submit information online at tips.fbi.gov.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation along with Tulsa Police Department and Broken Arrow Police Department are investigating the case. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Alicia Hockenbury and Kenneth Elmore are prosecuting the case.

A Criminal Complaint is merely an allegation. The defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
title: Child Victim Identified After Years of Investigation and an Oklahoma Couple Now Faces Federal Charges

text:
USITC Appoints Lisa Murray and Benjamin Richards as New Administrative Law Judges
Brett W. Doyle, Chairman of the U.S. International Trade Commission (Commission or USITC), announced today that Lisa A. Murray and Benjamin S. Richards have been named USITC Administrative Law Judges (ALJs). Murray and Richards will manage an active litigation docket, preside over evidentiary hearings, and make initial determinations in the Commission’s investigations involving unfair practices in import trade under section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930. These investigations most often involve allegations of patent and trademark infringement.
About Lisa A. Murray
Prior to her appointment as ALJ, Murray served as an Administrative Patent Judge (APJ) on the Patent Trial and Appeal Board at the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office from 2024 to 2026. Prior to her appointment as APJ, Murray worked as an investigative attorney in the USITC’s Office of Unfair Import Investigations from 2008 to 2024, where she represented the public interest in section 337 investigations involving patent infringement and trade secret misappropriation.
Murray began her career as a judicial law clerk to the Hon. Dominick L. DiCarlo, Chief Judge of the U.S. Court of International Trade, and practiced intellectual property and international trade law at various private firms before rejoining the federal government.
Murray holds a juris doctor degree, cum laude, from the University of Michigan Law School, a master of science degree in computer science from the George Washington University, a masters of arts degree in political science (world politics) from the University of Michigan, and a bachelor of arts degree, with honors, in history and music performance from Oberlin College.
About Benjamin S. Richards
Before his appointment as ALJ, Richards served as Of Counsel at Winston Taylor LLP in Washington, DC. Previously, he served as an attorney-advisor in both the Office of the General Counsel and the Office of the Administrative Law Judges at the USITC. In those roles, he advised the Commission and ALJs on section 337 investigations and represented the Commission in appellate litigation before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit.
Earlier in his career, he served as a trial attorney in the Intellectual Property Section of the U.S. Department of Justice's Civil Division, where he represented the United States in patent, trademark, and copyright litigation.
He holds a juris doctor degree from the George Washington University Law School and a bachelor's degree in mathematics from the University of Utah.
About the U.S. International Trade Commission
The USITC is an independent, nonpartisan, factfinding federal agency that investigates and makes determinations in proceedings involving imports claimed to injure a domestic industry or violate U.S. intellectual property rights; provides independent analysis and information on tariffs, trade, and competitiveness to the President and the Congress; and maintains the U.S. Harmonized Tariff Schedule.
title: USITC Appoints Lisa Murray and Benjamin Richards as New Administrative Law Judges

GREAT FALLS – A Browning man who strangled one girlfriend and beat another almost to death was sentenced today to five years in prison, followed by three years of supervised release, U.S. Attorney Scott Twito said.

Jeremiah James Harwood, 23, pleaded guilty under a global plea agreement in August 2026 to three charges from two separate cases: strangulation, assault resulting in serious bodily injury, and witness tampering.

Chief U.S. District Judge Brian M. Morris presided.

The government alleged in court documents that Harwood strangled one intimate partner and beat another almost to death. After beating his partner, he then tried to convince her to change her testimony against him.

Harwood strangled his first partner using a lanyard she was wearing. The two were fighting and Harwood tackled the victim while trying to take her phone. He then grabbed the lanyard she had around her neck and began to choke her until she couldn’t breathe. At that point she stopped resisting and Harwood let go.

Roughly a year later, while on pretrial release for the strangulation charge, Harwood was in a new relationship with a different partner. Harwood attacked that partner on two occasions about two weeks apart, each time sending her to the hospital with significant head injuries. After the second assault, his partner was diagnosed with a traumatic brain injury that required intubation and surgery.

Law enforcement began an investigation after the assault, at which point Harwood reached out to the victim and attempted to convince her to redo her statement and tell investigators he was not involved. Instead, she reported him to the FBI.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office prosecuted the case. The Blackfeet Law Enforcement Services and the FBI conducted the investigation.
title: Browning man sentenced to five years in prison for strangling one victim, beating another, and witness tampering

text:
Statement from U.S. Attorney’s Office and DEA El Paso Division

ALBUQUERQUE – An Albuquerque woman is facing federal drug trafficking and firearm offenses after an HSTF investigation allegedly recovered large quantities of fentanyl, heroin, cash, and firearms from her Albuquerque residence.

According to court documents, law enforcement is investigating a drug trafficking organization allegedly importing large quantities of fentanyl, heroin and other narcotics into Albuquerque, New Mexico. On October 28, 2026, a U.S. Magistrate Judge authorized a federal search warrant for the residence of Angel Ramirez , 45, in northwest Albuquerque.

On October 29, 2026, agents executed the warrant and encountered Ramirez , the sole adult in the home. Inside the master bedroom, investigators allegedly located multiple duffel bags containing large quantities of narcotics, bulk U.S. currency, and numerous firearms. Laboratory field testing confirmed the presence of fentanyl and heroin.

In total, agents recovered approximately 43.75 kilograms of fentanyl powder, the largest seizure in New Mexico in the DEA history, 7.70 kilograms of fentanyl pills, 4.40 kilograms of heroin, and an additional 1,036 grams of fentanyl in a separate container. Investigators also located approximately 29 firearms and assorted ammunition inside and around a gun safe directly beneath the narcotics and cash.

Court documents state that Ramirez was employed as a paralegal with the State of New Mexico’s Department of Justice, a taxpayer‑funded position of public trust. Investigators allege that Ramirez leveraged her government employment, clean criminal history, and internal access to the justice system to create a veneer of legitimacy while her residence operated as a distribution hub for narcotics, drug proceeds, and firearms.

“Nearly 50 kilograms of fentanyl powder in a single Albuquerque home tells us just how serious the drug trafficking problem has become in New Mexico,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison. “This is a tremendous accomplishment by the agents who got these drugs off our streets, but it is no cause for celebration. With fentanyl overdose deaths on the rise in New Mexico, we have a lot more work to do. We will continue targeting the organizations bringing these drugs into our state and aggressively prosecuting those responsible.”

“Nearly 50 kilograms of fentanyl powder in a single Albuquerque home tells us just how serious the drug trafficking problem has become in New Mexico,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison. “This is a tremendous accomplishment by the agents who got these drugs off our streets, but it is no cause for celebration. With fentanyl overdose deaths on the rise in New Mexico, we have a lot more work to do. We will continue targeting the organizations bringing these drugs into our state and aggressively prosecuting those responsible.”

“As members of the community, I want you to know that our agents remain deeply committed to protecting and serving the city of Albuquerque,” said DEA El Paso Division Special Agent in Charge Robert “Eric” Castañeda. “I’m proud of their professionalism, dedication, and the outstanding work they demonstrated throughout this operation. DEA remains steadfast in our mission to keep our communities safe.”

“As members of the community, I want you to know that our agents remain deeply committed to protecting and serving the city of Albuquerque,” said DEA El Paso Division Special Agent in Charge Robert “Eric” Castañeda. “I’m proud of their professionalism, dedication, and the outstanding work they demonstrated throughout this operation. DEA remains steadfast in our mission to keep our communities safe.”

Ramirez is charged with possession with intent to distribute fentanyl and using and carrying a firearm during and in relation to a drug trafficking crime. She will remain in custody pending trial which has not been scheduled. If convicted of the current charges, Ramirez faces no less than 15 years and up to life in prison.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison made the announcement today on behalf of HSTF. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Mark Probasco, Timothy Piatt and Oliver Stephanz are prosecuting the case.

This arrest is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States.

HSTF Region II CORE 7 is comprised of agents and officers from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the Federal Bureau of Investigations (FBI), the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI), Customs and Border Protection – Office of Field Operations (OFO), U.S. Border Patrol (USBP) and Air and Marine (AMO), Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR), United States Department of the Interior – Bureau of Land Management (BLM), Joint Task Force North (JTF-N), United States Postal Inspection Service (USPIS), United States Marshal Service (USMS), Department of State, Bureau of Diplomatic Security (DSS), U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), Texas Department of Public Safety (TXDPS), El Paso Police Department (EPPD), New Mexico State Police (NMSP), West Texas / New Mexico High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas (HIDTA), Albuquerque Police Department, New Mexico Sixth Judicial District, Las Cruces/Dona Ana County Metro Narcotics Agency, and the prosecution is being led by the Office of the United States Attorney for the Districts of Western Texas and New Mexico.

The Sandoval County Sheriff’s Office, Bernalillo County Sheriff’s Office, Rio Rancho Police Department and Pueblo of Pojoaque Tribal Police Department provided invaluable assistance in this arrest.

A criminal complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

text:
Fort Myers, Florida – Rudy Perez (41, Fort Myers) has been sentenced by U.S. District Judge Sheri Polster Chappell to 21 years and 8 months in federal prison for enticing minors to engage in sexual activity, receiving and possessing images and videos depicting the sexual abuse of children, and transferring obscene matter to a minor. Perez was found guilty on August 3, 2026, following a bench trial. Perez was also sentenced to a term of life of supervised release and ordered to register as a sex offender. United States Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe made the announcement.

According to court documents, between January and April 2022, Perez used a social media application to persuade, induce, and entice a minor to engage in sexual activity. In January 2025, a social media application made a Cybertipline Report to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) that Perez was involved with the online enticement of children for sexual acts.

During the course of the investigation, law enforcement obtained a search warrant for Perez’s social media account. The FBI observed that Perez had enticed and solicited numerous other users who had identified themselves as children for sexually explicit images, and several minor children sent sexually explicit material to Perez at his request. Further, Perez sent photographs and sexually explicit videos and images of adults to numerous users who had identified themselves as children.

Pursuant to a search warrant, Perez’s cellphone was seized and a subsequent forensic analysis revealed that Perez possessed child sexual abuse material, including numerous videos depicting the sexual abuse of minors.

This case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Fort Myers Child Exploitation and Human Trafficking Task Force, which includes the Lee County Sheriff’s Office. It was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Yolande G. Viacava.

This is another case brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by the United States Attorneys’ Offices and the Criminal Division’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who sexually exploit children, and to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.justice.gov/psc.
title: Fort Myers Man Sentenced to More than 21 Years in Federal Prison for Child Exploitation Offenses

Robert Bowers, Senior Inspector
NORFOLK, Virginia – A fugitive investigation that spanned several states and lasted over 18 months came to an end today when the U. S. Marshals Service (USMS) arrested a fugitive who was wanted in relation to a homicide that occurred in Hampton on April 11, 2025.
The USMS Capital Area Regional Fugitive Task Force (CARFTF), in conjunction with the USMS New York/New Jersey Regional Fugitive Task Force arrested Curtis Shermaine Frazier, Jr., 27, shortly after 9:30 a.m., in the 5000 block of Farragut Avenue in Brooklyn, New York. Frazier was wanted on charges of second-degree murder, use of a firearm in the commission of a felony, shooting in a public place, and reckless handling of a firearm.
All charges were related to a Hampton homicide at the Karma Lounge that took the life of 25-year-old D’Angelo Osborne.
Shortly after the homicide, investigators with the Hampton Police Division requested assistance from the USMS Capital Area Regional Fugitive Task Force with locating and apprehending Frazier. The USMS CARFTF followed up on leads in North Carolina and Georgia before ultimately apprehending Frazier in New York.
Frazier was arrested without incident and is being held at Brooklyn Central Booking, where he will await extradition to Virginia to face charges.
The USMS Capital Area Regional Fugitive Task Force was established in June of 2004, has partnership agreements with over 100 federal, state, and local agencies and has 8 fully operational offices. To date, the USMS CARFTF has arrested more than 111,488 fugitives.

SIOUX FALLS - United States Attorney Ron Parsons announced today that Assistant U.S. Attorney Megan Poppen has been selected to receive the 2026 Director’s Award from the U.S. Department of Justice’s Executive Office for United States Attorneys (EOUSA) in recognition of her Superior Performance in Indian Country for the Department of Justice.

“AUSA Megan Poppen was nominated for her prodigious contribution to the safety of citizens of the Oglala Sioux Tribe,” said U.S. Attorney Parsons. “For more than a decade, she has prosecuted and convicted hundreds of dangerous defendants who victimized the most vulnerable persons living within the Pine Ridge Reservation. The lives of countless tribal citizens, especially children, are better and safer because of her efforts. She is extremely worthy of this nationwide honor, and we could not be prouder of Megan and her work.”

“AUSA Megan Poppen was nominated for her prodigious contribution to the safety of citizens of the Oglala Sioux Tribe,” said U.S. Attorney Parsons. “For more than a decade, she has prosecuted and convicted hundreds of dangerous defendants who victimized the most vulnerable persons living within the Pine Ridge Reservation. The lives of countless tribal citizens, especially children, are better and safer because of her efforts. She is extremely worthy of this nationwide honor, and we could not be prouder of Megan and her work.”

AUSA Poppen was honored among 183 Department of Justice staff recognized during a ceremony in the Great Hall of the Robert F. Kennedy Building, the Justice Department’s headquarters in Washington, D.C., on October 27, 2026, and accepted the award from Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter and EOUSA Director Francey Hakes. Department leadership commended AUSA Poppen for her exceptional work in promoting public safety and safeguarding the communities of the Pine Ridge Reservation through the prosecution of violent crimes, including homicide, sexual abuse, and assaults involving dangerous weapons. This marks the second time AUSA Poppen has received this prestigious award for her exemplary service in Indian Country.
title: Rapid City Federal Prosecutor Receives National Award from the Department of Justice for Superior Performance in Indian Country

American manufacturing is surging under President Donald J. Trump. A new report shows the sector expanding for the tenth consecutive month, with production growing at its fastest pace in nearly five years. Factories are expanding. Jobs are returning. Paychecks are rising faster than inflation. And companies are investing trillions to build their futures in America.
- Manufacturing jobs are coming back. Manufacturers have added 72,000 jobs this year, reversing the 202,000 manufacturing jobs lost in the final two years of the Biden Administration. Employment in factory construction has climbed by nearly 112,000 since President Trump took office.
- Paychecks are growing. Manufacturing workers’ weekly earnings are up 5% over the past year — outpacing inflation and boosting purchasing power.
- Investment is accelerating. Business investment jumped 12.7% in the third quarter of 2026, the fastest growth in 15 years. Private investment in plants and equipment rose 9.4% — more than twice the 2025 rate and triple the pace of Biden’s final year. Capital goods imports hit a record share of total goods imports in September while consumer goods imports fell to a historic low, signaling businesses are equipping American factories, not just importing finished products.
- Demand for American machinery is strong. U.S. machine tool orders reached their third-highest monthly total on record, up more than 36% from a year earlier.
Companies are matching the momentum with major new commitments. In just the past few weeks:
- Audi announced a $4 billion factory in Georgia — its first U.S. manufacturing plant — creating 4,500 jobs.
- Westinghouse Electric announced a $1 billion investment in South Carolina to build a next-generation nuclear fuel factory.
- U.S. Steel announced a $3 billion investment near Pittsburgh to construct a new hot strip mill and increase annual capacity by roughly 1.3 million tons.
- Apple announced up to $100 million to strengthen American titanium production.
- Bombardier announced $270 million in U.S. manufacturing investment, creating thousands of jobs.
- Carrier announced more than $600 million in an advanced manufacturing facility in Fort Worth.
More jobs. Rising wages. New factories. Record investment. Under President Trump, American manufacturing is being rebuilt — and made great again.

Foreign Military Sales: Congressional Notification

Bureau of Political-Military Affairs

November 2, 2026

Transmittal #26-95

The U.S. Department of State has made a determination approving a possible Foreign Military Sale to the Government of Jordan for Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System II and related equipment. The estimated total cost is $100 million.

The Government of Jordan has requested to buy up to one thousand five hundred (1,500) WGU-59A/B or B/B Single Variant Block Upgrade (air-to-air, ground-to-air, or air-to-ground) Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System II (All-up-rounds or guidance sections). The following non-major defense equipment items will also be included: launchers; Mk-152 high explosive warheads; MK66 rocket motors; proximity fuzes; WTU-1/B practice warheads; inert MK66 rocket motors; support equipment; publications and technical documentation; transportation; U.S. Government and contractor engineering, technical, training, and logistical support services; and other related elements of logistics and program support. The estimated total cost is $100 million.

This proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by helping to improve the security of a Major Non-NATO Ally that is an important force for political stability and economic progress in the Middle East.

The proposed sale will improve Jordan’s capability to meet current and future threats by providing enhancement to its air defense capability in support of the Middle East Air Defense pillar of the Regional Security Construct. The acquisition of additional APKWS II guided rockets will increase Jordan’s capacity to defend itself, allow for the reduction of sustained U.S. support over time, and provide increased security for U.S. military assets stationed in Jordan. Jordan will have no difficulty absorbing these articles and services into its armed forces.

The proposed sale of this equipment and support will not alter the basic military balance in the region.

The principal contractor will be BAE Systems, Inc., located in Nashua, NH. At this time, the U.S. Government is not aware of any offset agreement proposed in connection with this potential sale. Any offset agreement will be defined in negotiations between the purchaser and the contractor.

Implementation of this proposed sale will not require the assignment of any additional U.S. Government or contractor representatives to Jordan. Only additional periodic participation in program and technical reviews, training, and maintenance support will be required.

There will be no adverse impact on U.S. defense readiness as a result of this proposed sale.

For further information, please contact the Bureau of Political-Military Affairs Outreach Team at T_Outreach_PM@State.gov .

BY THE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
A PROCLAMATION
For more than a century, human freedom has been threatened by communist and socialist ideologies that eliminate individual opportunity, subjugate individuals to the state, and extinguish the God-given rights upon which free nations are built. This Anti-Communism Week, we are reminded of the devastating consequences of state control over human thought, creativity, and political expression, resulting in suffering, poverty, exploitation, violence, and misery for millions, and we renew our commitment to protect the sacred values of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness from the chains of tyranny.
Our Republic was founded upon the enduring conviction that our rights are inherent, our liberties are sacred, and our Government derives its just powers from the consent of the governed. These principles have defined our national character for over 250 years and continue to distinguish our way of life from that of all other countries on Earth.
Today, however, our American experiment faces renewed threats as socialist, communist, and radical leftist ideologies find increased expression in our Nation. We must remain vigilant in defending the principles that sustain our Republic and ensure the lessons of history are never forgotten nor repeated. Under my leadership, America will never fall victim to these evil ideologies, and the United States will never become a communist country.
The story of America is, above all, a story of a Nation uniting as one, standing up to tyranny, and charting its own destiny as a free and self-governing Republic. As President, I will always protect the founding principles for which so many fought and died. Together, we will defend our Constitution, which protects our freedoms; uphold the dignity of every individual; strengthen the free market, which has made us the most prosperous country ever to exist; and ensure that the promise of America remains alive and well for generations to come.
This week, we honor the victims of socialism and communism by remembering their lives, defending the freedoms that were denied, renewing our resolve to safeguard the Republic entrusted to us, and reminding ourselves that what we have created as a Nation stands as the greatest testament to human freedom in the history of the world.
NOW, THEREFORE, I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of America, by virtue of the authority vested in me by the Constitution and the laws of the United States, do hereby proclaim the week of November 1 through November 7 as Anti-Communism Week. I call upon all Americans to stand firm in their defense against any threat to the American way of life and to protect our burning flame of liberty from the darkness of communism.
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand this third day of November, in the year of our Lord two thousand twenty-six, and of the Independence of the United States of America the two hundred and fifty-first.
DONALD J. TRUMP
title: ANTI-COMMUNISM WEEK, 2026
