A man who sexually exploited a child in Vinton, Iowa, in 2022, pled guilty today in federal court in Cedar Rapids. Dennis Tomas Greehy, age 38, most recently from Melbourne, Florida, was convicted of sexual exploitation of a child and possession of child pornography.

In a plea agreement, Greehy admitted that he started talking online with a 13‑year‑old child in 2020. He asked the child to send him nude photos and videos, and the child did so. On multiple occasions, starting when the child was 14 years old, Greehy traveled from North Carolina to Iowa City and had sex with the child. In the summer of 2022, he rented an apartment in Vinton and he had sex with the child in that apartment. He also recorded the child engaging in sexually explicit conduct. Greehy then moved to Florida but continued to communicate with the child, asking for photos and videos of the child engaged in sex acts. He also traveled back to Iowa to have sex with the child. In June 2026, law enforcement officers arrested Greehy in Florida and seized his phone. On his phone were several depictions of the child engaging in sexually explicit conduct.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and CEOS, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit Justice.gov/PSC .

Sentencing before United States District Court Chief Judge C.J. Williams will be set after a presentence report is prepared. Greehy remains in custody of the United States Marshal pending sentencing. Greehy faces a mandatory minimum sentence of 15 years’ imprisonment and a possible maximum sentence of 40 years’ imprisonment, a $500,000 fine, $77,200 in special assessments, and a lifetime term of supervised release following any imprisonment.

The case is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Devra T. Hake and was investigated by the Iowa City Police Department, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Brevard County, Florida, Sheriff’s Office, and the Melbourne, Florida, Police Department.

Court file information at https://ecf.iand.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/login.pl .

The case file number is 26-CR-46.

HUNTINGTON, W.Va. – Anton Marcel Jeffries, 32, of Akron, Ohio, was sentenced to one year and nine months in prison, to be followed by four years of supervised release, for violating supervised release.

According to court documents and statements made in court, September 18, 2025, Jeffries was arrested and charged with intent to deliver a controlled substance in Kanawha County Magistrate Court. Jeffries was arrested after law enforcement officers investigated the source of a significant increase in drug overdoses in Charleston between September 17 and September 18, 2025. Jeffries pleaded guilty to possession of a controlled substance, fentanyl, in Kanawha County Circuit Court on September 14, 2026.

At the time of this offense, Jeffries was serving a term of supervised release following his conviction for possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine, heroin, and fentanyl in United States District Court for the Southern District of West Virginia on August 27, 2019. Jeffries began his term of supervised release on September 12, 2025, six days before his arrest.

WASHINGTON – U.S. Representative Pramila Jayapal (WA-07) released the following statement following the announcement that the City of Seattle’s Department of Transportation (SDOT) was awarded $9,675,459 through the United States Department of Transportation Safe Streets and Roads for All grant. This grant will support the implementation of safety improvements at six high-injury locations across Seattle to ensure safer conditions for drivers and pedestrians.
“This funding is a big win for our city as we continue our work to invest in enhanced street safety in vulnerable and high-risk areas,” said Jayapal. “I was proud to support this project, and in Congress, I will continue to work to bring home federal money to support projects that prioritize safety for pedestrians, bikers, and drivers across our city.”
“Thank you to Congresswoman Jayapal, and our congressional delegation for supporting Seattle and helping to secure this $10 million street safety grant. Safety is my top priority, and traffic safety is one of our community’s top concerns. This funding will make a meaningful impact and support our work to prevent traffic injuries and deaths and ensure that everyone in Seattle can get around our city safely,” said Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson.
“This Safe Streets grant will add to our Vision Zero traffic safety efforts, funding street pavement upgrades to prevent people driving from skidding off the street and harming themselves or others. It also means we can enhance traffic signals in Pioneer Square and the Chinatown – International District to be more responsive to pedestrians and emergency vehicles. We are deeply appreciative of the ongoing leadership of our congressional delegation for your ongoing work to help Seattle secure this and several other federal traffic safety grants in recent years,” said SDOT Acting Director Angela Brady.
This project, titled Safer Streets for Seattle: Addressing Our City’s Evolving Roadway Safety Needs, addresses roadway issues that contribute to serious injuries and fatal crashes throughout Seattle’s most impacted and at-risk intersections and roadways. Through its Vision Zero Action Plan, SDOT is committed to eliminating traffic fatalities and serious injuries on city streets by prioritizing the corridors and intersections where crashes are most severe and happen most often. With the support of this grant, SDOT will install high-friction surface treatments to reduce skidding, upgrade traffic signals, and conduct further data analysis to identify crash patterns and risks.
Jayapal’s letter of support for this grant can be found here.

U.S. Coast Guard Awards $114 Million Contract to Modernize Critical Water Infrastructure at Base Kodiak, Bolstering Arctic Readiness
WASHINGTON — The U.S. Coast Guard awarded a $114 million contract on Oct. 29, 2026 to Gilbane Federal of Providence, Rhode Island, to modernize the water distribution system at Base Kodiak, Alaska. Funded through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, this project directly strengthens operational readiness and quality of life at the Coast Guard’s largest operational installation.
As a vital hub for projecting U.S. presence and defending national sovereignty across Alaska and the Arctic approaches, Base Kodiak supports surface and aviation operations in a demanding maritime environment. The contract encompasses all design, labor, material, equipment, and site work necessary to deliver a resilient, modern water utility network, with completion scheduled for Oct. 2031.
Project Key Highlights:
- System Recapitalization: Replaces and upgrades more than 8 miles of main water distribution lines across Base Kodiak.
- Storage Capacity: Replaces four large-scale water storage tanks critical to base operations.
- Aviation and Facility Fire Suppression: Delivers dedicated water supply and pressure reliability for fire suppression systems protecting two operational aircraft hangars and key shore facilities.
- Workforce Quality of Life: Ensures safe, dependable potable water for the active-duty, reserve, civilian, and family members living and working on base.
- Execution and Oversight: Civil Engineering Unit (CEU) Juneau is executing this project, operating under the Shore Infrastructure Logistics Center within the Coast Guard’s Program Executive Office (PEO) Shore.
“Every day, the Coast Guard delivers value to our Nation by controlling, securing, and defending our northern border and maritime approaches in the Arctic,” said Rear Adm. Jon Hickey, Deputy Commandant for Systems. “Our crews need modern, resilient shore capabilities to answer the call and get the mission done. By investing $114 million to modernize Base Kodiak’s critical water and fire-suppression infrastructure, we are directly supporting our forces and their families while building the foundation for our expanding polar fleet and long-term mission readiness.”
Driving Holistic Arctic Transformation
Base Kodiak is central to the Coast Guard’s strategic posture in the high latitudes and designated as the future homeport for the Service’s first two Arctic Security Cutters. The water distribution modernization complements a comprehensive suite of infrastructure projects currently planned or underway at Base Kodiak to support expanding mission capabilities and workforce growth, including:
- Construction of a new fuel pier and upgrades to the cargo wharf to support major cutters and icebreakers.
- Construction of 30 additional family housing units and a new child development center to support Coast Guard personnel and their families.
Using the nearly $25 billion investment in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the largest capital investment in the Service’s history, the Coast Guard has already ordered over $20 billion in new assets and capabilities, critical depot maintenance, and shore facilities. This rapid investment demonstrates the Coast Guard’s commitment to modernizing acquisition, delivering next-generation technology, restoring readiness, and revitalizing shore infrastructure.
For media inquiries contact mediarelations@uscg.mil.
###
About the U.S. Coast Guard 
With more than 95,000 miles of shoreline, 25,000 miles of navigable rivers and 4.5 million square miles of U.S. exclusive economic zone, the U.S. Coast Guard defends the Nation, protects the marine transportation system, regulates and safeguards ports and waterways, leads the Nation in maritime drug interdiction and secures the maritime border. As a member of the joint force, a law enforcement organization, a regulatory agency and a member of the U.S. intelligence community, the Coast Guard employs a unique mix of authorities to ensure the safety and integrity of the maritime domain to protect the economic and national security of the nation. More than 76,000 members of the Coast Guard operate a multi-mission, interoperable fleet of more than 220 cutters, 185 fixed and rotary-wing aircraft, 1,300 boats and its own dedicated cyber command to protect critical maritime infrastructure.
More information about the U.S. Coast Guard can be found at www.uscg.mil Follow @USCG on X and Instagram, like us on Facebook, subscribe on YouTube and follow LinkedIn—connect with us.
Make a difference on land, at sea or in the air with the Coast Guard. Visit GoCoastGuard.com to find out how to be part of our team.

Gainesville, Florida – Kensha Eugene Williams, 26, of Gainesville, Florida, has pleaded guilty in federal court on a charge of possession of a firearm and ammunition by a convicted felon. John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida announced the guilty plea.

U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “Our state and federal law enforcement officers work hard every day to keep our citizens safe from dangerous, violent felons, like this defendant, and I am proud to back up their hard work with successful prosecutions like this one.”

According to court records, on June 28, 2026, law enforcement observed the defendant in possession of a suspected drugs. Once detained and searched, the officer located a firearm and ammunition in the defendant’s pocket. The defendant has prior convictions for Aggravated Assault with Firearm and Carrying a Concealed Firearm and therefore cannot legally possess a firearm and ammunition.

Sentencing is scheduled for February 16, 2027, at 2:30pm before Chief United States District Court Judge Allen Winsor in Gainesville, Florida. The Defendant faces up to 15 years’ imprisonment.

The case was jointly investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the Gainesville Police Department. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Tyler Fleming.

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities .

The United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Florida is one of 94 offices that serve as the nation’s principal litigators under the direction of the Attorney General. ALEXANDRIA, Va. – A Venezuelan national who resided in Miami was sentenced today to 12 years in prison for conspiracy to launder money. Jorge Figueira, 60, laundered billions of dollars for numerous and varied illicit actors, including drug trafficking organizations. Figueira also agreed to a $1 billion money judgment.

According to court documents, the laundering network of Figueira used various bank accounts, cryptocurrency exchange accounts, private cryptocurrency wallets, and shell companies to launder voluminous amounts of illicit money into and out of the United States. Figueira used a series of steps, including the conversion of money to cryptocurrency that was directed to a series of digital wallets. Figueira would send the funds to liquidity providers to exchange the cryptocurrency for dollars, then transfer the dollars to Figueira's bank accounts and ultimately to the intended recipient. These transactions were performed to conceal the nature of the funds from law enforcement authorities.

More than a billion dollars moved through the identified cryptocurrency wallet and various financial accounts. Within Figueira’s financial accounts, the majority of the inbound funds were received from cryptocurrency trading platforms. The majority of outbound funds were sent to various businesses and individuals located in the United States and overseas, including high-risk jurisdictions such as Colombia, China, Panamá, and Mexico.

Theophani K. Stamos, First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia, and Jeffrey L. Tyler, Special Agent in Charge of the FBI Washington Field Office's Criminal Division, made the announcement after sentencing by U.S. District Judge Rossie D. Alston Jr.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Catherine Rosenberg and Edgardo Rogriguez are prosecuting the case.

Related court documents and information are located on the website of the District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia or on PACER by searching for Case No. 1:26-cr-74.

WASHINGTON —The U.S. Small Business Administration is reminding eligible businesses and private nonprofit organizations in Pennsylvania of the Dec. 4 deadline to apply for low-interest federal disaster loans to offset losses caused by the Hotel Hampton Fire occurring Feb. 20.
The declaration covers the Pennsylvania counties of Bucks, Carbon, Lehigh, Monroe, and Northampton, as well as the New Jersey county of Warren, which are eligible for Economic Injury Disaster Loans from SBA.
The SBA’s Economic Injury Disaster Loan (EIDL) program is available to eligible small businesses, small agricultural cooperatives, and private nonprofits — including faith-based organizations — impacted by financial losses directly related to this disaster. The SBA is unable to provide disaster loans to agricultural producers, farmers, or ranchers, except for aquaculture enterprises.
EIDLs are for working capital needs caused by the disaster and are available even if the business did not suffer any physical damage. The loans may be used to pay fixed debts, payroll, accounts payable, and other bills which could not be paid due to the disaster.
“SBA loans help eligible small businesses and private nonprofits cover operating expenses after a disaster, which is crucial for their recovery,” said Chris Stallings, Associate Administrator of the Office of Disaster Recovery at SBA. “These loans not only help business owners get back on their feet but also play a key role in sustaining local economies in the aftermath of a disaster.”
The loan amount can be up to $2 million with interest rates are as low as 4% for businesses and 3.625% for private nonprofits, with terms up to 30 years. Interest does not begin to accrue, and payments are not due until 12 months from the date of the first loan disbursement. The SBA determines eligibility and sets loan amounts and terms based on each applicant’s financial condition.
To apply online, visit sba.gov/disaster. Applicants may also call the National Support Network Center at (866) SBA-HELP or email disastercustomerservice@sba.gov for more information on SBA disaster assistance. For people who are deaf, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability, please dial 7-1-1 to access telecommunications relay services.
The deadline to return economic injury applications is Dec. 4. However, after the deadline has passed, there is a 60-day grace period in which SBA will accept applications.
###
About the U.S. Small Business Administration
The U.S. Small Business Administration helps power the American dream of business ownership. As the only go-to resource and voice for small businesses backed by the strength of the federal government, SBA empowers entrepreneurs and small business owners with the resources and support they need to start, grow or expand their businesses, or recover from a declared disaster. It delivers services through an extensive network of SBA field offices and partnerships with public and private organizations. To learn more, visit www.sba.gov.

TULSA, Okla. – Three employees of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Oklahoma and a detective with the Bartlesville Police Department were among 183 Department of Justice employees recognized by Attorney General Todd Blanche and Executive Office for U.S. Attorneys (EOUSA) Director Francey Hakes at the 2026 Director’s Awards Ceremony held Oct. 28 in Washington, D.C. The annual event honored DOJ employees for outstanding service and achievement and recognized exceptional accomplishments by employees of U.S. Attorneys’ Offices nationwide.

"These awards reflect the extraordinary talent, professionalism, and dedication found throughout our office and community," said U.S. Attorney Christopher J. Nassar. "We are incredibly proud of Thomas, Alicia, Taelyn, and Detective Andrew Bailey for their accomplishments and grateful for their continued service to the Northern District of Oklahoma and the Department of Justice."

Superior Performance in Indian Country

Assistant United States Attorney Alicia Hockenbury and Victim Assistance Specialist Taelyn Langford were recognized with the Director's Award for Superior Performance in Indian Country, alongside the case agent, and Detective Andrew Bailey with Bartlesville Police Department whose critical investigative work was instrumental to the case.

This recognition stems from their outstanding efforts in United States v. Kaleb Smith , in which the defendant was convicted by a jury of Sexual Abuse of a Minor in Indian Country and two counts of Abusive Sexual Contact with a Minor in Indian Country. Court records established that Smith sexually abused two teenage victims, ages 13 and 14. Through the dedication and collaboration of the prosecution team, a sentence of 228 months of imprisonment was secured.

The work of Alicia, Taelyn, and Detective Bailey reflects the highest standards of public service and demonstrates an unwavering commitment to seeking justice for vulnerable victims. Their efforts have made a lasting impact on the lives of those they serve and on the communities they protect.

Excellence of an Appellate Assistant United States Attorney

Thomas Duncombe, Appellate Coordinator for the Northern District of Oklahoma, received the Director's Award for Excellence as an Appellate Assistant United States Attorney. His exceptional legal analysis, advocacy, and steadfast commitment to justice have strengthened the district and advanced the Department of Justice's mission. Thomas was recognized for his written and oral advocacy before the Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals, including his work in United States v. McCarthy . In that case, he successfully argued to the Tenth Circuit to reverse the dismissal of an indictment by demonstrating that the district court had erred in finding that the Controlled Substance Precursor Statutes did not apply to defendants who distributed unwashed poppy seeds while knowing their customers would use them to manufacture opiates. We are grateful for Thomas's leadership and the expertise he brings to every case.

Please join us in congratulating these award recipients on their well-deserved honors. Their achievements exemplify excellence in public service and reflect the strength and commitment of the entire Northern District of Oklahoma team.

EOUSA provides oversight, general executive assistance, and direction to the 94 United States Attorneys’ offices around the country. For more information on EOUSA and its mission, visit http://www.justice.gov/usao .

SAN JOSÉ, CA — Today, Congresswoman Zoe Lofgren (CA-18), Chair of the California Democratic Congressional Delegation, released the following statement after the Associated Press projected that Democrats have retaken the majority in the U.S. House of Representatives:
“I’m so proud of the millions of Americans who cast their votes over the last few weeks to make their voices heard. Regardless of who you voted for, the new Democratic majority in the House is committed to lowering your costs, protecting your healthcare, and defending your rights," said Rep. ICE arrests citizen of the Philippines for federal election fraud
TULSA, Okla. — On Oct. 28, ICE arrested Maria Elenor Lopez Rios, a citizen of the Philippines who is also a U.S. lawful permanent resident. Her arrest was the culmination of an investigation that alleges she committed federal election fraud, made false citizenship claims and made a false statement in voter registration.
In 2022, Rios registered to vote by falsely claiming U.S. citizenship under oath, voted in the November 2022 federal election, and was subsequently arrested while returning home from work while her naturalization application was pending.
“Every illegal vote undermines the integrity of our elections and the rights of Americans who are legally entitled to cast a ballot,” said ICE Assistant Director for Public Affairs Micah Bock. “American citizens have the exclusive right to choose their leaders, and we are here to help protect that right. Anyone who illegally casts a ballot or lies about their citizenship to influence an election must be held accountable.”
This investigation reflects HSI Tulsa’s continued commitment to protecting the integrity of the nation’s electoral process through coordination with federal, state and local law enforcement partners.
Under President Trump, ICE is focused on its core mission: enforcing immigration law and protecting the American people.
You can report crimes, including voter fraud, by calling (866) DHS-2-ICE (3472423) or completing the online tip form.
Learn more about ICE’s public safety mission on X, Facebook, Instagram, Threads, Bluesky and Truth Social.
title: ICE arrests citizen of the Philippines for federal election fraud

Joint Base Andrews marked a historic milestone Nov. 2, with the arrival of the first HH-60W Jolly Green II, bringing a new generation of Air Force rotary-wing capabilities to the nation’s capital for the first time in 60 years.
"Our leaders recognized the need for change and decided to rapidly modernize the equipment that we use to protect our nation,” said Col. Karl W. Seekamp, 316th Wing and installation commander. “...this critical mission deserves the modern capability and safety upgrades that are available today.”
With a larger airframe and bigger fuel capacity, the Jolly Green II can fly faster and farther, extending the operational reach of the Air Force’s response in times of crisis and contingency. It also provides nearly three times the airlift capability of the UH-1N.
The arrival of the Jolly Green II represents a new chapter in the Air Force's rotary-wing history, building on a legacy established by the 1st Helicopter Squadron, which served as the Air Force's only rotary-wing unit in the National Capital Region for six decades.
The aircraft will first be assigned to the 5th Helicopter Squadron, which is charged with training the force and establishing the new fleet, while the 1st HS will fly the UH-1N to provide continuous support of Andrews’ 24/7 no-fail national security mission.
Since 1969, the 1st HS has conducted immediate-response contingency operations in support of critical national security requirements while maintaining a rigorous training schedule to ensure mission readiness. The squadron has flown the UH-1N Huey since 1971, and three of the aircraft that flew during the Vietnam War remain in service today.
That history is an important part of the transition to the Jolly Green II.
“It is important that we honor the legacy of what the Huey has done for safety and operations as a whole,” noted Lt. Col. Jonathan Bonilla, 5th HS commander. “We must remember this while we, as an Air Force, continue to look into the future.”
While the Huey has a storied history of saving lives through its light-lift capabilities, particularly during the Vietnam War, the arrival of the HH-60W represents an investment in modernizing the Andrews’ rotary-wing capabilities and providing a more versatile aircraft to meet evolving operational requirements.
"I think the [HH-60] Whiskey is absolutely the right call," said Capt. Joshua Lemon, 316th Operations Group executive officer and UH-1N instructor pilot, who will be part of the first class of aircrew transitioning to the new aircraft. "It is inherently a joint airframe, meaning that almost any branch or agency in the area can call on us and we can lend a hand, or an aircraft. It makes us part of a bigger team.” 
Although rotary-wing aircraft represent a small but vital part of the Air Force, their maneuverability and ability to operate in areas inaccessible to many fixed-wing aircraft make them essential to a wide range of missions. The arrival of the Jolly Green II ensures JB Andrews' long-term ability to respond to national security requirements across the nation’s capital.
Introducing a new airframe also strengthens the Wing’s readiness for future mission needs and modernizes a crucial fleet of aircraft that supports U.S. senior leaders. Beginning in 2027, designated classes of Airmen from JB Andrews’ helicopter squadrons will receive familiarization training from certified Sikorsky aircrews. Following the course, select Airmen will be qualified to instruct their fellow crewmembers in HH-60W safety and familiarization procedures. As each class graduates, both the 1st and 5th HS will have a growing team of aircrew who can fly both the HH-60W and the UH-1N, enabling 24/7 continuous support.
As the Jolly Green II takes its place on the JB Andrews flightline, it carries forward a mission shaped by decades of service. The Huey's legacy remains an enduring part of that history, while the arrival of the HH-60W ensures the installation is equipped to meet the demands of the future.
title: First HH-60W arrives at JB Andrews, marking new era for Air Force rotary-wing operations

Release Number 9320-26
CFTC Secures Court Order Directing Texas Man and His Company to Pay Over $13 Million in Commodities Fraud
November 03, 2026
WASHINGTON — The Commodity Futures Trading Commission today announced the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas entered a default judgment against defendants Walter Dunning Larrick III and Cambridge Financial Advisors LLC for their participation in a commodities fraud scheme.
In entering the default judgment, the court found the defendants fraudulently solicited and misappropriated more than $3 million from participants.
The court found the defendants falsely represented they would use participant funds to trade futures and options, including those involving natural gas, oil, and gold; made material misrepresentations and omissions about the profitability of commodity trading with them; and issued false account statements to conceal their misconduct.
The court further found the defendants misappropriated participant funds by making payments to existing participants in a manner akin to a Ponzi scheme, paying Larrick’s personal expenses, and sending funds to offshore accounts in Costa Rica.
The court ordered the defendants to pay a $9,767,625 civil monetary penalty and $3,255,875 in restitution. It also permanently enjoined them from further violations of the Commodity Exchange Act and Commission regulations, as charged, and imposed permanent trading and registration bans.
The default judgment resolves all claims in the CFTC’s 2023 complaint. [See CFTC Press Release No. 8768-23.]
-CFTC-
title: CFTC Secures Court Order Directing Texas Man and His Company to Pay Over $13 Million in Commodities Fraud

ICE HSI New Jersey arrests Jamaican national accused of voting illegally over 22-year span
WASHINGTON — ICE’s Homeland Security Investigations New Jersey arrested Antonio Mitchell Oct. 28 for illegally voting in a range of elections between 2000 and 2022. Mitchell, a 54-year-old lawful permanent resident from Jamaica, has arrests for burglary, resisting arrest, and possession of marijuana for sale. These charges were ultimately dropped.
“Voting in American elections is a right reserved for eligible voters,” said ICE Assistant Director of Public Affairs Micah Bock. “Those who knowingly violate federal election laws should understand that their actions carry serious consequences. ICE cannot ignore suspected federal crimes simply because they involve elections. The law applies to everyone, and we intend to enforce it.”
According to investigators, Mitchell registered to vote and participated in multiple federal primary and general elections over a 22-year span, despite being ineligible because he was not a U.S. citizen.
In January 2025, Mitchell submitted a naturalization application in which he allegedly falsely stated he had never registered to vote or voted in a federal, state or local election. Those statements became part of a joint investigation involving HSI, the FBI and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.
Federal law generally prohibits noncitizens, including lawful permanent residents, from voting in elections for federal office. Knowingly making materially false statements during the naturalization process carries criminal penalties.
title: ICE HSI New Jersey arrests Jamaican national accused of voting illegally over 22-year span

ABERDEEN PROVING GROUND, Md. — Two Soldiers representing the Defense Health Agency-Public Health overcame training injuries, postpartum recovery hurdles, and a rain-soaked course to complete the 42nd Annual Army 10-Miler, with one securing the top finishing spot for the Aberdeen Proving Ground garrison team.
Army Captain Francesca Metzler, an audiologist with the Clinical Public Health and Epidemiology Directorate, and Army Staff Sgt. Lewis A. Simuel II, the noncommissioned officer in charge of the Deployed Health Services Division, proved that team motivation across officer and NCO ranks translates directly from the laboratory to the pavement.
Partners in the Lab, Partners on the Pavement
For Metzler and Simuel, the road to the starting line began long before race day. As members of the APG team, they participated in early-morning group workouts that built camaraderie and helped them overcome the challenges of race preparation.
“Having colleagues from DHA-PH made the experience even more meaningful,” said Metzler. “The APG team spent many early mornings training together.”
Overcoming the odds: Injury and postpartum milestones
Neither runner had an easy path to the race. For Simuel, a habitual runner, the opportunity to join the APG 10-Miler team came up just days before the tryouts, right as he was recovering from a severe iliotibial, or IT, band injury that had sidelined him for nearly two months.
“My training in all honesty was not optimal,” said Simuel. “I was coming off an IT band injury where I wasn’t able to run for seven weeks and had just started running again when the APG tryouts were happening. I was only running around 14 to 18 miles per week, which is half of what I was doing prior to my injury.”
For Metzler, the race represented a deeply personal milestone in her military career and life postpartum.
“My goal was to challenge myself, celebrate how far I had come, and remind myself that becoming a mother doesn’t mean losing the parts of yourself that existed before motherhood,” said Metzler. “Training while balancing military responsibilities and motherhood has been an exercise in time management and flexibility. Some workouts required early mornings, while others had to fit into whatever time was available, most involved pushing [my daughter] Mackenzie in the stroller.”
Their dedication paid off on race day, where Metzler crossed the line in 1:13:02, securing her place as the top female finisher for the APG garrison team.
“Crossing the finish line was a moment to reflect on everything it took to get there,” said Metzler. “As an Army audiologist, I take pride in serving our Soldiers and supporting the mission. I hope my participation also reminds other parents, especially mothers, that their personal goals and identities still matter.”
Pushing through the crux: Rocks and rain
When race day arrived, the weather was far from ideal. Heavy rain threatened to dampen spirits, but both Soldiers leaned on their military training to push through the toughest miles.
For Simuel, the physical test came in the form of a literal obstacle inside his shoe.
“The hardest moment of the race was mile eight,” said Simuel. “For some context, I had a small rock in my shoe for half the race up to this point. I didn’t stop because I knew it would throw me off my pace.”
Despite this obstacle in his shoe, Simuel wanted to give it his all.
“I really started to feel the pain in my feet, and I was also experiencing heavy fatigue,” said Simuel. “All I could do is take it one mile at a time. I would keep telling myself, ‘I can go one more mile’ each time I wanted to stop.”
Metzler chose to use the wet conditions as a mental catalyst rather than a setback.
“The toughest part of this year’s race was actually the weather—rain,” said Metzler. “I continually reminded myself that I couldn’t control the weather, only how I responded to it. I reminded myself how much I loved running in the rain early on in my career. I embraced the suck and kept moving!”
Advice for the ranks
Both competitors hope their journey inspires other junior enlisted, NCOs, and officers to take on the challenge next year.
“Do it!” Metzler urged. “You don’t have to be the fastest runner or the most experienced athlete to run the Army 10-Miler. You just have to be willing to set a goal and work toward it.”
Simuel emphasized the importance of disciplined training.
“To anyone running next year, I would say to prepare well,” said Simuel. “Run and do speed and tempo work weekly. Monitor your recovery and sleep. Ensure you’re eating enough and that 80% of your runs are easy.”
The Defense Health Agency is a Combat Support Agency, serving as a force multiplier for the joint services by optimizing lethality through warfighter medical readiness.

title: Soldiers push through grit, rain during Army 10-Miler

KANSAS CITY, Mo. – Two Kansas City, Kan., men were charged in an eighteen-count indictment by a federal grand jury for their roles in an early morning March 25, 2026, violent crime spree involving several victims.

Following their initial appearances in federal court, Michael T. Lomax, 57, and Mario O. Lomax, 19, were charged with multiple federal crimes including: conspiracy to commit Hobbs Act Robbery, conspiracy to commit kidnapping, kidnapping, Hobbs Act Robbery, discharging/brandishing/using firearms during and in relation to crimes of violence, carjacking, and other related offenses. Both men had initially been charged in Jackson County, Missouri Circuit Court. That case was dismissed in favor of federal charges.

According to the probable cause statement, two men wearing dark clothing, facemasks, and armed with handguns stormed into the house of 63-year-old Victim #1 at 6:20 a.m. Victim #1 was ordered on the floor at gunpoint to direct the men to any money or guns inside the residence. Victim #1 was then forced around their home at gunpoint, with the defendants discharging their firearms at least once for their compliance. Victim #1 was forced into their basement and told to remain there while they fled the residence. The defendants stole U.S. Currency, firearms, Victim #1’s car keys, and their cell phone.

While fleeing the area, the defendants came upon a Chevy Silverado, sitting in the driveway of a home, with the engine idling. The adult owner of the Silverado, Victim #3, was outside of the vehicle assisting one of their children. Sitting in the backseat of the Silverado was their other child, a juvenile, Victim #2. The two defendants got into the front driver and passenger seats of the vehicle, noticed the child in the backseat, then pointed their handguns at them while telling the child to get out of the vehicle. Victim #2 got out of the vehicle and the defendants fled in the Silverado. In taking the Silverado, the defendants also stole Victim #3’s cell phones, bag, and medication.

Using surveillance video, witness statements, witness identification, GPS, and numerous other investigative tools, Michael T. Lomax and Mario O. Lomax were identified as the assailants from the morning of March 25, 2026.

The charges contained in the indictment are simply accusations, and not evidence of guilt. Evidence supporting the charges must be presented to a federal trial jury, whose duty is to determine guilt or innocence.

Under federal statutes, both Michael T. Lomax and Mario O. Lomax are currently subject to a minimum sentence of 24 years imprisonment, with a maximum sentence of up to life in federal prison without parole. The minimum and maximum statutory sentences are prescribed by Congress and are provided here for informational purposes only.

This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Jeffrey Q. McCarther and Kelly Collins. It was investigated by the Kansas City, Missouri Police Department.

Project Safe Neighborhoods

This case is part of Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN), a program bringing together all levels of law enforcement and the communities they serve to reduce violent crime and gun violence, and to make our neighborhoods safer for everyone. On May 26, 2021, the Department launched a violent crime reduction strategy strengthening PSN based on these core principles: fostering trust and legitimacy in our communities, supporting community-based organizations that help prevent violence from occurring in the first place, setting focused and strategic enforcement priorities, and measuring the results.
title: Grandfather and Grandson Charged in Early Morning Armed Robbery, Kidnapping, Carjacking Crime Spree

U.S. Special Operations Forces (SOF) are active duty and reserve components of the military services that are designated as SOF by the Secretary of Defense, who is using "Secretary of War" as a "secondary title" under Executive Order (EO) 14347, dated September 5, 2025. SOF are selected, organized, trained, and equipped to conduct and support special operations. Special operations frequently require unique modes of employment, tactics, techniques, procedures, and equipment. SOF often conduct special operations in hostile, politically, and/or diplomatically sensitive environments. Special operations are characterized by one or more of the following: being time-sensitive and/or clandestine, occurring in low-visibility conditions, happening with or through indigenous forces, requiring regional orientation and cultural expertise, or carrying a high degree of risk. SOF's core activities are
SOF operational personnel (often referred to as "operators") undergo a rigorous screening and selection process resulting in a low selection rate. After selection, they receive mission-specific training to instill proficiency in a variety of special operations skills. Selected operators have regional, cultural, and linguistic expertise. Some SOF personnel require highly technical and advanced training for anticipated missions, such as Military Freefall parachute training, Combat Diver training, and Sniper training.
In 1986, Congress, concerned about the status of SOF within overall U.S. defense planning and budgeting, enacted legislation to strengthen special operations' position within the defense community and to strengthen interoperability among the branches of U.S. SOF. The National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for Fiscal Year 1987 (P.L. 99-661) established an Assistant Secretary of Defense for Special Operations and Low Intensity Conflict (ASD (SOLIC)) and a new four-star command to prepare SOF to carry out assigned missions and, if directed by the President or Secretary of Defense, to plan for and conduct special operations.
The ASD (SOLIC), who is using Assistant Secretary of War for Special Operations and Low Intensity Conflict as a secondary title under EO 14347, is the principal civilian advisor to the Secretary of Defense on special operations and low-intensity conflict matters. The ASD (SOLIC) has, as their principal duty, overall supervision (to include oversight of policy and resources) of special operations and low-intensity conflict activities. The ASD (SOLIC) falls under and reports to the Under Secretary of Defense for Policy. Congress, wanting the ASD (SOLIC) to exercise greater oversight of U.S. Special Operations Command (USSOCOM), enacted Section 922 of the FY2017 NDAA (P.L. 114-328) to strengthen and provide resources for the ASD (SOLIC), as originally intended, to assume Service Secretary-like authorities.
Activated on April 16, 1987, and headquartered at MacDill Air Force Base in Tampa, FL, USSOCOM is the unified Combatant Command responsible for organizing, training, and equipping all U.S. SOF units. As of 2026, Headquarters, USSOCOM, consists of around 3,500 military and civilian personnel, and overall, the command has approximately 70,000 personnel assigned to its headquarters, service components, and sub-unified commands. The USSOCOM commander is a four-star general from any service who reports directly to the Secretary of Defense. After the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, USSOCOM's responsibilities were expanded in the 2004 Unified Command Plan, assigning USSOCOM responsibility for coordinating Department of Defense plans against global terrorism and conducting global operations as directed. USSOCOM has also been assigned the roles coordinating authority over countering violent extremist operations and countering weapons of mass destruction operations.
On December 1, 1989, USASOC was established at Fort Bragg, NC, as a major Army command to enhance the readiness of Army SOF active duty and reserve components. With an allocated strength of approximately 36,000 personnel, USASOC consists of Special Forces (Green Berets), Rangers, Special Operations Aviators, Civil Affairs Soldiers, Psychological Operations Soldiers, training cadre, and Sustainment Soldiers. USASOC has three major subordinate commands: the 1st Special Forces Command (Airborne), U.S. Army John F. Kennedy Special Warfare Center and School, and the U.S. Army Special Operations Aviation Command.
Established April 16, 1987, and based in Coronado, CA, the NSWC is responsible for organizing training and equipping five Naval Special Warfare Groups, the Naval Special Warfare Center, and the Development Group (DEVGRU). With approximately 11,000 personnel, the NSWC consists of Sea, Air, Land operators (SEALs), Special Warfare Combatant-Craft Crewmen (SWCC), and Combat Support and Combat Service Support personnel.
Established May 22, 1990, with its headquarters at Hurlburt Field, FL, AFSOC is responsible for organizing, training, and equipping five Active Component Special Operations Wings (SOWs), three Reserve Component SOWs, and the Air Force Special Operations Air Warfare Center. AFSOC consists of about 17,000 personnel, comprising Special Operations Aviators, Air Commandos, Special Tactics Airmen, and Support Air Commandos.
Headquartered in Camp Lejeune, NC, and established February 24, 2006, MARSOC consists of the Marine Raider Regiment, the Marine Raider Group, and the Marine Raider Training School. MARSOC's almost 3,500 personnel consist of Marine Raiders, Marine Raider Officers, Special Operations Independent Duty Corpsmen, Special Operations Capabilities Specialists, and Combat Service Support Specialists.
U.S. SOF frequently operate with conventional forces of the Joint Force. SOF theater-level command and control (C2) responsibilities are vested in TSOCs. TSOCs are special operational headquarters elements designed to support the National Command Authority, the Joint Force, and the Global Combatant Commands' special operations logistics, planning, and operational command and control requirements. Following are the current TSOCs.
Established October 22, 1980, JSOC is a sub-unified command of USSOCOM. JSOC "prepares assigned, attached and augmented forces and, when directed, conducts special operations against threats to protect the homeland and U.S. interests abroad."
SREC is responsible for
[s]ynchronizing, integrating, and enabling special reconnaissance (SR) capabilities across the joint force. It serves as a [C2] body that focuses on leveraging and optimizing SR assets, which include technical, environmental, and human intelligence collection, to support special operations. The command works to improve the network architecture, data sharing, and collaboration between special reconnaissance units and other elements of the joint force to enhance overall mission effectiveness.

Prescription drug prices are plummeting for the first time in decades under the leadership of President Donald J. Trump — delivering real, measurable relief to millions of Americans. In City Journal, Dr. Joel Zinberg explains why this is a major accomplishment:
“Yet few Americans realize that drug prices—a major complaint—are actually falling.
The Consumer Price Index for prescription drugs has either fallen or been flat every month of 2026. The latest inflation data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics show that while the overall CPI rose 3.7 percent year to year, prescription drug prices fell 4.5 percent—the largest year-over-year decline since 1963—and nonprescription prices fell 0.9 percent…
The Trump administration has pursued multiple policies to bring drug prices down. TrumpRx, launched in February 2026, provides cash-paying patients with large discounts on over 800 drugs, including many of the most popular medicines. Chief among these are the GLP-1 weight-loss drugs. U.S. prescription drug spending surged in 2025, driven by increased utilization of the GLP-1s tirzepatide and semaglutide at approximately $60 billion each. Consumers’ use of the TrumpRx discounts—particularly for GLP-1s—has been a major factor in lowering prescription prices throughout 2026.
Agreements with pharmaceutical companies Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk reduce the cost of GLP-1 medications for government programs and TrumpRx while expanding Medicare coverage for obesity with a $50 monthly copay. TrumpRx prices are most valuable to uninsured patients and those whose private plans do not cover GLP-1s to treat obesity. (Less than a third of employer-provided health plans cover GLP-1s for obesity.) By providing low, transparent prices to consumers, these programs create downward pressure on drug prices in all insurance plans.”
Read the full article in City Journal here.
title: ICYMI: Drug Prices Are Falling at the Fastest Rate in Over 60 Years Under President Trump

BIRMINGHAM, Ala. – A convicted felon has been sentenced for illegal possession of multiple firearms, announced U.S. Attorney Phillip W. Williams Jr.

U.S. District Court Judge Anna M. Manasco sentenced Timothy Shane Postell, 40, of Bessemer, Alabama, to 130 months in prison. Postell pleaded guilty to being a felon in possession of a firearm in two separate and unrelated cases.

According to the plea agreements, Postell illegally possessed firearms on two separate occasions.

On April 16, 2022, an officer with the Leeds Police Department responded to a call at a retail store in Leeds. The officer arrived on the scene and found a female and Postell on a couch, and both appeared to be under the influence of narcotics. They were arrested for public intoxication. The officer searched Postell and recovered a stolen pair of tennis shoes, narcotics, and a loaded SCCY 9mm pistol.

On February 7, 2026, an officer with the Hueytown Police Department initiated a traffic stop on a vehicle driven by Postell. As the officer approached the vehicle, Postell fled the scene recklessly—speeding and passing vehicles with oncoming traffic and in no-passing zones. The pursuit continued until Postell stopped at the end of a dirt road. Postell exited the vehicle and ran. An officer deployed his taser with no effect but eventually got close enough to tackle Postell and handcuff him. The officer searched Postell and recovered a loaded Canik 9mm pistol from one of Postell’s inside jacket pockets and a loaded Glock 10mm pistol from the other inside jacket pocket. During a search of Postell’s vehicle, officers recovered a loaded Marlin .22 rifle, body armor plates, methamphetamine, and drug paraphernalia.

“Keeping firearms out of the hands of convicted felons is critical in protecting our communities,” said U.S. Attorney Williams. “This defendant repeatedly demonstrated disregard for the law. This 130-month sentence sends a clear message that illegal firearm possession by repeat offenders will have serious consequences. We are grateful to our law enforcement partners for their dedication and continued efforts to keep our communities safe.”

“ATF prioritizes public safety and is committed to bringing individuals who unlawfully possess firearms to justice” said ATF Special Agent in Charge James VanVliet. “Mr. Postell, a four-time convicted felon, showed a pattern of criminal behavior in this case, illegally possessing firearms in multiple incidents. ATF will continue to work with our state and local law enforcement partners to make our communities safe by pursuing, apprehending, and prosecuting such individuals who demonstrate a propensity for lawlessness and recklessness.”

Postell is prohibited from possessing firearms because of his four prior felony convictions that span from 2007 to 2021. Postell was convicted in the Superior Court of Paulding County, Georgia in February 2007, of Robbery by Intimidation, Theft by Taking, and Aggravated Assault and in September 2013, of Possession of Cocaine; in the Circuit Court of Jefferson County, Alabama in May 2014 for Robbery, Second Degree; and in the District Court of Shelby County, Alabama in February 2021, of Burglary, Third Degree.

The ATF investigated the case along with the Leeds Police Department and Hueytown Police Department. Assistant United States Attorney Darius C. Greene prosecuted the case.
title: Four-Time Convicted Felon Sentenced to More than 10 Years in Prison for Illegal Possession of Multiple Firearms

WASHINGTON – The United States Attorney for the District of Columbia announced today that Strand Book Store, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,482,560 because the New York City bookstore violated the False Claims Act by improperly applying for and receiving a second draw loan under the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) for which it was not eligible. Strand was ineligible because Senator Ron Wyden’s wife was the owner.

“The Paycheck Protection Program was created to save American jobs, not to enrich those who aren’t eligible for taxpayer-funded relief, especially the wife of a U.S. Senator,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “Strand Book Store, owned by Nancy Bass Wyden, wife of U.S. Senator Ron Wyden, received $932,350 in second draw PPP funds despite a federal law barring businesses controlled by a member of Congress or their spouse from receiving those loans. Our Fraud and Asset Recovery Division will expose this abuse, pursue those who exploit taxpayer dollars, and hold them accountable. No one gets a pass when it comes to defrauding the American taxpayer.”

“The Paycheck Protection Program was created to save American jobs, not to enrich those who aren’t eligible for taxpayer-funded relief, especially the wife of a U.S. Senator,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “Strand Book Store, owned by Nancy Bass Wyden, wife of U.S. Senator Ron Wyden, received $932,350 in second draw PPP funds despite a federal law barring businesses controlled by a member of Congress or their spouse from receiving those loans. Our Fraud and Asset Recovery Division will expose this abuse, pursue those who exploit taxpayer dollars, and hold them accountable. No one gets a pass when it comes to defrauding the American taxpayer.”

When Congress enacted the Coronavirus, Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act in March 2020, it authorized forgivable PPP loans to eligible small businesses and nonprofit organizations for job retention and certain other expenses. The PPP loan program was administered by the Small Business Administration. In the Economic Aid to Hard-Hit Small Businesses, Nonprofits, and Venues Act enacted in December 2020, Congress provided additional funding for PPP loans and allowed eligible entities to apply for a “second draw” of PPP funding. The Economic Aid Act included a prohibition against businesses obtaining second draw PPP funds if a member of Congress or their spouse directly or indirectly held a controlling interest in the PPP loan applicant.

In February 2021, Strand applied for a second draw PPP loan in the amount of $932,350. At the time, the controlling owner of Strand was Nancy Bass Wyden, the wife of U.S. Senator Ron Wyden. On behalf of Strand, Ms. Wyden made a number of certifications as part of the loan application, including that the spouse of a Member of Congress does not directly or indirectly hold a controlling interest in the applicant. Ms. Wyden’s certification was knowingly and materially false and Strand was not eligible for the second draw loan it received.

The settlement resolves claims brought under the qui tam or whistleblower provisions of the False Claims Act. Under these provisions, a private party can file an action on behalf of the United States and receive a portion of the recovery. The qui tam complaint was filed by a corporate Relator Blockquote Inc. and is captioned U.S. ex rel. Blockquote Inc. v. Strand Book Store, Inc., Civ. No. 25-3609 (D.D.C.) . Blockquote Inc. will receive a total share of approximately $148,256 in connection with the settlement.

The civil settlement resulted from an investigation by Assistant United States Attorney Sean M. Tepe with the support of attorney Christopher J. McClintock of SBA’s Office of the General Counsel. This is the second recovery on behalf of the United States since U.S. Attorney Pirro announced the creation of the Fraud and Asset Recovery Division, headed by Assistant U.S. Attorney Dan Schiffer.

Tips and complaint regarding potential fraud affecting COVID-19 government relief programs can be reported by calling the Department of Justice’s National Center for Disaster Fraud (NCDF) Hotline at (866) 720-5721 or by submitting a NCDF Web Complaint form at https://www.justice.gov/disaster-fraud/ncdf-disaster-complaint-form .

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

The claims resolved by the civil settlement are allegations only, and there has been no determination of liability.

WASHINGTON – One of the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) most important missions is ensuring election integrity, supporting free and fair elections, and protecting the right to vote for U.S. citizens across the United States. The DOJ has sent election monitors in support of this mission since the enactment of the Voting Rights Act in 1965 across all Administrations.

Today, the DOJ will further this mission by engaging in its largest monitoring effort in history—with approximately 1,000 election monitors and observers deployed, and, for the first time, in all 50 states. The effort is coordinated by the Civil Rights Division. Monitors will include personnel from the Division, other DOJ divisions/components, U.S. Attorney’s Offices and federal observers from the Office of Personnel Management. Throughout Election Day, Division personnel will maintain contact with state and local election officials.

“Election integrity has been one of the top priorities for this Administration and this Division,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Civil Rights Division at the Department of Justice. “I am very proud we are deploying the largest monitoring effort in DOJ history, and pursuing transparency for elections in an assertive and nondiscriminatory manner.”

Election monitors will be checking for compliance with the federal voting rights statutes that fall within the jurisdiction of the Division. The Division’s Voting Section enforces the civil provisions of federal statutes that protect the right to vote, including the Voting Rights Act, National Voter Registration Act, Help America Vote Act, Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act, and Civil Rights Acts.

The Division’s Disability Rights Section enforces the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) to ensure that persons with disabilities have a full and equal opportunity to vote. The Division’s Criminal Section enforces federal criminal statutes that prohibit voter intimidation and voter suppression based on race, color, national origin, or religion.

Throughout the day and week, Division personnel will be available to receive questions and complaints from the public related to federal voting rights laws. If you have a question or complaint, please call our election issues hotline at 1-800-253-3931, email us at VEM@usdoj.gov , or submit a complaint through our website at www.civilrights.justice.gov/report .

Individuals with questions or complaints related to the ADA may call the Division’s toll-free ADA information hotline at 1-800-514-0301 or 1-833-610-1264 (TTY) or submit a complaint through our ADA website at www.ada.gov .

Complaints related to any disruptions at a polling place should always be reported to local election officials (including officials based in the polling place). Complaints related to violence, threats of violence or intimidation at a polling place should be reported immediately to local police authorities by calling 911. These complaints should also be reported to the department after local authorities have been contacted.

To learn more about what the DOJ and the Civil Rights Division has done historically to protect the vote and ensure free and fair elections, go to www.civilrights.justice.gov/electionintegrity .

BOSTON – A Mexican national unlawfully residing in Jamaica Plain, Mass. pleaded guilty to unlawfully reentering the United States after deportation.

Carlos Altunar-Rueda, 33, pleaded guilty to a one count indictment. U.S. District Court Leo T. Sorokin scheduled sentencing for Jan. 27, 2027. Altunar-Rueda was indicted by a federal grand jury in June 2026. In January 2026, he was charged by criminal complaint with the same offense.

Altunar-Rueda is a citizen of Mexico who was deported from the United States in 2013 and again in 2019. In May 2018 , he was convicted in federal court in Massachusetts for unlawful reentry of a deported alien. In November 2015, he was convicted in New York state court for sexual abuse in the 3rd degree, sexual abuse in the 2nd degree and forcible touching. The charge of unlawful reentry of a deported alien provides for a sentence of up to 10 years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. The defendant is subject to deportation upon completion of any sentence imposed. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley and David T. Wesling, Acting Field Office Director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Enforcement and Removal Operations in Boston made the announcement. Assistant U.S. Attorney Suzanne Sullivan Jacobus of the Major Crimes Unit is prosecuting the case.
title: Illegal Alien from Mexico Pleads Guilty to Illegal Reentry

Tennessee Prison Escapee Captured in Missouri
For immediate release
Kansas City, MO – Around 12:00 p.m. on November 3, 2026, Jacob Morley was captured in Norborne, Missouri near Kansas City by federal, state and local law enforcement.
The U.S. Marshals Service (USMS) in the Western District of Tennessee was requested by the Tennessee Department of Correction to assist in the search after Morley escaped from the Northwestern Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, Tennessee on the night of October 25, 2026.
Morley was serving a life sentence after being convicted of First-Degree Murder.
“Over the past nine days, the U.S. Marshals Service, alongside our partners, was engaged in a relentless pursuit of prison escapee, Jacob Morley, which ended today with his capture in Missouri,” said Tyreece Miller, U.S. Marshal for the Western District of Tennessee. “We are glad to assist in his return back to the Tennessee Department of Correction.”
The following USMS Offices assisted in the investigation: Eastern Tennessee, Kansas, Missouri, Wisconsin, Ohio, South Carolina, North Carolina, and Southern Illinois.
Other federal agencies who assisted: Federal Bureau of Investigation, Homeland Security Investigations.
The following state and local agencies in Tennessee assisted: Tennessee Department of Correction, Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, Tennessee Highway Patrol, Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency, Tiptonville Police Department, Lake County Sheriff’s Office, Bartlett Police Department, Madison County Fire Department, Williamson County Sheriff’s Office, Obion County Sheriff’s Office, Dyer County Sheriff’s Office.
Law enforcement agencies outside of Tennessee who assisted: Marion, Illinois Police Department, Williamson County, Illinois Sheriff’s Office; Illinois State Police; Kentucky State Police; Independence, Missouri Police Department; Kansas City, Missouri Police Department; Carroll County, Missouri Sheriff’s Office; Missouri State Police, and the Missouri Career Criminal Unit.

PORTLAND, Ore.— U.S. Attorney Scott E. Bradford announced today that Andy Robert Perovici , 36, of Portland, has pleaded guilty to federal charges for his role in a multi‑state scheme that targeted public assistance recipients and caused more than $550,000 in losses in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) benefits in Oregon and Washington.

“Public assistance benefits are a lifeline for families who rely on them,” said U.S. Attorney Scott E. Bradford. “Stealing from these programs harms some of the most vulnerable members of our communities. Today’s guilty plea reflects our commitment to holding accountable those who exploit federal benefits systems for personal gain.”

According to court documents, between April 2025 and November 2025, Perovici and his coconspirators obtained stolen SNAP and EBT card numbers and PINs and used this information to withdraw cash, purchase goods, and access benefits without authorization.

Investigators determined that on multiple occasions, including August 1 and September 1, 2025, Perovici used stolen EBT account information to make fraudulent withdrawals and purchases totaling thousands of dollars. He also possessed and trafficked device‑making equipment, including skimming devices and other hardware used to capture and clone EBT card data. Skimming devices were installed at retail locations in Portland, Tigard, Lake Oswego, and Salem, Oregon.

A forensic review of electronic devices seized from Perovici revealed EBT account information and PINs associated with hundreds of SNAP and TANF recipients . The cumulative value of the compromised accounts was approximately $554,215.

Perovici pleaded guilty to Conspiracy to Defraud the United States , Unauthorized Use of Access Devices , and Aggravated Identity Theft . The Aggravated Identity Theft charge carries a mandatory two‑year prison term that must run consecutive to any other sentence imposed.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Office of Inspector General is investigating the case with assistance from federal and state partners. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Geoffrey A. Barrow and Nicholas D. Meyers are prosecuting the case.
title: Portland Man Pleads Guilty to Federal Conspiracy, Access Device Fraud and Aggravated Identity Theft Related to SNAP EBT Skimming Scheme

Representative Min and Senator Welch Demand Answers from Former Trump Attorney Alina Habba-Mildon on Influence over President’s Pardon of Corrupt Venezuelan Banker Julio Herrera Velutini
Washington, DC. — U.S. Representative Dave Min (D-CA-47), Member of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform and Chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus’ Anti-Corruption Task Force and U.S. Senator Peter Welch (D-Vt.), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, are demanding answers from former Senior Adviser to the Attorney General Alina Mildon on her reported role in President Trump’s decision to grant Julio Herrera Velutini—who pleaded guilty to violating U.S. campaign finance laws—a full presidential pardon. The letters come as President Trump criticized his former attorney’s $50 million agreement with Mr. Herrera as “totally obnoxious and outrageous,” and “not acceptable.”
In their letters, the lawmakers express concern that the timing of Ms. Habba-Mildon’s hiring and Mr. Herrera’s daughter’s contribution to MAGA Inc. raise questions about whether improper considerations, including quid pro quo or “pay-to-play” dynamics, may have affected President Trump’s decision to pardon him. These letters are part of a broader bicameral investigation led by Representative Min and Senator Welch into potential corruption surrounding President Trump’s decisions to grant presidential pardons.
The lawmakers write: “Article II, Section 2, Clause 1 of the U.S. Constitution authorizes the President to ‘grant Reprieves and Pardons for Offenses against the United States, except in Cases of Impeachment.’ The U.S. Supreme Court has characterized executive clemency as ‘an act of grace’ exercised for the ‘public welfare.’ President Trump’s use of this authority appears to deviate from this traditional purpose. Congress has a compelling interest in ensuring that the constitutional pardon power is exercised with fairness and transparency. Given these circumstances, we are seeking additional information to better understand the extent to which influence and access may have overridden the standard pardon review process.”
In August 2022, Mr. Herrera was criminally charged with providing $300,000 to a super political action committee (PAC) in violation of a campaign finance law barring contributions or donations by foreign nationals to U.S. federal, state, or local elections. Mr. Herrera financially supported the reelection campaign of Puerto Rico’s governor in exchange for her pledge to remove a top banking regulator who had scrutinized one of Mr. Herrera’s banks.
According to public reporting, Ms. Mildon entered into an employment agreement with Mr. Herrera’s family in late 2025, while she was serving as an adviser at the Justice Department. She also previously served as President Trump’s personal lawyer and as the Acting U.S. Attorney for New Jersey. In the hiring contract, Mr. Velutini’s family agreed to pay her $50 million over four years to be general counsel at Concord Partners, a company set up by Mr. Velutini’s daughter days before she signed the contract. Ms. Mildon finalized the deal with Concord Partners while she was still serving at the Justice Department.
Ms. Mildon then began working for Concord Partners on January 1, 2026, while serving as a senior adviser to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi, overseeing U.S. attorneys. Two weeks later, Mr. Herrera received a pardon on January 15, 2026. Since President Trump’s election in November 2024, his 27-year-old daughter, a self-employed financial consultant, also donated $3.5 million to MAGA Inc., a Trump-supporting super PAC.
Read and download the lawmakers’ full letters to Alina Habba-Mildon and Julio Herrera Velutini.
In May, Senator Welch and Rep. Min sent letters to 17 individuals who received pardons or commutations under circumstances that warrant further congressional scrutiny, including several individuals connected to major fraud schemes, financial crimes, and high-profile political or financial relationships tied to President Trump and his associates. The earlier letters sought information regarding the clemency process, including whether financial contributions, lobbyists, intermediaries, or personal connections played a role in securing presidential clemency.
Among the individuals who received letters are convicted fraudsters, political fundraisers, corporate executives, and wealthy donors, such as Changpeng Zhao, whose cases have generated public reporting suggesting unusual access to Trump’s network of political allies and associates, direct lobbying efforts, large political donations, or other concerning connections surrounding their clemency requests.
The lawmakers continued their investigation in June, sending four additional letters to the Department of Justice’s Office of the Pardon Attorney, the White House Office of Records Management, the White House Pardon Czar, and the United States Secret Service. In October, the lawmakers initiated a probe into the influence of cabinet members, U.S. Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., and Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin, in Trump’s decision to pardon convicted felons.
