FRESNO, Calif. — Ron Cook, 58, of Fresno, has been indicted on multiple charges of making false statements to the federal government, wire fraud, aggravated identity theft, and money laundering for running a nearly $65 million fraud scheme through his company, Corporate America Lending (CAL), U.S. Attorney Eric Grant announced today.

Cook was arrested at his office this morning and will make his initial court appearance this afternoon.

According to court records, CAL is a lending company based in Fresno that originates loans for farmers, ranchers, and others who work in the agriculture industry. Once CAL originates the loans, it sells the interest in them to others, including investors, financial companies, and the Federal Agricultural Mortgage Company (Farmer MAC). Farmer MAC is a company backed by the federal government that provides increased access to affordable financing for the agriculture industry.

Beginning in 2023, the borrowers of a $58 million loan that Cook had originated and sold to one financial company refinanced the loan with another financial company. The first financial company did not know about the refinancing. Cook then made several misrepresentations to the borrowers, the first financial company, and the second financial company so that he would receive the $58 million refinance amount without the first financial company becoming aware and could keep the money for himself. When the first financial company found out about the refinancing, Cook transferred the money to his friends and associates to conceal its location. It was these transfers that resulted in the money laundering charges.

During this period, Cook also defrauded his other customers and investors. He defrauded his customers by stealing their identities and taking out loans in their names from Farmer MAC without their knowledge, and he defrauded his investors by selling them interests in loans that did not actually exist. It was Cook’s stealing his customers’ identities to get loans from Farmer MAC that resulted in the false statements to the federal government charge against him.

Cook obtained at least $64 million through his fraud scheme. He used the money to pay for his lifestyle and to pay debts that he owed to some of his customers and investors who had detected the fraud and threatened to file criminal charges against him. He also used the money to make political donations.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation conducted the investigation. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Arelis Clemente and Joseph Barton are prosecuting the case.

If convicted, Cook faces 30 years in prison and a $250,000 fine for the making false statements to the federal government charge. He faces 20 years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000 for each of the wire fraud and money laundering charges. Finally, he faces a mandatory two years in prison, consecutive to the sentence he receives for any other charges, for each of the aggravated identity theft charges. Any sentence, however, would be determined at the discretion of the court after consideration of any applicable statutory factors and the federal Sentencing Guidelines, which take into account a number of variables. The charges are only allegations; the defendant is presumed innocent until and unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
title: Fresno Executive Indicted for $65 Million Fraud Scheme that Defrauded Farmer MAC and Others

text:
Stamford Man Sentenced to Additional Prison Time for Distributing Crack Prior to Reporting to Prison
STAMFORD, Conn. - David X. Sullivan, United States Attorney for the District of Connecticut, announced that DANNY TURKVAN, also known as “Smooth” 55, of Stamford, has been sentenced by U.S. District Judge Stefan R. Underhill in Bridgeport to an additional 14 months of imprisonment for distributing crack cocaine after he had been sentenced in another federal case and prior to reporting to prison.
On August 13, 2025, Turkvan was sentenced in Hartford federal court to 46 months of imprisonment and three years of supervised release for his participation in a southwestern Connecticut narcotics trafficking conspiracy. Turkvan, who was released on a $150,000 bond, was ordered to report to prison on October 16, 2025. An investigation revealed that Turkvan continued to distribute narcotics after his August 2025 sentencing. Stamford Police arrested Turkvan on state charges on October 11, 2025, and seized crack cocaine that he intended to distribute.
Turkvan has been detained since his arrest. On July 8, 2026, he pleaded guilty in federal court to possession with intent to distribute cocaine base (“crack”).
This investigation was conducted by the Stamford Police Department and the Drug Enforcement Administration. The case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Patricia Stolfi Collins.
title: Stamford Man Sentenced to Additional Prison Time for Distributing Crack Prior to Reporting to Prison

SYRACUSE, N.Y.— The Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Army for Financial Management and Comptroller, Jake Fischer, recently visited Syracuse University to strengthen the Army’s longstanding academic partnership and explore opportunities to develop the next generation of financial management leaders.
The visit included engagements with Army ROTC cadets, students enrolled in the Defense Comptrollership Program (DCP), and senior faculty from the Whitman School of Management and Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs.
During his visit with DCP students, Fischer emphasized the evolving role of financial management professionals as the Army accelerates its modernization efforts. As emerging technologies and super intelligence reduce the burden of routine financial transactions, the Army must increasingly leverage its workforce’s knowledge, analytical expertise, and judgment to inform senior leader decisions.
These discussions reinforced priorities outlined in the Army’s FY27 Financial Management Strategy and Transformation Plan, including the Fiscal Frontline financial dashboard, Army Audit Acceleration, and ongoing efforts to modernize how the Army allocates resources.
When meeting with Army ROTC cadets, Fischer discussed Army transformation, leadership, and the importance of financial accountability in supporting warfighter readiness.
A tour of Syracuse’s National Veterans Resource Center highlighted the university’s extensive support to service members, veterans, and transitioning Soldiers, including educational opportunities, professional certifications, and career transition programs.
Dialog with university leadership explored new opportunities for academic collaboration, particularly in artificial intelligence, strategic resource management, and executive communication. These efforts emphasized strengthening the workforce’s ability to translate complex financial information into clear, actionable recommendations.
The visit underscored the Army’s continued commitment to investing in its people and leveraging academic partnerships to build a more agile, analytically capable financial management workforce—one prepared to transform financial information into decision advantage for the warfighter.
title: Army PDASA FM&C Jake Fischer strengthens partnership with Syracuse University to modernize workforce

text:
Rep. Summer Lee, House Labor Leaders Demand Answers Over Corporate Union-Busting, Enforcement of Federal Transparency Laws
PITTSBURGH, PA – NOVEMBER 2, 2026 — Today, Congresswoman Summer L. Lee (PA-12) joined House Education and Workforce Committee Ranking Member Robert C. “Bobby” Scott (VA-03) and Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions Ranking Member Mark DeSaulnier (CA-10) in demanding answers from the Trump Administration over its failure to adequately enforce federal transparency laws governing corporations and union-busting consultants.
In a letter to Office of Labor-Management Standards (OLMS) Director Elisabeth Messenger, the lawmakers raised serious concerns about widespread failures by employers and anti-union consultants to disclose how much money they spend attempting to influence workers' decisions to organize.
Too often, when workers exercise their right to organize a union, corporations and bosses hire outside consultants to wage anti-union campaigns. Over the last several decades, union-avoidance has become a multi-billion-dollar industry. The latest analysis found that companies spend approximately $1.7 billion every year, including nearly $500 million on union-busting consultants, to break their organizing drives. Some consultants are reportedly paid $500 per hour or $4,000 per day for their services.
Under the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act (LMRDA), employers and consultants are required to file public reports about their matter because it allows workers to see how much their bosses are spending to influence their decision to unionize. However, for decades, employers and union-busting consultants have routinely failed to meet this requirement, allowing bosses and their consultants to operate in the shadows. Under the Trump Administration, the problem is only becoming worse. A recent watchdog report found that, as of August 8, 2026, nearly 60 percent of employers required to file a disclosure in 2025 have still not submitted their reports—the largest year-over-year decline on record.
“Over the last several years, while worker organizing has skyrocketed, employers have increasingly responded with hostile anti-union campaigns, including by hiring well-compensated outside consultants. As more employers seek to quash their workers’ unionization drives, it is imperative that employer and consultant disclosure requirements under the LMRDA are robustly enforced by OLMS, so workers have a complete picture of who is attempting to influence their decision as they exercise their right to organize,” wrote the Members.
To determine whether OLMS is effectively carrying out its responsibility to enforce the LMRDA, the Members requested a response to their extensive questions by no later than November 16, 2026.
To read the full letter to OLMS Director Elisabeth Messenger, click here.
Congresswoman Summer Lee serves on the House Committee on Judiciary and the Committee on Education and Workforce. Since taking office in January 2023, she has delivered historic levels of federal investment totaling over $2.7 Billion brought back to Western PA, including over $580 million for infrastructure, over $110 million for affordable transit, over $500 million to keep clean energy manufacturing at home in Pennsylvania, and over $55 million on clean energy efforts in and around schools to help keep our kids and communities safe. These investments will help improve Western Pennsylvania’s infrastructure and transit, ensure cleaner air and drinking water, lower housing costs, fund research institutions, fuel clean manufacturing, fund STEM innovation and entrepreneurship, boost workforce development, and create thousands of good paying union jobs. Lee and her team have also delivered casework and constituent services to over 4,000 constituents with issues ranging from helping our seniors and disabled community access Medicare and social security to helping folks secure housing and helping families with immigration support and passports.
title: Rep. Summer Lee, House Labor Leaders Demand Answers Over Corporate Union-Busting, Enforcement of Federal Transparency Laws

text:
Secretary Kennedy Advances MAHA in Michigan and Iowa with Focus on Nutrition, Recovery, and Maternal Health
WASHINGTON, D.C.—NOVEMBER 2, 2026— U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. advanced President Trump's Make America Healthy Again agenda last week during four days of stops in Michigan and Iowa on his "Take Back Your Health Tour." Secretary Kennedy celebrated more than 250 hospitals committing to healthier food, highlighted a $12 million investment in Detroit's treatment and recovery services, and announced new infant formula actions to support growing families.
"Under President Trump's leadership, we are bringing real food into hospitals, investing in addiction recovery, and helping mothers give their children a healthy start," said Secretary Kennedy. "In Michigan and Iowa, I met people turning these priorities into action. HHS is backing their work to Make America Healthy Again."
On October 26, Secretary Kennedy visited Corewell Health's Lifestyle and Culinary Medicine Practice in Grand Rapids, Michigan, for a roundtable, tour, and cooking demonstration. He met with healthcare leaders, clinicians, and culinary medicine professionals to discuss how hospitals can serve healthier meals and give patients practical skills to continue eating well at home. During the visit, Secretary Kennedy celebrated more than 250 hospitals signing the Make Hospital Food Healthier Pledge. The visit also highlighted Corewell Health's work to connect clinical care with cooking instruction, nutrition education, and community programs.
"As part of our commitment to make health better, Corewell Health supports HHS' Make Hospital Food Healthier Pledge, which builds on work we have been doing for years to improve the meals we serve our patients. We appreciated the recent visit from the Secretary which showcased our focus on serving whole foods, cutting back on sugar and sodium and using healthier cooking methods. Nutrition is an important part of patient care, which we train our current and future physicians to incorporate. The right food choices are always guided by conversations between patients, physicians and their care teams," said Tina Freese Decker, Corewell Health president and CEO.
On October 27, Secretary Kennedy toured Detroit Wayne Integrated Health Network's crisis care facility and joined a roundtable with city officials, healthcare providers, faith leaders, and Americans who confronted addiction and embraced the path of recovery. The visit highlighted Detroit's selection as one of eight communities receiving funding through the HHS STREETS program. The Detroit Health Department will receive $12 million over four years to establish its Prevention and Access to Treatment, Housing, and Stability program, known as PATHS. Through coordinated outreach and services, PATHS will connect people experiencing homelessness and serious mental illness, substance use disorders, or both with treatment, recovery support, and stable housing.
"We are grateful to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and its Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration for recognizing the urgent needs of our community. This STREETS funding strengthens DWIHN's ability to connect people experiencing homelessness and co-occurring mental health and substance use disorders with the treatment and support they need to move toward recovery, stability, and independence," said James E. White, President and CEO, Detroit Wayne Integrated Health Network (DWIHN).
Secretary Kennedy also announced new analysis from the HHS Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation highlighting how actions across President Trump's two terms to reduce unnecessary opioid prescribing, combat illicit fentanyl, and strengthen treatment and recovery have led opioid-related deaths in the United States to plummet to the lowest since President Trump declared a public health emergency in 2017.
On October 28, Secretary Kennedy, joined by Kathryn Burgum and HHS Center for Faith Director Monty Burks, visited Sheepgate in Colfax, Iowa. The trio toured the residential recovery facility, met with program leaders, and engaged with clients sharing their journeys from addiction to sobriety. The discussion focused on faith-based recovery, mentoring, and helping people return to their families and communities. Sheepgate's structured program combines Biblical teaching, fellowship, practical work experience, and support for re-entry. The visit highlighted the role of faith and community partnerships in advancing President Trump's Great American Recovery.
"Addiction affects so much more than the person struggling. It impacts families and entire communities. For more than 50 years at Sheepgate, a division of Adult and Teen Challenge of the Midlands, we've seen firsthand how Jesus Christ can completely transform lives. We were grateful for the opportunity to welcome Secretary Kennedy, Kathryn Burgum and Monty Burks to share what's working in faith-based recovery and discuss the challenges we face. As we fight this crisis together, our hope is to build stronger partnerships and make sure finances never stand in the way of someone getting the help they need," said Michael Hunsberger, President of Sheepgate.
Secretary Kennedy concluded the trip on October 29 at Everystep in West Des Moines, Iowa, where he joined Health Resources and Services Administration Administrator Tom Engels for a maternal health roundtable. During the visit, Secretary Kennedy delivered a Newborn Essentials Support Toolkit (NEST) to an expectant mother and announced new FDA actions on infant formula including proposed updates to nutrient requirements and an online dashboard giving families easier access to formula information.
"Every child and their family deserves access to the care and support they need to be healthy and thrive," said Tray Wade, president and CEO of EveryStep. "At EveryStep, we have seen firsthand the difference maternal and child health programs have made for Iowa families, from supporting healthy pregnancies to helping parents navigate the challenges of raising young children. We were honored to have welcomed Secretary Kennedy and national health care leaders to share the important work happening in our communities and discuss why continued state and federal support remains so important to the families who rely on these services."
Together, these visits underscored the Trump Administration's commitment to healthier food, lasting recovery, and stronger families — turning national priorities into practical support in communities across America.

Justice Department Announces Charges Involving 63 Individuals for Election-Related Crimes
Today, the Justice Department announced charges involving 63 individuals, including four illegal aliens, in connection with illegal voting, fraudulent voter registration, and related election crimes across the country. The cases include voting by aliens in federal elections, false claims of U.S. citizenship to register to vote or to vote, and the fraudulent submission of a voter registration application in another state.
“Today’s announcement marks the largest surge of voter-fraud arrests since President Trump returned to office,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “These foreign nationals allegedly took advantage of the trust of the American people and flouted the laws that govern our nation’s elections. This Department of Justice will continue investigating and prosecuting voter fraud to restore confidence in our electoral system.”
In the last nine weeks alone, the Department has charged 195 aliens across 25 states with illegal voting and registration offenses. Since the beginning of this Administration, we have charged 239 people with voting fraud-related offenses.
Case details are as follows:
Northern District of Georgia
Benito Covarrubias Iniguez, 64, an illegal alien from Mexico has been charged with making a false claim of U.S. citizenship in order to vote in a federal election.
Southern District of Texas
Five aliens, including an illegal alien, have been charged with election-related crimes.
- Ali Khan, 33, an illegal alien from the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago, has been charged with voting by an alien. Khan allegedly voted in the 2024 election.
- Nigerian national Mohammed Omar Hassan, 61, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by an alien. Hassan allegedly voted in the 2022 and 2024 elections.
- Mexican national Diego Benavides Rodriguez, 29, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by an alien and an additional charge of falsely claiming U.S. citizenship.
- Mexican national Jose Vasquez-Mendoza, 51, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by an alien. Vasquez-Mendoza allegedly voted in the 2022 special election for Congressional District 34.
- Mexican national Karen Hinojosa-Martinez, 37, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with lying on immigration documents after allegedly voting in a federal election.
District of Maryland
Mohammad Hachibur Rahman, 33, an illegal alien from Bangladesh, is charged by information with unlawful voting. Rahman allegedly voted in the November 2024 election. The election was held in part for the purpose of selecting a candidate for president, vice president, or member of the U.S. Senate or House of Representatives.
Eastern District of North Carolina
Nine aliens, including an illegal alien, have been charged with election-related crimes.
- Selvin Porfidio Gonzalez Escobar, 43, an illegal alien from Guatemala living in Robeson County, North Carolina, is charged with one count of falsely claiming citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. He registered to vote in 2020 and voted in the 2024 and 2020 general elections.
- Italian and British national Amerigo Di Nolfi, 53, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with one count of falsely claiming citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. Di Nolfi allegedly registered to vote in 2024 and voted in the 2024 general election.
- Kenyan national Elizabeth Margaret Crudup, 52, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with one count of falsely claiming citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. Crudup allegedly registered to vote in 2008 and voted in nine general elections in 2024, 2022, 2020, 2018, 2016, 2014, 2012, 2010, and 2008, as well as nine primary elections in 2026, 2024, 2022, 2020, 2018, 2016, 2014, 2010, and 2008.
- Bermudan national Gregory Eugene Wade, 64, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with one count of falsely claiming citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. Wade allegedly registered to vote in 2000 and voted in 12 general elections in 2024, 2022, 2020, 2018, 2016, 2014, 2012, 2010, 2008, 2004, 2002, and 2000, as well as the 2020 and 2002 primary elections.
- Singaporean national Jacqueline Yvonne Papandreou Brown, 63, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with one count of falsely claiming citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. Brown allegedly registered to vote in 2020 and voted in the 2024 general election.
- Jamaican national Karl Anthony Wilkins, 62, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with one count of falsely claiming citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. Wilkins allegedly registered to vote in 2018 and voted in the 2024, 2022, and 2020 general elections, as well as the 2020 primary election in Wake County, North Carolina.
- Colombian national Patricia Elena Valencia Cardona, 56, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with one count of falsely claiming citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. Cardona registered to vote in 2024 and voted in the 2024 general election.
- United Kingdom national Richard John Reid, 62, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with one count of falsely claiming citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. Reid registered to vote in 2002 and voted in four general elections in 2024, 2020, 2012, and 2008, as well as the 2012 and 2008 primary elections.
- Canadian national Taso Gretes, 58, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with one count of falsely claiming citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. Gretes allegedly registered to vote in 2022 and voted in the 2024 general election.
Middle District of North Carolina
Five aliens have been charged with election-related crimes.
- Dutch national Adrianus Marinus Van Der Staak, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged by indictment with one count of knowingly making a false statement or claim of U.S. citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien.
- Mexican national Saida Adali Hirachete Olivarez, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged by indictment with one count of knowingly making a false statement or claim of U.S. citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien.
- Cuban national Juan Florencio Ramos, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged by indictment with one count of knowingly making a false statement or claim of U.S. citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien.
- Barbadian national Phillip Alexander Carter, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged by indictment with one count of knowingly making a false statement or claim of U.S. citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien.
- Argentinian national Yamila Avalos, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged by information with one count of voting by an alien.
Western District of North Carolina
Four aliens have been charged with election-related crimes.
- Nigerian national Michael Agah, 74, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by an alien and making a false claim to U.S. citizenship to vote. Agah allegedly falsely stated and claimed that he was a U.S. citizen on an Authorization to Vote Form. Then on Nov. 5, 2024, Agah voted in a federal election.
- Dominican national Luis Alberto DeJesus, 50, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by an alien in a federal election and making a false claim to U.S. citizenship to vote. It is alleged that DeJesus falsely stated on an Early Voting Application that he was a U.S. citizen and thereafter voted on Oct. 30, 2024, knowing that he was not a U.S. citizen and was not legally permitted to cast a ballot.
- French national Serge Christian Dupont, 57, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by an alien and making a false claim to U.S. citizenship to vote. It is alleged that on Nov. 5, 2024, Dupont made a false statement and claimed that he was a citizen of the United States on an Authorization to Vote Form. Dupont then did vote on the same day in a federal election.
- St. Kitts and Nevis national Edread Ray Stanley, 63, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by an alien. It is alleged that Stanley, knowing that he was not a U.S. citizen, knowingly voted on Nov. 5, 2024, in a federal election.
Middle District of Tennessee
Three aliens have been charged with election-related crimes.
- Jamaican national Garfield St. Vincent Bruce, 48, a lawful permanent resident, allegedly voted in the 2024 election held in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for President, Vice President, Member of the U.S. Senate, or Member of the U.S. House of Representatives and allegedly falsely and willfully represented himself to be a citizen of the United States in a Tennessee voter registration application in 2024 in order to register to vote or to vote in a federal, state, or local election.
- Honduran national Mariela Elizabeth Avila Ortiz, 33, a lawful permanent resident, allegedly voted in the 2024 election held in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for President, Vice President, Member of the U.S. Senate, or Member of the U.S. House of Representatives and allegedly falsely and willfully represented herself to be a citizen of the United States in a Tennessee voter registration application in 2024 in order to register to vote or to vote in a federal, state, or local election.
- Trinidad and Tobago national Allison Melissa Wilkes, 49, a lawful permanent resident, allegedly voted in the 2024 election held in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for President, Vice President, Member of the U.S. Senate, or Member of the U.S. House of Representatives and allegedly falsely and willfully represented herself to be a citizen of the United States in a Tennessee voter registration application in 2024 in order to register to vote or to vote in a federal, state, or local election.
Western District of Tennessee
Two aliens have been charged with voting by an alien.
- Mexican national Cesar Sanchez Correa, 44, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with one count of unlawful voting by an alien. Sanchez Correa allegedly illegally voted in Haywood County, TN in the 2024 election held in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for President, Vice President, Member of the U.S. Senate, or Member of the U.S. House of Representatives, and allegedly falsely and willfully represented himself to be a citizen of the United States in a Tennessee voter registration application in order to vote in a federal, state, or local election.
- German national Andreas Van Der Werf, 62, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with two counts of unlawful voting by an alien. Van Der Werf allegedly illegally voted in Fayette County, TN in both the 2022 and 2024 elections held in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for President, Vice President, Member of the U.S. Senate, or Member of the U.S. House of Representatives, and allegedly falsely and willfully represented himself to be a citizen of the United States in a Tennessee voter registration application in order to vote in a federal, state, or local election.
Eastern District of Tennessee
Two aliens have been charged with illegally voting.
- Iraqi national Mark Adwar Odisho, 30, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with illegally voting in the U.S. presidential election on Nov. 5, 2024. He made his initial appearance in federal court on Oct.29.
- French national Frederic Jean Rene Sicard, 50, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with illegally voting in the U.S. presidential election on Nov. 5, 2024. He made his initial appearance in federal court on Oct. 30, 2026.
District of New Jersey
Two aliens have been charged with election-related crimes.
- Jamaican national Antonio Mitchell, 54, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by an alien and unlawfully attempting to procure U.S. citizenship. Mitchell has also been charged with an additional count of making false statements while applying for U.S. citizenship. Mitchell allegedly voted in-person in the 2022 general election. Mitchell falsely claimed that he had never registered to vote or voted in any federal elections. Additionally, after submitting his application for naturalization (N-400), Mitchell was interviewed by an Immigration Services Officer. In that interview and while under oath, Mitchell denied having registered to vote, or having voted, in any federal election.
- Italian national Andrea Morzetta, 72, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by an alien and unlawfully attempting to procure U.S. citizenship. Morzetta allegedly voted in-person in the November 2024 general election and falsely claimed that he had never registered to vote or voted in any federal elections when applying for U.S. citizenship.
Western District of Wisconsin
Two aliens have been charged with election-related crimes.
- Canadian national Monique Gignac-Yochum, 60, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with illegally voting as an alien in the November 2022 and November 2024 elections. Gignac-Yochum allegedly voted, knowing she was not a U.S. citizen, in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for the offices of Member of the Senate, Member of the House of Representatives, Vice President, and President.
- Canadian national Rodger Dedrick, 66, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with illegally voting as an alien in November 2024. He is also charged with falsely claiming U.S. Citizenship when registering to vote in August 2024.
Northern District of New York
Two aliens have been charged with voting by an alien.
- Indian national Pooja Pawse, 31, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by an alien. Pawse allegedly voted in the 2024 General Election while knowing that she was not a U.S. citizen.
- Afghan national Mobin Tora Kheil, 33, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by an alien. Kheil allegedly voted in the 2024 General Election while knowing that he was not a U.S. citizen.
District of Utah
Samoan national Valelia Toleafoa, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by an alien. Toleafoa allegedly voted in November 2024.
Western District of Missouri
Canadian national Christopher Doucet, 68, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with falsely claiming to be a U.S. citizen in order to register to vote. Doucet allegedly registered to vote in January 2024 and voted in a general municipal election at the Living Hope Restoration Branch polling place in Independence, Mo.
District of Nevada
Four aliens have been charged with illegally voting.
- Argentinian national Mariela Delia Mendoza, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by an alien. Mendoza allegedly voted in November 2024 in an election held in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for the office of President, Vice President, Member of the Senate, and Member of the House of Representatives. She was not a U.S. citizen.
- Sudanese national Moneir Elzobier Ali Yousif, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by an alien. Yousif allegedly voted in an election held in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for the office of President, Vice President, Member of the Senate, and Member of the House of Representatives.

Safi allegedly voted in an election held in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for the office of President, Vice President, Member of the Senate, and Member of the House of Representatives.

Mlebinge Riziki Ramadhani allegedly voted in an election held in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for the office of President, Vice President, Member of the Senate, and Member of the House of Representatives.
District of New Mexico
Robert Glenn Johnson, 63, of Annapolis, Maryland, has been charged for fraudulently submitting a voter registration application in New Mexico. Johnson allegedly submitted a voter registration application to the Bernalillo County Clerk’s Office Bureau of Elections in Albuquerque falsely claiming to be a New Mexico resident.
Central District of California
Six aliens have been charged with making false statements on their naturalization applications.
- Filipino national Sirgalahad Camua, 43, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with making false statements on his naturalization applications. Camua allegedly illegally registered to vote in August 2009 by falsely claiming to be a U.S. citizen. He voted by mail-in ballot in May 2020, November 2024, and June 2026. In May 2025, Camua filed paperwork seeking to become a naturalized U.S. citizen and, under penalty of perjury, falsely stated that he had neither claimed to be a U.S. citizen nor had he registered to vote in U.S. elections.
- Mexican national Krystel Capi Valle, 31, a lawful permanent resident has been charged with making false statements on her naturalization applications. Capi Valle in June 2026 swore under penalty of perjury on her naturalization form that she had never claimed to be a U.S. citizen nor had she registered to vote in U.S. elections. In fact, in October 2022 she illegally registered to vote by lying that she was a U.S. citizen. She then illegally voted by mail-in ballot in the November 2022 election.
- Israeli national Moria Dahan, 35, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with making false statements on her naturalization applications. Dahan allegedly illegally registered to vote and voted in person on Nov. 5, 2024, the date of the U.S. general election. She falsely claimed under penalty of perjury to be a U.S. citizen. On her naturalization form dated November 6, 2025, she falsely stated under penalty of perjury that she never claimed to be a U.S. citizen nor had she registered to vote in a U.S. election.
Canadian citizen Chad Goertz, 52, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with making false statements on his naturalization applications. Goertz allegedly illegally registered to vote in April 2018 and illegally voted by mail in the November 2022 and November 2024 U.S. elections. In February 2026, Goertz lied under oath on his naturalization form when he denied having ever claimed to be a U.S. citizen and denied having ever registered to vote in a U.S. election.
- Iranian national Mahyar Nikzad, 35, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with making false statements on his naturalization applications. Nikzad allegedly illegally registered to vote and under penalty of perjury checked the box on his voter registration form reading, “I am a U.S. citizen.” Records indicate that Nikzad voted in the March 2024 and November 2024 U.S. elections. In February 2026, under penalty of perjury, he falsely stated that he never claimed to be a U.S. citizen and denied ever registering to become a U.S. voter.
- Mexican national Gilberto Ruiz, 46, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with making false statements on his naturalization applications. Ruiz in July 2022 allegedly registered to vote and he voted by mail-in ballot in three elections: November 2022, March 2024, and November 2024, falsely claiming to be a U.S. citizen. In August 2025, under penalty of perjury, Ruiz denied ever claiming to be a U.S. citizen and denied having ever registered to vote.
Eastern District of California
Six aliens have been charged with illegally voting.
- Filipino national Lorie Jane Alcala, 44, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with illegally voting. Alcala allegedly voted in November 2024 in the U.S. presidential election.
- Filipino national Edith San Pedro Carter, 59, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with illegally voting in the U.S. presidential election in November 2024.
- Portuguese national Maria Joao Bettencourt, 49, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with illegally voting in the U.S. presidential election in November 2024.
- Portuguese national Rosa Bento Silva Anderson, 26, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with illegally voting in the U.S. presidential election in November 2024.
- Filipino national Janelyn Stewart, 38, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with illegally voting in the U.S. presidential election in November 2024.
- Filipino national Meryll Joy Quirong Costi, 36, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with illegally voting in the November 2024 presidential election and the November 2022 midterm election.
Eastern District of Arkansas
Mexican national Juan Manuel Gudino, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by an alien. Gudino allegedly registered to vote in 2022 and voted in the 2022 general election.
Eastern District of Pennsylvania
Five aliens have been charged with election-related crimes.
- Dominican Republic national Rosanny Fabre Villa, 28, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with making a false statement of citizenship in order to vote. Villa allegedly submitted a voter registration application that she knew was fraudulent, because on it she falsely claimed to be a United States citizen, when, as she knew, she was not a U.S. citizen.
- Canadian national Gavin Moir, 55, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with four counts of voting by an alien. Moir allegedly voted in the 2022 and 2024 general elections, and the 2022 and 2026 primaries.
- Jamaican national Antonio Lyttle, 68, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by an alien. Lyttle allegedly voted in the 2024 general election.
- Indonesian national Widarto, 56, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by an alien. Widarto allegedly voted in the 2024 general election.
- Finnish national Eija Annikki Yaroma, 66, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by an alien. Yaroma allegedly voted in the 2024 general election.
A complaint, indictment, and information merely contain accusations. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

JOINT BASE SAN ANTONIO-FORT SAM HOUSTON, Texas – Brooke Army Medical Center participated in the annual San Antonio Mass Casualty Exercise and Evaluation Oct. 21 to test the hospital’s emergency preparedness and response capabilities in case of a mass casualty incident.
SAMCEE is designed to assess the surge capabilities of hospitals in the 26,000-square-mile region covered by the Southwest Texas Regional Advisory Council. The exercise specifically covers participating hospitals’ treatment processes, patient tracking abilities, and family reunification procedures.
“As one of two Level 1 trauma centers, we not only treat military members and their beneficiaries, but also civilian trauma patients,” Emergency Manager George Wible said. “So, if there ever was a mass casualty incident, BAMC will be one of the primary recipients of patients.”
As part of the simulated drill, BAMC physicians, nurses, medical personnel and staff received news via mass text shortly after 8 a.m. that a mid-air collision had been reported near San Antonio International Airport. Soon after, about 55 “victims,” or volunteer role players, began arriving at BAMC in emergency vehicles with various life-threatening mock injuries.
Army Lt. Col. (Dr.) Michael Rowland, trauma medical director, said the Trauma Department’s participation in the exercise each year is vital. “By treating patients through a variety of emergency scenarios, the exercise allows our trauma surgeons to provide quality care for critically injured patients should an incident ever happen,” he said.
One role player, Army Pvt. Angelina Doss, portrayed a 9-year-old who arrived at the emergency room with severe chest pain and breathing problems. Emergency physicians diagnosed her with a collapsed lung after conducting medical tests.
“It was a lot of fun,” she said. “I liked the staging area where they put the moulage (simulated injuries) on us, and then coming in and seeing how the entire hospital was involved to prepare for an actual emergency.”
BAMC was one of 50 hospitals and healthcare facilities in the region to participate in SAMCEE.
Air Force Col. Amy Brown, deputy commander of surgical services, who executed her role in the Hospital Command Center along with other key leadership, said BAMC takes an “all-hands on deck approach” while conducting the disaster drill.
“Disaster response is directed by the hospital incident commander with additional team members having assigned roles and areas of responsibility,” Brown said. “We have playbooks that allow for dynamic collaboration between departments such as the ED (Emergency Department), Logistics, Facilities, Public Affairs, OR (Operating Room), Manpower, and Patient Registration. Security, Mental Health and Chaplain services play a vital role in assisting families separated from victims and providing reunification.”
Army Capt. Cristina Western, dietitian, volunteered to be an observer/controller and was responsible for tracking patient movements from point of entry to placement in an inpatient unit. She also noted any procedures that could be improved on.
“I didn’t realize how widespread across San Antonio that SAMCEE was and how many external entities were involved,” Western said. “It was eye-opening to see what the whole process involves.”
According to STRAC, the South Texas medical community uses a four-pronged approach to emergency preparedness: plan, equip, train, and exercise. Results from the exercise are used to improve emergency plans, identify equipment shortages, and other areas for improvement.
After the four-hour exercise ended, Wible provided an early assessment of the simulated drill.
“I’ve heard positive remarks that things went a lot more smoothly and effectively than previous exercises,” he said. “Of course, not everything went flawlessly. Ultimately, what we hope to have accomplished is that we identify any gaps or inconsistencies that we can improve upon. We will take those lessons learned and put them into a revised plan, and when we do it again, hopefully we will do even better.”
title: BAMC tests emergency readiness, patient influx capabilities during mass casualty exercise

BUFFALO, N.Y.-U.S. Attorney Michael DiGiacomo announced today that Barry Wright, 57, of Marietta, GA, pleaded guilty before U.S. District Judge Richard J. Arcara to conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute, and to distribute, controlled substances, which carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison, and fine of $1,000,000.

Between July 2024 and January 2025, Tandel conspired with others to sell Tapentadol and Amphetamine/Dextroamphetamine. During the conspiracy, MEDDZONLINE.COM, PHARMACYSTORESONLINE.com, and related websites were part of a larger organized drug trafficking organization operating domestically and internationally. After orders were received, the organization sent bulk shipments of drugs via international mail to a US based bulk re-shipper. The drugs were then sent to smaller re-shippers, who were paid for each package they mailed out to customers. Wright was a smaller re-shipper.

On November 20, 2024, the DEA Buffalo conducted a controlled purchase from MEDSHEALTHONLINE.com. for 60 Zolpidem pills for $475. On November 27, 2024, the DEA obtained the USPS parcel that contained blister packs of Zolpidem, which was mailed by the defendant. During the investigation, law enforcement obtained a spreadsheet related to the organization detailing drugs mailed out by Wright to customers around the United States. Wright mailed out a total of 333 parcels, receiving $48.50/per package. In some instances, Wright was listed as taking drugs from his stock for himself.

This investigation was part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of U.S. law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Buffalo comprises agents and officers from Homeland Security Investigations, the FBI, ATF, IRS Criminal Investigations, Department of Homeland Security Emergency Removal Operations, Customs and Border Protection, the DEA, the U.S. Coast Guard Investigative Service, the U.S. Marshals Service, U.S. Postal Inspection Service, the U.S. Secret Service, and the Diplomatic Security Service, with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Western District of New York.

The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Joshua A. Violanti. The plea is the result of an investigation by the Drug Enforcement Administration, under the direction of Special Agent-in-Charge Farhana Islam, New York Field Division. Additional assistance was provided by the Drug Enforcement Offices in St. Louis, MO, Atlanta, GA, and Mobile, AL.

Sentencing is scheduled for March 18, 2027, at 10:00 a.m. before Judge Arcara.

CINCINNATI – U.S. Attorney Dominick S. Gerace II announced today results of the Southern District of Ohio’s continuing work to reduce violent crime, firearms offenses and fraud in fiscal year 2026.

Fiscal year 2026 includes Oct. 1, 2025, through Sept. 30, 2026.

Violent and Gun Crime

“I am extremely proud of what my Office has accomplished since I became U.S. Attorney just over a year ago,” said U.S. Attorney Gerace. “My tenure began amid a significant uptick in violent and gun crimes, particularly in downtown Cincinnati, and I promised the public that we would aggressively pursue federal charges against those offenders. The statistics show that we have done just that. I asked my prosecutors to target repeat violent offenders and to focus on the safety of the streets in our communities and they continue to answer the bell.”

As indicated below, in Cincinnati alone, the Office increased prosecutions of firearms offenders by 250% when compared to FY2025. More generally, violent crime prosecutions increased by 148.5% in Cincinnati and by 92.7% districtwide.

The total number of defendants charged with firearms offenses and violent crimes across the District sets a Southern District of Ohio record based on available statistics going back to FY2004. The total number of defendants charged with firearms offenses represents an increase of 93.5% from FY2025.

Defendants Charged with Violent Crimes

Defendants Charged with Firearms Offenses (18 U.S.C. 922(g) and 924(c))

“None of these cases are possible without strong partnerships with our local, state and federal law enforcement agencies who investigate these crimes. I thank them for joining us in the fight against violence,” said U.S. Attorney Gerace. “I am also grateful to Ohio Attorney General Andy Wilson for his continued support and for providing us with a Special Assistant United States Attorney dedicated to federal gun cases.”

Fraud and White-Collar Crime

“The fight against fraud, especially fraud against taxpayer-funded government benefits programs, is a top priority for this Office,” said U.S. Attorney Gerace. “This fiscal year, we brought charges against several individuals who allegedly stole tens of millions of dollars from government programs designed to provide healthcare and food benefits to Americans in need—including a Medicaid fraud scheme involving $30 million and a SNAP fraud scheme involving $29.7 million. We will continue to hold fraudsters accountable for stealing taxpayer dollars and for depriving vulnerable citizens of these services.”

As indicated below, the District increased prosecution of white-collar defendants by 46.3% when compared to FY2025, with the largest increases coming from the Dayton and Columbus areas.

Defendants Charged with White-Collar Crimes

“These statistics represent just a few of the areas that our dedicated public servants focus on every day to keep the people of the Southern District of Ohio safe,” added U.S. Attorney Gerace. “In addition to violent, gun and white-collar crime, my Office remains steadfast in combatting child exploitation, protecting our homeland security, ridding our streets of deadly drugs, enforcing immigration laws, and dismantling transnational criminal organizations. We are proud to do our jobs in service to our communities and this great country.”

text:
The federal "farm safety net" refers to a collection of programs administered by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) that provide risk protection and income support to farmers in the United States in response to natural disasters, adverse growing conditions, and/or low market prices. Farm safety net programs include the Federal Crop Insurance Program (FCIP), farm-bill-authorized commodity support and disaster assistance programs, and commodity support and disaster assistance programs authorized outside of a farm bill (i.e., ad hoc farm support programs). The FCIP and farm-bill-authorized programs provide payments to farmers that are triggered automatically based on production, weather, and/or market conditions. Ad hoc programs provide payments to farmers in response to certain conditions, depending on the funding provided.
Congress has authorized commodity support programs for specific crop years in farm bills since the 1930s. Congress has permanently authorized the FCIP and farm-bill-authorized disaster assistance programs under various laws and included provisions to amend these programs in farm bills since 2008. Congress has authorized ad hoc support intermittently and, at certain times, allowed USDA to use the authorities of the Commodity Credit Corporation (CCC) to initiate ad hoc support.
The FCIP and farm-bill-authorized commodity support and disaster assistance programs are funded with mandatory appropriations of "such sums as necessary." The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimates the cost of these programs in the farm bill budget baseline. Ad hoc programs are funded with discretionary appropriations, and CBO typically does not include the cost of these programs in the farm bill budget baseline.
The Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018 (2018 farm bill; P.L. 115-334) made relatively limited changes to expected FCIP and farm-bill-authorized support program payments. Between 2018 and 2025, Congress appropriated and USDA initiated various ad hoc farm support in response to disasters and other market disruptions. The FY2025 budget reconciliation law (P.L. 119-21) reauthorized the farm-bill-authorized commodity support programs through the 2031 crop year and made changes to the FCIP and the farm-bill-authorized commodity support and disaster assistance programs to increase financial assistance and risk management options for farmers.
The FCIP offers insurance policies that farmers can purchase to mitigate the financial risks of natural disasters, adverse growing conditions, and certain commodity price declines. USDA regulates the insurance offered and subsidizes the premiums that farmers pay. Premium subsidies were approximately $15 billion in 2026, equal to about 66% of the total premium on average for all insurance policies sold in 2026. Federal crop insurance is available for field crops (e.g., corn, cotton), specialty crops (e.g., fruits, vegetables), certain types of livestock and animal products, and grazing lands. USDA Risk Management Agency administers the FCIP. There are no statutory caps on maximum premium subsidies or indemnities per farmer.
USDA Farm Service Agency (FSA) administers commodity support programs that provide price and income support for eligible farmers. The Agriculture Risk Coverage (ARC) and Price Loss Coverage (PLC) programs provide payments triggered automatically by relatively low revenues or prices, respectively, for eligible field crops. The Marketing Assistance Loan (MAL) and Loan Deficiency Payment (LDP) programs provide low-interest loans and payments triggered automatically by relatively low prices for eligible stored field crops and certain other commodities. The Dairy Margin Coverage (DMC) program provides payments for dairy producers based on the difference between the price of milk and the cost of feed for dairy cows. Producers of sugar beets, sugar cane, and refined sugar benefit from programs that support U.S. sugar prices.
ARC, PLC, and LDP are free for eligible farmers. Farmers must pay premiums for most DMC coverage. Except when market prices drop below MAL price support levels, farmers must repay MAL loans with interest rates set at 1% above the cost of borrowing from the U.S. Treasury. Farmers cannot combine ARC and PLC for the same commodity. Also, farmers cannot combine MALs and LDPs for the same commodity. Statute caps the maximum total ARC and PLC payments for each eligible farmer.
USDA FSA administers agricultural disaster assistance programs that provide financial assistance to help producers recover from certain natural disasters. The Noninsured Crop Disaster Assistance Program (NAP) offers farmers the opportunity to purchase coverage for losses due to natural disasters in areas where FCIP coverage is unavailable, with limited exceptions. NAP support is available for a wide variety of crops and grazing lands. The Tree Assistance Program (TAP) provides payments for losses to qualifying tree, bush, and vine crops. The Livestock Indemnity Program (LIP) provides payments for qualifying injuries and deaths of eligible livestock. The Livestock Forage Disaster Program (LFP) provides payments for grazing losses due to qualifying droughts or wildfires. The Emergency Assistance for Livestock, Honeybees, and Farm-Raised Fish Program (ELAP) provides payments for losses involving certain livestock, honeybees, or farm-raised fish not covered by LIP and LFP.
These programs do not require federal disaster designations to automatically trigger payments. ELAP, LFP, LIP, and TAP are free for eligible farmers. Farmers must purchase NAP coverage. Statute caps the maximum total NAP and LFP payments for each eligible farmer.
FCIP and farm-bill-authorized program outlays vary by year based on program enrollments, market prices, and natural disasters and adverse growing conditions (Figure 1). Using CBO's February 2026 baseline for USDA mandatory farm programs, CRS estimates that the combined federal cost of these programs will average about $30.6 billion annually for FY2027-FY2031.
FCIP and farm-bill-authorized program payments are proportional to a farm's production. As a result, larger-scale farms tend to receive more in total payments than small-scale farms, subject to applicable program payment limits and eligibility criteria.
Congress created ARC and PLC and expanded the FCIP and farm-bill-authorized disaster assistance programs in the Agricultural Act of 2014 (2014 farm bill; P.L. 113-79). Between 2014 and 2017, Congress did not authorize ad hoc farm support and restricted USDA's ability each year to use the CCC for providing farm support and for other purposes. In enacting the 2018 farm bill, Congress made limited changes to expected FCIP and farm-bill-authorized program payments.
Since 2018, Congress appropriated funds for ad hoc support programs and discontinued annual restrictions on USDA's use of the CCC. In response, USDA created multiple ad hoc farm support programs, which provided various types of relief: ad hoc disaster assistance for the 2018-2024 crop years, additional FCIP premium subsidies in 2019 and 2021-2022, ad hoc commodity support in 2018-2019 in response to retaliatory tariffs imposed by foreign trading partners, ad hoc commodity support in 2020-2023 in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, and ad hoc commodity support in 2024 and 2025 in response to market disruptions and perceived high farm input costs, among other ad hoc farm support. In general, the ad hoc disaster assistance and other supplemental assistance programs compensated for losses not covered by the FCIP or farm-bill-authorized programs. Some of the ad hoc commodity support programs provided payments only for commodities eligible for farm-bill-authorized commodity support programs; other programs provided payments for a broader range of commodities.
Both versions of the 2026 farm bill—House-passed H.R. 7567 and Senate committee-reported S. 5526—would make limited changes to expected FCIP and farm-bill-authorized program payments.
Farm safety net programs have been established and amended over time to provide a measure of financial stability for the farm sector and to promote an adequate supply of certain agricultural products while allowing producers to respond to market signals. In P.L. 119-21, Congress made changes to expand payments to farmers from the FCIP and farm-bill-authorized commodity support and disaster assistance programs. The 2026 farm bill proposals would make some changes that would further modify expected program payments.
The prices of some farm inputs (e.g., fuel, fertilizers, seeds, and labor) have increased in recent years for a variety of reasons. Except for the DMC program, farm-bill-authorized commodity support programs do not provide automatic payments in response to rising farm input prices. Congress authorized and USDA initiated ad hoc support in 2025 and 2026, in part to address potential effects of high farm input prices. Some stakeholders support providing additional ad hoc assistance and/or increased farm-bill-authorized support to help farmers defray input prices and maintain commodity production. Other stakeholders suggest that if the United States produced smaller harvests, market prices would increase and farmers could achieve profitability with reduced farm support payments. Higher market prices could increase costs for the individuals and businesses that purchase agricultural commodities. Congress may consider what level of farm support and types of programs would fulfill current policy objectives and whether the programs are sufficiently flexible to address changing farm circumstances.
title: Farm Bill Primer: Farm Safety Net Programs

The annual session of the United Nations (UN) General Assembly is held at UN Headquarters in New York City. The President generally (but not always) appoints one Democrat and one Republican to serve as U.S. representatives to the session, alternating each year between the House and Senate. The 81st General Assembly session began on September 8, 2026. Two Members of Congress are serving as U.S. representatives during the session: Senator Dave McCormick and Senator Jeanne Shaheen.
The UN General Assembly is composed of 193 UN member states, including the United States. It is the primary deliberative, policymaking, and representative organ of the United Nations. Each country, including the United States, has one vote. A two-thirds majority vote is required for decisions related to key issues such as peace and security, admission of new members, and the budget. A simple majority vote applies for all other matters.
The Assembly's annual regular session opens in September and runs for one year. The main part of the session, from September to December, includes most of the work of the Assembly's six committees. The annual meeting of heads of state and government, often referred to as the "general debate," is held at the beginning of the Assembly session. Selected Members of Congress generally serve as U.S. representatives during this period.
The concept of congressional representation to the UN General Assembly emerged from extensive participation by both Senators and Representatives in the 1945 San Francisco Conference on International Organization, which led to the adoption of the UN Charter. The practice began at the first Assembly session in 1946, when Members of the Senate and House held positions as representatives and alternate representatives, respectively. Since that time, with few exceptions, congressional representatives have served as part of U.S. delegations to the UN General Assembly, which are typically led and coordinated by the Department of State. Each year two Senators have alternated with two Representatives—with the Senate typically serving in years when the House holds elections. In most cases, both parties have been represented and, when possible, the Administration and Congress have aimed to select Members who have not previously served as delegates. (See Table 1
After the adoption of the UN Charter, Congress enacted the United Nations Participation Act of 1945 (UNPA; 22 U.S.C. 287 et seq.), which provides legislative authority for U.S. engagement in the United Nations. UNPA does not require congressional participation in sessions of the General Assembly, but anticipates and permits participation of Members of Congress, among other U.S. representatives, in such sessions. Section 2 of the act sets out the authorities for U.S. representation the United Nations. Specifically, Section 2(a) specifies that the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, shall designate not more than five U.S. representatives to attend a specified session or specified sessions of the General Assembly. UNPA does not specify whether Members are eligible to be appointed as U.S. representatives; however, Section 2(g) prohibits compensation for Members serving as U.S. representatives, signaling that Members might serve.
The role and duties of congressional representatives are not formalized; thus, the level and extent of congressional engagement during the Assembly session depends on the interests and priorities of individual Members. Delegates generally travel to New York at the beginning of the regular session. In the past, some Members have attended the general debate and the President's reception for visiting heads of state, while others have stayed for several additional days or returned for other parts of the Assembly session. Congressional representatives have also followed the activities of one of the General Assembly's six main committees, with at least one Member tracking the work of the fifth committee, which is responsible for administrative and budgetary matters related to the organization. Before or during the session, Members may also schedule appointments on policy issues of interest; these might include one-on-one visits with heads of state, foreign representatives, or UN officials.
Congressional representatives have often received support from congressional committee staff and State Department officials. For example, staff from the House Foreign Affairs Committee (HFAC) and Senate Foreign Relations Committee (SFRC) might write statements, provide background materials and briefings, or arrange meetings for Members. State Department officials have traditionally coordinated meetings and briefed Members on U.S. policy and key issues facing the Assembly. The Department also historically provided some Members with office space and services in the U.S. Mission to the United Nations in New York City.
As outlined in UNPA, the President, with the advice and consent of the Senate, may designate congressional representatives. In practice, SFRC has developed a policy of not holding hearings for temporary or part-time positions, including General Assembly representatives. Instead, both HFAC and SFRC have provided the President with their choices, who are nominated by the President and confirmed by vote of the full Senate, with some exceptions. For example, nominees for the 72nd (2017) and 73rd (2018) Assembly sessions were confirmed by the Senate by voice vote. From 2013 to 2016, however, it appears that while SFRC reported out nominees, the full Senate did not vote on the nominations and they were returned to the President pursuant to Senate Rule XXXI, paragraph 6. For the 74th (2019) and 75th (2020) sessions, President Trump did not transmit nominations to SFRC, and thus no committee or full Senate consideration took place. In each of those years, two Members of Congress served as representatives to the Assembly (except in 2020 due to COVID-19). During the Biden Administration, nominees were transmitted to the Senate from 2021 through 2024; Senators Leahy and Risch were confirmed in 2022, while the nominations in other years were returned to the President.
President Trump did not transmit nominations for the Assembly's 80th session in 2025. On September 22, 2025, Representative Sara Jacobs stated, "The Trump Administration has refused to send a bipartisan congressional delegation to the UN this year – blocking my official participation but not my Republican counterpart's." On September 23, Representative Young Kim stated that she was representing the United States at the 80th session. As noted previously, Senator Dave McCormick and Senator Jeanne Shaheen are serving as U.S. representatives to the 81st General Assembly session. The Trump Administration has not transmitted their nominations to the Senate.
Although both HFAC and SFRC have at different times documented procedures for selecting congressional representatives, in practice the process appears to be informal and has varied over time depending on the priorities and preferences of committee leadership.
House of Representatives. HFAC does not appear to have a formal process for selecting congressional representatives to the General Assembly. In past practice, it has assigned one Member from each political party on the basis of seniority, starting with those who have not served as representatives; however, HFAC members have increasingly selected participants based on the Member's level of interest in UN-related issues and availability to attend the session.
Senate. SFRC also does not appear to have a formal process for selecting congressional representatives to the Assembly. In practice, the chairperson and ranking member select the representatives, who are usually chosen from among SFRC members. Similar to the House, congressional representatives from the Senate appear to be selected based on their interest in UN issues and availability.
In accordance with the President's authority to appoint U.S. representatives to the UN General Assembly, the executive branch is responsible for sending a letter of invitation to the individual Member appointing him or her to the U.S. delegation. At the same time, it might customarily forward the names of the selected Members to the Senate for confirmation. The first public notice is usually a press statement from individual Members, a White House announcement, or a notice of intention to nominate as part of the Assembly delegation, subject to Senate confirmation.
The State Department has historically provided funding for U.S. representatives to the General Assembly, including per diem, transportation, and lodging expenses. These activities are typically financed through the Diplomatic Programs account, which funds the Office of International Conferences in the International Organization Affairs Bureau (IO/C). IO/C is responsible for accrediting, instructing, and managing U.S. delegates to multilateral conferences, including the General Assembly.
title: United Nations Issues: Congressional Representatives to the UN General Assembly

The Air Force Research Laboratory and Air Combat Command’s Experimental Operations Unit recently flew the XQ-67A Autonomous Collaborative Platform in the Nevada Test and Training Range marking a technology milestone in autonomous capabilities for the future fight.
The flight, which was completed under the Demonstration of ACP Performance and Effectiveness project, directly supports National Defense Strategy priorities for the Department of the Air Force by accelerating ACP development and delivery.
“By pairing AFRL’s rapid prototyping with ACC's operational test units, the Air Force is shortening the timeline between concept and warfighter capability,” said Col. Matthew Caspers, DAF Deputy Technology Executive Officer for Air.
During the flight, the XQ-67A demonstrated integration of several advanced mission systems, including state-of-the-art sensors, mission computers, and power and thermal management hardware, all designed to work collaboratively in demanding combat environments.
Additionally, the integration of Beyond Line-of-Sight datalinks and live, virtual and constructive simulations during the flight demonstrated management of uncrewed platforms across distributed theaters, bolstering deterrence through resilient, layered command and control.
“This proved that AFRL’s autonomous architectures, aligned with Autonomy and Agile Mission Suite Government Reference Architectures, can reliably process and relay combat-relevant data in real-world scenarios,” said Trenton White, aerospace engineer in AFRL’s Air Warfare directorate.
The research and development investment in unified platforms like the XQ-67A validates how uncrewed systems can extend the operational reach of crewed fighter formations. It provides solutions for equipping commanders with deep situational awareness and adding affordable operational mass to the fleet, all while significantly reducing risk to human aircrews.
About AFRL
The Air Force Research Laboratory is the Department of the Air Force’s primary scientific research and development center and one of six centers within Air Force Materiel Command. AFRL leads the discovery, development and delivery of technologies for air, space and multidomain operations. With a workforce spanning seven mission areas at more than 40 locations worldwide, AFRL conducts research ranging from basic science to advanced technology development. For more information, visit afresearchlab.com.
title: Air Force Research Laboratory completes flight of XQ-67A, advancing autonomous technology

LAREDO, Texas–U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Homeland Security Investigations, the Drug Enforcement Administration, and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Texas announced major enforcement results from Operation Southern Surge, a coordinated Homeland Security Task Force initiative targeting drug trafficking and other cross-border criminal activity.
At a Nov. 2 press conference at the Juarez-Lincoln International Bridge, officials highlighted the operation’s early results and reaffirmed their commitment to stopping dangerous narcotics, weapons, and illicit proceeds before they reach American communities.
Since Oct. 19, Operation Southern Surge has resulted in the seizure of more than 1,600 pounds of narcotics, 15 firearms, more than 3,000 rounds of ammunition, and over $360,000 in illicit currency. These enforcement actions have also led to 89 arrests.
Among the significant enforcement actions under Operation Southern Surge are:
Hidalgo Port of Entry - After a K-9 alert, officers discovered cylindrical packages hidden among a shipment of leeks. A total of 909 packages were discovered and tested positive for methamphetamine. The total weight of the narcotics was 1,082.47 pounds with a street value of $984,063.
Juarez-Lincoln Bridge - CBP officers recently referred a vehicle for secondary inspection. Using nonintrusive inspection technology and their training and experience, an anomaly was detected and officers discovered 49.3 pounds of cocaine concealed in 20 packages.
The officials present at the news conference reiterated that these numbers represent more than enforcement statistics and further reflect the commitment of CBP personnel and law enforcement partners to stop dangerous drugs, weapons, and criminal proceeds from entering our communities.
“Operation Southern Surge leverages tactical intelligence and coordinated enforcement actions to dismantle the trafficking infrastructure, intercept illicit supply chains, and bolster situational awareness across the southwest border,” said Director Jennifer De La O of the Laredo Field Office, Office of Field Operations. “International drug trafficking presents a direct threat to U.S. national security, public safety and economic stability and our partnerships are a force multiplier in detecting these crimes and protecting the public.”
“Securing the border requires more than making seizures or stopping a single smuggling attempt. HSI’s role is to follow the evidence, identify the people behind these crimes, and dismantle the organizations moving drugs, weapons, money, and people across the border,” said Acting Deputy Special Agent in Charge Charles Kerby, HSI Laredo. “Through the Homeland Security Task Force, we are working closely with CBP, DEA, the FBI, and our law enforcement partners to hold these criminal networks accountable and protect communities across the country.”
Under the leadership of President Donald J. Trump and Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, the dedicated men and women of U.S. Customs and Border Protection, alongside our law enforcement partners and with the support of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF), are combating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and drug trafficking networks.
The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership that coordinates law enforcement efforts to identify, investigate, and prosecute these organizations and the crimes they commit in the United States and abroad. The HSTF prioritizes combating child trafficking and other crimes involving children, while supporting efforts to investigate, prosecute, and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States.
Click here for more photos of Operation Southern Surge.
title: CBP, HSI, DEA, USAO in Coordination with the Homeland Security Task Force Tout Successes of Major Drug, Weapons and Cash Seizures in Operation Southern Surge

WASHINGTON — Today, Ambassador Jamieson Greer issued a statement following President Trump notifying Congress and the governments of Rwanda and South Africa of his intent to terminate these countries from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) trade preference program, as of January 1, 2027.
“The Office of the United States Trade Representative led the annual interagency review of sub-Saharan African countries’ eligibility for the AGOA trade preference program. Based on the review, President Trump found that the governments of Rwanda and South Africa are engaging in practices that are inconsistent with AGOA’s eligibility criteria,” said Ambassador Greer. “These concerning and pervasive practices include, but are not limited to, barriers that undermine American trade and investment and practices that pose a threat to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests in the region. The Trump Administration is working to ensure our African partners take the necessary steps to meet the eligibility criteria.”
Background:
In Rwanda, the Trump Administration is deeply concerned by the following issues: trade and investment barriers, rule of law, political pluralism, internationally recognized worker rights, human rights, and threats to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. In South Africa, the Trump Administration is deeply concerned by barriers to U.S. trade and investment, corruption, and threats to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.
###
title: Ambassador Greer Issues Statement on President Trump’s Intent to Terminate Rwanda and South Africa from the AGOA Trade Preference Program
