Labor Leaders Press Trump Administration on Union-Busting Consultants’ and Corporations’ Compliance with Federal Law
WASHINGTON – Today, House labor leaders demanded information from Office of Labor-Management Standards (OLMS) Director Elisabeth Messenger on whether corporations and their union-busting consultants comply with federal transparency requirements.
The letter was sent by House Education and Workforce Committee Ranking Member Robert C. “Bobby” Scott (VA-03), Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions (HELP) Ranking Member Mark DeSaulnier (CA-10), and Education and Workforce Member Rep. Summer L. Lee (PA-12).
Too often, when workers exercise their right to organize a union, corporations and bosses hire outside consultants to wage anti-union campaigns. Over the last several decades, union-avoidance has become a multi-billion-dollar industry. The latest analysis found that companies spend approximately $1.7 billion every year, including nearly $500 million on union-busting consultants, to break their organizing drives. Some consultants are reportedly paid $500 per hour or $4,000 per day for their services.
Under the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act (LMRDA), employers and consultants are required to file public reports about their matter because it allows workers to see how much their bosses are spending to influence their decision to unionize. However, for decades, employers and union-busting consultants have routinely failed to meet this requirement, allowing bosses and their consultants to operate in the shadows. Under the Trump Administration, the problem is only becoming worse. A recent watchdog report found that, as of August 8, 2026, nearly 60 percent of employers required to file a disclosure in 2025 have still not submitted their reports—the largest year-over-year decline on record.
“Over the last several years, while worker organizing has skyrocketed, employers have increasingly responded with hostile anti-union campaigns, including by hiring well-compensated outside consultants. As more employers seek to quash their workers’ unionization drives, it is imperative that employer and consultant disclosure requirements under the LMRDA are robustly enforced by OLMS, so workers have a complete picture of who is attempting to influence their decision as they exercise their right to organize,” wrote the Members.
To determine whether OLMS is effectively carrying out its responsibility to enforce the LMRDA, the Members requested a response to their extensive questions by no later than November 16, 2026.

WASHINGTON – Edward Allen Anderson, 40, a previously convicted “armed career criminal” residing in the District, was sentenced today in U.S. District Court to 135 months in prison in connection with illegally possessing a loaded firearm, a Glock Model 25 9mm pistol with an obliterated serial number that police found in the back of his car, announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro.

Anderson, aka “Man Man,” pleaded guilty July 2 before U.S. District Judge Timothy J. Kelly to a single count of unlawful possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. In addition to the 135‑month prison term, Judge Kelly ordered Anderson to serve three years of supervised release.

According to court documents, on Sept. 15, 2023, Metropolitan Police Department officers observed a Volkswagen Touareg with Virginia tags parked in the 700 block of Otis Place NW. During a plain view check of vehicles on the block, an officer saw a firearm on the rear passenger floorboard of the Touareg.

Officers recovered a Glock Model 25 9mm handgun from the Touareg. The serial number had been scratched off or obliterated. The gun was loaded with one round in the chamber and 16 rounds in an extended magazine.

The vehicle was registered to Anderson, and officers found mail addressed to him inside. DNA analysis linked the firearm to Anderson.

Anderson was prohibited from possessing any firearm because he had previously been convicted of a drug felony punishable by more than one year in prison.

The investigation was conducted by the Metropolitan Police Department.

The matter was prosecuted under the Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful initiative by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nihar Mohanty. Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful is a law enforcement initiative in support of President Trump’s Executive Order to crack down on gun violence, prioritize federal firearms violations, pursue tougher penalties, and seek detention for federal firearms violators.

MACON, Ga. – A Central Georgia woman faces up to 30 years in prison for altering hundreds of thousands of dollars in stolen checks and posting them for sale on social media.

“This case marks the second federal prosecution by our office in just a matter of days involving defendants accused of stealing checks from the mail and exploiting hardworking citizens and small businesses for personal gain,” said U.S. Attorney William R. “Will” Keyes. “Our office remains committed to working with our law enforcement partners to identify, investigate, and prosecute those who prey on the public.”

“This case demonstrates our dedication to safeguarding the integrity of the nation's mail system. Our collaboration with our law enforcement partners to combat mail theft serves as a force multiplier in conducting these types of investigations,” said Jonathan Ulrich, Special Agent in Charge, U.S. Postal Service Office of Inspector General. “If you abuse the Postal Service and exploit the public’s trust for personal gain then you will be held accountable.”

Mikela Kendrick, 24, of Byron, Georgia, pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit bank fraud before U.S. District Judge C. Ashley Royal on Oct. 29. Kendrick faces a maximum sentence of 30 years in prison, to be followed by five years of supervised release, and a maximum fine of $1 million. The sentencing date will be determined by the court. There is no parole in the federal system.

According to court documents and statements made in court, Kendrick and another individual obtained numerous checks stolen from the mail between August 2024 and September 2025. They then completed a process known as “check washing,” in which information on stolen checks, including the payee’s name and dollar amount, was removed and altered.

Kendrick advertised the stolen and altered checks for sale through her social media account. In one exchange with a prospective buyer, she stated that she typically sold checks in bundles, offering three checks for $600. Each check carried a face value of at least $10,000. A review of images of stolen checks posted to Kendrick's social media account showed she possessed checks totaling at least $299,789.57.

On Sept. 4, 2025, law enforcement executed a search warrant at Kendrick's residence and recovered 112 stolen personal and business checks, money orders, and cashier's checks. Investigators also found blank check stock, bank cards, and identification cards bearing different names. Additionally, officers seized items commonly used in check-washing schemes, including ink cartridges, cotton swabs with ink stains, antifreeze, water-removal products, printers, and computer devices.

The total face value of the 112 stolen checks was $395,101.43, with individual checks ranging from $5 to $155,408.81. The checks belonged to various payees and with accounts at federally insured and chartered financial institutions.

During an approximately three-week period in August 2025, at least four stolen and altered checks, each valued at $1,000, were deposited into Kendrick's checking account. In addition, a $17,550 check that had been stolen and altered by Kendrick was deposited into her account.

The case was investigated by the U.S. Postal Service Office of Inspector General (USPS-OIG), the Monroe County Sheriff's Office, the Bibb County Sheriff's Office, and the Warner Robins Police Department, with assistance from the Centerville Police Department.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Elizabeth Howard is prosecuting the case for the Government.
title: Central Georgian Faces 30 Years in Prison for Stolen Check-Washing Scheme

BOSTON – A Rockland man was sentenced today in federal court in Boston for conspiring to distribute fentanyl following a series of controlled drug purchases in Brookline and Boston.

Kerry Charlotin, a/k/a “KG,” 36, of Rockland, was sentenced by U.S. District Court Judge Leo T. Sorokin to 88 months in prison, to be followed by four years of supervised release. In July 2026 , Charlotin pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to distribute fentanyl. Charlotin was arrested and charged in December 2025 along with co-conspirator Shaquylle Burden.

In June 2025, an investigation began into drug trafficking activities conducted by Charlotin and his co-conspirator Burden. The investigation revealed that the defendants were actively trafficking significant quantities of fentanyl and other controlled substances in the greater Boston area.

On various dates in 2025, Charlotin coordinated with Burden and met repeatedly with a federal cooperating witness to conduct controlled sales of fentanyl. During the course of the investigation, Charlotin and Burden sold more than 280 grams of fentanyl, along with other controlled substances.

Following the controlled purchases, search warrants were executed in December 2025, including of Charlotin’s person after he was located and arrested in South Carolina, and at multiple residences in Massachusetts. During the searches, additional cocaine base, a loaded 9mm pistol and approximately 131.5 grams of cocaine were recovered. The cocaine was packaged in plastic bags that had been unsuccessfully attempted to be flushed down a toilet. One firearm was also recovered from Burden’s Roslindale residence at the time of his arrest.

At the time of these offenses, Charlotin was serving a term of supervised release following a prior federal conviction for being a felon in possession of a firearm and ammunition, for which he had previously served a five-year federal prison sentence.

Burden was sentenced to five years in prison for his role in the conspiracy on Oct. 19, 2026 .

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley; Ted E. Docks, Special Agent in Charge of the Federal Bureau of Investigation in Boston; and Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox made the announcement today. Valuable assistance was provided by the FBI’s Columbia Field Office in South Carolina. Assistant U.S. Attorney John T. Dawley of the Organized Crime & Gang Unit is prosecuting the case.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations, and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.
title: Rockland Man Sentenced to More Than Seven Years in Prison for Drug Conspiracy

text:
Title III of the Trade Act of 1974 (Sections 301-310, 19 U.S.C. §§2411-2420), titled "Relief from Unfair Trade Practices," is often collectively referred to as "Section 301." Under Section 301, Congress grants the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) a range of responsibilities and authorities to investigate and take action (e.g., impose a tariff) to enforce U.S. rights under trade agreements or respond to certain foreign trade practices. As of October 2026, the second Trump Administration has initiated six investigations; four are ongoing and two investigations were completed in June 2026 (see Table 1th Congress could consider whether to urge or require the Administration to limit or expand its use of Section 301. Congress could also consider whether the use of Section 301 to investigate and impose tariffs on multiple trading partners is consistent with Congress's intent for the authorities granted by Section 301.
Section 301 investigations determine if the rights of the United States under any trade agreement are being denied, or an act, policy, or practice of a foreign government is burdening or restricting U.S. commerce. The statute defines "commerce" to include services and investment.
Initiation. Any interested person may file a petition with USTR requesting that the agency initiate an investigation under Section 301. USTR must determine whether to initiate an investigation within 45 days. USTR also may "self-initiate" a case. The statute requires that USTR publish notice of an investigation in the Federal Register and provide opportunity for public comment and hearing.
Administration. Section 301 investigations are conducted by a "Section 301 Committee," established in 15 C.F.R. §2002.3 as a subordinate, staff-level body of the USTR-led, interagency Trade Policy Staff Committee (TPSC). The Section 301 Committee reviews petitions, conducts public hearings, and makes recommendations to the TPSC regarding potential actions under Section 301. USTR bases its decision on recommendations provided by the TPSC.
Consultations. USTR is required to request consultations with the foreign government at the initiation of an investigation. If consultations do not result in a mutually acceptable outcome, USTR is required to request formal dispute settlement proceedings under a governing trade agreement, if applicable.
Determination and Implementation. Following consultations, USTR is to conduct an investigation to determine if the statutory criteria for action are met and, if so, what action, if any, to take. Section 301 divides actions into mandatory and discretionary categories. If USTR concludes there is a violation of a trade agreement or that an act, policy, or practice of a foreign government is "unjustifiable" and "burdens or restricts" U.S. commerce, responsive action is mandatory. If USTR determines that an act, policy, or practice of a foreign government is "unreasonable or discriminatory" and "burdens or restricts" U.S. commerce, action is discretionary. Section 301 specifies that USTR make a determination 12 months after an investigation begins for cases not involving a trade agreement or for "Special 301" cases involving countries identified as "priority foreign countries" for "onerous or egregious" violations against intellectual property rights.
Action. To remedy a foreign trade practice, Section 301 authorizes USTR to (1) impose tariffs or other import restrictions, (2) withdraw or suspend trade agreement concessions, and (3) enter into a binding agreement with the foreign government either to cease the conduct in question or compensate the United States. USTR must prioritize tariffs if it opts for import restrictions. Mandatory actions must "affect goods or services of the foreign country in an amount that is equivalent in value to the burden or restriction being imposed by that country on" U.S. commerce. The statute requires USTR to give interested persons an opportunity to comment on proposed actions. Section 301 does not specify a tariff exclusion process.
Subsequent Actions. Section 301 specifies requirements for monitoring, modifying, and terminating actions. USTR must report to Congress the reasons for any modification or termination of an action. Under Section 301, foreign noncompliance is considered a violation of a trade agreement and subject to mandatory action. Section 301 actions terminate after four years, unless USTR receives a request for continuation and conducts a review of the case. In some instances, USTR may reinstate a previously terminated Section 301 action.
From the establishment of the World Trade Organization (WTO) in 1995 until the first Trump Administration, the United States used Section 301 primarily to build cases and pursue dispute settlement at the WTO. The first Trump Administration initiated six investigations under Section 301. The expanded use of the authority was part of a trade strategy that emphasized unilateral action and tariff actions by the United States after decades of multilateral coordination on tariff-setting through U.S. participation in free trade agreements and the WTO.
The Biden and second Trump Administrations have continued to utilize Section 301 to investigate foreign trade practices and impose tariff actions. USTR has initiated six investigations during the second Trump Administration. In July 2025, USTR began an investigation into Brazil's practices related to digital trade and electronic payment services, ethanol market access, and other issues. USTR concluded this investigation in June 2026, finding that the acts, policies, and practices of Brazil at issue are actionable under Section 301 and implementing a 25% tariff with exemptions for certain goods in July 2026.
In March 2026, following a February U.S. Supreme Court decision invalidating tariffs imposed by the second Trump Administration under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), USTR initiated two investigations under Section 301 into the practices of dozens of countries related to excess industrial capacity and action on forced labor on an "accelerated timeframe." USTR may seek to utilize the findings of these investigations to impose a regime of country-specific tariffs similar in scope to the global tariffs imposed under IEEPA in 2025. USTR concluded the investigation into action on forced labor in June 2025, imposing a 10% tariff for economies it found have failed to enforce an import ban on products made with forced labor and a 12.5% tariff on economies that it found do not impose such a ban with exemptions for certain goods. USTR finalized that tariff action in July 2026, when a 10% tariff imposed in February 2026 under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 expired. The second Trump Administration has also initiated investigations into the People's Republic of China's (PRC's or China's) implementation of the U.S.-China "Phase One" deal (see "2017 Investigation into PRC Practices"), intellectual property protection in Vietnam, and underpayment for pharmaceuticals in Germany.
In 2024, the Biden Administration initiated three investigations under Section 301 that were completed in 2025. In each case, USTR determined the policies under investigation were actionable under Section 301 but did not take actions that would immediately increase tariffs or other import restrictions. Investigations into labor and human rights practices and the rule of law in Nicaragua and PRC policies in the semiconductor industry, both initiated in 2024, found actionable conduct under Section 301 in 2025 but resulted in no immediate additional tariffs. An investigation into PRC shipping and shipbuilding practices, initiated in 2024, resulted in a January 2025 finding by the Biden Administration that PRC practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce, but proposed port fees and tariffs were suspended in 2025.
The first Trump Administration initiated an investigation into PRC practices related to forced technology transfer, intellectual property rights, and innovation in 2017. In 2018, USTR imposed four rounds of tariffs ranging from 7.5% to 25% on around $370 billion worth of U.S. imports from China; China retaliated with tariffs on $100 billion worth of U.S. goods. The two sides negotiated the "Phase One" deal, concluded in 2020, to address U.S. concerns. In 2024, USTR concluded the statutory four-year review of Section 301 actions and their impact on the U.S. economy. USTR maintained existing tariffs and increased tariffs on certain products (e.g., electric vehicles). In May 2026, USTR initiated a second four-year review.
Congress may debate whether to maintain, limit, or expand the scope of the authority it has delegated under Section 301 or whether to urge or require the Administration to pursue additional investigations or otherwise modify or review its use of Section 301. Some Members in the 119th Congress have called on the Administration to utilize Section 301 to investigate foreign drug pricing or seafood practices. Other Members have introduced legislation to require notification to and review by Congress of tariffs imposed (e.g., H.R. 2665/S. 1272). The 119th Congress could also consider whether the broad use of Section 301 to simultaneously investigate dozens of U.S. trading partners and potentially impose a broad-based tariff regime is in line with the way Congress intended the authorities to be used. Congress may also consider the effectiveness of Section 301 actions in deterring certain foreign trade practices or the impact of tariff actions on the U.S. economy. For example, H.R. 2287 calls for a study by the Federal Reserve on the impact of tariffs on prices. The 117th Congress directed the U.S. International Trade Commission to study the impact on the U.S. economy of Section 301 tariffs in a joint explanatory statement accompanying P.L. 117-103. Previous congressional efforts related to Section 301 were related to establishing a formal product exclusion process (e.g., 117th Cong., §73001 in S. 1260).
title: Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974

Washington, D.C. — Today, Rep. Robert Garcia, Ranking Member of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, demanded answers from Secretary of State Marco Rubio after the Trump Administration allegedly helped bring Flávio Bolsonaro, a Brazilian politician under investigation for money laundering and corruption, into the United States.
“Donald Trump appears to have no problem pulling out all the stops for a far-right Brazilian politician who lost his election and is under investigation for corruption. Secretary Rubio should send Bolsonaro home to face justice and fully explain why this Administration helped bring him here. We are demanding answers,” said Ranking Member Robert Garcia.
In the letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Ranking Member Garcia wrote, “While President Trump uses ICE as his personal police force to terrorize kids and hardworking people trying to support their families and communities, he has bent over backwards to bring to the U.S. Flávio Bolsonaro, a disgraced Brazilian politician under investigation for money laundering, corruption, and other serious crimes. If the President claims he doesn’t want criminals to come to the U.S., why allow Mr. Bolsonaro entry? Trump Administration officials’ ties to Mr. Bolsonaro—including your own—cast doubt on the motives for giving him such special treatment. The fact that Vice President Vance’s former firm has connections to one of the ongoing criminal investigations raises further questions about political considerations in this process. You should immediately return Mr. Bolsonaro to Brazil to face justice and be prepared to explain why the Trump Administration is welcoming a corrupt politician and government official fleeing accountability into our country while terrorizing Americans and lawful residents of the U.S. that you have falsely labeled as criminals.”
In September 2026, Ranking Member Robert Garcia demanded answers from Secretary Rubio and Attorney General Todd Blanche after they allegedly helped white collar criminal Alejandro Betancourt lead the Trump Administration’s unprecedented scheme to take an ownership stake in a Venezuelan oil company.
In August 2025, Ranking Member Garcia demanded answers following reports that President Trump and Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele entered into a secret, backdoor deal that resulted in America’s release of dangerous MS-13 leaders back to El Salvador.

WASHINGTON – The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) kicks off Critical Infrastructure and Resilience Month today, recognizing the systems and assets that keep the country running as well as the people who operate them. This year’s Critical Infrastructure Security and Resilience Month aligns with President Trump’s National Resilience Strategy and comes as we continue to see new and evolving threats, including those driven by rapid advances in technology like super intelligence. Through it all, we rely on frontline operators who keep essential services moving even when things are disrupted.
“Our work depends on people who understand their systems and stay prepared,” said Acting CISA Director Nick Andersen. “Resilience comes from knowing what matters most and having a plan you can actually use when something goes wrong.”
All month, CISA will highlight four practices that help infrastructure owners and operators stay prepared:
- Know your most important systems and the outside services they depend on
- Understand the risks that matter most to your organization
- Make clear plans that guide response and recovery
- Track progress and update plans based on real lessons learned
As threats continue to emerge, it’s imperative that everyone does their part to be more resilient. Strong resilience in critical infrastructure helps protect lives and jobs, keeps communities connected, and reduces disruptions. Critical Infrastructure Security and Resilience Month empowers American industry, state and local governments, and the Federal Government to each do their part to protect our nation’s security, prosperity, and freedom.
Organizations can participate in Critical Infrastructure Security and Resilience Month with CISA’s toolkit, which includes graphics and plain language text that organizations can use to show the steps they are taking this November to be more resilient.
###
About CISA
As the nation’s cyber defense agency and national coordinator for critical infrastructure security, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency leads the national effort to manage, uncover, and reduce risk to our digital and physical infrastructure Americans rely on every hour of every day.
Visit CISA.gov for more information and follow us on X, Facebook, LinkedIn, Instagram.
title: CISA Kicks Off Critical Infrastructure Security and Resilience Month 2026

PHILADELPHIA – FEMA will evaluate a Biennial Radiological Emergency Preparedness Exercise at the Salem & Hope Creek Nuclear Generating Stations. The exercise will occur during the week of Nov. 16, 2026, to assess and improve the ability of the state of Delaware to respond to an emergency at the nuclear facility.
“These drills are held every other year to evaluate government’s ability to protect public health and safety,” said Andre C. McCoy, Regional Administrator for FEMA Region 3. “We will assess state and local government emergency response capabilities within the 10-mile Emergency Planning Zone and the 50-mile Ingestion Pathway Zone in the state of Delaware.”
Within 90 days, FEMA will send its evaluation to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission for use in licensing decisions. The final report will be available to the public approximately 120 days after the exercise.
FEMA will present preliminary findings of the exercise during a public meeting at 12:30 pm EST on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026. Planned speakers include representatives from FEMA and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. The meeting will take place in-person at:
SpringHill Suites by Marriott Frederica
208 Dominus Drive 
Frederica, DE 19946
At the public meeting, FEMA may request that questions or comments be submitted in writing for review and response. Written comments may also be submitted after the meeting by emailing FEMAR3NewsDesk@fema.dhs.gov or by mail to:
Andre C. McCoy, Regional Administrator
FEMA Region 3
615 Chestnut Street, 6th Floor
Philadelphia, PA  19106
FEMA created the Radiological Emergency Preparedness Program to ensure that residents living near commercial nuclear power plants would be adequately protected in the event of a nuclear power plant accident. The program also helps inform and educate the public about radiological emergency preparedness.
Radiological Emergency Preparedness Program responsibilities cover only “offsite” activities: state and local government emergency planning and preparedness activities that take place beyond the nuclear power plant boundaries. Onsite activities continue to be the responsibility of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
Additional information on FEMA’s Radiological Emergency Preparedness Program is available online at FEMA.gov/Radiological-Emergency-Preparedness-Program.

PICATINNY ARSENAL, N.J. - With decades of fuze experience and knowhow at risk of disappearing as engineers begin to transition out, the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM) Armaments Center has stepped up to the task of readying the workforce.
Between Monday, Oct. 19 and Friday, Oct. 23, the Armaments Center hosted a course related to munition fuzes for 30 business professionals from small and big business alike. Taught by Senior Fuze Subject Matter Expert Tom Emanski, Acting Army Fuze Management Office Chief Sandy Picinic, Army Fuze Safety Review Board Executive Secretary Briar Ostar-Exel and Armaments Center Fuze Division Engineer Lam Vo, the course provided an open forum for engineers to examine the fundamentals of fuze design, safety philosophies, operational environments and emerging threats, while engaging directly with the experts who help shape military safety standards and evaluations. Fuzes, being the component in a munition that decides when and under what conditions the warhead should function, are a critical component in munitions directly responsible for providing both safety to the warfighter and down range lethality.
According to Emanski, the course was conceived after industrial partners repeatedly signaled how few options there were to learn about fuzing in academia. The field is very rarely taught in traditional academic programs, so many professionals must learn the fundamentals on the job, and while the Armaments Center’s Armament Graduate School (AGS) does have a fuze elective, it is only open to students at the school, making it difficult to preserve knowledge as prior subject matter experts in industry begin to retire. Built from the elective, the course provided training to help both new hires and established professionals develop a shared foundation on fuzes and pass their knowledge forward.
The National Armaments Consortium helped advertise, process applications and coordinate logistics, and Emanski, Picinic and Vo signed on as instructors as they already supported a related elective at AGS. Though the course was planned for some time, it only took about nine weeks to screen applicants and select attendees, Emanski said. The course was capped to 30 students to preserve interactive two-way discussion and deep learning, as any larger would approach a lecture.
“It’s to help as a starting point to understand this very unique item called ‘fuze’, which plays a critical role in our munitions,” noted Picinic.
During the course, attendees received a basic overview of fuzes, delved into the fundamentals of fuze safety design architectures and environments, discussed hand-placed ordnance, target detection, among other topics. The syllabus also addressed the ever-changing landscape of unmanned systems, in which fuzes are a quintessential component, and explained both electronic and mechanical aspects.
“Fuzes are on just about every munition out there. It’s challenging to teach a course when there’s so many use cases,” said Emanski. “Each fuze for every commodity item is different, so we’re teaching a course where there are many different examples, use cases and CONOPs (concepts of operation).”
The students themselves came from both small and large businesses; some had a decade of experience with fuzes, while others had never touched one before. This spectrum of experience, alongside the wide variety in business backgrounds, led to meaningful engagement throughout the week.
“My group designs and builds seekers and tracking missile interceptors. We're expanding our capabilities, and this was an area identified as a key gap where we wanted to deepen our expertise,” said Boeing Integrated Air and Missile Defense engineer Erik Stein.
Several students noted not only the broad omnibus, but how different the course was from what they expected. Falcata AI Engineer Adam Tuck showed surprise at spending a full day talking about interrupted fuzes, which use purely mechanical components to keep the fuze from setting a munition off too early, and non-interrupted fuzes, which use electronics. Wild West Systems Chief Engineer of Munitions and Energetics John Granier called the discussion about balancing cost and safety “fascinating,” while TETAC Incorporated Chief Executive Officer Mark Benson noted the section on fuze safety boards and how it humanized a force usually unseen.
Participants praised the course universally for offering information otherwise not available to industry and expressed hope that a similar course would be offered again in the future.
“I think a lot of the reason why this is so niche is that there’s no awareness of this at the collegiate level. It’d be cool, now that we’re opening this up to industry, if that eventually bleeds down to universities and maybe gets more people interested earlier on rather than as we go through our careers. I didn’t know what a fuze was when I started,” said Day and Zimmermann Munitions Director of Business Development Christopher Stemple.
According to Emanski, there have already been inquiries from industry members about when the Armaments Center can offer the course again in the future. Seeing the success of the course, the Armaments Center has already started working with NAC representatives and industry to expand the course offering in 2027.
title: Armaments Center hosts first industry fuzing course to preserve critical expertise

Comisionado Residente presenta comentarios sobre las reglas propuestas para el Censo 2030 y su impacto en Puerto Rico
Los comentarios profundizan en las preocupaciones expresadas por el Comisionado Residente al firmar, junto a otros miembros del Congreso, una carta el 30 de octubre que solicitó retirar la propuesta.
Caguas, Puerto Rico — El Comisionado Residente Pablo José Hernández presentó comentarios ante el Negociado del Censo de Estados Unidos para advertir sobre los posibles efectos de las reglas propuestas para el Censo 2030 en la contabilización de la población de Puerto Rico y de las comunidades puertorriqueñas en Estados Unidos.
El 30 de octubre, Hernández firmó junto a otros miembros del Congreso una carta dirigida al Negociado del Censo en la que expresaron su oposición a la propuesta y solicitaron su retiro. La comunicación planteó preocupaciones sobre los nuevos criterios de residencia, el uso de récords administrativos y las restricciones a la recopilación de información sobre raza, origen étnico y orientación sexual. En sus comentarios específicos sobre Puerto Rico, el Comisionado Residente detalla cómo estos cambios podrían afectar el conteo de nuestra población.
“Nos preocupa que esta propuesta limite la información demográfica esencial que se recopila sobre nuestra población. Sin datos precisos, se hace más difícil identificar las necesidades de nuestras comunidades y priorizar lo básico: los servicios, los recursos y la atención que nuestra gente necesita. Por eso, me opuse a esta regla y solicité su retiro”, expresó el Comisionado Residente.
Entre sus señalamientos, Hernández advierte que utilizar únicamente récords contributivos federales podría excluir a residentes bona fide de Puerto Rico que no tienen obligación de radicar una planilla federal. Por ello, plantea considerar también información del Departamento de Hacienda, incluidos los formularios W-2PR. Asimismo, señala que los sistemas automatizados podrían dejar fuera hogares en comunidades rurales cuyas direcciones no siguen los formatos convencionales.
Los comentarios también cuestionan las posibles restricciones a las preguntas sobre raza y origen hispano, cuya información permite identificar a las comunidades puertorriqueñas dentro y fuera de la Isla. Además, señalan la importancia de considerar los movimientos de personas entre Puerto Rico y los estados para evitar que sean omitidas o contadas incorrectamente.
La importancia de un conteo preciso queda reflejada en los resultados de 2020. Según el propio Negociado del Censo, en el Censo de 2020 se estima que aproximadamente 217,000 residentes de Puerto Rico, equivalentes al 7.1% de la población estimada en hogares, fueron omitidos del conteo.
Los datos del Censo ayudan al Gobierno de Puerto Rico a planificar los servicios que necesitan los municipios y las comunidades, revisar los distritos legislativos y administrar programas federales. Por eso, Hernández plantea que las reglas del Censo 2030 deben evitar que Puerto Rico y su población queden insuficientemente representados en la información oficial.

Tallahassee, Florida — The Department of Justice’s Office on Violence Against Women has awarded a $400,000 federal grant to Florida State University to support on-campus approaches to combat domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking. United States Attorney John P. Heekin highlighted the recently announced award following the conclusion of Domestic Violence Awareness Month that took place during October 2026.

U.S. Attorney John P. Heekin said: “October was Domestic Violence Awareness Month, but our efforts to provide safety, dignity, and justice to victims and survivors of domestic violence continue year-round. Through this critical investment of federal grant monies, we provide vital resources to FSU’s on-campus programs that ensure victim safety and assistance while holding offenders accountable. Together, we can put an end to domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking on campus.”

The award, paid through the Office on Violence Against Women Fiscal Year 2025 Grants to Reduce Domestic Violence, Dating Violence, Sexual Assault, and Stalking On Campus Program, provides institutions of higher education the resources to establish multidisciplinary approaches to combat domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking on campuses. The Campus Program supports comprehensive approaches designed to enhance victim services (including legal services), implement prevention and education programs, and develop and strengthen security and investigation strategies to prevent, prosecute, and respond to domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Florida is committed to prosecuting those who violate federal laws, collaborating with local & campus law enforcement, and ensuring victims have access to the resources they need. By understanding the signs of abuse and connecting victims to resources, we can all play a role in creating safer communities. For more information on domestic violence or to access resources, please visit https://www.justice.gov/ovw/domestic-violence .

The Department of Justice funds essential victim services through its grantmaking. Grantees of OVW and the Department’s Office for Victims of Crime (OVC) run programs that support victims in the aftermath of domestic violence. There is help available, including the National Domestic Violence Hotline, 1-800-799-SAFE (7233), and the Strong Hearts Native Helpline, 1-844-7NATIVE (762-8483). In addition, OVW’s Resources for Victims and Survivors webpage lists national hotlines as well as state, territorial, and Tribal domestic violence and sexual assault coalitions that can direct victims to local resources and services, as well as opportunities to get involved.

The United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Florida is one of 94 offices that serve as the nation’s principal litigators under the direction of the Attorney General. To access public court documents online, please visit the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida website. For more information about the United States Attorney’s Office, Northern District of Florida, visit https://www.justice.gov/usao-ndfl .
title: Justice Department Awards FSU Federal Grant to Combat Domestic Violence, Dating Violence, Sexual Assault, & Stalking on Campus

Operation Guardian arrested more than 230 illegal aliens, including more than 40 CDL holders in 72 hours
WASHINGTON – On Monday, United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin hosted a press conference in Oklahoma to announce the results of Operation Guardian, a three-day operation that arrested hundreds of illegal aliens, including dozens with commercial driver’s licenses (CDLs).
Operation Guardian was conducted by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and state and local partners from October 26 to October 28. Spanning 15 states, the operation targeted illegal aliens with unauthorized CDLs and other public safety threats in the trucking industry. The operation resulted in the arrests of more than 230 illegal aliens, including more than 40 CDL holders.
The press conference was held at the headquarters of Melton Truck Lines, in Tulsa, Oklahoma. Secretary Mullin was joined by Melton Truck Lines CEO Bob Peterson, Melton Truck Lines President Robert Ragan, Senior Advisor Richard Schroyer, ICE Assistant Director Russell Hott, Oklahoma Department of Public Safety Commissioner Tim Tipton, Colonel Freeman Martin of the Texas Department of Public Safety, and Colonel Joe Williams of the Oklahoma Highway Patrol. Prior to the press conference, Secretary Mullin participated in a closed-door roundtable with the press conference’s attendees.
“Thanks to the hardworking patriots of ICE, and our state and local partners, Operation Guardian was an incredible success. In just three days, we arrested more than 230 illegal aliens, including over 40 illegal aliens with commercial driver’s licenses, across 15 states,” said Secretary Mullin.“Operation Guardian proves how federal and local law enforcement can work together to get threats like these off of our roadways and protect the homeland. Since day one, President Trump promised to Make American Roads Safe Again, and he continues to deliver for the American people. Our roads are safer with these illegal aliens no longer behind the wheels of semi-trucks.”
In one notable arrest during Operation Guardian on October 26, the Oklahoma Highway Patrol stopped a vehicle on I-35 after they observed the driver looking down at his cell phone while driving. After a registration check revealed that the vehicle had been reported stolen in Texas, the trooper attempted to arrest the driver, Luis Armando Garlo Rodriguez, an illegal alien from Honduras. Rodriguez resisted arrest and broke the trooper’s arm before fleeing on foot. Additional officers tracked him down and arrested him. ICE's Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Tulsa has filed charges against Rodriguez for assaulting, resisting, and impeding certain officers or employees.
The next day, on October 27, the Oklahoma Highway Patrol stopped a vehicle on I-40 and determined that all seven occupants were illegal aliens, including an unaccompanied child (UAC). The driver was Arturo Alvarado-Islas, an illegal alien from Mexico, who illegally entered the United States at an unknown date and location. Alvarado-Islas was turned over to ICE custody the same day.
Arturo Alvarado-Islas
The states which participated in Operation Guardian were Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Indiana, Iowa, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Tennessee, and Texas.
This operation is a part of the Trump Administration’s broader nationwide crackdown on illegal aliens with CDLs:
- On September 25, 2026, ICE launched Operation Guardrail, a nationwide operation targeting commercial vehicles operating in violation of U.S. laws. As of October 29, ICE has arrested 303 aliens through Operation Guardrail.
- From January 20, 2025 to October 28, 2026, ICE has made 4,795 CDL-related arrests nationwide and 1,233 arrests involving CDL holders.

title: Secretary Mullin Announces Results of Operation Guardian Crackdown on Illegal Aliens with Commercial Driver’s Licenses

text: St. Thomas, USVI –United States Attorney Adam Sleeper announced today that Assistant United States Attorney Erik Tate has been appointed to serve as the District Election Officer and, in that capacity, will be responsible for overseeing the District’s handling of election day complaints related to voting rights concerns, threats of violence to election officials or staff, and election fraud. The Department of Justice has an important role in deterring and combatting discrimination and intimidation at the polls, threats of violence directed at election officials and poll workers, and election fraud and will address these violations wherever they occur. The Department’s longstanding Election Day Program furthers these goals and seeks to ensure public confidence in the electoral process by providing local points of contact within the Department for the public to report possible federal election law violations. “Every citizen must be free to cast his or her vote without interference or discrimination,” United States Attorney Sleeper said. “The Department of Justice will work tirelessly to protect the integrity of the election process.” Federal law protects against such crimes as threatening violence against election officials or staff, intimidating or bribing voters, buying and selling votes, impersonating voters, altering vote tallies, voting by non-citizens, stuffing ballot boxes, and marking ballots for voters against their wishes or without their input. It also contains special protections for the rights of voters, and provides that they can vote free from interference, including intimidation, and other acts designed to prevent or discourage people from voting or voting for the candidate of their choice. The Voting Rights Act protects the right of voters to mark their own ballot or to be assisted by a person of their choice (where voters need assistance because of disability or inability to read or write in English). Assistant United States Attorney Tate and other Assistant United States Attorneys will be on duty in this District while the polls are open and can be reached by the public at 340-774-5757. The FBI will also have special agents available to receive allegations of election fraud and other election abuses on election day. The FBI can be reached by the public at 787-987-6500. Complaints about possible violations of the federal voting rights laws can also be made directly to the Civil Rights Division in Washington, DC by phone at (855) 856-1247 (toll free) or by complaint form at https://civilrights.justice.gov/electionintegrity .
title: United States Attorney Names District Election Officer to Oversee Election Day Complaints

WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of the Treasury today announced its current estimates of privately-held net marketable borrowing for the October–December 2026 and January–March 2027 quarters.
- During the October–December 2026 quarter, Treasury expects to borrow $618 billion in privately-held net marketable debt, assuming an end-of-December cash balance of $850 billion. The borrowing estimate is $10 billion lower than announced in August 2026, primarily due to the higher-than-assumed beginning of quarter cash balance, partially offset by lower projected net cash flows. Excluding the higher-than-assumed beginning-of-quarter cash balance, the current quarter borrowing estimate is $24 billion higher than announced in August.
- During the January–March 2027 quarter, Treasury expects to borrow $800 billion in privately-held net marketable debt, assuming an end-of-March cash balance of $1.000 trillion.
- During the July–September 2026 quarter, Treasury borrowed $742 billion in privately-held net marketable debt and ended the quarter with a cash balance of $984 billion. In August 2026, Treasury estimated borrowing of $739 billion and assumed an end-of-September cash balance of $950 billion. The $4 billion in higher privately-held net marketable borrowing resulted primarily from the higher-than-assumed end-of-quarter cash balance, offset by higher net cash flows. Excluding the higher-than-assumed end-of-quarter cash balance, actual borrowing was $30 billion lower than announced in August.
Additional financing details relating to Treasury’s Quarterly Refunding will be released at 8:30 a.m. on Wednesday, November 4, 2026.
###
1. Privately-held net marketable borrowing excludes rollovers (auction “add-ons”) of Treasury securities held in the SOMA but includes financing required due to SOMA redemptions. Secondary market purchases of Treasury securities by SOMA do not directly change privately-held net marketable borrowing but, all else equal, when the securities mature and assuming the Federal Reserve does not redeem any maturing securities, would increase the amount of cash raised for a given privately-held auction size by increasing the SOMA “add-on” amount. Additionally, buybacks are not expected to significantly affect privately-held net marketable borrowing as new issuance replaces securities that are bought back.

The Department of the Air Force’s Spark Tank program concludes its final year with the Top 5 ideas selected out of 350 total submissions. These ideas endured strict subject matter evaluation from 1,394 members casting nearly 26,000 votes, evaluation from command leadership, and final determination by a panel of innovation leaders.
Out of 350 total submissions from across the Air and Space Forces, the Spark Tank 2026 Top 5 are:
Automated Master Storage Plan (Air Combat Command) – Leverages artificial intelligence to plan warehouse layouts for munitions, enabling weeks of planning to be executed in minutes.
M-UAS-D, MANET-enabled UAS Detector (Air Combat Command) – Low-cost for large scale deployment, a counter sUAS to detect drones, share real-time range data to users and response teams.
Project CAPYBARA (Air Mobility Command) – A set of tutorials and parts lists provided to any organization to build custom rovers for any capability needed in the field, replacing costly TDYs and certification programs.
Secure STIG Checker (Air Force Special Operations Command) – Replaces Enterprise Network manual compliance checks with a tool capable of analyzing millions of lines of code in under 500 seconds.
Tac-Hub: Agile Communications for the Modern Mission (Air Force Global Strike Command) – Modular command and control suite to enable rapid deployment; designed for military and emergency response teams.
Spark Tank is the Department of the Air Force's premier campaign where Guardians and Airmen present their innovative solutions to top leaders and industry experts, seeking sponsorship to bring their concepts to life.
The Top 5 teams will now accelerate prototypes and forge strategic partnerships with the help of AFWERX Refinery and DAF Enterprise Innovation support.
A panel of judges also reviewed the following semi-finalist submissions, which will be migrated for support and progression:
Aerial Minefield (Air Combat Command) – Low cost solution to create dense clouds of aerial obstacles to defend against and disable low-cost adversarial drones.
Agile Cyber Training Environment: Portable Cyber Ops Center (Air Combat Command) – Portable, battery-powered, network-independent center globally deployable by a single person in less than a minute for agile cyber operations.
Contingency Remote Optical Charging Spacecraft (Space Systems Group) – Charges dead spacecraft with ground lasers to prevent abandoned spacecraft and lost satellites due to loss of power.
Energy Resilience Command Platform (Air Force Reserve Command) – Dashboard unifying all base energy, power, water, heating, and mission critical data into a real time “Base Resilience Percentage”, indicating operational sustainment during disruptions.
Flight Room 3D Models (Air Education and Training Command) – Standardizes and institutionalizes 3D printed models of pilot curriculum items.
Project HOPLITE (Air Force Special Operations Command) – Integrates key components from Land Phalanx Weapon System, tactical truck, or FMTV load handling system to create a flexible and rapidly deployable air defense solution, transportable by C-130.
(ReSearch) an Advanced Search Engine for EPubs (Air Force Material Command) – Integrates Advana’s advanced search engine, natural language processing, and data analytics into the EPubs platform to allow Airmen to find exactly what they are looking for.
SpartReg 36-2903 Pictures of Dress Right vs. Wrong (Pacific Air Forces) – Digital interactive guide with side-by-side “correct vs. incorrect” examples, hyperlinks, and visual decision trees for dress and appearance standards.
Streamline 1205 Narrative Sync (Pacific Air Forces) – Standardize Air Force writing style by switching from character count format that matches EPB/ORB narrative standards.
The Sheppard Blueprint: A Proven Model for CONUS MTF Pharmacy Recapture (Air Education and Training Command) – Low-cost and highly replicable, a text message outreach and 24/7 prescription lockers to prevent lost cost in on-base pharmacies.
Vehicle Diagnostic System (Air National Guard) – Consolidates 5 tools and 7 software licenses into 1 tool for vehicle diagnostics.
title: DAF announces Spark Tank 2026 Top 5

BOISE – Khadijah Chapman, 62, of Georgia, was sentenced to an extra year in federal prison for failing to self-surrender for a prison sentence, U.S. Attorney John C. Shirts announced today.

According to court records, a Grand Jury indicted Chapman for bank fraud in 2022 for fraudulently obtaining Paycheck Protection Program funds during the COVID-19 pandemic. A jury convicted Chapman of the charge in 2023. In 2024, the District Court sentenced Chapman to 46 months’ imprisonment for the crime but allowed Chapman to remain out-of-custody and self-surrender to federal prison on a later date. Chapman, however, intentionally failed to surrender to Federal Prison Camp Alderson in West Virginia on the date required, and the United States Marshals Service arrested Chapman approximately two months later in Las Vegas, Nevada. Chief U.S District Judge Amanda K. Brailsford sentenced Chapman to an additional year of imprisonment to run consecutively to her initial prison sentence.

U.S. Attorney Shirts commended the work of the United States Marshal Service, which led to the charge, and the efforts of Assistant U.S. Attorneys Sean Mazorol and Robert Firpo, who prosecuted the case.

###
title: Convicted Felon Sentenced To Extra Year In Federal Prison For Failing To Self-Surrender

Gainesville, Florida – Samonta Leondre James, 26, of Gainesville, Florida, has pleaded guilty in federal court on a charge of possession of a firearm and ammunition by a convicted felon. John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida announced the guilty plea.

U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “I applaud the excellent investigative work by the Gainesville Police Department to remove this dangerous felon from our streets. My office will continue to aggressively prosecute these offenders to make abundantly clear that the Northern District of Florida has zero-tolerance from crime.”

According to court records, Gainesville Police Department conducted a traffic stop on a vehicle where the Defendant was a passenger. When asked by law enforcement if he had any weapons, the defendant stated that he had a firearm in his possession. A search of the defendant uncovered a Glock 29 10-millimeter handgun with seven rounds of ammunition. The defendant has prior convictions for Possession with Intent to Sell Cannabis within 1000 Feet of a Place of Worship and Possession with Intent to Sell Cannabis, and he is legally prohibited from possessing a firearm and ammunition.

Sentencing is scheduled for February 16, 2027, at 1:30pm before Chief United States District Court Judge Allen Winsor in Gainesville, Florida. The Defendant faces up to 15 years’ imprisonment.

The case was jointly investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, and the Gainesville Police Department. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Tyler Fleming.

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities .

MUSKOGEE, OKLAHOMA – The United States Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Oklahoma announced that Leobaldo Espinoza-Hinojosa, age 45, a Mexican national unlawfully present in LeFlore County, Oklahoma, pleaded guilty to one count of Unlawful Reentry of Removed Alien, punishable by a term of imprisonment of not more than ten years, and a fine of not more than $250,000.00.

The charge arose from an investigation by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s Immigration and Customs Enforcement Division and the Arkoma Police Department.

The Indictment alleged that on September 18, 2026, Espinoza-Hinojosa, an alien, was found in Arkoma, Oklahoma, without obtaining the express consent of the Secretary of Homeland Security to reapply for admission to the United States after having been previously removed on July 13, 2006.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America , a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

The Honorable Gerald L. Jackson, Magistrate Judge in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Oklahoma, accepted the plea and ordered the completion of a presentence investigation report.

A U.S. District Court Judge will determine the sentence to be imposed after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

Espinoza-Hinojosa will remain in the custody of the United States Marshals Service pending sentencing.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Chuck Sullivan represented the United States.
title: Illegal Alien Pleads Guilty To Unlawful Reentry

MONROE – On October 21, 2026, United States Chief District Judge Terry A. Doughty sentenced Justavious K. “Tae Tae” Williams , 25, of Bastrop, to 336 months in federal prison for Conspiracy to Possess a Controlled Substance with Intent to Distribute and for Possessing a Firearm in Furtherance of a Drug Trafficking Crime, followed by five years of supervised release. Williams previously pled guilty to the charges on July 10, 2026.

According to court documents, between May 16, 2025, and October 9, 2025, Williams participated in a methamphetamine trafficking organization. Investigators executed a wiretap on one of Williams’ co-conspirator’s phones and intercepted calls and messages in which Williams discussed acquiring and distributing large quantities of methamphetamine. On October 1, 2025, communications revealed that Williams’ co-conspirators were arranging the pickup of a large shipment of methamphetamine from Texas. Williams then traveled to Garland, Texas, where agents observed him and a co-conspirator load a bright orange suitcase into a vehicle. After the vehicle returned to Louisiana, Louisiana State Police (LSP) later attempted a traffic stop. Williams fled the stop, leading troopers on a brief pursuit before Williams and the co-conspirator were caught and arrested. A search of the vehicle revealed approximately 25 kilograms of methamphetamine in the suitcase. Roughly a week later, Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) agents executed a search warrant at a local address where Williams was found with the same co-conspirator as in the car stop. Inside the residence, agents recovered seven firearms along with various quantities of ecstasy pills, methamphetamine, marijuana, and other controlled substances. A cook lab trailer located behind the residence contained 20,000 methamphetamine pills and more than three kilograms of additional powder methamphetamine.

U.S. Attorney Zachary A. Keller for the Western District of Louisiana made the announcement.

The case was investigated by DEA, LSP, and Monroe Metro Narcotics. It was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney J. Aaron Crawford with assistance from Legal Assistant Amanda Morgan.

You may find a copy of this press release (and any updates) at www.justice.gov/usao-wdla.

Related court documents and information may be found on the website of the District Court for the Western District of Louisiana at www.lawd.uscourts.gov or at https://www.lawd.uscourts.gov/cmecf-pacer, under Case Number 3:25 cr 299.

text:
United States Attorney Lesley A. Woods announced that David John Groth, 38, of Omaha, Nebraska, was sentenced on October 30, 2026, in federal court in Omaha for receipt and distribution of child pornography. United States District Judge Robert F. Rossiter, Jr. sentenced Groth to 168 months’ imprisonment. There is no parole in the federal system. After Groth’s release from prison, he will begin a six-year term of supervised release. Judge Rossiter ordered Groth to pay $5,000 in restitution to each of two identified victims and a $5,000 special assessment pursuant to the Amy, Vicky, and Andy Child Pornography Victim Assistance Act of 2018, which supports the Defined Monetary Assistance Victims Reserve to provide compensation for victims of child sexual abuse material.

Between October 5, 2024, and April 30, 2025, Kik/Media Lab Inc. (Kik), an electronic service provider, made 12 Cyber Tip reports to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC). Each Cyber Tip reported a Kik user uploaded and then distributed to another Kik user, via the application’s chat function, videos depicting child pornography. Location information associated with each Cyber Tip resolved to Groth’s residence in Nebraska. Through investigative legal processes, a task force officer with the FBI located 110 child pornography videos and 30 child pornography images across all related Kik accounts. The agent observed pictures of Groth within the Kik accounts and confirmed Groth sent child pornography files to other Kik users using the Kik accounts reported in the Cyber Tips. Groth discussed his sexual attraction to children and the sexual abuse of children with other Kik users. Groth invited Kik users to connect with him on Telegram to further exchange child pornography.

On August 7, 2025, agents executed a search warrant at Groth’s residence in Bellevue, Nebraska, and seized electronic devices including computers, hard drives, and cell phones. Agents forensically analyzed Groth’s iPhone. Groth admitted using Kik on the iPhone. Agents located 38 child pornography images and 71 child pornography videos on Groth’s iPhone. The child pornography recovered from Groth’s Kik accounts and his iPhone depicted the sexual abuse and exploitation of pubescent and prepubescent children, toddlers, and infants. Groth’s child pornography included sadistic and masochistic conduct, children being bound and lead around on a leash.

“It is a victory for Nebraska every single time that a sex offender of this kind is taken off our streets, out of neighborhoods, and kept locked up and away from our children,” said United States Attorney Lesley A. Woods. “This conviction and outcome are just, and the United States Attorney’s Office will continue to prioritize going after offenders that target kids until none remain inside our borders.”

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by United States Attorney’s Offices and the Criminal Division's Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS), Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.projectsafechildhood.gov.

This case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

EL PASO, Texas – An illegal alien from Mexico was sentenced in a federal court in El Paso today to life in prison for his role in a deadly conspiracy to smuggle and harbor illegal aliens, announced U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons for the Western District of Texas.

According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Juan Carlos Lara-Quezada aka Ironman, 33, was a leader of an alien smuggling organization operating in the Western District of Texas and District of New Mexico. The organization is responsible for smuggling hundreds of illegal aliens into the U.S. via the desert in Santa Teresa, New Mexico. After successfully entering the U.S., the aliens were picked up and then driven to a stash house in El Paso where they would remain until they were transported further into the United States.

In 2024, the organization smuggled a woman and her son-in-law into the U.S., using a foot guide to lead them on an eight-hour journey through the desert. On the journey, the woman fell ill. The smugglers were directed to drop her off at an El Paso hospital instead of the stash house. En route to the hospital, the foot guide and driver instead abandoned the woman and her son-in-law on the sidewalk of a residential neighborhood. A passing motorist noticed the two abandoned aliens and called emergency services. The woman was transported to a hospital where she was pronounced dead due to environmental heat exposure.

An investigation led by Homeland Security Investigations resulted in Lara-Quezada’s arrest on Dec. 20, 2024. He was charged in a second superseding indictment on April 2, 2025, with conspiracy to transport aliens resulting in death, conspiracy to harbor aliens, transporting aliens resulting in death, conspiracy to bring in aliens, and conspiracy to launder monetary instruments. Lara-Quezada was convicted of all five charges by a federal jury in August.

“My message about the motivations of human smugglers has been consistent and clear. These organizations care nothing about the human lives from which they profit,” said U.S. Attorney Simmons. “These smugglers abandoned a woman in their care and left her to die in the streets. Like all the alien smugglers we prosecute, they are now being held accountable. And, while his co-defendants will be subject to removal from the United States following their respective sentences, Lara-Quezada will never again see the outside world in this country or any other.”

FORT WAINWRIGHT, Alaska — From hand-sewn prototypes to custom-built web platforms, Soldiers of the 11th Airborne Division demonstrated the power of grassroots innovation during Angel Ascent, held Oct. 28 at the division theater.
Col. Matthew Adamczyk, Deputy Commanding Officer for Operations, 11th Airborne Division, praised the competitors’ efforts.
“Soldiers across the 11th Airborne Division continue to demonstrate that many of the best ideas come from the bottom up. Events like Angel Ascent prove the ability of our troops to solve problems, our job is to help provide the right resources. When our Soldiers and leaders are empowered, there's no limit to what we can achieve in the Arctic and beyond.” said Col. Adamczyk.
Spc. Leighton Keilen, 1st Battalion, 24th Infantry Regiment, 1st Infantry Brigade Combat Team, 11th Airborne Division, earned first place for his Skydio Drone Relay and modular payload delivery system that significantly extends tactical drone range and utility in Alaska’s rugged, mountainous terrain. Col. Matthew Adamczyk presented Keilen with a Meritorious Service Medal. All other competitors received Army Commendation Medals, and every participant was awarded a four-day pass in recognition of their efforts.
The competition provided Soldiers of all ranks a direct platform to present practical solutions to senior military leaders, civilian officials and innovation experts. Each innovator received 10 minutes to brief their project followed by five minutes of questions from the judging panel, which evaluated entries on problem identification, solution quality, operational value, resource requirements and presentation.
The event highlighted a key truth: some of the Army’s most effective solutions come from the Soldiers who live with the problems every day. Whether serving in Arctic extremes or supporting complex administrative demands, these warfighters refused to accept “the way it’s always been done.”
The competitors’ backgrounds highlight the wide range of skills, experiences and perspectives that strengthen today’s Army. Pfc. Michael Pereira, a Tactical Unmanned Aircraft Systems specialist from Miami, Florida, hand-sewed his first prototype of a passive thermal battery vault designed to keep drone batteries viable in sub-zero temperatures using only body heat and radiant barriers. Staff Sgt. Baddeley, a respiratory therapist from Petaluma, California, developed TroopToTask.org after years of watching small-unit leaders struggle with fragmented spreadsheets. His intuitive web platform consolidates personnel data, training records, duty rosters and mission tracking, allowing commanders, first sergeants and leaders at every echelon to focus on leading Soldiers instead of chasing administrative tasks.
Other standout projects included a low-cost battery eliminator for PRC-158 radios in extreme cold, a modular power and heating system for man-hauled Ahkio sleds, 3D-printed explosively formed penetrators for FPV drones, and a unit-fabricated ring mount hatch for FMTVs that protects convoy gunners in Arctic conditions for a fraction of the cost of commercial systems.
By formally recognizing these efforts with awards and command emphasis, the 11th Airborne Division is cultivating a culture where initiative is expected and innovation is accelerated. Events like Angel Ascent serve as a powerful example for the broader Army of how to empower Soldiers at the tactical edge to solve real problems, reduce logistical burdens, and increase lethality in austere environments.
title: Soldiers from across 11th Airborne Division shine at Angel Ascent innovation competition

OKLAHOMA CITY – TAYLOR RYAN PRIGMORE , 31, of McLoud, Oklahoma, has pleaded guilty to threatening to murder federal law enforcement officers, communicating a threat, assaulting federal officers, and brandishing a firearm in the furtherance of a crime of violence, announced U.S. Attorney Robert J. Troester.

“Threats and attempts to harm federal agents are serious crimes that result in severe consequences,” said U.S. Attorney Robert J. Troester. “We will always support the men and women of law enforcement who work hard each day to maintain our safety, and we will hold accountable those who threaten or obstruct their work.”

"Mr. Prigmore’s guilty plea represents an important step toward accountability for his disgraceful actions that endangered the lives of FBI agents as they carried out their sworn duties,” said FBI Oklahoma City Acting Special Agent in Charge Joe Skarda. “Violence and intimidation have no place in our society, and the FBI will continue working alongside our law enforcement and prosecutorial partners to ensure those who engage in such conduct are brought to justice."

According to court records, between May 9, 2025, and January 17, 2026, a YouTube account belonging to Prigmore posted multiple comments on various videos threatening to kill Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents and others. Prigmore also threatened to kill law enforcement officers who came to his residence, stating that he wanted to kill “as many as possible.”

On January 19, 2026, FBI agents arrested Prigmore following a brief standoff at his residence. During the standoff, Prigmore fired multiple rounds at federal agents. No one was injured.

On November 2, 2026, Prigmore was charged with, and pleaded guilty to, a four-count Superseding Information, charging Prigmore with threatening to murder federal law enforcement officers, communicating a threat, assaulting federal officers, and brandishing a firearm in the furtherance of a crime of violence. As part of his plea, Prigmore admitted he willfully threatened to murder Federal law enforcement officers, sent another threat to injure others, and intentionally assaulted and interfered with federal officers with a firearm which he brandished.

At sentencing, Prigmore faces up to life in federal prison, and fines of up to $1,000,000.

The FBI Oklahoma City Field Office’s Joint Terrorism Task Force investigated the case, with assistance from Homeland Security Investigations and the Oklahoma Highway Patrol. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Arvo Mikkanen and Matt Dillon are prosecuting the case.

This case is part of the nationwide National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 initiative, which is a White House directed, interagency effort to integrate federal, state, and local partners in protecting First Amendment rights while targeting individuals and organizations engaged in political violence.

Reference is made to public filings for additional information.
title: McLoud Man Pleads Guilty after Firing at FBI Agents, Threatening to Kill Federal Officers and Others on YouTube
