WASHINGTON – Representatives Yassamin Ansari (AZ-03) and Don Bacon (NE-02) recently led a bipartisan effort calling on the Department of State and the Department of Homeland Security to provide urgent answers regarding the conditions and future resettlement plans for Afghan allies and their families currently housed at Camp As Sayliyah (CAS) in Doha, Qatar.
“Our Afghan allies stood alongside us, and we have the responsibility to ensure they and their families are treated with dignity and compassion,” said Rep. Ansari. “These women and children deserve access to medical care, education, and safe living conditions. We must uphold our country’s commitments and ensure these families have a clear path permanent resettlement and asylum. I’m glad to lead this bipartisan effort with my colleague, Congressman Don Bacon, to deliver the answers and accountability our Afghan allies deserve.”
“We made a commitment to the Afghan allies who stood alongside our servicemembers, and we have an obligation to honor it,” said Rep. Bacon. “We need clear answers about the care these families are receiving, particularly women and children, and the steps being taken to ensure their safe and orderly resettlement.”
With Afghan families enduring prolonged stays at CAS, the lawmakers are demanding accountability for the conditions they face and the services available to them. The letter calls for answers on access to essential maternal and OB-GYN care for pregnant women, routine pediatric services for young children, and safe, adequate living conditions. It also urges the provision of structured educational programming, English-language instruction, and recreational activities to support children’s development and well-being. Additionally, the lawmakers demand transparency around proposed third-country transfers, including clear assurances that any agreements uphold U.S. humanitarian standards, protect Afghan families’ well-being, and provide concrete pathways to safe, supported resettlement.
“More than 1,000 Afghan allies are waiting at Camp As Sayliyah, and most of them are women and children. They include family members of U.S. service members, and every one of them was brought there on an American promise. Representatives Ansari and Bacon are asking the right questions: Are pregnant women getting care? Are children learning? Is there a real path to resettlement? These families have kept their word to us, and they deserve clear answers and a way forward. AfghanEvac is grateful to every member who signed on,” said Shawn VanDiver, President and Founder of AfghanEvac.
“Last year, my team and I were at Camp As Sayliyah (CAS) helping secure flights and resettlement for hundreds of our wartime allies. Many of our allies, including the family members of U.S. veterans and service members, are still waiting for a safe path forward and still depend on health care and education at the camp,” said Andrew Sullivan, Executive Director of No One Left Behind. “We applaud this bipartisan recognition that a safe resolution for these allies, reached by Congress and the executive branch working in partnership, is in America’s best interest,” said Andrew Sullivan, Executive Director of No One Left Behind.
Ansari’s letter was cosigned by Representatives Don Bacon (NE-02), Jason Crow (CO-06), María Elvira Salazar (FL-27), Stephen F. Lynch (MA-08), Jasmine Crockett (TX-30), Diana DeGette (CO-01), Eleanor Holmes Norton (DC-AL), Seth Moulton (MA-06), George Latimer (NY-16), James R. Walkinshaw (VA-11), Mike Quigley (IL-05), Adelita S. Grijalva (AZ-07), Ami Bera (CA-06), Deborah K. Ross (NC-02), Julia Brownley (CA-26), Veronica Escobar (TX-16), Emily Randall (WA-06), Jennifer L. McClellan (VA-04), William R. Keating (MA-09), Dina Titus (NV-01), and Sara Jacobs (CA-51).
The letter is also endorsed by One Left Behind, AfghanEvac, Afghans For A Better Tomorrow, Association of Wartime Allies (AWA), FAER, With Honor, USAHello, Center for Gender & Refugee Studies, Borderlands Resource Initiative, Human Rights First, Humanitarian Legal Assistance Project, Special Operations Association of America (SOAA), Refugee Council USA (RCUSA), Lawyers for Good Government, Feminist Majority, Frontera Federation, Keeping Our Promise Inc., Instant Aid, Cross Cultural Communications, LLC, Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America, Hearts & Homes for Refugees, Unitarian Universalists for Social Justice, The 5ive Pillars Organization, Allied Shepherd, International Institute of New England, Dialogue Center for Resilience and Empowerment (DCRE), Paws Unite People Inc, SunEx Aviation, Our Culture is Giving, U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants, Asian Americans Advancing Justice Southern California, Afghan Scout Relief Fund, Afghan Advantage, Global Refuge, Union for Reform Judaism, and Immigrant Defenders Law Center.
Read the letter HERE and below.
Dear Secretary Rubio and Secretary Mullin,
We write to follow up on the ongoing transit operations at Camp As Sayliyah (CAS) in Doha, Qatar, where Afghan allies and their families remain in temporary housing awaiting final resettlement processing. In particular, we wish to learn more about the conditions faced by the hundreds of women and the young children currently in processing at the facility, and to request an update on plans for their safe resettlement.
These individuals were brought out of Afghanistan on U.S.-provided flights with the promise and understanding that CAS would serve as a short-term transit hub for temporary stay in the final stages of their processing for secure resettlement to the United States. With this sacred promise to the heroes who supported our forces in Afghanistan at the heart of our inquiry, we want to ensure that the most vulnerable among those at CAS receive the necessary processing support, health care, and clear communications on their next steps.
- Health and Support Services for Women and Children
Given the extended stays for many families, maintaining adequate specialized care remains a priority. We request an assessment of the medical services available at CAS, particularly maternal and OBGYN health resources for pregnant women and routine pediatric care for young children. Ensuring appropriate living conditions and consistent medical oversight for these families is essential as their immigration processing moves forward.
- Educational Opportunities and Developmental Support for Children
Beyond immediate health and security considerations, we also ask for an evaluation of the educational and developmental resources available to the school-aged children residing at CAS. Given the extended length of stay for many families, access to structured educational programming, English language learning, and recreational activities is essential to minimize learning disruptions and support childhood development. Ensuring there are routine learning environments at the facility not only helps prepare these children for integration into American schools and communities, but also provides critical stability and psychological support during a period of prolonged transition.
- Pathways to Final Resettlement
Clear and transparent communication regarding resettlement pathways is vital for maintaining the trust of our allies now and in future engagements. We ask for clarification on the open U.S. Refugee Admissions Program (USRAP) P-1/P-2 applications and family reunification cases at CAS. Additionally, we request information on how the Department of State and the Department of Homeland Security are handling any proposed third-country transfers to ensure the underlying bilateral agreements align with U.S. humanitarian standards and provide established resettlement support in the receiving country.
To inform Congress’ collaboration with your departments to shape an effective path forward, we
request your response addressing the following questions by November 27, 2026:
- What medical care is available for the Afghan evacuees at CAS, particularly maternal and OBGYN health resources for pregnant women and routine pediatric care for young children?
- What learning support is available to school aged children? What cultural and educational resources are available to prepare adults for employment and resettlement in the United States?
- How many individuals have ongoing USRAP referrals? What resources do your departments need to ensure all these individuals can renew their requisite documents and medical panels?
- What specific steps are your departments taking to communicate the status of resettlement options (including USRAP and third country agreements) to the individuals at CAS?
Thank you for your continued work to uphold U.S. national security by fulfilling our commitments to Afghan allies and their families. We look forward to working with your departments to ensure a swift, safe, and organized resolution for those at CAS.
Sincerely,
Yassamin Ansari
Member of Congress
Follow @RepYassAnsari on all social media platforms and visit Ansari.House.gov to learn more.

title: Ansari Leads Bipartisan Effort in Demanding Answers on Care and Resettlement of Afghan Women and Children in Qatar

PRESIDIO OF MONTEREY, Calif. (Nov. 2, 2026) – October was Domestic Violence Awareness and Prevention Month and staff at the Presidio of Monterey and Naval Support Activity Monterey worked together to educate their communities on domestic violence prevention and survivor support.
The month of events began Oct. 2 with a superhero run for military families in La Mesa Village. On Oct. 6, Julia Sibilla, deputy garrison commander of U.S. Army Garrison Presidio of Monterey and Capt. Ryan Easterday, commanding officer of Naval Support Activity Monterey, held a proclamation signing at NSAM Headquarters. The joint proclamation called upon all members of the community to help prevent domestic violence through education and increased awareness, ultimately strengthening our communities.
Additional trainings were held throughout the month at the NSAM Chapel and concluded with training for Defense Language Institute Foreign Language Center students at PoM, Oct. 30.
“We had a fantastic month of getting the word out on domestic violence prevention,” said Karlette Anderson, a family advocacy victim advocate at Fleet & Family Support Center Monterey. “Turnout was much greater than we had anticipated and we were excited for our first training at the Presidio of Monterey. We have a young population at DLI and some may not have the experience to identify domestic violence.”
Anderson educated service members about the different kinds of behaviors an abusive partner may exhibit. She encouraged attendees not to normalize physical, emotional, sexual or neglectful conduct from a partner and not to fall into the cycle of domestic violence.
“Domestic violence looks different in every case but normally follows a cycle,” Anderson said. “The tension phase is when we are walking on eggshells around the abuser and don’t want to make them angry. The next phase is the actual act of abuse. The last phase is what we call the honeymoon phase. This is where the partner apologizes and promises to never do that again.”
Anderson asked everyone to stand up to abuse, stand up for themselves and to get help if they cannot safely leave a harmful relationship. “We are here for you to help in any way that we can,” Anderson said. “You do not have to go through this alone and everything that you share with us will be strictly confidential unless you decide to disclose your information.”
Guest speaker Jessica Macias, the CEO of YWCA Monterey County, also spoke at the training. “We don’t ask gender, military affiliation or any unnecessary background information,” Macias said. “If someone comes to us and says they’re a victim of domestic violence, we will figure out the best way to support them.”
Domestic violence impacts all communities and socioeconomic groups. Any member of the military community who experiences domestic violence or thinks someone they know is facing abuse can call and receive support anonymously from Army Community Service at 831-242-7660, Fleet & Family Support Center at 831-656-3060 or either command’s emergency hotline at 520-725-7089 (PoM) or 831-744-2800 (NSAM). Anyone can call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 800-799-7233.
title: Presidio of Monterey, Naval Support Activity Monterey combine efforts in support of Domestic Violence Awareness and Prevention Month

SALT LAKE CITY, Utah – A Utah man admitted to his involvement in a multimillion-dollar Ponzi scheme in the District of Utah that collected funds of more than $60 million from hundreds of investors.

Matthew Morrison Bates, 42, of Lehi, Utah, appeared in court today for his initial appearance and pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and money laundering. He was initially charged by felony information on September 30, 2026.

According to court documents and admissions made at Bates’ change of plea hearing, beginning in or around May 2020 and continuing in or around June 2025, within the District of Utah and elsewhere, Bates and others devised and executed a scheme to defraud investors in an investment scheme involving short-term promissory notes that investors were falsely promised would be exclusively used by Bates’ company, Hedgehog Investments LLC, to extend “bridge loans” to companies seeking financial assistance to reduce debt and maximize companies’ creditworthiness, among other benefits. Investors were promised significant returns would be generated as the “bridge loans” were repaid by recipient businesses, but Hedgehog Investments did not extend “bridge loans” and any investor returns were paid with new investor funds, giving the false appearance of profitability. Investor loss is more than $60 million.

Bates is scheduled to be sentenced on January 12, 2027, at 11:00 a.m. in courtroom 3.4 before a U.S. District Court Judge at the Orrin G. Hatch United States Courthouse in downtown Salt Lake City.

United States Attorney Melissa Holyoak of the District of Utah made the announcement.

This case was investigated jointly by the Utah Division of Securities and the FBI Salt Lake City Field Office.

Assistant United States Attorneys Mark E. Woolf, Tanner Zumwalt, and Brian Williams of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Utah are prosecuting the case.
title: Utah County Man Admits His Part in a Multimillion-Dollar Ponzi Scheme

PHILADELPHIA – United States Attorney David Metcalf announced that five non-citizens have been charged with illegally voting or fraudulently registering to vote, despite knowing that they were not U.S. citizens. Under both federal and state law, only United States citizens may vote in Pennsylvania.

“Upholding the integrity of our electoral process is more than ‘important’ — it’s critical to the wellbeing of our democracy,” said U.S. Attorney Metcalf. “American citizens alone have the right to determine the outcome of our national elections.”

“Every unlawful vote compromises the principle that elections must be decided by eligible American citizens,” said HSI Philadelphia Special Agent in Charge Nathan Abel. “Voters deserve confidence that the law is enforced, and HSI will continue to investigate anyone who violates it.”

Rosanny Fabre Villa , 28, of Reading, Pennsylvania, a citizen of the Dominican Republic and lawful permanent U.S. resident, was arrested and charged by indictment with making a false statement of citizenship in order to vote.

The indictment alleges that, on or about March 3, 2026, in Berks County, Pa., the defendant submitted a voter registration application that she knew was fraudulent, because on it she falsely claimed to be a United States citizen, when, as she knew, she was not a U.S. citizen.

If convicted, Villa faces a maximum possible sentence of a fine, five years in prison, or both.

Gavin Moir , 55, of Atglen, Pa., was charged by information with four counts of voting by an alien. The information alleges that the defendant, a citizen of Canada and lawful permanent U.S. resident, illegally voted in the 2022 and 2024 general elections, and the 2022 and 2026 primaries.

If convicted, Moir faces a maximum possible sentence of a fine, four years in prison, or both.

Antonio Lyttle , 68, of Philadelphia, Pa., was charged by information with voting by an alien. The information alleges that the defendant, a citizen of Jamaica and lawful permanent U.S. resident, illegally voted in the 2024 general election.

Widarto , 56, also of Philadelphia, was charged by information with voting by an alien. The information alleges that the defendant, a citizen of Indonesia and lawful permanent U.S. resident, illegally voted in the 2024 general election.

Eija Annikki Yaroma , 66, of Doylestown, Pa., was charged by information with voting by an alien. The information alleges that the defendant, a citizen of Finland and lawful permanent U.S. resident, illegally voted in the 2024 general election.

If convicted, Lyttle, Widarto, and Yaroma each face a maximum possible sentence of a fine, one year in prison, or both.

These cases were investigated by Homeland Security Investigations.

The charges and allegations contained in the indictment and informations are merely accusations. Every defendant is presumed to be innocent unless and until proven guilty in court.
title: Five Non-Citizens Charged with Election Fraud Offenses

ELKINS, WEST VIRGINIA — An Augusta, West Virginia man has admitted to selling fentanyl in an Elkins, West Virginia business parking lot, U.S. Attorney Matthew L. Harvey announced today.

Johnny Foster Biggs, 47, pleaded guilty today to distribution of fentanyl analogue. According to court documents, Biggs sold 3.339 grams of a fentanyl mixture to someone in a business parking lot.

As a part of the plea agreement, Biggs agreed to forfeit a pistol and ammunition associated with this case. Biggs faces up to 30 years in prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Stephen Warner is prosecuting the case on behalf of the government. The investigation was conducted by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the Mountain Region Drug Task Force, a HIDTA-funded initiative.

Fentanyl has been designated by President Donald Trump as a weapon of mass destruction due to its extreme lethality which poses a grave threat to public safety, even in trace amounts. This case is part of Operation Take Back America , a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime, and repel the invasion of illegal immigration.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Michael John Aloi presided.
title: Hampshire County Man Admits to Fentanyl Trafficking

CINCINNATI – In keeping with past practice, United States Attorney Dominick S. Gerace II announced today that he has designated Election Officers in each of the District’s three offices to serve as points of contact for the upcoming election.

“The Department of Justice plays an important role in ensuring that our elections are free and fair,” said Gerace. “My Office will always work to protect the integrity of the election process.”

U.S. Attorney Gerace appointed:

Deputy Criminal Chief Emily N. Glatfelter in Cincinnati;

Assistant United States Attorney Peter K. Glenn-Applegate in Columbus; and

Deputy Criminal Chief Brent G. Tabacchi in Dayton.

As District Election Officers, they are responsible for overseeing the District’s handling of complaints of election fraud and voting rights concerns in consultation with the Justice Department’s Headquarters in Washington.

The Department's long-standing Election Day Program seeks to ensure public confidence in the integrity of the election process by providing local contacts for the public to report possible election fraud and voting rights violations.

Federal law protects against such crimes as non-citizen voting, intimidating or bribing voters, buying and selling votes, impersonating voters, altering vote tallies, stuffing ballot boxes, and marking ballots for voters against their wishes or without their input. It also contains special protections for the rights of voters and provides that they can vote free from acts that intimidate or harass them.

The local FBI field office can be reached by the public regarding allegations of election fraud and other election abuses at 1-800-CALL-FBI.

Complaints about possible violations of the federal voting rights laws can be made directly to the Civil Rights Division in Washington, DC by phone at 800-253-3931 or by complaint form at https://civilrights.justice.gov/ .

# # #
title: U.S. Attorney Gerace announces District Election Officers

HUNTINGTON, W.Va. – Samuel Jermaine Caples, also known as “EJ,” 26, of Pontiac, Michigan, was sentenced today to three years and six months in prison, to be followed by five years of supervised release, for distribution of 50 grams or more of methamphetamine.

According to court documents and statements made in court, on January 9, 2026, Caples sold approximately 216.7 grams of 100 percent pure methamphetamine to a confidential informant at a Huntington residence in exchange for $1,600. As part of his guilty plea, Caples admitted that he conducted the transaction after the confidential informant arranged it with another individual.

Caples further admitted that he sold a mixture containing approximately 30.18 grams of methamphetamine in exchange for $450 on December 2, 2025, and sold approximately 7.11 grams of fentanyl in exchange for $800 on January 14, 2026. Each transaction took place in Huntington.

United States Attorney Moore Capito made the announcement and commended the investigative work of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Cabell County Sheriff's Office.

United States District Judge Robert C. Chambers imposed the sentence. Assistant United States Attorney Joseph F. Adams and third-year law student intern Chloe A. Bailey prosecuted the case.

text:
PICATINNY ARSENAL, N.J. - Engineers at the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM) Armaments Center researchers say a new explosive initiator could remove environmental and safety risks from the supply chain.
DBX-1, full name copper (I) 5-nitrotetrazolate, provides the U.S. Military with an alternative to lead azide, used for decades because of its military reliability despite known risks to human health due to its volatility and toxic composition. DBX-1 maintains a lower toxicity than its legacy counterpart, is more efficient to manufacture and transport and supports a modernized supply chain with no compromise to weapon production or reliability.
As a copper-based compound, DBX-1 eliminates exposure risk to lead while handling, and at the same time opens an avenue towards automation. Instead of a dry powder, DBX-1 is prepared as a wet slurry and is dispensed into initiators via automated equipment, ensuring no dry handling and significantly reducing worker contact with sensitive primary explosives.
Lead azide has been a ubiquitous compound in explosives for decades, mostly used as the initiator in an explosive train, found at the heart of most armaments. Initiators are the first materials in the train, converting a trigger into a reliable detonation that sets off the rest of the sequence.
Lead azide and similar compounds like lead styphnate work well as initiators, but they come with significant caveats – lead is highly toxic, and due to supply chain disruptions and a limited domestic manufacturer base, warfighters must rely on aged stockpiles and single source suppliers for initiation and ignition. Lead azide, according to the National Institute of Health, produces toxic fumes when set alight, and is highly sensitive to heat, friction and impact when dry.
However, as these compounds are highly effective in the field, interests in finding alternatives have historically been muted. Lead azide only requires a small stimulus to trigger a large blast and does so consistently.
According to Senior Lead Chemical Engineer Neha Mehta, the DBX-1 project started from a desire to find a drop-in replacement to lead azide and similar compounds, which evolved into the pursuit of an azide alternative over time. The Primary Explosives and Detonator Lab Team encountered DBX-1 while at a primary explosive workshop, being presented by Pacific Scientific, said Mehta. The team was captivated by promises of lower toxicity, safer handling and strong energetic output, and several years of rigorous testing have thoroughly validated those beliefs.
“We did a lot of in‑house testing, and aside from a couple small confusions, we had zero no‑go’s. We’re always optimizing, always looking for how to make things better. Our goal has never been to change the hardware; we work with what already exists,” she explained.
DBX‑1 is fully sourced and produced within the United States, thus strengthening availability, providing a manufacturing base at home and mitigating supply disruption. Testing is ongoing in different applications, but so far, the compound has performed well across detonators, some primers, and fuze configurations, including anti-personnel obstacle breaching systems and grenade and artillery fuzes. It has also proved reliability across the Army’s smallest commonly used stab detonator (M55) and its largest (C70).
“If we can prove it in the smallest detonator and the largest detonator, everything in between will work, and that’s exactly what we’ve shown,” noted Mehta.
The team has already exhibited DBX‑1 as an alternative to lead azide and lead styphnate by completing the full fuze qualification test matrix for an artillery fuze, funded by the Safer Alternative for Readiness – Airborne Lead Reduction (SAFR ALR) and the Project Manager Combat Ammunition Systems. They also proved DBX‑1’s suitability for grenade fuzes, successfully finishing the full performance tests and mini‑arena evaluation of complete grenades equipped with a toxic‑free delay, lead‑free primer and lead‑free detonator, funded by Environmental Security Technology Certification Program (ESTCP).
The program has conducted extensive test series across numerous electric blasting‑cap configurations using the Army Remote Activation Munitions System and has met all its operational requirements. DBX-1 has also cleared qualification for tactical breaching initiators and point-detonating artillery fuzing systems.
According to lead mechanical engineering technicians Jason Semanek and John Marin, DBX-1 required not only laboratory success but also demonstrating manufacturability. Rocky Mountain Scientific Laboratory, based in Colorado with a growing facility in Texas, is positioned to manufacture DBX‑1. Innovative Materials and Processes in South Dakota, under Army contract, is developing the automated slurry‑loading process, while Action Manufacturing in Pennsylvania assisted in optimizing precursor synthesis, providing a significant boost to American manufacturing.
Additionally, both the DBX-1 manufacturing process and its automated loading equipment are being designed to operate inside transportable Conex containers. This means no need for dedicated permanent buildings, streamlines site approvals and reduces transportation risks, along with further simplifying stockpiling logistics. DBX-1 had its pre-pilot testing finished in 2025 and its full-scale pilot plant should be ready by the end of 2027 or early 2028, where it will be produced on-demand.
Mehta stated that funding for DBX-1 has been inconsistent, thus complicating the testing required to validate it across dozens of munition systems. She gave thanks to the SAFR program for giving the team financial support continuously, to the ESTCP, Army ManTech, the OSW’s Manufacturing Science and Technology Program and project managers for support and to the rest of her team for its dedication in helping ensure project success.
Despite its lengthy timeline, the team expressed pride and excitement over the program’s progress, noting that a few outside organizations have shown interest in DBX-1, particularly in mining. For the engineers, seeing DBX‑1 move toward full qualification and adoption feels like guiding a long-developed project into maturity, one they hope will be fully integrated across military systems within the near future.
“It’s like a child - slow progress, lots of work and now it’s finally ready to go out into the world,” quipped Marin.
title: A new class of blast: DBX 1 compound pushing Army towards cleaner, smarter firepower

KNOXVILLE, Tenn. – On October 30, 2026, Darrell Moore, 44, currently of Knoxville, Tennessee, was sentenced to 126 months imprisonment by the Honorable Katherine A. Crytzer, United States District Judge, in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Tennessee at Knoxville. Following his imprisonment, Moore will be on supervised release for 20 years and will be required to register with state sex offender registries and comply with special sex offender conditions during his supervised release.

As part of the plea agreement filed with the court, Moore agreed to plead guilty to an indictment charging him with one count of distribution of child pornography in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 2252A(a)(2) and §2252A(b)(1).

According to court filed documents, in June 2022, during a Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) operation, Moore sent videos of children under the age of eight years using the username “supercooldaddy,” to an undercover FBI agent. Subsequently, federal agents executed a search warrant at Moore’s Knoxville residence. Among items seized during the search warrant was Moore’s cellphone containing approximately 40 child pornography images and 62 child pornography videos. Moore admitted to knowingly distributing child pornography to others over the Kik chatting platform.

U.S. Attorney Francis M. Hamilton III of the Eastern District of Tennessee, and Special Agent in Charge Terrence G. Riley, of the Nashville Field Office’s Knoxville Resident Agency, made the announcement.

The criminal indictment was the result of an investigation by the Knoxville Police Department ICAC, Knoxville Police Department Special Crimes, and the FBI Knoxville Resident Agency, with assistance from the Johnson City Police Department and Tennessee Bureau of Investigation.

Assistant United States Attorney Suzanne H. Sullivan represented the United States.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood (PSC), a nationwide initiative launched in May 2006, by the Department of Justice to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by the United States Attorney’s Offices and the Criminal Division’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, PSC marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who sexually exploit children, and to identify and rescue victims. For more information about PSC, please visit www.justice.gov/psc .

For more information about internet safety education, please visit www.justice.gov/psc/resources.html and click on the tab “resources.”

FORT GEORGE G. MEADE, Md. — Baltimore Ravens players, former players and cheerleaders visited Fort George G. Meade Oct. 27, giving service members an opportunity to interact with professional athletes while highlighting the importance of military service, community partnerships and quality of life.
The visit, coordinated through a partnership involving the National Football League, USAA and Fort Meade’s Directorate of Family and Morale, Welfare and Recreation, included a military working dog demonstration and an autograph and photo session.
Command Sgt. Maj. Richard Moore welcomed the Ravens delegation at the installation’s Visitor Control Center before escorting the group to the military working dog kennels.
At the kennels, Lt. Col. Heather George, Headquarters Command Battalion commander, welcomed the visitors and introduced the military working dog team. The delegation received a briefing on the dogs’ training, capabilities and role in supporting military operations before watching a demonstration.
“The Baltimore Ravens visit provided a tremendous opportunity to showcase the professionalism, training and capabilities of our military working dog teams while strengthening the connection between our service members and the community,” George said.
Following the demonstration, Moore presented Ravens representatives with an American flag flown here that same day in appreciation for their visit and support of the military community.
The delegation then traveled to the Freedom Inn Warrior Restaurant, where service members met Ravens players, took photographs and collected autographs.
“Seeing the excitement and enthusiasm of our service members as they interacted with the Baltimore Ravens was truly rewarding,” said Command Sgt. Maj. Karen Bryant. “These engagements go beyond autographs and photographs. They help build morale, strengthen camaraderie and remind our Soldiers that the community values their service and sacrifices.”
For Staff Sgt. Lamar Riddick, the opportunity to meet professional athletes was a meaningful acknowledgment of military service.
“I think it shows great appreciation,” Riddick said. “It makes me feel valued.”
Pfc. Jaydon Green, a Ravens fan, shared that excitement. After learning about the visit, he immediately contacted his wife and made plans to attend.
“It feels like I’m respected,” Green said. “It feels like some of the service that we do here is kind of makes us feel like we get a little bit back from it.”
For former Ravens wide receiver Torrey Smith, whose father served in the military, the visit carried personal significance.
“I think it’s important to know that people matter, right? And that you appreciate them,” Smith said. “It’s a major sacrifice. It’s a major commitment that so many people make.”
Moore said the engagement highlighted the shared values of military service and professional athletics.
“Collaborating with world-class organizations like the Baltimore Ravens powerfully highlights our shared ethos,” Moore said. “We are both driven by core values and the relentless pursuit of excellence.”
The visit reinforced Fort Meade’s commitment to supporting service member morale, strengthening community relationships and providing opportunities to recognize the dedication and sacrifice of military personnel and their families.
title: Baltimore Ravens visit Fort Meade service members

WASHINGTON — In response to a Presidential disaster declaration issued Oct. 30, the U.S. Small Business Administration announced the availability of low-interest federal disaster loans to businesses, private nonprofits, and residents affected by severe storms, straight-line winds, tornadoes, and flooding occurring July 7 –Aug. 4.
The disaster declaration covers the Texas counties of Bandera, Bexar, Comal, Crockett, Dimmit, Frio, Gillespie, Kendall, Kerr, Kimble, Kinney, La Salle, Maverick, Medina, Real, Schleicher, Sutton, Uvalde, Val Verde, and Zavala which are eligible for both physical damage loans and Economic Injury Disaster Loans from SBA. Small businesses and most private nonprofit organizations in the following adjacent Texas counties are eligible to apply only for SBA EIDLs: Atascosa, Blanco, Concho, Crane, Duval, Edwards, Guadalupe, Hays, Irion, Llano, Mason, McMullen, Menard, Pecos, Reagan, Terrell, Tom Green, Upton, Webb, and Wilson.
Businesses and nonprofits are eligible to apply for physical disaster loans and may borrow up to $2 million to repair or replace disaster-damaged or destroyed real estate, machinery and equipment, inventory, and other business assets.
Homeowners and renters are eligible to apply for home and personal property loans and may borrow up to $100,000 to replace or repair personal property, such as clothing, furniture, cars, and appliances. Homeowners may apply for up to $500,000 to replace or repair their primary residence.
Applicants may also be eligible for a loan increase of up to 20% of their physical damage, as verified by SBA, for mitigation purposes. Eligible mitigation improvements include strengthening structures to protect against storm damage, upgrading to wind rated garage doors, and installing a safe room or storm shelter to help protect property and occupants from future damage.
The SBA’s Economic Injury Disaster Loan program is available to eligible small businesses, small agricultural cooperatives, and private nonprofits — including faith-based organizations —impacted by financial losses directly related to this disaster. The SBA is unable to provide disaster loans to agricultural producers, farmers, or ranchers, except for aquaculture enterprises.
Economic Injury Disaster Loans are for working capital needs caused by the disaster and are available even if the business or private nonprofit did not suffer any physical damage. The loans may be used to pay fixed debts, payroll, accounts payable, and other bills which could not be paid due to the disaster.
“A presidential disaster declaration opens the door to SBA assistance at a time when families and businesses are facing difficult decisions,” said Chris Stallings, Associate Administrator of SBA's Office of Disaster Recovery. “These loans can help eligible homeowners and renters repair or replace what was damaged while giving businesses and private nonprofits the resources to continue operating as their communities recover.”
Interest rates are as low as 4% for businesses, 3.625% for private nonprofits, and 2.875% for homeowners and renters, with terms up to 30 years. Interest does not begin to accrue, and payments are not due until 12 months from the date of the first loan disbursement. The SBA determines eligibility and sets loan amounts and terms based on each applicant’s financial condition.
Customer service representatives will be at the below Disaster Loan Outreach Center to answer questions and assist with the disaster loan application process. Walk-ins are welcome, and in-person appointments can be scheduled in advance at appointment.sba.gov.
The center’s hours of operation are:
BEXAR COUNTY
Disaster Loan Outreach Center
Las Palmas Library
515 Castroville Rd.
San Antonio, TX  78237
Monday &Tuesday, noon – 8 p.m.
Wednesday – Friday, 10 a.m. – 6 p.m.
Closed Wednesday, Nov. 11 for Veterans Day
To apply online, visit sba.gov/disaster. Applicants may also call SBA’s National Support Network Center at (866) SBA-HELP or email disastercustomerservice@sba.gov for more information about disaster assistance. For people who are deaf, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability, please dial 7-1-1 to access telecommunications relay services.
The filing deadline to return applications for physical property damage is Dec. 30. The deadline to return economic injury applications is July 30, 2027.

About the U.S. Small Business Administration
The U.S. Small Business Administration helps power the American dream of business ownership. As the only go-to resource and voice for small businesses backed by the strength of the federal government, the SBA empowers entrepreneurs and small business owners with the resources and support they need to start, grow, expand their businesses, or recover from a declared disaster. It delivers services through an extensive network of SBA field offices and partnerships with public and private organizations. To learn more, visit www.sba.gov.

SACRAMENTO, Calif. — A federal criminal complaint has been filed charging Antoine Rashad Polite, 35, of Sacramento, with delaying and obstructing the delivery of U.S. mail, U.S. Attorney Eric Grant announced.

According to court documents, Polite was employed as a letter carrier by the U.S. Postal Service in Sacramento County and was responsible for delivering mail along an assigned route. Between Sept. 23, 2026, and Oct. 27, 2026, Polite improperly withheld and delayed the delivery of hundreds of pieces of political mail intended for residents on his route.

The investigation began after postal management discovered approximately 493 pieces of political mail that had been placed in an area designated for undeliverable bulk business mail, despite the mail bearing valid, deliverable addresses located on Polite’s route. Investigators later identified an additional 527 pieces of political mail that had not been delivered and were found in undeliverable mail containers and inside Polite’s assigned postal vehicle. Many of the pieces of mail had the addresses marked through and were labeled with notations indicating they were vacant or undeliverable, even though postal officials determined the addresses were valid and deliverable.

According to the complaint, the withheld mail included campaign materials relating to candidates and ballot propositions appearing on the Nov. 3, 2026, California general election ballot. Postal officials ultimately recovered and delivered the vast majority of the mail to their intended recipients.

The U.S. Postal Service Office of Inspector General investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Kevin Khasigian is prosecuting the case.

If convicted, Polite faces a maximum statutory penalty of six months in prison for obstruction of mail and one year in prison for delay or destruction of mail. Any sentence, however, would be determined at the discretion of the court after consideration of any applicable statutory factors and the federal Sentencing Guidelines, which take into account a number of variables. The charges are only allegations; the defendant is presumed innocent until and unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.
title: Sacramento postal employee charged with obstructing delivery of political campaign mail

Media accreditation is open for the next launch to deliver NASA science investigations, supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station. A Northrop Grumman Cygnus XL spacecraft will launch in November to the orbital laboratory on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket for NASA.
The mission is known as NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25, or NASA’s Northrop Grumman CRS-25. Liftoff is targeted for no earlier than 10:49 a.m. EST, Sunday, Nov. 29, from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.
Following launch, astronauts aboard the space station will use the Canadarm2 robotic arm to capture Cygnus and install the spacecraft to the Unity module’s Earth-facing port for cargo unloading. The spacecraft will remain at the space station until May 2027. This is the company’s 25th spacecraft built to deliver supplies to the International Space Station under contract with NASA.
Credentialing to cover prelaunch and launch activities is open to U.S. media. The application deadline for U.S. citizens is 11:59 p.m. EST, Thursday, Nov. 12. All accreditation requests must be submitted online at:
Credentialed media will receive a confirmation email following approval. NASA’s media accreditation policy is available online. For questions about accreditation, or to request special logistical support, email: ksc-media-accreditat@mail.nasa.gov. For other questions, please contact NASA’s Kennedy Space Center newsroom at: 321-867-2468.
In addition to food, supplies, and equipment for the crew, Cygnus will deliver several new experiments, including hardware to manufacture tiny, DNA-inspired particles in space that could improve drug delivery for cancer and osteoarthritis, as well as a study that could guide cancer treatments by predicting whether a patient’s cancer is likely to spread to other parts of the body. Cygnus also will carry human muscle cells and medications to test therapeutics for muscle loss associated with spaceflight and aging on Earth, and a compact radiation sensor designed to improve crew safety on future missions.
Each resupply mission to the station delivers scientific investigations in the areas of biology and biotechnology, Earth and space science, physical sciences, and technology development and demonstrations. Cargo resupply from U.S. companies ensures a national capability to deliver scientific research to the space station, increasing NASA’s ability to conduct new investigations aboard humanity’s laboratory in space.
For 26 years, people have lived and worked continuously aboard the International Space Station, advancing scientific knowledge and making research breakthroughs that are not possible on Earth. The space station is an important testbed for NASA to understand and overcome the challenges of long-duration spaceflight and to expand commercial opportunities in low Earth orbit. As commercial companies concentrate on providing human space transportation services and destinations as part of a strong low Earth orbit economy, NASA is focusing its resources on deep space missions to the Moon as part of the Artemis and Moon Base programs to build on our foundation for the first astronaut missions to Mars.

Media Note

Office of the Spokesman

November 2, 2026

Today, the Department of State signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the United Parcel Service (UPS). Through this MoU, the Department of State and UPS will leverage UPS’s unrivaled logistics network, cargo transportation, and supply chain expertise in support of Department of State-led disaster response efforts around the world – helping deliver life-saving assistance faster and more effectively.

When disasters strike, speed and reach save lives. This partnership with UPS brings the best of American private sector logistics capability to bear alongside the Department of State’s disaster response expertise. UPS is a proven partner, having provided logistics support to the Department of State and its implementers during recent crises, including Hurricane Melissa, earthquakes in Venezuela and Colombia, and floods in Nepal.

The Department of State looks forward to continued collaboration with UPS and reiterates its commitment to advancing American private sector involvement in disaster response efforts around the world.

Lofgren Secures Over $54 Million for Pajaro River Flood Protection As El Niño Is Expected to Strengthen
WATSONVILLE, CA — Today, Congresswoman Zoe Lofgren (CA-18) delivered a $54,830,000 check for the Pajaro River Flood Risk Management Project, one of her 13 community projects she submitted for the Fiscal Year 2026 congressional appropriations cycle. This is the largest single community project that Lofgren secured this year, which is being completed by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) San Francisco District, in partnership with the Pajaro Regional Flood Management Agency (PRFMA). Senators Alex Padilla (D-CA) and Adam Schiff (D-CA) also requested congressional funding for this project.
“With El Niño expected to intensify in the early months of 2027, it’s critical that the residents and businesses along the Pajaro River have necessary flood protection,” said Rep. Lofgren. “Last year, I was proud to announce nearly $40 million for levee and floodwall construction in Watsonville, and I’m proud to have submitted this additional $54 million as one of my community projects this year. That’s going to help save lives and property, and I’m proud to have worked with Senators Padilla and Schiff to prioritize this project funding.”
“Consistent funding for the Pajaro River flood control project is critically important, and we are grateful to Rep. Lofgren for her work to keep the project moving forward and fulfilling our commitments to the vulnerable residents and businesses in the Pajaro Valley,” said Mark Strudley, Executive Director of PRFMA.
“Future improvements to the levee will make a real difference in reducing flood risks and protecting the people who call Watsonville and the Pajaro Valley home,” said Watsonville City Manager Tamara Vides. This is an investment in the safety, stability, and future of our community. We are thankful for the advocacy and support provided by Congresswoman Lofgren.”
The residents and businesses of Watsonville and Pajaro have been waiting for 50 years for flood protection and during that time have suffered significant damage and loss of life due to weather events. On March 11, 2023, a serious levee failure resulted in the evacuation of more than 2,000 people in the Town of Pajaro, 200 water rescues, significant flooding of farms, and closure of Highway 1. The farms impacted by flooding are vital contributors to the regional agricultural industry, where none of the fruit and vegetable crops are federally subsidized and floods can result in the loss of 2-3 growing seasons.
According to the National Weather Service, El Niño continues to strengthen with a strong-to-very strong El Niño likely through January-March 2027. Lofgren has urged Californians to prepare for storm season and sign up for emergency alerts. Tips and resources for El Niño can be viewed on her website.
Rep. Lofgren’s community project submissions this year have delivered a total of $58,022,000 for Watsonville and Santa Cruz County. This includes $1.2 million to renovate the Watsonville Veterans Hall, $1,092,000 to replace Watsonville’s wastewater infrastructure, and $900,000 for the Sí Se Puede Behavioral Health Center.
title: Lofgren Secures Over $54 Million for Pajaro River Flood Protection As El Niño Is Expected to Strengthen

CAMP HUMPHREYS, South Korea — Lt. Col. Jason A. Supnet, military deputy chief of contracting for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers – Far East District (USACE FED), was named the 2026 USACE 51C Commissioned Officer of the Year, earning the recognition for the second consecutive year.
As part of the USACE Excellence in Contracting Awards Program, the honor recognizes outstanding leadership, contracting expertise and professional development. This year, Supnet was selected amongst 99 nominations across individual, team and district categories.
"It is a real honor, and I am very grateful for it," Supnet said. "Receiving it once was already something I never expected, so receiving it a second year in a row is humbling."
With over two decades of military service, Supnet has built a career spanning in combat arms, contracting and contingency operations. At FED, his expertise has supported critical infrastructure projects, from the Space Force Operations Complex and the Hardened Aircraft Shelter at Osan Air Base to the Millet Gate Access Control Point redesign at Camp Humphreys, all contributing to military readiness across the Korean Peninsula.
Beyond supporting these projects, Supnet has played a key role in the district's efforts to explore innovative contracting approaches and strengthen collaboration with industry partners.
His most recent accomplishment was leading the planning and execution of the district's first-ever Reverse Industry Day, held Oct. 6, 2026 in Suwon, South Korea. The event brought together more than 250 attendees, providing an opportunity for industry representatives to share their expertise in innovative construction methods, acquisition strategies and discuss alternative project delivery approaches.
Unlike traditional industry engagement events, Reverse Industry Day allowed Korean industry partners to present their capabilities and perspectives directly to the district's workforce. Discussions included Other Transaction Authority (OTA), Progressive Design-Build (PDB) and other emerging practices that could help improve the delivery of complex construction projects.
Jisun Kang, chief of contracting at FED, praised Supnet's leadership in transforming the initiative from an idea into a successful district-wide event.
"I gave him the initial direction that we needed to make this event happen, and he took it from there," Kang said. "He coordinated across the district, developed the necessary operational plans and orders, and led countless planning meetings and rehearsals to ensure everything came together successfully."
For Supnet, the event represented an important step toward modernizing the district's contracting practices and identifying new opportunities to improve project delivery.
"We are in a period where contracting is evolving, and the district is doing a good job of taking a hard look at new tools and authorities that may help us better support the mission in Korea," Supnet said.
He emphasized that while these approaches may not be suitable for every project, they offer opportunities to improve early collaboration, manage risks and provide greater flexibility in meeting mission requirements.
Kang credited Supnet's continued success to more than his technical expertise, highlighting his ability to build relationships and foster a collaborative working environment.
"What sets LTC Supnet apart is his exceptional people skills, positive attitude, and ability to bring people together to accomplish a common goal," she said.
Kang, who was also recognized as the 2026 USACE Contracting Manager of the Year, reflected on her leadership alongside Supnet's accomplishments.
"It's truly an honor to see both of us recognized at the USACE enterprise level, but I see these awards as a reflection of the exceptional team we have at the Far East District," Kang said.
Supnet echoed that sentiment, emphasizing the importance of teamwork and the dedication of the contracting professionals who support the district's mission.
"Ms. Kang and I may receive recognition, but it is really a reflection of the hard work and dedication of the people around us," he said.
Looking ahead, Supnet remains committed to advancing innovative contracting practices, strengthening the district's acquisition capabilities and investing in the professional development of its workforce.
"I am grateful for the recognition, but I do not look at it as something to sit on," Supnet said. "If anything, it is a reminder to keep doing the work and to keep helping the team move forward. With the mission we have here, there is still a lot left to do."
title: USACE 51C Commissioned Officer of the Year: Far East District's Supnet earns back-to-back recognition

Fort Myers, Florida – Angel Rey Rivera (35, Fort Myers) was sentenced today by U.S. District Judge Kyle Dudek to five years in federal prison to be followed by 3 years of supervised release for possessing a firearm as a convicted felon. Rivera pleaded guilty on July 28, 2026. United States Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe made the announcement.

According to court records, Rivera was captured on video throwing a stolen firearm into a trash can after fleeing from officers from the Fort Myers Police Department on Palm Beach Boulevard. Upon arrest, Rivera exclaimed, “I don’t care about none of that. I already did 11 years. I’ll go lay down again.” Rivera had recently been released from the Tennessee Department of Corrections after serving nearly 11 years for multiple felony convictions, including two counts of attempted second-degree murder and attempted aggravated robbery.

This case was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the Fort Myers Police Department. It was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Matthew Redavid.

This case is part of Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) – the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities.
title: Violent Fort Myers Felon Sent Back to Prison for Possessing a Stolen Gun

text:
LITTLE ROCK—A federal jury has convicted Elbert Nichols of drug trafficking, possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime, and assault on a federal law enforcement officer. The trial, which spanned four days, ended on Thursday, October 29, 2026, with guilty verdicts on all counts for Nichols, 52, of Cordova, Tennessee. Jonathan D. Ross, United States Attorney for the Eastern District of Arkansas, announced the verdict.

Nichols was indicted by a federal grand jury on August 4, 2026, and went to trial facing six charges, including one count of distribution of fentanyl, one count of possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine, one count of possession with intent to distribute fentanyl, one count of being a felon in possession of a firearm, one count of possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime, and one count of assault on a federal officer.

The evidence at trial proved that on April 12, 2024, officers of the West Memphis Police Department’s Narcotics Unit conducted a controlled purchase of fentanyl pills from Nichols using a confidential informant (CI). During the buy, the CI purchased 20 pills from Nichols, who arrived at the transaction in an orange Jeep Renegade that was registered to him. The evidence at trial further proved that the pills purchased on April 12 were confirmed to contain fentanyl.

On May 9, 2024, officers arranged for the CI to make another controlled purchase from Nichols at the same location as the previous transaction. Again, Nichols arrived in the orange Jeep Renegade; but instead of Nichols approaching the CI for the pills, he was confronted by officers who had pulled in behind him to execute a felony arrest. Upon seeing the officers, Nichols threw his car into reverse which caused the officers to move out of the way so they would not be struck by Nichols, who did strike the officers’ vehicle, causing damage. Nichols then fled the area driving through a chain link fence and at a high rate of speed through a school zone at the end of a school day.

Officers continued to pursue Nichols and were able to disable his vehicle quickly after the pursuit began. Nichols, the only occupant of the vehicle, stopped and fled the vehicle, running towards an apartment complex. Before Nichols could escape, officers deployed a taser striking Nichols and ending the pursuit. During a search of Nichols’ vehicle, officers located approximately 50 fentanyl pills and over 80 grams of methamphetamine that were divided between seven baggies. The Drug Enforcement Administration Laboratory confirmed the pills contained fentanyl and the substance in the seven baggies contained methamphetamine. Officers also located during the search a loaded Smith & Wesson firearm in a backpack. In a post-Miranda interview, Nichols admitted that the drugs and firearm located during the search belonged to him.

After deliberating for approximately six hours, the jury found Nichols guilty of all counts, including distribution of fentanyl, possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine, possession with intent to distribute fentanyl, being a felon in possession of a firearm, possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime, and assault on a federal officer.

Following the guilty verdicts on the charges, and after the presentation of evidence regarding Nichols’ criminal history, the jury then found that Nichols had the requisite prior convictions to qualify him as an armed career criminal.

Nichols has a 2005 federal conviction out of the Middle District of Tennessee for being a felon in possession of a firearm, receiving a sentence of 110 months in the Bureau of Prisons (BOP). After his release from the BOP, Nichols was convicted of aggravated robbery in Shelby County, Tennessee, in 2015. This conviction was Nichols’ third time being convicted for aggravated robbery, having been convicted of the same crime in 1992 and 2005. Nichols also has a 2015 conviction out of Desoto County, Mississippi, for conspiracy to commit armed robbery.

Nichols was detained following the jury’s verdict and will be sentenced at a later date. Because of his classification as an armed career criminal, Nichols’ felon in possession of a firearm charge carries a sentence of not less than 15 years to life imprisonment. The most serious drug charges also carry a minimum sentence of 15 years and a maximum of life imprisonment. Nichols faces a sentence of five years to life imprisonment, consecutive to any other sentence, on the possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime, effectively making his minimum sentence 20 years with all charges. The possible sentence for assaulting a federal law enforcement officer is not more than eight years. There is no parole in the federal system.

This case was investigated by the West Memphis Police Department with assistance from the Second Judicial Drug Task Force and the Drug Enforcement Administration. This case was prosecuted and tried by Assistant United States Attorneys Lauren Eldridge and Claire Maddox.

Illegal alien from Venezuela passes away in Texas after lengthy hospital stay
SAN ANTONIO, Texas — Fran Gregory Portillo-Zapata, a 53-year-old illegal alien from Venezuela, died Oct. 29, 2026, at North Central Baptist Hospital in San Antonio, Texas. Portillo-Zapata was detained at the Karnes County Immigration Processing Center and was admitted to the hospital on Sept. 30. He suffered from severe sepsis, acute pancreatitis, and end-stage kidney disease. The official cause of death remains pending further medical examination.
Fran Gregory Portillo-Zapata was encountered in June 2023 by U.S. Border Patrol and removed to Mexico. On July 12, 2023, Portillo-Zapata attempted to enter illegally again, and he was released on an order of recognizance and issued a notice to appear before an immigration judge from the Executive Office for Immigration Review.
On Aug. 30, 2026, ICE San Antonio conducted an enforcement action in San Antonio, Texas. ICE identified Fran Gregory Portillo-Zapata, 53, a Venezuelan illegal alien living in the United States. Following a vehicle stop and field interview, ICE determined that Portillo-Zapata was amenable to administrative immigration arrest while pending removal proceedings with EOIR and took him into custody without incident.
Consistent with ICE policy, Enforcement and Removal Operations San Antonio completed the required notifications to the Department of Homeland Security, the ICE Office of Inspector General, and the ICE Office of Professional Responsibility through the Joint Intake Operations Center. ERO San Antonio notified Portillo-Zapata’s next of kin and sent an email notification to the Venezuelan Embassy.
ICE makes official notifications to Congress, non-governmental organization stakeholders, and the media upon reports of in-custody deaths and posts news releases with relevant details on its public website. Information is available in the ICE Newsroom and on the Detainee Death Reporting page.
ICE is committed to ensuring that all those in custody reside in safe, secure, and humane environments. Comprehensive medical care is provided from the moment individuals arrive and throughout their stay. All people in ICE custody receive medical, dental, and mental-health intake screenings within 12 hours of arriving at each detention facility; a full health assessment within 14 days of entering ICE custody or arriving at a facility; access to medical appointments; and 24-hour emergency care. At no time during detention is a detained alien denied emergency care.
title: Illegal alien from Venezuela passes away in Texas after lengthy hospital stay

PHILADELPHIA – United States Attorney David Metcalf announced that Sean Gerlach, 50, of Fairview, North Carolina, and Dawn Hawa, aka Dawn Benitez, 50, of Ephrata, Pennsylvania, have each been charged by information with offenses targeting the Liberty Bell.

Gerlach has been charged with tampering with property in a National Park, and trespassing on National Park property. Hawa has been charged with vandalism of property in a National Park.

As detailed in court filings, the Liberty Bell is housed inside the Liberty Bell Center, located within Independence National Historic Park in Philadelphia. During visiting hours, the public may visit and view the Liberty Bell, which is surrounded by a barrier to prevent visitors from approaching it too closely.

The information filed against Gerlach alleges that, on or about May 16, 2026, he, Hawa, and others visited the Liberty Bell Center. Gerlach then jumped over the barrier protecting the Liberty Bell and forcefully pushed the Liberty Bell until it swayed several times.

The information filed against Hawa alleges that, during this May 16, 2026, visit to the Liberty Bell Center, she flicked an oily substance over the barrier protecting the Liberty Bell. The substance hit and remained on the Liberty Bell and surrounding areas.

If convicted, Gerlach faces a maximum of one year in prison and Hawa faces a maximum of six months in prison.

This case was investigated by the FBI and the National Park Service.

The charges and allegations contained in the informations are merely accusations. Every defendant is presumed to be innocent unless and until proven guilty in court.
title: North Carolina Man and Pennsylvania Woman Charged With Offenses Targeting Philadelphia’s Liberty Bell

Homeland Security Task Force: Two Connecticut Men Found with 21 Kilos of Cocaine Sentenced to 10 Years in Federal Prison
BRIDGEPORT, Conn. - David X. Sullivan, United States Attorney for the District of Connecticut, today announced that REGINALD ROGERS 38, of Woodbridge, and LESTER ARRINGTON, 34, of Naugatuck, have each been sentenced by U.S. District Judge Stefan R. Underhill in Bridgeport to 120 months of imprisonment and five years of supervised release for trafficking cocaine. Rogers was sentenced today and Arrington was sentenced on October 27.
According to court documents and statements made in court, as part of a Homeland Security Task Force investigation, on February 23, 2026, Connecticut State Police troopers stopped a 2024 Subaru Crosstrek in Trumbull. Rogers was driving the vehicle and Arrington was a passenger. A K9 sniff of the vehicle alerted for the presence of narcotics, and a subsequent search revealed approximately 21 kilograms of cocaine hidden in two compartments (“traps”) that were installed under each front seat. Rogers and Arrington were arrested on state charges at that time.
Rogers and Arrington each pleaded guilty to possession with intent to distribute five kilograms or more of cocaine. Each is released on a $150,000 bond and they are required to report to prison on January 13.
Arrington and Rogers agreed to the forfeiture of the vehicle.
This investigation was led by the Drug Enforcement Administration with the assistance of the Bridgeport, Danbury, Stamford, and Stratford Police Departments. The case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Justyn P. Stokely and Lauren C. Clark.
This prosecution is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement toward identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States.
HSTF New Haven comprises agents and officers from the FBI, DEA, HSI, ATF, U.S. Postal Inspection Service, Internal Revenue Service – Criminal Investigation, U.S. Department of Transportation – Office of Inspector General, U.S. Department of Labor – Office of Inspector General, U.S. Department of Commerce – Bureau of Industry and Security’s Office of Export Enforcement, and Connecticut State Police, with prosecutions led by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Connecticut.
title: Homeland Security Task Force: Two Connecticut Men Found with 21 Kilos of Cocaine Sentenced to 10 Years in Federal Prison
